meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Exam 2 set 3. Each section has 25 case based questions: 20 regular (ids -m01 to -m20, no difficulty field) and 5 hard (ids -x01 to -x05, "difficulty": "difficult"). Questions follow 6 to 8 clients per section over time; "caseGroup" and "caseStep" link the steps, and every question also stands alone. "coverage" states the source and "objective" names the slide objective. Temperatures are Celsius only. No question carries the daily set flag.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man who walks without help at home was admitted 6 hours ago with heart failure. Which findings increase his risk for injury during this hospital stay? Select all that apply.

options.text: A loop diuretic was started today
options.rationale: A new medication is a listed reason hospitalization raises injury risk, and medication effects are an intrinsic fall risk factor.

options.text: He has an IV line and oxygen tubing attached
options.rationale: Tubes, lines and equipment are a hospital hazard he does not have at home.

options.text: He was woken four times last night for checks
options.rationale: Sleep disruption is one of the reasons hospitalization raises injury risk.

options.text: The bathroom is on the opposite side from his bathroom at home
options.rationale: Unfamiliar surroundings. His home habits now point him the wrong way.

options.text: He walks without help at home
options.rationale: This is his normal ability. It is a baseline to protect, not a risk factor.

options.text: The call light is clipped to his gown
options.rationale: A call light within reach is a universal fall precaution. It lowers risk.

questions.takeaway: Hospitalization itself adds risk: unfamiliar surroundings, new medications, sleep disruption, and tubes, lines and equipment. A client who is independent at home is still at risk in the hospital.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding: is this new since admission and does it make moving around harder? His home independence and a reachable call light do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New diuretic, IV and oxygen tubing, broken sleep, unfamiliar room layout.
Walking without help at home is what he normally does.
A call light within reach protects him.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: injury risk factors (patient, environment, health care)

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man who walks without help at home arrived on the unit 20 minutes ago with an IV line. He has not been shown the room, and he says he will manage alone. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Show him the room and have him demonstrate the call light
options.rationale: He has not been oriented. Familiarizing the client with the environment and a return demonstration of the call light are universal fall precautions that come before anything individualized.

options.text: Start scheduled toileting with staff every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: The right intervention for urgency or frequency. The stem gives no urgency, and he still does not know the room.

options.text: Ask a family member to stay at the bedside overnight
options.rationale: Family presence is an alternative for a confused client. The stem gives no confusion, and it does not replace orienting him.

options.text: Tell him the call light is on the bed rail whenever he needs it
options.rationale: Right idea, one step short. The slides call for the client to demonstrate call light use, not just be told.

questions.takeaway: Universal fall precautions come first for every client: orient to the room and have the client show you he can use the call light.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Scheduled toileting is a real fall intervention, but it matches a risk factor the stem does not give. The stated gap is that he has not been shown the room.

steps.detail: He has not been shown the room.
Toileting rounds fit urgency. Family presence fits confusion.

steps.action: Compare the two call light options
steps.detail: Telling is weaker than having him demonstrate.

elimination.verdict: Orient him and get a return demonstration of the call light.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man started a loop diuretic this morning. Twice in 3 hours he hurried to the bathroom alone, pulling his IV pole, because he could not wait for help. Which addition to the plan fits this risk?

options.text: A bed alarm that sounds at the station when he stands up
options.rationale: An alarm tells staff after he is already up and hurrying. It does not remove the reason he gets up.

options.text: A urinal at the bedside so he stays in bed until evening
options.rationale: Keeping him in bed is excessive restriction. Immobility worsens weakness, and the goal is safe mobility.

options.text: Scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours with staff
options.rationale: The risk factor is urgency. Scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours gets him to the bathroom before the urge makes him rush.

options.text: Reorientation to the room and call light every hour
options.rationale: The right intervention for confusion. The stem gives no confusion: he reached the bathroom, and his problem is that he cannot wait.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the risk factor. Urgency or frequency gets scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Name the reason he got up alone. He was not lost and not weak in the stem. He could not wait.

steps.detail: Urgency after a diuretic.

steps.action: Cut the intervention for another risk
steps.detail: Reorientation treats confusion.
A urinal in bed limits mobility. An alarm sounds after he is up.

elimination.verdict: Scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man taking a loop diuretic was placed on scheduled toileting every 2 hours after rushing to the bathroom alone. Which finding 24 hours later best shows the plan is working?

options.text: He had no falls and used a urinal in bed for the whole 12 hour shift
options.rationale: No falls, but through immobility. Fall prevention does not mean keeping him in bed.

options.text: He walked to the bathroom with staff each round and made no trips alone
options.rationale: The goal of scheduled toileting is to reduce urgency-driven unsafe movement while he keeps moving. He is walking, with help, and not rushing alone.

options.text: He drank less during the day so that he needed the bathroom less often
options.rationale: Fewer trips for the wrong reason. Cutting fluids is not a goal of the plan.

options.text: He used the call light for the bathroom once between the scheduled rounds
options.rationale: A good sign that he calls, but one call does not show whether unassisted trips stopped.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the goal of the intervention. For scheduled toileting, that is fewer urgency-driven unsafe trips, with mobility kept.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options report a good result. Check how the result was reached: by safe walking or by staying in bed.

steps.detail: No rushed trips alone, and he still walks.

steps.action: Cut the results reached the wrong way
steps.detail: Staying in bed and drinking less.
One call light use is partial evidence. No trips alone at every round is the outcome.

elimination.verdict: Walked with staff at each round, no trips alone.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman with pneumonia and new confusion is tugging at her IV line and picking at her gown. She last voided 7 hours ago. Her daughter asks for wrist restraints. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply hand mitts as the least restrictive device available
options.rationale: Least restrictive is the right rule once a restraint is needed. A mitt is still a restraint, and the cause has not been looked for.

options.text: Reassess her orientation to person, place and time
options.rationale: An assessment, but of something already known. Her confusion is established, and it does not look for the unmet need behind the tugging.

options.text: Explain to the daughter why restraints can cause harm
options.rationale: True and worth saying. It does not address why the client is tugging at the line.

options.text: Take her to the toilet and check for pain or other needs
options.rationale: Before any restraint, ask why. Toileting needs and pain are listed causes of this behavior, and 7 hours without voiding is a stated cue.

questions.takeaway: Before using a restraint, ask why the behavior is happening: pain, toileting, hunger, thirst, delirium, medication effects, fear, too much stimulation, an unfamiliar environment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options assess. One rechecks what is already known. The other checks the cause the stem hands you: 7 hours without voiding.

steps.detail: No void for 7 hours.
Orientation repeats a known finding. Toileting and pain look for the cause.

steps.action: Cut the restraint and the true statement
steps.detail: Mitts are still a restraint. Teaching the daughter does not help the client yet.

elimination.verdict: Toilet her and look for unmet needs.

questions.objective: restraints, alternatives and monitoring of a restrained client

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman with new confusion still reaches for her IV line after toileting and pain relief. Her daughter is in the waiting room. Which plan does the nurse try next?

options.text: Bring the daughter in, reorient the client, offer towels to fold
options.rationale: Reorientation, family presence and diversional activity are the listed alternatives, and they are tried before any restraint.

options.text: Raise all four side rails and check on her every 30 minutes
options.rationale: Rails raised to keep her in place restrict movement, which makes them a restraint. They do nothing about the IV line.

options.text: Apply hand mitts and remove them every 2 hours for skin care
options.rationale: Careful restraint care, used too early. Alternatives have not been tried yet.

options.text: Dim the lights and leave her alone to lower the stimulation
options.rationale: Lowering stimulation is a real environmental change, but leaving a confused client alone removes observation.

questions.takeaway: Use alternatives first: reorientation, family presence, diversional activity, observation, environmental modification, meeting unmet needs, alarms.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: One option is good restraint care. Good restraint care is still a restraint, and the stem says only the unmet needs have been tried.

steps.detail: Four rails and mitts both restrict movement.
Leaving her alone drops observation.
The daughter is nearby.

elimination.verdict: Family presence, reorientation and a diversion.

questions.objective: restraints, alternatives and monitoring of a restrained client

questions.stem: A 79-year-old confused woman has pulled out two IV lines despite family presence, reorientation and close observation, and she needs IV antibiotics. A restraint is prescribed. Which plan follows restraint guidelines?

options.text: Wrist restraints, kept on until the last antibiotic dose has infused
options.rationale: The plan ties removal to the end of treatment, not to her behavior. Guidelines say reassess and remove as early as possible.

options.text: Hand mitts, reassessed often and removed as early as possible
options.rationale: Least restrictive option, continued reassessment of need, and removal as early as possible are the stated guidelines.

options.text: Hand mitts during the night shift, when fewer staff can watch her
options.rationale: Right device, wrong reason. Restraints are never used for staff convenience.

options.text: Wrist restraints plus a vest so that she cannot slide down in bed
options.rationale: More restriction than the problem needs. Her hands are the risk, and mitts cover that.

questions.takeaway: When a restraint is needed: least restrictive option, keep reassessing the need, remove as early as possible, follow policy. Never for staff convenience, punishment or routine fall prevention.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options use mitts. Read the reason attached to each one.

steps.detail: Mitts stop pulling without tying her arms.
One is driven by her need, one by staffing.
Removal follows reassessment, not the antibiotic schedule.

elimination.verdict: Mitts, reassessed, off as early as possible.

questions.objective: restraints, alternatives and monitoring of a restrained client

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old confused woman has had bilateral wrist restraints for 5 hours after pulling out IV lines. The nurse reassesses her.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the nurse continues current care or must intervene now.

rows.text: Left hand is pale and cool below the restraint
rows.rationale: Circulation is impaired. Neurovascular injury is a listed complication.

rows.text: Skin under both restraints is intact and its usual color
rows.rationale: Skin integrity is being maintained.

rows.text: She has not been offered fluids or the toilet since the restraints were applied
rows.rationale: Hydration and elimination are on the monitoring list, and 5 hours have passed.

rows.text: She has slid down so the straps pull her arms above her head
rows.rationale: Positioning is on the monitoring list. This position strains her arms and invites escape injury.

rows.text: She moves her fingers, wrists and elbows fully when each restraint is released
rows.rationale: Range of motion is preserved.

rows.text: She is shouting and thrashing more than before the restraints were applied
rows.rationale: Increased agitation and confusion are a listed complication, so the need and the cause are reassessed.

questions.takeaway: A restrained client is checked for skin integrity, circulation, positioning, range of motion, hydration, elimination, comfort and mental status. A problem in any one of them needs action.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Run the monitoring list down the rows. A row passes only if that area is intact.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pale, cool hand fails. Intact skin passes.
No fluids or toileting in 5 hours fails.
Arms pulled overhead fails, full motion passes, more agitation fails.

elimination.verdict: Intervene, continue, intervene, intervene, continue, intervene.

questions.objective: restraints, alternatives and monitoring of a restrained client

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman has worn hand mitts for 6 hours after pulling out IV lines. She is now calm, knows she is in the hospital, and left her IV alone during two 15 minute releases. The prescription runs until morning. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Keep the mitts on and reassess at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: Tempting because it is cautious and the order allows it. The reassessment is already done and shows no need, so waiting is restraint without a reason.

options.text: Keep the mitts on overnight, when confusion often worsens
options.rationale: A fair worry about the night, but it restrains her for a risk she is not showing now. Observation covers that worry.

options.text: Remove the mitts now and continue close observation
options.rationale: The behavior that justified the restraint has stopped, shown twice with the mitts off. Guidelines say remove as early as possible, and a valid prescription does not require using it.

options.text: Remove the mitts and raise all four side rails for the night
options.rationale: Trades one restraint for another. Her risk was her hands on the IV line, which rails do not address.

questions.takeaway: Restraints come off as early as possible. When reassessment shows the reason is gone, remove them and go back to alternatives, even if the prescription has time left.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Waiting for the next check sounds safe. Ask what that check would add: she is calm, oriented to place and left the IV alone twice.

steps.detail: Calm, oriented to place, IV untouched in two releases.
Side rails are another restraint.
Both wait options keep a restraint with no current reason.

elimination.verdict: Remove the mitts and keep observing.

questions.objective: restraints, alternatives and monitoring of a restrained client

questions.stem: A nurse walking past a room sees a 74-year-old man sitting on the floor beside his bed. No other staff are in the room. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Call for assistance from the room
options.rationale: First. Help is needed, and calling from the room lets the nurse stay.

options.text: Stay with him and assess for injury before he is moved
options.rationale: The nurse stays and assesses. Moving him before assessment could worsen an injury.

options.text: Notify the provider of the fall and the findings
options.rationale: The provider is notified once there are assessment findings to report.

options.text: Reassess his fall prevention plan
options.rationale: The plan did not prevent this fall, so it is reviewed and changed.

options.text: Document the event and complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: Last. The record and the report can then include the event, the assessment, the notification and the plan change.

questions.takeaway: After a fall: call for assistance, stay with the client, assess for injury, notify the provider, follow agency policy, reassess the prevention plan, then document and complete an occurrence report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The pull is to get him off the floor or to call the provider at once. Neither appears before assessment.

steps.detail: Call from the room.
The provider needs findings.
Plan review, then documentation and the occurrence report.

elimination.verdict: Call for help, stay and assess, notify, reassess the plan, document.

questions.objective: clinical judgment about hazards (culture of safety, delegation, post fall response and huddle)

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man fell at 0300 walking to the bathroom. He is uninjured and says he could not see the floor. His glasses were in a drawer across the dark room. Low bed, locked brakes and nonslip socks were in place. Which change fits?

options.text: Begin scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours overnight
options.rationale: Fits urgency or frequency. He was going to the bathroom, but the stem gives poor vision as the reason he fell, not rushing.

options.text: Move him to a room that is closer to the nurses' station
options.rationale: More observation suits confusion. It does not let him see the floor.

options.text: Raise all four side rails from 2200 until 0600
options.rationale: Rails used to keep him in bed restrict movement, and restraint is not for routine fall prevention.

options.text: Keep a night light on and his glasses in reach
options.rationale: The cause was vision: a dark room and glasses out of reach. Improved lighting and accessible glasses are the matched intervention.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, find the cause and match the fix to it. Visual impairment gets better lighting and glasses within reach.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The bathroom trip makes toileting rounds look right. Read his own words for the cause: he could not see.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: Dark room, glasses out of reach.

steps.action: Cut the interventions for other risks
steps.detail: Toileting rounds for urgency, closer room for confusion.
Four rails restrain him.

elimination.verdict: Night light on, glasses within reach.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: Staff hold a post fall huddle for a 74-year-old man who fell at night. The plan listed the call light within reach, but it was found clipped to the wall behind the bed. Which contribution best serves the huddle?

options.text: "The call light was out of reach. How do we get it checked on every round?"
options.rationale: A huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether interventions were in place, and what needs to change. This names a planned intervention that was missing and moves to the change.

options.text: "We should find out who last left the room so that person can be counseled."
options.rationale: It looks at whether the intervention was in place, then turns to blame. A culture of safety is blame free and aims at the process.

options.text: "He was taught to call for help. We need to teach him again more firmly."
options.rationale: Reinforcing teaching has value, but he could not have called. The call light was not within his reach.

options.text: "Let us wait for the manager to read the occurrence report before we discuss it."
options.rationale: The occurrence report is required. It does not replace the team reviewing the event.

questions.takeaway: The post fall huddle asks four things: what happened, what contributed, were the interventions in place, and what needs to change. It is about the process, not blame.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options notice the call light problem. One fixes the process and one looks for a person.

steps.detail: The planned call light was not within reach.
Counseling a person, waiting for a manager.

steps.action: Cut the fix that misses the cause
steps.detail: Teaching him to call does not put the light in his hand.

elimination.verdict: Name the missing intervention and ask what changes.

questions.objective: clinical judgment about hazards (culture of safety, delegation, post fall response and huddle)

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man fell beside his bed. Two staff have arrived. The nurse's assessment shows his right leg is shorter than his left and turned outward, with right hip pain of 8 of 10. What is the nurse's next action?

options.text: Lift him to bed with the two staff, then notify the provider
options.rationale: Tempting because help is here and the floor is hard. The shortened, outward turned leg signals an injury that moving could worsen.

options.text: Keep him still and notify the provider of the findings
options.rationale: The assessment is done and it shows an injury. The next step in the fall response is to notify the provider, and he stays where he is meanwhile.

options.text: Complete a head to toe assessment before deciding who to call
options.rationale: Assessment comes first in most falls, and here the deciding findings are already in hand. More assessment delays the report.

options.text: Review which fall precautions were in place when he fell
options.rationale: Part of the response and of the huddle. It comes after the injured client is cared for.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, assess for injury, then notify the provider. When the assessment already shows an injury, the next step is to report it, not to move the client or assess further.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Enough help has arrived, so moving him to bed feels kind and safe. The leg findings are the cue that it is not.

steps.detail: Yes. Leg shorter, turned outward, pain 8 of 10.
Those findings mean keep him still.
Provider now, precaution review later.

elimination.verdict: Keep him still and notify the provider.

questions.objective: clinical judgment about hazards (culture of safety, delegation, post fall response and huddle)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman admitted after surgery is scored as a fall risk. She says, "I am careful. I never fall at home." Which response best helps the nurse identify her injury risk?

options.text: "Hospitals are different from home, so please call before you get up."
options.rationale: True, and good teaching later. It tells her the rule without finding out what has changed for her.

options.text: "Do you understand why your score puts you at risk for falling?"
options.rationale: A yes or no question about the tool. It gathers nothing about her abilities or routines.

options.text: "What do you manage alone at home, and what is harder since surgery?"
options.rationale: Safety through the client's eyes: ask about home routines, usual abilities and which limitations are new. Her answer shows where the risk is.

options.text: "I will set a bed alarm so that we know when you are getting up."
options.rationale: An intervention chosen before her risk is understood, and chosen without her.

questions.takeaway: See safety through the client's eyes: what does she believe is safe, what are her routines, what can she normally do, and which limitations are new? Include her in the plan.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The question asks what helps the nurse identify risk. Three options tell or act. One asks.

steps.detail: Identify risk, which means gather information.
A rule, an alarm.
A yes or no question about a score, or an open question about abilities and new limits.

elimination.verdict: Ask about her home abilities and what is new.

questions.objective: injury risk factors (patient, environment, health care)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is dizzy for about 2 hours after her 0800 blood pressure medication. Her walk with staff is scheduled for 0900, and yesterday she nearly fell during it. Which plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Ask the pharmacist about timing and walk her after the dizziness
options.rationale: For medication dizziness: monitor symptoms, adjust timing, and assist with mobility, with the pharmacist involved. She keeps walking, at a safer time.

options.text: Hold the 0800 dose on the days she is scheduled to walk with staff
options.rationale: Recognizes the medication link, but holding a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision, and the slides call for adjusting timing.

options.text: Cancel the walks until the dizziness has stopped for 24 hours
options.rationale: Prevents the near fall by stopping mobility. Immobility worsens weakness.

options.text: Keep the 0900 walk and add a second staff member to steady her
options.rationale: More assistance is part of the answer. The walk still falls inside the 2 hours when she is dizzy.

questions.takeaway: Medication dizziness: monitor symptoms, adjust timing, assist with mobility, and work with the pharmacist. The goal is to lower the medication-related risk, not to stop walking.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Adding a helper is right as far as it goes. Check the clock: 0900 is inside the 2 hour window.

steps.detail: Dose 0800, dizzy until about 1000, walk 0900.

steps.action: Cut stopping the walk or the drug
steps.detail: Neither is the matched intervention.

steps.action: Compare the two that keep her walking
steps.detail: Only one moves the walk out of the dizzy period.

elimination.verdict: Pharmacist on timing, assisted walk after the dizziness passes.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman at risk for falls walks three times a day with one staff member. Her son says, "I will make sure she stays in bed so she cannot fall." Which reply is best?

options.text: "Thank you. Please press the call light if she tries to get up."
options.rationale: Uses the call light well and accepts his help, but it agrees to a plan of keeping her in bed.

options.text: "Staff handle her walking, so you do not need to watch her."
options.rationale: She does walk with staff. Shutting out the son goes against involving family caregivers.

options.text: "She is allowed to walk whenever she feels steady enough."
options.rationale: Supports mobility but drops the assistance her plan specifies.

options.text: "Bed rest weakens her. Here is the help she needs to walk."
options.rationale: Fall prevention does not mean keeping her in bed. Family teaching explains the risk, specifies the assistance needed and involves the caregiver.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention is safe mobility, not immobility. Teach the family why she is at risk, exactly what help she needs, and how they can take part.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The son means well, so agreeing feels polite. Check each reply for two things: does she keep walking, and does she keep her helper?

steps.action: Cut the reply that keeps her in bed
steps.detail: Thanking him accepts his plan.

steps.action: Cut the reply with no helper
steps.detail: Walking when she feels steady.

steps.action: Cut the reply that excludes family
steps.detail: The slides say involve caregivers.

elimination.verdict: Explain that bed rest weakens her and show the help she needs.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with a seizure disorder begins a tonic-clonic seizure in bed. His teeth are clenched. The nurse has noted the time and called for help. Which action comes next?

options.text: Insert an oral airway between his teeth to keep the airway open
options.rationale: Airway is the right concern. Nothing is placed in the mouth once the teeth are clenched, because it injures the mouth.

options.text: Hold his arms and legs firmly so that he cannot strike the rails
options.rationale: Protecting him from injury is right. He is not restrained during a seizure, and limbs are held only loosely.

options.text: Turn him onto his side, remove pillows and raise the rails
options.rationale: Side lying lets secretions drain and protects the airway. Pillows come out and rails go up to protect a client seizing in bed.

options.text: Lower him to the floor with help, where he cannot fall
options.rationale: The floor is right for a client who is standing or sitting. A client in bed stays there during the seizure.

questions.takeaway: During a seizure: time it, stay, call for help, turn the client to the side, clear and protect the area, do not restrain, and put nothing in the mouth when the teeth are clenched.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Every option aims at airway or injury. Each wrong one does the right thing in a harmful way.

steps.action: Protect the airway without the mouth
steps.detail: Side lying, because the teeth are clenched.
Firm holding restrains him.
He is already in bed.

elimination.verdict: Side lying, pillows out, rails up.

questions.objective: fire, electrical, chemical and seizure safety

questions.stem: A nurse sees flames in a wastebasket beside the bed of a 29-year-old man. He is awake and able to walk. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Aim an extinguisher at the base of the flames
options.rationale: Correct technique for putting it out. Extinguishing comes after the client is safe, the fire is reported and it is contained.

options.text: Walk him out of the room to a safe area
options.rationale: Protect the client from immediate injury first. Anyone close to a fire, whatever its size, is moved, and a client who can walk leaves on foot.

options.text: Go to the nearest alarm and report the exact location
options.rationale: Reporting the exact location is the second step. Going now leaves him beside the fire.

options.text: Close the room door to contain the fire and smoke
options.rationale: Containing is the third step. Done now, it shuts him in with the fire.

questions.takeaway: In a fire: protect clients from immediate injury, report the exact location, contain the fire, and extinguish it if possible, in that order.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: All four are real fire steps. The question is only the order, and the client is beside the flames.

steps.detail: A client next to the fire.
Protect, report, contain, extinguish.
He can walk, so he walks out.

elimination.verdict: Move him out first.

questions.objective: fire, electrical, chemical and seizure safety

questions.stem: A nurse plugs in an infusion pump for a 29-year-old man and sees a spark at the plug. The pump then powers on and passes its self test. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Use the pump for this infusion and report the spark at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Reporting is right. Using it first keeps a shock and fire hazard at the bedside until the end of the shift.

options.text: Move the plug to a different outlet and watch for another spark
options.rationale: Tests the outlet. The pump is still suspect and still in use.

options.text: Run the pump on battery power until someone has inspected the cord
options.rationale: Avoids the outlet, but faulty equipment stays in use on a client.

options.text: Remove the pump from use, label it for repair and report it
options.rationale: Equipment that sparks when plugged in is taken out of service, marked for repair, and reported, even if it then appears to work.

questions.takeaway: Equipment that sparks or is not in proper working order is removed, marked for repair and reported. A passed self test does not clear it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The passed self test is there to make continued use look reasonable. Three options keep the pump on the client.

steps.detail: Three options.
It reports, but only at the end of the shift.

steps.action: Take the one that removes the hazard
steps.detail: Out of service, labeled, reported.

elimination.verdict: Remove it, label it, report it.

questions.objective: fire, electrical, chemical and seizure safety

questions.stem: An 85-year-old woman with leg weakness has a fall prevention plan: one person assists with walking, and toileting is every 2 hours. Which part does the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Rescore her on the fall risk tool after her afternoon nap
options.rationale: Assessing fall risk is the nurse's responsibility, even when it uses a standard tool.

options.text: Walk her to the toilet every 2 hours and report unsafe attempts
options.rationale: Assisting with toileting and mobility according to the plan and reporting concerning behavior may be delegated.

options.text: Decide each time whether she needs one helper or two
options.rationale: Assisting is delegable. Determining the level of help is determining the prevention plan, which the nurse does.

options.text: Judge at the end of the shift whether the toileting schedule is working
options.rationale: Evaluating effectiveness stays with the nurse. Assistive personnel report what they saw.

questions.takeaway: The nurse assesses fall risk, determines the plan and evaluates it. Assistive personnel assist with toileting and mobility according to the plan, keep the environment safe and report concerning behavior.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Each option involves hands-on time with her. Look at the verb: rescore, decide and judge are the nurse's work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rescore, decide, judge, walk and report.
Three options.

steps.action: Keep the task done according to the plan
steps.detail: Toileting every 2 hours with one person.

elimination.verdict: Toileting rounds according to the plan, with reporting.

questions.objective: clinical judgment about hazards (culture of safety, delegation, post fall response and huddle)

questions.stem: An 85-year-old woman with leg weakness walks with one staff member. Over 2 days she has needed more tries to stand from her chair. She is oriented to person, place and time and denies dizziness. Which change to her plan fits?

options.text: Continue assisted walks and involve physical therapy for strength
options.rationale: The risk factor is weakness. Its matched intervention is mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation, with physical therapy among those who assist, and the goal is safe movement and strength maintenance.

options.text: Use a wheelchair for all trips until her legs are stronger
options.rationale: Protects her on each trip, but immobility worsens weakness. Her legs will not get stronger in a wheelchair.

options.text: Ask the pharmacist to review the timing of her medications
options.rationale: The right step for medication dizziness. She denies dizziness.

options.text: Reorient her to the room and call light before each transfer
options.rationale: The right step for confusion. She is oriented to person, place and time.

questions.takeaway: Weakness gets mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation, with physical therapy involved. The goal is safe movement and keeping strength, so growing weakness is not answered with less walking.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: A wheelchair looks like the safest choice for weaker legs. Ask what it does to her strength over the next week.

steps.detail: Worsening leg weakness. Oriented, no dizziness.

steps.action: Cut the interventions for other risks
steps.detail: Medication timing fits dizziness. Reorientation fits confusion.

steps.action: Compare the two that address weakness
steps.detail: A wheelchair removes walking. Assisted walks with physical therapy keep strength.

elimination.verdict: Keep assisted walking and bring in physical therapy.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: A nurse finds an 85-year-old woman's bed raised to its highest position with the brakes unlocked after she returned from radiology. She did not fall. The nurse lowers and locks the bed. What else does the nurse do?

options.text: Nothing further, because the hazard is corrected and she was not harmed
options.rationale: The bed is safe now. The handoff process that left it unsafe is unchanged for the next client.

options.text: Remind the transporter in private and keep it between the two of them
options.rationale: Speaking up is good. Kept private, it teaches one person and nobody else learns from it.

options.text: Report the hazard through the agency's reporting system
options.rationale: A culture of safety encourages reporting hazards and errors and learning from them, including events that caused no harm.

options.text: Ask the transporter's supervisor to discipline the transporter
options.rationale: Does bring it to someone with authority, but as blame. That discourages the reporting a culture of safety depends on.

questions.takeaway: A culture of safety is blame free, encourages reporting of hazards and errors, and learns from them. A hazard that hurt no one still gets reported.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: No harm makes the first option feel complete. Ask which choice lets the unit learn from it.

steps.detail: The bed is fixed. The process is not.
Discipline discourages reporting.
One person learns.

elimination.verdict: Report the hazard.

questions.objective: clinical judgment about hazards (culture of safety, delegation, post fall response and huddle)

questions.stem: An 83-year-old man with weakness and new confusion is found in the hall three times in 2 hours, looking for "my kitchen." He walks steadily with his walker and voided 20 minutes before each time. Which intervention fits best?

options.text: Start toileting rounds every 1 to 2 hours with staff
options.rationale: Often right when an older client keeps getting up. He had voided 20 minutes before each trip, so urgency is not the cause.

options.text: Have staff assist him with every transfer and every walk
options.rationale: Fits weakness, which he has. The stem says he walks steadily with the walker, and it is where he is going that is unsafe.

options.text: Keep a night light on and place his glasses within his reach
options.rationale: Fits visual impairment. Nothing in the stem points to a vision problem.

options.text: Reorient him often and have family bring familiar objects
options.rationale: Disorientation is driving the unsafe trips. Frequent reorientation and familiar cues, with family, are the matched intervention.

questions.takeaway: A client can have several risk factors. Treat the one causing the unsafe behavior now. Confusion gets frequent reorientation and familiar cues.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: He has weakness and confusion, and toileting is the usual suspect. Use the cues that rule causes out: he just voided and he is steady.

steps.detail: Voided 20 minutes before each trip.

steps.action: Rule out weakness as the cause now
steps.detail: Steady with the walker.
He is looking for his kitchen.

elimination.verdict: Reorientation and familiar cues with family.

questions.objective: individualized fall prevention matched to the risk factor

questions.stem: An 83-year-old confused man was placed in wrist restraints 1 hour ago after pulling out a feeding tube. Since then he shouts and twists against them, and both wrists are red. His last pain medication was 9 hours ago. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Release them with staff present, assess for pain, and try alternatives
options.rationale: Increased agitation is a complication of restraints, and it began after they were applied. Pain is a listed cause of the behavior, and 9 hours without pain medication is a stated cue.

options.text: Pad both wrists, loosen the straps one notch, and recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats the red wrists, a real skin problem. It leaves him fighting the restraints and the cause unexamined.

options.text: Request a sedative so that he stops straining against the restraints
options.rationale: Adds a chemical restraint to a physical one and treats the shouting, not its cause.

options.text: Add a vest restraint so that twisting cannot injure his wrists
options.rationale: More restriction for a problem the restraint is causing. Injury from escape attempts would become more likely.

questions.takeaway: Restraints can cause the agitation they were meant to control. When a restrained client gets worse, reassess the need and the cause before adding anything.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Padding answers the wrists. Read the timing: the shouting and twisting started after the restraints went on.

steps.detail: Agitation began after the restraints.
No pain medication for 9 hours.
A sedative and a vest. Padding alone keeps him fighting.

elimination.verdict: Release with staff present, assess for pain, try alternatives.

questions.objective: restraints, alternatives and monitoring of a restrained client

questions.stem: An 83-year-old man's plan says one person assists him to the toilet. He received a sedating medication 1 hour ago and is now drowsy and slow to answer. Assistive personnel offer to take him to the toilet. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Let the assistive personnel take him, since toileting according to the plan is delegable
options.rationale: True on an ordinary day, which makes it tempting. The plan no longer matches him, so following it is not safe delegation.

options.text: Assess him before he gets up and decide what assistance he needs now
options.rationale: The plan was written before he became drowsy. Assessing fall risk and determining the plan belong to the nurse when the client's condition changes.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to bring a second helper if he seems unsteady
options.rationale: Sounds careful, but it hands the judgment about the level of help to assistive personnel.

options.text: Let them take him and reassess his drowsiness once he is back in bed
options.rationale: The right assessment at the wrong time. The risk is during the trip, so the assessment has to come before he stands.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel assist according to the plan. When the client changes, the nurse reassesses and resets the plan before the task is delegated.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Toileting is on the delegable list, and that pulls you toward yes. The new drowsiness after the medication is the cue.

steps.action: Compare the plan with the client now
steps.detail: One person assist was set before the sedating medication.

steps.action: Ask who decides the level of help
steps.detail: The nurse.

steps.action: Check the timing of the assessment
steps.detail: Assessing after the trip comes too late.

elimination.verdict: Assess first, then set the assistance.

questions.objective: clinical judgment about hazards (culture of safety, delegation, post fall response and huddle)

questions.stem: A 78-year-old on bed rest for 3 days with pneumonia is helped to sit at the side of the bed. After 40 seconds the client leans backward, needs the nurse's hands to stay upright, and cannot reach across midline. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Continue to the stretch and point test while a second nurse supports the client's trunk
options.rationale: The right next test at the wrong time. Stretch and point is only attempted after sit and shake is passed, and a supported trunk hides the very deficit being tested.

options.text: Stop the testing, treat the client as level 1 total assist, and plan moves at that level
options.rationale: The client could not sit unassisted for more than 2 minutes or reach across midline, so sit and shake is failed. That is level 1, total assist, the testing stops there, and moves are planned at that level.

options.text: Ask the client to rise toward standing so leg strength can be judged before deciding
options.rationale: Standing is the level 3 test. A client who cannot hold a seated balance has no safe way to attempt it.

options.text: Record level 2 maximum assist because the client reached a sitting position
options.rationale: Level 2 means sitting balance is present and the legs are the limit. Here the sitting balance itself is missing.

questions.takeaway: The BMAT stops at the first task the client fails. Failing sit and shake (sit unassisted more than 2 minutes, reach across midline, shake a hand) is level 1, total assist.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options keep testing or score the client higher. Ask what the first failed task is, because that task names the level.

steps.detail: Sitting balance lasted 40 seconds with hands on, and midline reach failed.

steps.action: Cut the options that move up the tool
steps.detail: Stretch and point and standing both come after a passed sit and shake.
Level 2 needs sitting balance, which this client lacks.

elimination.verdict: Stop the testing and treat the client as level 1 total assist.

questions.objective: assessing mobility, range of motion, functional ability and activity tolerance (BMAT)

questions.stem: A 78-year-old recovering from pneumonia now sits unassisted for 3 minutes and shakes the nurse's hand across midline, but cannot straighten either knee or point the toes. Assistive personnel ask how to move the client to the chair. Which direction is correct?

options.text: Stand the client with a gait belt and pivot to the chair using two staff
options.rationale: A real technique, for a client whose legs can take weight. This client could not even extend a knee against gravity while seated.

options.text: Walk the client three steps to the chair with a walker and standby assist
options.rationale: Standby assist with a device belongs to level 4. Stretch and point has just been failed.

options.text: Have the client lift the buttocks and hold for a count of 5 before choosing
options.rationale: That is the level 3 stand test. It is not attempted after a failed stretch and point.

options.text: Use a mechanical lift for the transfer, with the client helping while seated
options.rationale: Failed stretch and point is level 2, maximum assist: sitting balance is present, but the legs cannot support progress toward standing, so the transfer is done with equipment.

questions.takeaway: Passing sit and shake but failing stretch and point is level 2, maximum assist. The client can take part while seated, and the legs are not ready to bear weight.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The pivot transfer sounds like good teamwork. The deciding cue is that neither knee would straighten, so no number of staff makes standing safe.

steps.detail: Sit and shake passed, stretch and point failed: level 2.

steps.action: Remove everything that loads the legs
steps.detail: Pivot, walker steps and the stand test all require leg strength this client did not show.

steps.action: Keep what the client can do
steps.detail: Seated balance is present, so the client joins in seated tasks.

elimination.verdict: Mechanical lift for the transfer; the client participates while seated.

questions.objective: safe patient handling chosen from the BMAT level

questions.stem: A 78-year-old on day 5 of a pneumonia admission passes sit and shake and stretch and point. Asked to rise from the bed, the client lifts the buttocks, holds for a count of 2, and sits back down. Which plan fits this result?

options.text: Level 3 moderate assist: support standing and do not start the walk test
options.rationale: The client must hold the buttocks off the bed for a count of 5. A count of 2 fails the stand test, which is level 3: some leg strength, not enough to progress to walking.

options.text: Level 4 standby assist: the client cleared the bed, so begin marching in place with a walker
options.rationale: Clearing the bed is only half of the task. Without the count of 5 the stand test is not passed and the walk test is not started.

options.text: Level 2 maximum assist: any failed standing attempt means the legs cannot bear weight
options.rationale: Level 2 is assigned when stretch and point fails. This client passed it and showed some standing strength.

options.text: Level 3 moderate assist: repeat the stand test every 15 minutes until a count of 5 is reached
options.rationale: The level is right, and repeated testing to fatigue is not the plan. The client stays at level 3 with matching assistance until reassessed.

questions.takeaway: The stand test needs the buttocks off the surface for a count of 5. Lifting without holding fails it, and the client is level 3, moderate assist.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options name the correct level. Read what each one does after naming it.

steps.detail: Count of 2 against a required count of 5.

steps.action: Cut the level that is too high and the one that is too low
steps.detail: Level 4 needs a passed stand test. Level 2 needs a failed stretch and point.
One supports the client at this level. The other drills a failed test until the client tires.

elimination.verdict: Level 3 moderate assist, no walk test yet.

questions.objective: assessing mobility, range of motion, functional ability and activity tolerance (BMAT)

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with pneumonia lifts the buttocks off the bed and holds for a count of 5. Since last night the client is disoriented to place, pulls at the oxygen tubing, and follows only some commands. What does the nurse decide?

options.text: Go on to the walk test with a gait belt, because the leg strength criterion was met
options.rationale: Defensible on strength alone. The walk test also judges safety awareness, and the tool directs the nurse to weigh cognition, orientation and delirium before the standing levels.

options.text: Go on to the walk test with two staff, giving one short command at a time
options.rationale: Extra staff and simple commands are good practice with confusion. They do not supply the safety awareness that stepping away from the bed requires.

options.text: Hold progression and keep moves assisted until directions are followed
options.rationale: Cognition, orientation and delirium are considered before attempting to stand and progress. A client who cannot follow commands reliably is not safe to advance, even with a count of 5.

options.text: Return the client to bed rest and score level 1 total assist until the delirium clears
options.rationale: Too far back. Seated balance and leg strength were shown, and bed rest adds the immobility that worsens the situation.

questions.takeaway: Leg strength alone does not pass a client up the BMAT. Cognition, orientation and delirium are weighed before standing and walking, because the client must be able to follow directions.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options advance the client with extra precautions. The cue that tips it is new disorientation with commands followed only some of the time.

steps.detail: Count of 5 was met. Orientation and command following were not.

steps.action: Pair the two walk test options
steps.detail: Both advance a client who cannot reliably follow directions, so both fall together.
Demonstrated sitting balance and leg strength do not fit level 1.

elimination.verdict: Hold progression and keep moves assisted until the client can follow directions.

questions.objective: safe patient handling chosen from the BMAT level

questions.scenario: A 78-year-old recovering from pneumonia reaches BMAT level 4 and walks 20 meters in the hallway with a walker. Resting values before the walk: heart rate 82 per minute, respiratory rate 18 per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the client is tolerating the activity or not tolerating the activity.

rows.text: Heart rate 98 per minute at the end of the walk and 84 per minute after 3 minutes of sitting
rows.rationale: A rise with activity is expected. The return to the resting rate within minutes is the recovery the nurse looks for.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 30 per minute, pausing for breath in the middle of sentences
rows.rationale: Dyspnea that interrupts speech is more work than this client can sustain.

rows.text: Oxygen saturation 88% on room air at the turnaround point
rows.rationale: A fall from 95% to 88% means oxygenation is not keeping up with demand.

rows.text: Reports the legs feel tired, and says the tiredness is gone after sitting for 2 minutes
rows.rationale: Mild fatigue that clears quickly with rest is an expected response to progressive activity.

rows.text: Reports dizziness and reaches for the wall rail
rows.rationale: Dizziness during activity is a listed sign of intolerance and an immediate fall risk.

rows.text: Heart rate 118 per minute 10 minutes after returning to the chair
rows.rationale: The heart rate has not come back toward 82 per minute. Failure to recover after activity shows the load was too great.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is judged by the response and by the recovery: heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and how fast the client returns to baseline.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: A higher heart rate during a walk is not a failure. Ask whether each value came back to the resting level after the client sat down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare each value with the resting value
steps.detail: 82, 18 and 95% are the reference points.
84 per minute after 3 minutes recovered. 118 per minute after 10 minutes did not.
Broken speech and dizziness are intolerance. Tiredness that clears in 2 minutes is not.

elimination.verdict: Tolerating: r1 and r4. Not tolerating: r2, r3, r5, r6.

questions.objective: assessing mobility, range of motion, functional ability and activity tolerance (BMAT)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a stroke can raise the left arm halfway to shoulder height and then stops, unable to go further. The right arm moves through its full range without help. Which exercise plan does the nurse choose for the left shoulder?

options.text: Passive range of motion, with the nurse moving the joint while the arm stays relaxed
options.rationale: Right for a limb with no voluntary movement. This arm can do half the work, and doing all of it for the client wastes the muscle effort available.

options.text: Active range of motion, with the nurse counting repetitions from the bedside
options.rationale: Right for the right arm. The left arm stops halfway, so the rest of the range would never be exercised.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion, with the nurse completing the arc
options.rationale: The client moves the joint as far as the muscle allows and the nurse finishes the range, which uses the remaining strength and keeps the whole joint flexible.

options.text: Isometric shoulder contractions held against the mattress in place of joint movement
options.rationale: Isometric work builds static strength without moving the joint, so it does nothing for the half of the range the shoulder is missing.

questions.takeaway: Match the type of range of motion to what the limb can do: full voluntary movement is active, partial is active-assistive, none is passive.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Passive range of motion is the tempting choice for a stroke arm. The stem says the arm gets halfway by its own effort.

steps.detail: Halfway to shoulder height, not zero and not full.
Passive ignores the movement present. Active leaves half the range untouched.

steps.action: Check the exercise that moves no joint
steps.detail: Isometric contraction cannot maintain joint range.

elimination.verdict: Active-assistive range of motion for the left shoulder.

questions.objective: range of motion types and isotonic vs isometric exercise

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a stroke has no voluntary movement of the left ankle. The left foot rests pointed downward under tight blankets, and the nurse can still bring it to a right angle by hand. Which plan does the nurse start?

options.text: Support the foot in neutral alignment and give ankle range of motion
options.rationale: Prolonged plantar flexion leads to foot drop. While the joint still moves fully, neutral alignment, a supportive device and range of motion prevent the contracture.

options.text: Teach the client to pump the left ankle up and down ten times every hour
options.rationale: Ankle pumps are a good exercise for a client who can move the ankle. This ankle has no voluntary movement.

options.text: Place a pillow under both knees so the legs rest in slight flexion
options.rationale: This relaxes the legs and leaves the foot pointing down. It also holds the knees flexed, which invites a second contracture.

options.text: Leave the foot as it rests and compare both ankles again at the next shift
options.rationale: Comparing sides is sound assessment. The cue is already present, and waiting lets a correctable position become a fixed one.

questions.takeaway: A foot left in plantar flexion becomes a plantar flexion contracture (foot drop). Prevent it with neutral alignment, range of motion and supportive devices.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The foot still reaches a right angle by hand, so this is the window for prevention. Pick the option that changes the position of the foot itself.

steps.detail: Pointed foot plus pressure from bedding equals plantar flexion held for hours.

steps.action: Cut what the client cannot do
steps.detail: No voluntary ankle movement rules out self-performed pumps.

steps.action: Cut what leaves the foot down
steps.detail: Knee pillows and watchful waiting do not move the ankle to neutral.

elimination.verdict: Neutral alignment with a supportive device and passive ankle range of motion.

questions.objective: effects of immobility on body systems

questions.stem: During range of motion on a 66-year-old with left-sided weakness from a stroke, the left elbow stops 30 degrees short of where the right elbow straightens. The client reports stiffness without pain. Yesterday both elbows straightened equally. What does the nurse do with this finding?

options.text: Push the left elbow steadily through the resistance until it matches the right
options.rationale: Range of motion is taken to the point of resistance, not through it. Forcing a stiff joint injures the tissue the nurse is trying to keep supple.

options.text: Rest the left arm flexed across the chest on a pillow, since that position is not painful
options.rationale: Absence of pain makes this look kind. Holding the elbow flexed for long periods is how the shortening becomes permanent.

options.text: Record it as an expected result of the stroke and continue the same schedule
options.rationale: The stroke explains the weakness. A range that was equal yesterday and is limited today is a new change.

options.text: Add range of motion sessions for an early contracture and position the elbow extended
options.rationale: New stiffness, limitation and asymmetry on side to side comparison point to muscle and tendon shortening. More frequent range of motion and proper positioning prevent a permanent contracture.

questions.takeaway: Compare range of motion bilaterally and note pain, stiffness, limitation or asymmetry. A new one-sided limitation in an immobile limb is an early contracture until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The word that matters is "yesterday". The same finding with no change over time would be read very differently.

steps.detail: Equal yesterday, 30 degrees short today, on the weak side.
Forcing the joint and resting it flexed both make things worse.
A new asymmetry is acted on, because contractures are permanent once set.

elimination.verdict: Early contracture: more range of motion and extended positioning.

questions.objective: assessing mobility, range of motion, functional ability and activity tolerance (BMAT)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with left-sided weakness from a stroke has sat in a chair for 90 minutes and now leans left, with the trunk curved and the left shoulder hanging lower. The client reports tiredness and back ache. Which action is best?

options.text: Return the client to bed for the rest of the day to relieve the tired back muscles
options.rationale: Rest eases the ache for now. It trades a positioning problem for more immobility, when the sitting position itself can be corrected.

options.text: Recenter the trunk in an upright position and support the left side and arm
options.rationale: Proper alignment minimizes stress on joints, reduces fatigue and improves balance. The lean explains the ache and tiredness, so the nurse fixes the lean.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess the back ache in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Treats the symptom and leaves the cause in place. The curved trunk will keep straining the back.

options.text: Ask the client to hold the trunk upright with the right arm on the armrest
options.rationale: Uses the strong side, and it cannot be kept up. Muscles working to hold a poor position are the source of the fatigue.

questions.takeaway: Poor alignment costs energy and loads joints. When a client who cannot hold a position reports fatigue or ache, correct and support the alignment first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Every option does something about the ache. Only one removes what is producing it.

steps.action: Link the symptoms to the posture
steps.detail: Curved trunk and dropped shoulder for 90 minutes, then ache and tiredness.
Analgesic and bed rest leave the alignment unchanged.

steps.action: Cut the plan that depends on effort
steps.detail: Holding upright with one arm adds fatigue.

elimination.verdict: Recenter the trunk and support the weak side.

questions.objective: movement, posture, balance and alignment

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a stroke stands with a therapist, and the left leg holds weight without buckling. The client does not know where the left foot is unless looking at it, and it slides sideways unnoticed. How does the nurse plan standing at the bedside?

options.text: Stay hands-on with a gait belt and have the client watch the left foot while standing
options.rationale: Balance depends on the nervous system as well as muscle. Without awareness of body position the client cannot correct a foot that drifts, so strength alone does not make standing safe.

options.text: Add leg strengthening exercises and progress to standing alone as the leg strength improves
options.rationale: Strengthening is the usual answer to an unsafe stand. Here the leg already holds weight, and the missing piece is position sense, which exercise for strength does not restore.

options.text: Allow standing with standby assist from the doorway, since the leg bears full weight
options.rationale: Standby assist fits a client with adequate strength and balance. This client has the first and not the second.

options.text: Keep the client seated for all care until the left foot sensation has fully returned
options.rationale: Removes the fall risk by removing the activity. Guarded standing is still possible and prevents the losses of immobility.

questions.takeaway: Movement needs strength and proprioception. A leg that is strong but not sensed is an unstable leg, so the nurse guards balance and substitutes vision for position sense.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options rest on the leg being strong. The stem says the strength is present and something else is absent.

steps.action: Find what is intact and what is lost
steps.detail: Weight bearing is intact. Awareness of foot position is lost.

steps.action: Drop the options that answer a strength problem
steps.detail: More strengthening and standby assist both assume strength was the limit.
Seated for all care adds immobility without need.

elimination.verdict: Hands-on guarding with a gait belt, and the client watches the foot.

questions.objective: movement, posture, balance and alignment

questions.nursesNote: 0800: 58-year-old, day 2 after abdominal surgery, has stayed flat in bed since surgery and declines to turn or sit up. Respiratory rate 24 per minute and shallow. Breath sounds diminished in both lung bases. Cough is weak, with secretions heard in the upper airway after coughing. Oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Incision edges together and dry. Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants. Pain 3 of 10 at rest.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up as respiratory effects of immobility.

segments.text: Has stayed flat in bed since surgery and declines to turn or sit up
segments.rationale: The cause. Lying flat and still limits lung expansion, and it is the part the nurse can change.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 24 per minute and shallow
segments.rationale: Shallow breaths do not open the bases, which is how atelectasis starts.

segments.text: Breath sounds diminished in both lung bases
segments.rationale: Less air is reaching the bases. With decreased lung expansion this points to atelectasis.

segments.text: Cough is weak, with secretions heard in the upper airway after coughing
segments.rationale: Reduced cough effectiveness and retained secretions raise the risk of pneumonia.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 91% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygenation is already affected and needs to be trended as the client is mobilized.

segments.text: Incision edges together and dry
segments.rationale: An expected wound finding on day 2, and not a respiratory effect.

segments.text: Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants
segments.rationale: A reassuring gastrointestinal finding.

segments.text: Pain 3 of 10 at rest
segments.rationale: Pain at this level at rest is not itself a respiratory effect of immobility, although the nurse reassesses it with movement.

questions.takeaway: Immobility decreases lung expansion, weakens the cough and lets secretions collect. Diminished bases with shallow breathing is atelectasis on the way to pneumonia.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Sort each phrase by body system first. The question asks only for the respiratory picture and its cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rate and depth, breath sounds, cough, saturation.
Flat and unwilling to move is what the plan must change.
Incision, bowel sounds and resting pain are not respiratory effects.

elimination.verdict: s1 to s5.

questions.objective: effects of immobility on body systems

questions.stem: A 58-year-old on day 2 after abdominal surgery, with diminished breath sounds in both bases, is raised to Fowler's position. Three pillows push the chin to the chest, the legs are straight, and the client has slid down the bed. What does the nurse correct?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to flat so the client stops sliding and the spine is straight
options.rationale: Stops the slide and gives up the upright position that the diminished bases call for.

options.text: Add a fourth pillow behind the shoulders and raise the head of the bed higher
options.rationale: More height with the same supports increases the neck flexion and the slide.

options.text: Use one small head pillow and support the hips and knees in slight flexion
options.rationale: Supported Fowler's permits flexion of the hips and knees and keeps the normal cervical, thoracic and lumbar curves. That stops the slide and frees the chest to expand.

options.text: Keep the pillows and place a firm footboard so the straight legs can brace
options.rationale: Bracing limits the slide while the neck stays flexed and the legs stay straight, so the alignment problem remains.

questions.takeaway: In supported Fowler's position the supports allow hip and knee flexion and keep the normal curves of the cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The position chosen is right. The question is about the supports, so the answer changes the supports and keeps the head of the bed up.

steps.detail: Neck forced forward, legs straight, body sliding down.
Diminished bases need it, so flat is out.
A small pillow frees the neck, and hip and knee flexion stops the slide.

elimination.verdict: One small head pillow and slight hip and knee flexion.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 58-year-old gets up for the first time 2 days after abdominal surgery. Lying blood pressure was 128/76 mm Hg. After 1 minute sitting at the bedside the client reports dizziness and blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg. What does the nurse do now?

options.text: Stand the client promptly with two staff so the calf muscles can pump blood upward
options.rationale: Leg muscle activity does help venous return. Standing a dizzy client whose systolic pressure has fallen 26 mm Hg invites a faint and a fall.

options.text: Return the client to lying and later raise the head of the bed in stages
options.rationale: A 26 mm Hg systolic fall with dizziness is orthostatic hypotension from bed rest. The client goes back down, and the next attempt uses gradual position changes.

options.text: Apply the sequential compression devices and continue the transfer to the chair
options.rationale: Compression devices reduce venous stasis in bed. They do not make it safe to keep moving a client who is symptomatic right now.

options.text: Coach slow deep breaths with the incentive spirometer until the dizziness passes
options.rationale: A useful respiratory measure aimed at the wrong system. The dizziness comes from the pressure drop.

questions.takeaway: Bed rest sets up orthostatic hypotension. A systolic drop of 20 mm Hg or more with dizziness means return to bed, then progress with gradual position changes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a real prevention measure for immobility. Match the measure to the complication in front of you.

steps.detail: 128 to 102 mm Hg systolic, with dizziness.
A symptomatic client does not continue upward.
Compression devices and spirometry answer stasis and lung expansion, not this drop.

elimination.verdict: Back to lying, then raise the head in stages.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 58-year-old 2 days after abdominal surgery has an order for bed rest for 24 more hours and no fluid restriction. The client drank 400 mL yesterday, and the sequential compression devices have been lying on a chair since the morning bath. Which actions reduce this client's risk of thrombus formation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reapply the sequential compression devices to both legs now
options.rationale: The devices move venous blood that the still calf muscles are not moving. They work only while they are on.

options.text: Teach ankle and leg exercises to be done in bed every hour while awake
options.rationale: Leg exercises are allowed on bed rest and counter venous stasis.

options.text: Offer fluids through the day, since no restriction is ordered
options.rationale: Adequate hydration as appropriate is a listed prevention, and 400 mL per day is low.

options.text: Plan progressive activity to begin as soon as the bed rest order ends
options.rationale: Progressive activity is the lasting answer to stasis, started when the order permits.

options.text: Keep a pillow under both knees so the legs rest comfortably flexed
options.rationale: Comfortable, and it holds the knees bent and presses on the vessels behind them, which slows venous flow further.

options.text: Have the client use the incentive spirometer ten times each hour
options.rationale: A correct order for this client's lungs. It does not act on venous stasis.

questions.takeaway: Venous stasis is prevented with leg exercises, sequential compression devices, adequate hydration as appropriate, gradual position changes and progressive activity.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options are good care for a different problem or for comfort. Ask of each one: does this move blood out of the legs?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Compression devices, leg exercises, later walking.
Fluids, because intake was 400 mL and no restriction exists.

steps.action: Drop comfort and the lung measure
steps.detail: Knee pillows slow flow. Spirometry treats the lungs.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 58-year-old had diminished bases, a weak cough and an oxygen saturation of 91% on room air after abdominal surgery. After 24 hours of upright sitting, deep breathing, coughing and incentive spirometry, which finding best shows the plan is working?

options.text: Respiratory rate 12 per minute and shallow, with the client dozing between checks
options.rationale: A lower rate looks like progress. Slow, shallow breathing in a drowsy client expands the bases even less.

options.text: The client reports no incisional pain while lying still and declines to cough
options.rationale: Comfort at rest is welcome. A client who will not cough is still retaining secretions.

options.text: Saturation 96% on oxygen at 2 L per minute, with both bases still diminished
options.rationale: The number is better only because oxygen was added. The bases are still not filling, so the plan has not yet changed lung expansion.

options.text: Breath sounds heard in both bases, a strong cough, and saturation 96%
options.rationale: Air is reaching the bases, secretions are being cleared, and oxygenation has risen from 91%. These are the three problems the plan targeted.
