questions.takeaway: Evaluate a respiratory plan for immobility by what it was meant to change: lung expansion, cough effectiveness, secretion clearance and oxygenation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: A better number is not the outcome by itself. Look for the option in which air and secretions are moving without added support.

steps.detail: Diminished bases, weak cough, saturation 91%.
Only one shows open bases, an effective cough and a higher saturation together.

steps.action: Reject the partial and quiet findings
steps.detail: Saturation raised by added oxygen with bases still diminished, drowsy shallow breathing and refusing to cough show no real gain.

elimination.verdict: Bases audible, strong cough, saturation 96%.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on bed rest for 10 days sits with the head of the bed at 60 degrees and slides down hourly. Assistive personnel pull the client up by the arms across the sheet. Sacral skin is intact. What does the nurse change?

options.text: Move the client up on a friction-reducing sheet with two staff, without dragging
options.rationale: Dragging across the sheet adds friction, and sliding down with the head raised adds shear. Both raise pressure injury risk before any skin change is visible.

options.text: Keep the method and inspect the sacrum at every reposition for early redness
options.rationale: Skin inspection is correct and comes too late on its own. It watches the damage instead of removing the forces that cause it.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees so the client stays fully upright
options.rationale: A steeper angle increases the downward pull of the trunk over the sacrum and with it the shear.

options.text: Massage the sacrum with lotion after each move to restore the circulation
options.rationale: Aimed at reduced circulation, and rubbing skin already exposed to friction adds to the injury.

questions.takeaway: Pressure, friction and shear are the integumentary threats of immobility. Sliding in bed is shear and dragging is friction, so the nurse changes how the client is moved.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Intact skin does not mean the method is safe. The cues are the slide and the pull across the sheet.

steps.detail: Slide equals shear. Drag equals friction.
The cause is already known, so watching the sacrum alone is not the fix.
A steeper bed and massage both increase stress on the skin.

elimination.verdict: Friction-reducing sheet and two staff instead of dragging.

questions.objective: effects of immobility on body systems

questions.stem: An 84-year-old in bed for 10 days, now cleared for activity as tolerated with no fluid restriction, drinks 700 mL per day, has had no stool for 4 days, and passes small amounts of dark, cloudy urine. Which plan addresses both elimination problems?

options.text: Request a laxative and continue offering the bedpan with the client lying flat
options.rationale: Helps the bowel for a day and leaves low intake, the flat position and inactivity untouched. The urine problem is not addressed.

options.text: Request a urinary catheter so that stagnant urine drains from the bladder continuously
options.rationale: Draining urine sounds like the answer to stasis. A catheter adds infection risk to a client whose immobility already raises it.

options.text: Increase fluids, use an upright commode, and add activity as tolerated
options.rationale: Immobility slows gut motility and lets urine pool. Fluids, an upright position that lets gravity help emptying, and movement act on both.

options.text: Limit evening fluids and offer the bedpan on a fixed schedule every 4 hours
options.rationale: A schedule is helpful, and less fluid concentrates the urine further and hardens stool.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes urinary stasis with infection and stone risk, and decreased gut motility with constipation. Fluids, upright positioning and mobility counter both.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem asks for both problems. Check each option against the bowel and then against the bladder.

steps.detail: Low intake, flat position, no activity.
A laxative serves the bowel only. A catheter serves the bladder only and adds risk.
Intake is already 700 mL per day.

elimination.verdict: Fluids, upright on a commode, more activity.

questions.objective: effects of immobility on body systems

questions.stem: An 84-year-old man on bed rest for 10 days has stopped talking with staff, sleeps through the day, and refuses his bath, saying, "What's the point, I can't do anything for myself." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "You are getting stronger every day, and you will be home before you know it."
options.rationale: Cheerful, and it steps over what he said. False reassurance closes the conversation.

options.text: Let him sleep and skip the bath today, because rest supports his recovery
options.rationale: Respects the refusal on the surface. More daytime sleep and less contact deepen the isolation that the cues show.

options.text: Ask the provider to evaluate him for an antidepressant before the next shift
options.rationale: Depression is a real risk of immobility. Reaching for a drug first skips the nursing measures that address the stated cause.

options.text: "It sounds hard to depend on others." Then offer him choices in his care
options.rationale: He named loss of independence. Reflecting the feeling and returning control over his care acts on the cause of the withdrawal.

questions.takeaway: Immobility brings boredom, isolation, loss of independence, anxiety, depression and altered self-concept. Give back control: choices, self-care the client can manage, and contact.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: His own words tell you which psychosocial effect this is. Choose the response that answers those words.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: "I can't do anything for myself" is loss of independence.

steps.action: Remove the reply that dismisses it
steps.detail: Promising he will be home soon denies the feeling.
Choices restore control. Sleep and a drug request do not.

elimination.verdict: Reflect the feeling, then offer him choices in his care.

questions.objective: effects of immobility on body systems

questions.stem: A 52-year-old is critically ill with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome and is on a ventilator. In supported Fowler's position oxygen saturation is 86% on high oxygen settings. Which position does the nurse prepare the team to use?

options.text: High Fowler's at 90 degrees with the arms supported forward on an overbed table
options.rationale: Upright positioning is the usual first move for difficult breathing, which makes this defensible. The client is already upright and is still at 86%.

options.text: Prone, lying on the stomach with the head turned to face the left or the right
options.rationale: Prone positioning is first-line therapy for a critically ill client with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. The words "severe" and "critically ill" select it.

options.text: Supine, flat on the back with the arms at the sides and the head midline
options.rationale: Supine gives easy access to the tubes and lines. It does nothing for oxygenation in this condition.

options.text: Left side-lying, alternated with right side-lying every 2 hours
options.rationale: Turning protects the skin and moves secretions. It is routine care, not the treatment for this degree of low oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Upright positions support breathing for most clients. For the critically ill client with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, prone positioning is first-line.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: "Raise the head of the bed" is the reflex for low saturation. The stem has already tried upright and names a diagnosis with its own first-line position.

steps.detail: Supported Fowler's with saturation 86%.
Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome in a critically ill client.
More of a position that has not worked loses to the first-line position.

elimination.verdict: Prone, head turned to one side.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome has just been turned prone on a ventilator. Oxygen saturation rose from 86% to 93%, and the ventilator tubing lies free. On reassessment, which finding does the nurse correct right away?

options.text: The head is turned to the left, with the left cheek resting on a cushion
options.rationale: This is how the head is placed in the prone position. The cheek is a pressure area to keep checking, and nothing here needs correcting now.

options.text: Both arms lie along the client's sides, with the palms facing upward
options.rationale: An acceptable arm placement that keeps the shoulders in a neutral position.

options.text: The left ear is folded forward and pinned between the head and the cushion
options.rationale: Pressure areas and skin are reassessed after every reposition. A folded ear under the weight of the head is pressure on thin skin over cartilage, and it is corrected before injury starts.

options.text: The client's oxygen saturation has not yet reached 95% in the new position
options.rationale: The value rose 7 points after the turn. The response is in the right direction and is trended, not corrected.

questions.takeaway: After repositioning, reassess alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and the ability to breathe. In the prone position the face and ears carry the pressure.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: A better saturation does not finish the evaluation. Walk the reassessment list and separate the expected placements from the one finding that will injure tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, breathing.
Head to one side, arms at the sides, free tubing and a rising saturation are all acceptable.
An ear folded under the head.

elimination.verdict: Free and flatten the left ear.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 52-year-old recovering from acute respiratory distress syndrome is returned to the supine position. Assistive personnel rest both of the client's arms on pillows, raised out to the sides above shoulder level at about 120 degrees. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Lower both arms to the sides, or out to the sides at less than 90 degrees
options.rationale: In the supine position the arms rest at the sides or abducted less than 90 degrees. Above that the shoulder joints and the nerves around them are strained.

options.text: Turn the client's head toward the left so that it is not resting in the midline
options.rationale: Turning the head belongs to the prone position. In supine it does nothing about the arms.

options.text: Leave the arms as placed and check the hands for swelling in 2 hours
options.rationale: Checking is good practice, and the arm position is already outside the limit, so the position is corrected first.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and flex the hips and knees with support
options.rationale: Describes supported Fowler's. It is a different position and leaves the arms where they are.

questions.takeaway: Supine means lying on the back with the arms at the sides or abducted less than 90 degrees. Check limb placement after every turn.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Three options describe a detail of another position or delay. The stem gives an angle, so find the option that answers the angle.

steps.detail: About 120 degrees of abduction.
Less than 90 degrees in supine.
Head turning is prone. Hip and knee flexion is Fowler's.

elimination.verdict: Bring the arms to the sides or below 90 degrees.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 52-year-old on oxygen by nasal cannula is turned onto the right side. The client lies aligned and denies pain. Saturation falls from 95% to 89%, and the cannula tubing runs under the right shoulder. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn the client back to the previous position and recheck the saturation
options.rationale: Reasonable when a new position is the only change. Here a specific cause is in view, and turning back would be a second move with the tubing still at risk.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees and coach slow, deep breaths
options.rationale: Supports breathing in general. It does not restore oxygen that is being cut off by the client's own weight.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the wall meter and recheck in 5 minutes
options.rationale: More flow cannot pass tubing that is compressed, and the cause stays in place.

options.text: Free the tubing from under the shoulder and confirm oxygen flow
options.rationale: Tubes and lines and the ability to breathe are reassessed after repositioning. Tubing pinned under the shoulder explains the fall, and freeing it is the fastest correction.

questions.takeaway: When a client worsens right after a turn, check what the turn changed. Tubes and lines come before repositioning again.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Turning the client back and freeing the tubing would both work. The stem tells you where the tubing is, and that is the cue that tips it.

steps.action: Link the drop to the turn
steps.detail: 95% to 89% right after repositioning.
The oxygen tubing runs under the right shoulder.
Restore the oxygen supply before changing position or settings.

elimination.verdict: Free the tubing and confirm flow.

questions.objective: interventions and positioning that prevent complications of immobility

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with leg weakness after 2 weeks of illness rises from a chair with the feet touching each other and reaches forward for a walker placed an arm's length away. The client sways as the trunk moves forward. What does the nurse teach?

options.text: Rise faster so that less time is spent in the unsteady part of the movement
options.rationale: Speed shortens the moment of sway. It gives weak muscles less time to control a shifting center of gravity.

options.text: Place the feet apart and bring the walker within easy reach before rising
options.rationale: The center of gravity shifts during movement, and weakness reduces stability. A wider base and a support within reach keep the shifting weight over the feet.

options.text: Keep the walker where it is and look straight ahead instead of at the floor
options.rationale: Looking ahead helps posture. The sway comes from the narrow stance and the long reach, which are unchanged.

options.text: Remain seated for transfers until leg strength has returned to its usual level
options.rationale: Avoids the sway by avoiding the movement. Supervised standing is how the strength returns.

questions.takeaway: Balance means keeping a shifting center of gravity over the base of support. With weakness, widen the base and bring the support close before moving.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The client does two things wrong before standing even begins. Choose the option that corrects the setup.

steps.detail: Feet together and walker at arm's length.
The trunk moves forward beyond a narrow base.
Faster adds risk. Staying seated adds immobility.

elimination.verdict: Feet apart, walker close, then rise.

questions.objective: movement, posture, balance and alignment

questions.stem: A 72-year-old recovering from 2 weeks of illness marches in place with a walker, then steps forward and back with each foot without losing balance. Assistive personnel plan to use the mechanical lift for the bathroom trip "to be safe." What does the nurse direct?

options.text: Use the mechanical lift today, then reassess the mobility level tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Sounds cautious. The assessment has just been done, and a lift takes away the walking this client is able to do.

options.text: Take the client by wheelchair, with a stand and pivot at the bedside and toilet
options.rationale: Less equipment than a lift, and it still replaces walking in a client who passed the walk test.

options.text: Let the client walk to the bathroom alone while staff prepare the room
options.rationale: Independence is the goal. After 2 weeks of illness, the first walks are done with someone within reach.

options.text: Have the client walk with the walker while staff stay close as standby assist
options.rationale: Advancing a step with balance is level 4, minimum or standby assist. The client walks with the assistive device and staff stay within reach.

questions.takeaway: Equipment is matched to the BMAT level. A client who can march in place and advance a step is level 4: walking with standby assist and the usual assistive device.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: More equipment is not automatically safer. Using more help than the level calls for costs the client strength.

steps.detail: Marching and stepping passed: level 4.
Lift and wheelchair remove the activity.
Walking alone drops the standby that level 4 names.

elimination.verdict: Walk with the walker and standby assist.

questions.objective: safe patient handling chosen from the BMAT level

questions.stem: A 72-year-old regaining strength after 2 weeks of illness has a painful, swollen right knee, and the provider has restricted bending of that knee while it heals. The client wants to keep the right thigh muscle strong. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Active range of motion, bending and straightening the right knee ten times each hour
options.rationale: Isotonic movement is the usual route to functional strength, which makes this defensible. It moves the one joint that is painful and restricted.

options.text: Passive range of motion to the right knee, performed gently by the nurse twice a day
options.rationale: Passive movement keeps a joint flexible and does not build muscle. It also bends the restricted knee.

options.text: Tightening the right thigh with the knee straight, then relaxing
options.rationale: An isometric contraction works the muscle without joint movement, so static strength and joint stability are built around a painful or healing joint.

options.text: Resting the right leg on a pillow until the swelling and the pain have resolved
options.rationale: Protects the knee and gives up the goal. An unused thigh muscle atrophies within days.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic exercise moves the joint and builds dynamic strength. Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without joint movement, which makes it the choice around a painful or healing joint.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options build strength. The provider's restriction on bending decides between them.

steps.action: State the goal and the limit
steps.detail: Keep thigh strength, no knee bending.
Active and passive range of motion both move the joint.
Rest alone lets the muscle waste.

elimination.verdict: Isometric thigh contractions with the knee straight.

questions.objective: range of motion types and isotonic vs isometric exercise

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with 3 days of diarrhea takes a diuretic and a daily laxative. Her daughter reports she became confused this morning. The client says she is not thirsty. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess heart rate, lying and standing blood pressure, and mucous membranes
options.rationale: In an older adult, acute confusion may be the first sign of a fluid imbalance, and she has three causes of loss: diarrhea, a diuretic and a laxative. These checks confirm or rule out a deficit now.

options.text: Complete a detailed orientation and memory screen, since she denies thirst
options.rationale: A mental status screen describes the confusion without looking for its cause. The thirst reflex is diminished with age, so no thirst does not rule out a deficit.

options.text: Hold the diuretic and laxative, then reassess her confusion after the next dose time
options.rationale: Both drugs do raise her risk, so this is a reasonable later step. It skips finding out how depleted she is right now.

options.text: Start an intake and output record and review the 24 hour totals tomorrow
options.rationale: Right tool, wrong time. Intake and output belongs in her care, but new confusion needs an assessment today.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion can be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance, and thirst is not a reliable guide.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a risk picture and one new change, with no measurements yet. That is the signal to collect data before choosing a treatment.

steps.detail: No pulse, blood pressure or mucous membrane findings are given.

steps.action: Drop the options that miss the cause
steps.detail: A memory screen and totals reviewed tomorrow both leave new confusion unexplained.
Holding drugs treats a cause before the deficit is measured.

elimination.verdict: Assess for fluid deficit now.

questions.objective: older adult risks

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 82-year-old woman with 3 days of diarrhea for fluid deficit. Skin pinched on the back of her hand stays tented. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Record the tenting as proof of dehydration and request IV fluids
options.rationale: Tenting does point to a deficit, but skin on an older adult's hand tents from age alone. A treatment request should not rest on this site.

options.text: Repeat the pinch on the back of her other hand to compare sides
options.rationale: Comparing sides sounds careful, but both hands have the same age related loss of elasticity.

options.text: Check skin turgor over her sternum before judging her hydration
options.rationale: In older adults turgor is assessed at the sternum, not the hands. That site gives a finding the nurse can trust.

options.text: Leave turgor out of the assessment and ask whether she feels thirsty
options.rationale: Thirst is diminished in older adults, so this swaps one unreliable cue for another.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, check skin turgor at the sternum. Tenting on the hand may only reflect age.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The age in the stem changes how a routine technique is done. Ask which option corrects the site instead of acting on the first result.

steps.detail: Two options still use the hand.
Thirst is weak in older adults.
The sternum is the site for her age group.

elimination.verdict: Recheck turgor at the sternum.

questions.objective: older adult risks

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with 3 days of diarrhea has dry mucous membranes, heart rate 104 per minute and tenting at the sternum. She is drowsy and coughs with each sip of water. Which plan does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Oral fluids every hour, with assistive personnel helping her drink
options.rationale: Scheduled oral replacement is the usual plan for a mild to moderate deficit. It requires a client who is alert and able to swallow, and she is drowsy and coughing with sips.

options.text: IV crystalloid replacement, with oral fluids held until she swallows safely
options.rationale: Oral replacement is only for a client who is alert, able to swallow and tolerating fluids by mouth. Her drowsiness and coughing move her to the IV route.

options.text: Thickened oral fluids offered whenever she says she is thirsty
options.rationale: Thickening addresses the coughing, but a drowsy client still cannot drink safely, and waiting for thirst fails in an older adult.

options.text: An albumin infusion to hold water inside her blood vessels
options.rationale: A colloid expands plasma volume. Diarrhea loses water and electrolytes together, which a crystalloid replaces.

questions.takeaway: Oral replacement needs an alert client who can swallow and tolerate fluids. If any of those is missing, the route becomes IV.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two plans replace fluid correctly. The cue that separates them is her swallowing and alertness, not how dry she is.

steps.detail: Drowsy and coughing with each sip means an unsafe swallow.
Both oral options put fluid into an unprotected airway.
Losses from diarrhea are water and electrolytes, so a crystalloid fits.

elimination.verdict: IV crystalloid, oral fluids held.

questions.objective: dehydration

questions.scenario: An 82-year-old woman admitted with dehydration from diarrhea had heart rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 lying and 94/58 standing, hematocrit 52% (above the reference range), new confusion and urine output of 15 mL per hour. She has now received IV crystalloid for 8 hours.
questions.stem: For each finding at 8 hours, indicate whether it shows that the fluid deficit is resolving.
columns: Does not show it is resolving

rows.text: Heart rate 88 per minute with a strong pulse
rows.rationale: The fast, weak pulse was compensation for low volume. A slower, stronger pulse means volume is returning.

rows.text: Blood pressure 120/72 lying and 116/70 standing
rows.rationale: The drop on standing has gone, so there is enough volume to hold pressure upright.

rows.text: Urine output 15 mL per hour, dark amber
rows.answer: Does not show it is resolving
rows.rationale: Unchanged from admission and still concentrated. At this rate she makes under 500 mL per day.

rows.text: Hematocrit 45%
rows.rationale: The high value was hemoconcentration. A fall from 52% means plasma water is being restored.

rows.text: She says she is not thirsty
rows.answer: Does not show it is resolving
rows.rationale: Thirst is diminished in older adults, so its absence says nothing about her volume.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place and time
rows.rationale: Confusion was a sign of the imbalance. Clear orientation shows the brain is being perfused again.

answer.r3: Does not show it is resolving
answer.r5: Does not show it is resolving

questions.takeaway: Judge fluid replacement by pulse, standing blood pressure, urine, hematocrit and mental status. In an older adult, do not judge it by thirst.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Compare each row with the admission value in the scenario. One row has not moved, and one row is a cue that does not work at her age.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each row to its admission value
steps.detail: Pulse, standing pressure, hematocrit and orientation have all moved toward normal.

steps.action: Find the row that did not move
steps.detail: Urine is still 15 mL per hour and dark.
Thirst is unreliable at 82.

elimination.verdict: Resolving: pulse, blood pressure, hematocrit, orientation. Not shown: urine output, thirst.

questions.objective: dehydration

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with diarrhea, now alert and swallowing safely, is receiving oral fluid replacement for dehydration. Assistive personnel report four findings from the past 24 hours. Which one does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: Weight 0.2 kg lower than yesterday on the same scale
options.rationale: A small loss worth tracking with daily weights. It is less urgent than evidence that the kidneys are not being perfused.

options.text: Heart rate of 92 per minute while resting in bed
options.rationale: A resting rate of 92 per minute is inside the usual 60 to 100 range. It is watched, but it is not the most concerning value here.

options.text: Oral intake of 1,400 mL, mostly water and broth
options.rationale: Intake is being taken, which is the plan. The question is whether it is enough, and the urine answers that.

options.text: Total urine output of 420 mL, dark amber in color
options.rationale: Output under 500 mL per day with concentrated urine is concerning. It shows that replacement is not keeping up with her losses.

questions.takeaway: In dehydration, urine output under 500 mL per day with concentrated urine means replacement is falling behind.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are real monitoring data. Pick the one with a stated threshold that it has crossed.

steps.detail: Intake of 1,400 mL is the plan working as ordered.
A 0.2 kg change is small and a rate of 92 is within the usual range.
420 mL is below 500 mL per day.

elimination.verdict: Follow up the urine output.

questions.objective: dehydration

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure received IV fluids for 2 days. The nurse wants the single best indicator of how much fluid he has retained. Which finding does the nurse rely on?

options.text: Intake exceeded output by 700 mL over the past 24 hours of care
options.rationale: Intake and output is part of monitoring and points the same way. It misses unmeasured losses and depends on every entry being recorded.

options.text: Pitting edema of 2+ in both of his ankles
options.rationale: Edema is a sign of overload, but it shows where fluid has settled, not how much he has gained.

options.text: Weight up 1.8 kg since yesterday on the same scale
options.rationale: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of fluid overload, and this weight was taken on the same scale as yesterday's.

options.text: Blood pressure of 152/90 with a bounding radial pulse
options.rationale: Both fit overload, and both are also changed by pain, anxiety and drugs. They do not measure the amount retained.

questions.takeaway: Rapid weight gain, measured at the same time, on the same scale, in the same clothing, is the best indicator of fluid overload.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Every option is a true sign of overload. The stem asks for the best indicator of amount, so pick the one that measures it.

steps.detail: Best indicator of how much.
Edema and blood pressure do not give a quantity.
Weight captures all fluid; intake and output captures only what was recorded.

elimination.verdict: The matched daily weight.

questions.objective: fluid overload

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure and fluid overload has four findings on the morning assessment. Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: New crackles in both bases, respiratory rate 26 per minute
options.rationale: The priority in fluid overload is preventing pulmonary edema. New crackles with fast breathing mean fluid is entering the lungs.

options.text: Pitting edema of 2+ in both ankles, present since admission
options.rationale: Edema needs skin care and tracking. It has been present since admission and does not threaten breathing.

options.text: Weight gain of 1 kg since yesterday morning, on the same scale
options.rationale: This confirms he is still retaining fluid and belongs in the report. The lungs show where that fluid is doing harm.

options.text: An enlarged liver edge felt below the right ribs
options.rationale: Liver enlargement is a finding of overload and is followed over days, not minutes.

questions.takeaway: In fluid overload the priority is preventing pulmonary edema, so new crackles and a rising respiratory rate come first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four belong to overload. Rank them by which one threatens breathing and which one is new.

steps.detail: Only one option involves the lungs.
The crackles are new; the edema dates from admission.
It measures the problem but is not the danger itself.

elimination.verdict: New crackles with a rate of 26.

questions.objective: fluid overload

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure has gained 2.8 kg in 2 days and has crackles in both bases, distended neck veins and a bounding pulse. A scheduled loop diuretic is due now. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Reweigh him on the same scale to confirm the gain before the dose
options.rationale: Checking a weight is good practice when it stands alone. Here crackles, neck veins and pulse already confirm it, so reweighing only delays treatment.

options.text: Hold the dose and tighten his fluid restriction until tomorrow's weight
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is part of the plan, but it removes nothing already retained, and his lungs are filling now.

options.text: Repeat the lung and neck vein assessment in 30 minutes, then decide
options.rationale: Assessing before acting is the usual rule. The assessment is already complete and consistent, so repeating it adds no new information.

options.text: Give the loop diuretic now and track his urine output and lung sounds
options.rationale: The data are complete and all point to overload, and the treatment is already prescribed and due. Acting now protects against pulmonary edema.

questions.takeaway: When the assessment is complete and the prescribed treatment is due, give it. More assessment is a delay, not caution.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Count what the stem already gives: weight, lungs, neck veins and pulse. Then ask whether another check would change the decision.

steps.detail: Four findings agree on overload.
A reweigh or repeat check would not change the plan.
It limits new intake and leaves the lungs wet.

elimination.verdict: Give the scheduled loop diuretic now.

questions.objective: fluid overload

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure received a loop diuretic 4 hours ago for fluid overload. Which findings tell the nurse the overload is getting worse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Urine output of 15 mL per hour for the past 2 hours
options.rationale: A diuretic should raise output. Decreased urine output is one of the findings to watch for in overload.

options.text: Crackles now heard halfway up both lungs
options.rationale: Crackles are a watch-for finding, and spreading crackles mean he is moving toward pulmonary edema.

options.text: Neck veins more distended than at the last check
options.rationale: Increasing neck vein distention shows rising volume in the vessels.

options.text: Radial pulse more bounding than it was 4 hours ago
options.rationale: A bounding pulse reflects excess volume, and a stronger one means more of it.

options.text: Weight 0.6 kg lower than this morning on the same scale
options.rationale: Weight loss after a diuretic means fluid is leaving, which is the goal.

options.text: Dry mouth and thirst while on his fluid restriction
options.rationale: An expected discomfort of restriction. Offer mouth care; it does not signal worsening overload.

questions.takeaway: After a diuretic, watch for a bounding pulse, more neck vein distention, crackles and falling urine output. Any of them means the overload is winning.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each finding separately against one question: does this show more fluid in the vessels and lungs, or less?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pulse, neck veins, crackles and urine output.
Down 0.6 kg is improvement.
Thirst on restriction is expected.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: fluid overload

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with SIADH has serum sodium of 124 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145). The nurse notes four findings on the morning assessment. Which finding does the nurse report first?

options.text: Weight 2 kg higher than 3 days ago on the same scale
options.rationale: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of how much water she has retained. It measures the cause, and the brain shows where that water is doing harm.

options.text: New confusion about where she is, with a headache
options.rationale: Low sodium moves water into cells, and the brain sits in a rigid skull with little room to swell. New confusion is a cerebral change, and seizures and coma come next.

options.text: Generalized weakness with decreased deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: These are neuromuscular findings of hyponatremia and call for fall precautions. They do not signal rising pressure inside the skull.

options.text: A bounding radial pulse at 88 per minute
options.rationale: A bounding pulse fits hyponatremia with excess water and confirms her volume status. It is expected with SIADH and is not the most dangerous finding.

questions.takeaway: The brain is the organ most sensitive to sodium imbalance because the skull leaves no room for swelling. In hyponatremia a new cerebral change outranks weight, pulse and reflex findings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four findings belong to hyponatremia with excess water. Rank them by which one shows the brain is being affected.

steps.detail: Weight gain and a bounding pulse describe her water excess.
Weakness and low reflexes are a fall risk, not a brain finding.
New confusion with a headache.

elimination.verdict: Report the new confusion and headache.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with SIADH and serum sodium of 124 mEq/L is on fluid restriction. Assistive personnel report scant, dark urine and ask to encourage water. How does the nurse direct them?

options.text: Offer 240 mL of water each hour until her urine lightens
options.rationale: Dark, scant urine usually calls for more fluid in dehydration. Hers comes from excess ADH, and more water lowers her sodium further.

options.text: Offer water freely and add salt to her meal trays
options.rationale: Oral sodium is used in mild cases along with restriction. Free water cancels the restriction that treats her.

options.text: Hold all fluids by mouth until her urine output increases
options.rationale: Limiting fluid is the right direction, but a restriction is a prescribed daily amount, not nothing by mouth. Urine output is also the wrong target while ADH is holding water.

options.text: Keep the restriction, since excess ADH is holding water
options.rationale: ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water, so in SIADH concentrated urine is expected and does not mean she needs fluid.

questions.takeaway: ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water. In SIADH, dark scant urine is the hormone at work, so the fluid restriction stays.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The same urine finding means opposite things in dehydration and in SIADH. Let the diagnosis and the sodium decide, not the urine color.

steps.detail: Two options add water, and one removes all of it.
124 mEq/L from retained water gets worse with more water.
ADH is causing the concentration.

elimination.verdict: Keep the restriction.

questions.objective: hormonal regulation of fluid balance

questions.scenario: A 54-year-old woman with SIADH has gained 2 kg in 3 days. Serum sodium is 124 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145). Her pulse is bounding, she has a headache and she is slow to answer questions.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Maintain the prescribed fluid restriction
options.rationale: Her sodium is low because of extra water, so limiting water is the treatment.

options.text: Give the prescribed vasopressin antagonist
options.rationale: This drug class is used for hyponatremia with fluid excess and for SIADH.

options.text: Infuse 0.45% sodium chloride as replacement
options.rationale: A hypotonic solution pushes water into cells. Her brain cells are already taking on water.

options.text: Encourage a glass of water every hour
options.rationale: Right for a client who is dry. She has retained water, and more of it dilutes her sodium further.

options.text: Dilutional hyponatremia from retained water
options.rationale: SIADH, a 2 kg gain and a bounding pulse with sodium of 124 mEq/L mean water excess.

options.text: Hyponatremia from sodium loss with fluid deficit
options.rationale: The sodium fits, but a deficit gives a thready pulse and weight loss. She has the opposite.

options.text: Hypernatremia from water loss
options.rationale: Her sodium is below 135 mEq/L, not above 145.

options.text: Isotonic dehydration
options.rationale: She has gained weight and her pulse is bounding, which is excess, not loss.

options.text: Level of consciousness
options.rationale: Headache and slow responses are cerebral changes. Confusion, seizures and coma are what follow if it worsens.

options.text: Serum sodium trend
options.rationale: Shows whether restriction and the drug are raising the level.

options.text: Hematocrit for hemoconcentration
options.rationale: Hemoconcentration is a dehydration finding. She has too much water.

options.text: Skin tenting over the sternum
options.rationale: Tenting is a sign of fluid deficit and would not be expected with a 2 kg gain.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium with weight gain and a bounding pulse is a water problem. Remove water, and watch the sodium and the brain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Settle the condition first from the pulse and the weight. The actions and parameters for a fluid deficit are offered as distractors.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sodium 124 mEq/L with gain and a bounding pulse means dilution.
Restriction and a vasopressin antagonist.
Sodium level and level of consciousness.

elimination.verdict: Dilutional hyponatremia; restriction and vasopressin antagonist; consciousness and sodium trend.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with SIADH had serum sodium of 124 mEq/L and slow responses. After 24 hours of fluid restriction and a vasopressin antagonist, which finding best shows the treatment is working?

options.text: Sodium 130 mEq/L, and she answers questions promptly
options.rationale: The level is rising toward 135 to 145 mEq/L and the cerebral change has cleared. Both the lab and the brain show improvement.

options.text: Weight down 0.5 kg, sodium 124 mEq/L, still slow to answer
options.rationale: Weight loss means water is starting to leave, which is the right direction. The sodium and her thinking, the two things that defined the problem, have not changed yet.

options.text: Weight up 0.5 kg, with a pulse that remains bounding
options.rationale: More weight and a bounding pulse mean she is still retaining water.

options.text: Urine output of 20 mL per hour, dark amber in color
options.rationale: Scant, concentrated urine shows her kidneys are still holding water, which is the problem being treated.

questions.takeaway: Treatment of dilutional hyponatremia is working when the sodium rises toward 135 mEq/L and the cerebral changes clear.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that shows change in the two things that defined her problem at the start: the sodium and her thinking.

steps.detail: Sodium 124 mEq/L and slow responses.
Weight gain, bounding pulse and scant dark urine.
130 has risen; 124 has not.

elimination.verdict: Sodium 130 mEq/L with prompt answers.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man has had fever and poor intake for 4 days. He is agitated with muscle twitching, and serum sodium is 156 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145). Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride IV by infusion pump
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is for severe hyponatremia. It would raise a sodium that is already high.

options.text: Fluid restriction of 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restriction treats sodium that is low from excess water. He has lost water and needs it replaced.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride IV by infusion pump
options.rationale: The goal in hypernatremia is to replace free water and lower sodium gradually. A hypotonic fluid on a pump does both, with sodium levels rechecked as it runs.

options.text: A loop diuretic IV to increase his sodium excretion
options.rationale: A diuretic is used when hypernatremia is kidney related. His comes from fever and poor intake, and a diuretic removes more water.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia from water loss is treated by replacing free water with isotonic or hypotonic fluid and lowering sodium gradually.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Fever plus poor intake tells you how the sodium got high: water left. Choose the order that puts water back under control.

steps.detail: Four days of fever and poor intake means water loss.
3% saline and fluid restriction.

steps.action: Match the diuretic to its use
steps.detail: Kidney related cases only.

elimination.verdict: Hypotonic saline by pump.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with serum sodium of 156 mEq/L began hypotonic IV fluid 4 hours ago for agitation and twitching. Sodium is now 141 mEq/L, and he has a new headache and is hard to rouse. Which judgment guides the nurse?

options.text: Sodium is in range and he is resting after agitation, so continue the rate
options.rationale: A value of 141 mEq/L looks like success. A fall of 15 mEq/L in 4 hours is not gradual, and a headache with poor arousal is not rest.

options.text: Sodium fell too fast and his brain is swelling, so slow the fluid and report
options.rationale: Rapid correction of hypernatremia causes cerebral edema. A steep fall with new headache and poor arousal fits, so the rate comes down and the provider hears now.

options.text: Lethargy means the hypernatremia is progressing, so request a faster rate
options.rationale: Hypernatremia does progress from agitation to lethargy and coma. That needs a high or rising sodium, and his is 141 mEq/L and falling fast.

options.text: One value may be a lab error, so reassess him in 1 hour
options.rationale: A repeat level is reasonable. Waiting an hour while fluid runs at the same rate lets swelling continue.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia is lowered gradually. A rapid fall with new neurologic change means cerebral edema until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Lethargy can mean worsening hypernatremia or overcorrection. The sodium value and the speed of its fall tell you which.

steps.detail: 156 to 141 mEq/L in 4 hours.
Progression needs a high sodium; his is now in range.
New headache and poor arousal are brain findings.

elimination.verdict: Too fast: slow the fluid and report.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man is returning to a care facility after treatment for hypernatremia caused by fever and poor intake. Which instruction to facility staff best prevents a recurrence?

options.text: Remind him to drink whenever he feels thirsty
options.rationale: Drinking is the right goal. The thirst reflex is diminished in older adults, so a plan that depends on thirst fails.

options.text: Restrict the sodium in his meals and weigh him once each month
options.rationale: Sodium restriction is used if needed, but his problem was water loss, and a monthly weight cannot catch a deficit that develops over days.

options.text: Check skin turgor on the backs of his hands every shift
options.rationale: Regular checks are a good idea. In older adults turgor is assessed at the sternum, and checking finds a deficit without preventing it.

options.text: Offer him water at set times without waiting for a request
options.rationale: Increasing water intake is the key measure for older adults. Scheduled offers replace the thirst signal that no longer prompts drinking.

questions.takeaway: Older adults have a diminished thirst reflex, so water is offered on a schedule instead of waiting for them to ask.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options contain a sensible idea with one detail that fails in an older adult. Find the option with no such detail.

steps.detail: Thirst is diminished at 79.
Hand turgor is the wrong site and monthly weights are too far apart.

steps.action: Keep the plan that supplies water
steps.detail: Scheduled offers.

elimination.verdict: Offer water on a schedule.

questions.objective: older adult risks

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man had large burns 12 hours ago. He has generalized swelling, weight unchanged from admission, heart rate of 124 per minute and blood pressure of 92/56. Assistive personnel say he has too much fluid. Which judgment is correct?

options.text: Swelling shows fluid overload, so he needs fluid and sodium restriction
options.rationale: Swelling does occur in overload, but overload gives a bounding pulse and high blood pressure. He has a fast heart rate and low pressure.

options.text: Plasma has shifted into his tissues, so his vessels are short of fluid
options.rationale: In vascular dehydration fluid moves from plasma to the interstitial space with no true water loss. That explains swelling, unchanged weight and low pressure together.

options.text: His unchanged weight shows that his fluid balance needs no action
options.rationale: Weight is unchanged because the fluid is still in the body. It is in the wrong compartment, and his pressure shows it.

options.text: Water has moved into his cells, so hypertonic saline should draw it out
options.rationale: Hypertonic fluid does pull water out of cells. His fluid is in the interstitial space, not in the cells.

questions.takeaway: Swelling with low blood pressure and a fast pulse means fluid has left the plasma for the tissues. The vessels are depleted even though the weight has not changed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Swelling appears in overload and in a plasma shift. The pulse and blood pressure tell you which compartment is short.

steps.detail: Heart rate 124 with 92/56 means low vascular volume.
No water has left the body.
Interstitial space, not cells.

elimination.verdict: A plasma to tissue shift with depleted vessels.

questions.objective: fluid compartments and water movement

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with burns has blood pressure of 92/56 and concentrated urine at 18 mL per hour. A new nurse asks whether to request a diuretic to raise his output. Which reply is correct?

options.text: Yes, a loop diuretic will keep his kidneys working while pressure is low
options.rationale: A loop diuretic does raise urine output. It does so by removing volume that he does not have.

options.text: Yes, but only if the output stays this low for a full 24 hours
options.rationale: Waiting does not change the reasoning. The low output comes from low volume at any hour.

options.text: No, low volume has triggered ADH and RAAS, so replacing fluid raises output
options.rationale: Low volume and low blood pressure trigger ADH and the renin system, which conserve water and cut urine output. Restoring volume removes the trigger.

options.text: No, natriuretic peptides are holding sodium, so restrict his sodium instead
options.rationale: Natriuretic peptides are released with high volume and make the body excrete sodium and water. Neither part fits him.

questions.takeaway: Low volume triggers ADH and RAAS, which cut urine output on purpose. The fix is fluid, not a diuretic.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Low urine output is a response here, not the disease. Find the option that treats what set the response off.

steps.detail: Blood pressure of 92/56 after burns.
A diuretic removes volume he lacks.

steps.action: Check the hormone in each no answer
steps.detail: ADH and RAAS conserve; natriuretic peptides excrete.

elimination.verdict: No diuretic. Replace fluid.

questions.objective: hormonal regulation of fluid balance

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with burns has blood pressure of 92/56 and urine output of 18 mL per hour from a plasma to tissue fluid shift. Albumin is infused. Which finding 2 hours later shows it did its job?

options.text: Blood pressure 108/66 and urine output 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: A colloid raises oncotic pressure, keeps water in the vessels and expands plasma volume. Better pressure and more urine show the plasma has filled.

options.text: Weight unchanged from the value recorded before the infusion
options.rationale: A plasma shift involves no true water loss, so weight does not track it in either direction.

options.text: He reports that his thirst has eased
options.rationale: Easier thirst is welcome, but it is a report and does not measure plasma volume.

options.text: Hematocrit has risen from 50% to 54%
options.rationale: A rising hematocrit means more hemoconcentration, so plasma volume is still falling.

questions.takeaway: A colloid holds water in the vessels and expands plasma. Judge it by blood pressure and urine output, not by weight.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Ask what albumin is meant to change, then look for a measurement of that compartment.

steps.detail: Plasma volume.
Weight and thirst.
Up means more concentrated.

elimination.verdict: Higher blood pressure and urine output.

questions.objective: dehydration

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with 4 days of vomiting has serum sodium of 118 mEq/L and has just had a seizure. 3% sodium chloride is prescribed, but the bag delivered is 0.45% sodium chloride. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Hang the delivered bag now, since any saline replaces her lost sodium
options.rationale: She did lose sodium. A 0.45% solution is hypotonic, so it adds more water than her serum can take.

options.text: Run the delivered bag slowly until the 3% bag arrives
options.rationale: A slow rate limits the dose but keeps the direction wrong: hypotonic fluid still moves water into cells.

options.text: Give oral sodium with sips of water while waiting for pharmacy
options.rationale: Oral sodium is for mild cases. She has just had a seizure and has been vomiting.

options.text: Withhold it, since hypotonic fluid swells brain cells
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells and hypertonic fluid pulls it out. After a seizure with a sodium of 118 mEq/L she needs the prescribed 3% solution, so the nurse obtains it.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells and hypertonic fluid pulls it out. In severe hyponatremia the tonicity of the bag is the treatment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The two bags are both saline and move water in opposite directions. Decide which direction her brain needs.

steps.detail: 0.45% is hypotonic; 3% is hypertonic.
Two options infuse the hypotonic bag.
Unsafe after a seizure with vomiting.

elimination.verdict: Do not hang the hypotonic bag.

questions.objective: fluid compartments and water movement

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman who takes a diuretic has vomited for 4 days. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145). Her pulse is 112 per minute and thready, and her blood pressure falls on standing. Which prescription fits?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV infusion
options.rationale: Vomiting and a diuretic cause actual sodium loss, and a thready pulse with a drop on standing shows a fluid deficit. Hyponatremia with deficit is treated with IV saline.

options.text: Fluid restriction of 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restriction is a standard hyponatremia treatment when water is in excess. She is volume depleted, and restriction would deepen the deficit.

options.text: A vasopressin antagonist by mouth once daily
options.rationale: This class treats hyponatremia with fluid excess. It makes her lose more water, and she is vomiting.

options.text: Sodium tablets with a modest fluid restriction
options.rationale: This is the plan for mild cases. Four days of vomiting and a falling blood pressure are not mild, and the restriction part harms her.

questions.takeaway: Determine the cause first. Low sodium with a fluid deficit gets IV saline; low sodium with fluid excess gets restriction.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Saline and restriction are both correct for hyponatremia in different clients. The pulse quality and standing blood pressure tell you which client this is.

steps.detail: Thready pulse and a drop on standing mean deficit.
Restriction and a vasopressin antagonist.
Vomiting and restriction both rule it out.

elimination.verdict: IV 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with vomiting had serum sodium of 126 mEq/L and a thready pulse. After 12 hours of IV saline, sodium is 131 mEq/L, her pulse is 84 per minute and strong, and she is oriented. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Request 3% sodium chloride to reach 135 mEq/L sooner
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is for severe or emergency hyponatremia. She is oriented and improving on the current fluid.

options.text: Begin a fluid restriction because sodium is still below 135 mEq/L
options.rationale: Restriction treats low sodium from excess water. Hers came with a deficit that saline is correcting.

options.text: Continue the current infusion with sodium and neurologic checks
options.rationale: Sodium, pulse and orientation all show the plan is working. The correct action is to keep it going and keep watching.

options.text: Request a vasopressin antagonist to finish the correction
options.rationale: That class is for hyponatremia with fluid excess, which she does not have.

questions.takeaway: When the sodium, the pulse and the mental status are all improving, continue the plan and keep monitoring. Do not escalate a treatment that is working.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: The sodium is still under 135 mEq/L, which tempts a change. Check the direction of every value before changing anything.

steps.detail: 126 to 131 mEq/L, pulse strong, oriented.
Three change the treatment and one keeps it.

steps.action: Match each change to its use
steps.detail: Severe cases, or fluid excess.

elimination.verdict: Continue the infusion and the checks.

questions.objective: sodium imbalances

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with right-sided heart failure has 3+ pitting edema in both legs. A new nurse suggests requesting albumin to pull the fluid back into his vessels. Which reply is correct?

options.text: Yes, albumin holds water in plasma, which is what his legs need
options.rationale: Albumin does hold water in plasma. His edema is not caused by too little plasma, so the remedy does not match the cause.

options.text: No, high capillary pressure pushes fluid out, and plasma adds to it
options.rationale: Right-sided heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, and filtration moves fluid from high pressure to low. Expanding plasma raises that pressure further.

options.text: No, his edema is water inside cells, so hypertonic saline fits better
options.rationale: Pitting edema is fluid in the interstitial space, not in the cells. Hypertonic saline also adds sodium to a client who is retaining fluid.

options.text: Yes, but only once his daily weight has been recorded
options.rationale: Timing the weight does not change whether the treatment suits the cause.

questions.takeaway: Edema in right-sided heart failure comes from high capillary hydrostatic pressure. Adding plasma volume makes it worse.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: A colloid fixes edema caused by a plasma shift. Ask what is driving this client's edema before borrowing that treatment.

steps.detail: High pressure in the capillaries from the failing right heart.
More plasma volume, more pressure.
Pitting edema is interstitial.

elimination.verdict: No. The cause is pressure, not low plasma.

questions.objective: fluid compartments and water movement

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with heart failure weighed 82.0 kg at 0600 yesterday on the bed scale in a gown. Today assistive personnel report 84.1 kg at 1100 on a standing scale, fully dressed. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Assess his lungs and neck veins, and standardize tomorrow's weight
options.rationale: Daily weights count only at the same time, on the same scale, in the same clothing. Until a valid weight exists, direct assessment shows whether he is retaining fluid.

options.text: Record a 2.1 kg gain and request an extra dose of loop diuretic
options.rationale: A true 2.1 kg gain would need action. This value differs in time, scale and clothing, so it cannot support a drug request.

options.text: Subtract 1 kg for his clothing, then chart the adjusted figure as today's weight
options.rationale: An estimate corrects one of three differences and creates a number nobody measured.

options.text: Stop weighing this client and follow his intake and output only
options.rationale: Intake and output helps, but rapid weight gain is the best indicator of overload and should not be dropped.

questions.takeaway: A daily weight is valid only at the same time, on the same scale, in the same clothing. If it is not, assess the client directly and fix the routine.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Before acting on a number, check how it was obtained. Three conditions changed between the two weights.

steps.detail: Time, scale and clothing all differ.
A diuretic request or an estimate both treat it as real.
Correct the weighing instead of abandoning it.

elimination.verdict: Assess now and standardize the weights.

questions.objective: fluid overload

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with heart failure has lost 3 kg in 2 days on a loop diuretic. Blood pressure is 88/54, pulse is thready, lungs are clear, and urine output fell to 20 mL per hour. Which judgment guides the nurse?

options.text: Falling output shows the overload is worsening, so give the next dose early
options.rationale: Decreased urine output is a warning sign in overload. Overload brings crackles and a bounding pulse, and his lungs are clear and his pulse is thready.

options.text: Natriuretic peptides are lowering his output, so restrict his sodium further
options.rationale: Natriuretic peptides respond to high volume and increase sodium and water excretion. His volume is low and his output is down.

options.text: Low pressure has triggered RAAS to conserve water, so hold the dose and report
options.rationale: Low blood pressure and low volume trigger renin, and angiotensin II decreases urine output. With a 3 kg loss and a thready pulse, he now has a deficit.

options.text: Lower output is expected after diuresis, so continue the dose and recheck tomorrow
options.rationale: Output does settle after a diuretic acts. A pressure of 88/54 with a thready pulse is not an expected endpoint.

questions.takeaway: Low urine output means overload only if the other signs agree. With low blood pressure, a thready pulse and weight loss, it is RAAS responding to a deficit.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Falling urine output appears in overload and in deficit. Use the lungs, the pulse and the weight trend to decide which.

steps.detail: Down 3 kg, 88/54, thready pulse, clear lungs.
No crackles and no bounding pulse.
Low pressure triggers renin and the kidneys conserve.

elimination.verdict: Deficit with RAAS active: hold the diuretic and report.

questions.objective: hormonal regulation of fluid balance

questions.stem: A 78-year-old on day 5 of contact isolation and bed rest, in a windowless room with no visitors, is newly bored, tearful and unsure of the date. Which problem best explains these cues?

options.text: Sensory overload from the constant hospital routine and care
options.rationale: Overload also causes confusion, but it comes from too much stimulation. This room has almost none.

options.text: Sensory deprivation from the restricted room
options.rationale: Isolation and bed rest are the common settings. Boredom, tearfulness and disorientation are its affective and cognitive effects.

options.text: A sensory deficit that was missed on admission
options.rationale: A deficit is a loss of vision or hearing. The stem gives no cue of either.

options.text: An expected change of aging in a person of 78
options.rationale: New changes over 5 days are not assumed to be age related.

questions.takeaway: Isolation, bed rest and restricted rooms cause deprivation: boredom, depression, confusion and disorientation. Look at the amount of stimulation in the room before naming the problem.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Confusion appears in both deprivation and overload. The setting decides it: count the stimuli.

steps.detail: Windowless, no visitors, bed rest, 5 days. Too little input.
Overload needs excess stimulation, which is absent.
New over 5 days is not aging.

elimination.verdict: Sensory deprivation. The setting gives too little meaningful stimulation.

questions.objective: normal sensation and types of sensory alteration

questions.stem: A 78-year-old on bed rest in contact isolation for 5 days has become bored, tearful and disoriented to the date. Which change to the plan of care best targets the cause of these cues?

options.text: Reorient the client to the date once every shift
options.rationale: Reorienting treats the result. The room still offers nothing meaningful between visits.

options.text: Cluster all care into fewer visits and schedule a daily quiet time
options.rationale: Correct action for the similar problem, sensory overload. Here it would remove even more stimulation.

options.text: Leave the television on through the day and night
options.rationale: Adds noise, not meaning, and constant sound can tip into overload.

options.text: Ask family to bring photos and music, and add a clock
options.rationale: Photos, music and a clock are meaningful stimuli, which are critical for preventing deprivation.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation is fixed with meaningful stimuli: family photos, music, pets, clocks. More noise is not more meaning.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options reduce or ignore stimulation and one adds meaningless stimulation. Only one adds meaning.

steps.detail: Too little meaningful stimulation.
Clustering and quiet time reduce input.
A television is quantity. Photos, music and a clock are meaning.

elimination.verdict: Bring in photos, music and a clock.

questions.objective: factors that affect sensory function

questions.stem: A 78-year-old in contact isolation has had no visitors for 5 days and is withdrawn and tearful. The daughter says gowning is a bother and he 'just sleeps anyway.' Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: 'without visitors he is becoming isolated. let me show you how to gown.'
options.rationale: Absence of visitors leads to isolation, loneliness and depression. This names the effect and removes her barrier.

options.text: 'you can phone the unit each day and we will pass on your messages.'
options.rationale: Keeps her informed, but the client still has no social interaction.

options.text: 'it is safer to wait until isolation ends before you visit again.'
options.rationale: Isolation precautions do not bar visitors who gown, and waiting prolongs the cause.

options.text: 'i will ask the provider whether a drug for his low mood would help him cope.'
options.rationale: Treats the result with a drug before fixing the missing social contact.

questions.takeaway: No visitors means isolation, loneliness and depression. Remove the barrier to visiting before reaching for anything else.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask which response puts a person back in the room with the client.

steps.detail: Social interaction is missing.
A phone message to staff and a drug do not replace a visitor.
Waiting extends the cause.

elimination.verdict: Explain the effect and teach her to gown.

questions.objective: factors that affect sensory function

questions.stem: A 78-year-old on bed rest in contact isolation was bored, tearful and unsure of the date. After 2 days of family visits, music and a bedside clock, which finding best shows the sensory deprivation is resolving?

options.text: The family says the visits are going well for them
options.rationale: A family outcome. It says nothing about the client's thinking or mood.

options.text: The client sleeps most of the day and seldom uses the call bell
options.rationale: Quiet is not recovery. Long sleep can be continued withdrawal.

options.text: The client states the correct date and asks about a grandchild
options.rationale: Orientation and interest have returned, the cognitive and affective effects that were present.

options.text: The client says the music is nice but still asks what month it is
options.rationale: Accepts the stimulus, yet the disorientation remains.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the cues you started with. Deprivation showed as disorientation and low mood, so resolution is orientation and interest.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Match each option to the original three cues: bored, tearful, unsure of the date.

steps.detail: Bored, tearful, disoriented to date.
The family's view is not the client's outcome.
Sleeping and not calling can be withdrawal.

elimination.verdict: Correct date and interest in family.

questions.objective: normal sensation and types of sensory alteration

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on day 3 in intensive care, with alarms, hourly checks and constant lighting, is restless, has scattered attention and keeps playing with the IV tubing. Pain is 2 of 10. Which problem do these cues suggest?

options.text: Sensory overload
options.rationale: Excess stimulation the brain cannot filter. Restlessness, scattered attention and playing with tubes are its listed effects, and intensive care is a common setting.

options.text: Sensory deprivation
options.rationale: Also alters thinking, but it needs too little stimulation. This room has alarms, checks and light around the clock.

options.text: Uncontrolled pain
options.rationale: Chronic pain can add to overload, but 2 of 10 does not explain this behavior.

options.text: A sensory deficit
options.rationale: A deficit is lost vision or hearing. No cue in the stem points to either.

questions.takeaway: Overload: racing thoughts, scattered attention, restlessness, anxiety, playing with tubes and dressings. Common in intensive care and emergency settings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Count the stimuli first. Alarms, hourly checks and constant light are too much, not too little.

steps.detail: Alarms, hourly checks, constant light.
Deprivation needs too little input.
Pain 2 of 10 is not the driver.

elimination.verdict: Sensory overload.

questions.objective: normal sensation and types of sensory alteration

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old on day 3 in the intensive care unit is restless, has scattered attention and plays with the dressing and IV tubing. Staff enter about every 20 minutes for separate tasks, and lights and alarms stay on overnight.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.

rows.text: Combine vital signs, drug doses and dressing care into one visit
rows.rationale: Combining activities cuts the number of interruptions.

rows.text: Schedule rest periods and a quiet time each afternoon
rows.rationale: Scheduled rest and quiet time are the slide's measures for controlling stimuli.

rows.text: Leave the television on so the room feels less clinical
rows.rationale: Adds one more stimulus to a brain that already cannot filter.

rows.text: Keep the call bell within reach
rows.rationale: A listed safety measure that adds no stimulation.

rows.text: Apply wrist restraints to protect the tubing
rows.rationale: Not the least restrictive choice. Lower the stimulation that drives the behavior first.

rows.text: Reorient the client during each combined visit and keep objects in the same places
rows.rationale: Frequent reorientation and consistent object placement are acute care measures.

questions.takeaway: Control overload by combining activities, scheduling rest and quiet time, reorienting, and keeping the call bell close. Do not add stimuli or restrain first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask of each row: does this lower the number of stimuli or keep the client safe without adding any?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Entries every 20 minutes plus overnight light and alarms: overload.
Combined care, rest, quiet time, reorientation, call bell.
Television and wrist restraints.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: r1, r2, r4, r6. Not indicated: r3, r5.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A 66-year-old in intensive care is restless and misreads staff who approach the bed. Alarm volume is already lowered and care is already combined. The client's glasses and both hearing aids are in a bedside drawer. Which action is best next?

options.text: Close the door and darken the room for a longer quiet time
options.rationale: Defensible for overload, but stimuli are already reduced, and more reduction risks deprivation while the deficits stay uncorrected.

options.text: Put the glasses and both hearing aids on the client
options.rationale: Clients often have more than one alteration. Without the devices the remaining stimuli arrive distorted, and the devices must be accessible, not in a drawer.

options.text: Reorient the client to place and staff every hour
options.rationale: Right action, but spoken reorientation is poorly received by a client who cannot see or hear clearly.

options.text: Arrange for a staff member to sit at the bedside
options.rationale: Adds a person the client may also misread, and does not correct the cause.

questions.takeaway: Clients often have more than one alteration. When overload measures are in place and the client still misreads the room, check that glasses and hearing aids are on and working.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem says the overload measures are done. The one new cue is the drawer.

steps.detail: Alarms lowered, care combined.
Glasses and hearing aids are in a drawer.
Reorientation works only after the client can see and hear.

elimination.verdict: Put on the glasses and hearing aids.

questions.objective: normal sensation and types of sensory alteration

questions.stem: A nurse started an afternoon quiet time and combined care for a 66-year-old in intensive care who was restless and playing with tubing. Which finding 4 hours later best shows the plan is working?

options.text: The client lies still and does not respond when spoken to
options.rationale: Stillness with no response is a new change that needs assessment, not a goal.

options.text: The client asks the time at every visit and then forgets the answer given
options.rationale: Constant reorientation is still needed, which is an effect of overload.

options.text: The client's hands are quiet while a staff member holds them
options.rationale: The behavior is being blocked by a person, not resolved.

options.text: The client rests, leaves the tubing alone and follows conversation
options.rationale: Restlessness and tube handling have eased, and the client still responds to people.

questions.takeaway: Overload is resolving when restlessness and tube handling ease and the client stays responsive.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A quiet client is not automatically a better client. Check that the client still responds.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Restless, playing with tubing.
No response to speech is a new problem.
Repeated time questions and held hands show the problem remains.

elimination.verdict: Rests, leaves tubing alone, follows conversation.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: During admission an 81-year-old gives answers that do not match the questions and nods at everything. The daughter says the client was sharp at home yesterday. Which assessment comes first?

options.text: Ask the daughter if the client uses hearing aids and has them
options.rationale: Establish the baseline: know whether a deficit already exists and whether the device is here and working before judging cognition.

options.text: Complete a full mental status examination with standard questions
options.rationale: A correct assessment at the wrong time. The result is not valid if the client cannot hear the questions.

options.text: Orient the client to the room, the bathroom and the call bell
options.rationale: A needed action, but teaching will not land until the communication barrier is known.

options.text: Review the drug list for agents that cloud thinking
options.rationale: Reasonable later. The mismatched answers with a sharp baseline point to hearing first.

questions.takeaway: In acute care, establish the baseline: does the client already have a deficit, and are glasses or hearing aids present and working? Do this before labeling confusion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are assessments. Pick the one the other depends on.

steps.detail: Mismatched answers, nodding, sharp yesterday.
Mental status testing needs working hearing.
Orientation comes after you know how to communicate.

elimination.verdict: Ask about hearing aids first.

questions.objective: assessing sensory deficits and safety risks

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with hearing loss in both ears cannot follow teaching about a new drug. The nurse is standing at the foot of the bed while writing notes and talking. Which change is best?

options.text: Speak much louder and closer to one ear
options.rationale: Shouting is to be avoided, and it takes the nurse's face out of view.

options.text: Face the client, speak slowly, and add written information
options.rationale: The slide's strategy for hearing loss: face to face, slow clear speech, written information, no shouting.

options.text: Leave the written sheet for the client to read later
options.rationale: Written information is right, but alone it gives no chance to check understanding.

options.text: Teach the daughter and ask her to explain it to the client at home
options.rationale: Bypasses the client instead of adapting the communication.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss: face to face, slow and clear, written information, no shouting.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: One option combines the parts that the others use alone or get wrong.

steps.detail: The nurse is not facing the client.
Louder is not clearer.
Face, pace and writing together.
