elimination.verdict: Face the client, slow clear speech, written information.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: An 81-year-old says the right hearing aid has made no sound since morning. It is switched on and seated in the right ear. Which check should the nurse make first?

options.text: Rinse the aid under warm running water to clear it
options.rationale: Cleaning is the right idea with the wrong method. Water damages a hearing aid.

options.text: Turn the volume to its highest setting
options.rationale: Volume does nothing if the aid has no power or the opening is blocked.

options.text: Check the battery and look for wax in the opening
options.rationale: The two common, fixable reasons an aid goes silent. This confirms whether the device is functional.

options.text: Send the aid home and use written notes instead
options.rationale: Written notes help, but giving up the device before a simple check reduces the client's communication.

questions.takeaway: Part of sensory assessment is whether the device works. A silent hearing aid: check the battery and look for wax before anything else, and keep it dry.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Start with the simplest cause you can fix at the bedside.

steps.detail: On and seated, so placement is not the issue.
Water damages the aid.
Check before replacing the device with notes.

elimination.verdict: Battery and wax.

questions.objective: assessing sensory deficits and safety risks

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with long standing hearing loss followed conversation with hearing aids on admission. On day 3, in a quiet private room with both aids working, the client cannot. Which chart item most needs follow up?

options.text: The client's age of 81
options.rationale: Age explains the long standing loss. A change over 3 days is not assumed to be age related.

options.text: A loop diuretic taken daily for the past 10 years
options.rationale: Right idea, wrong timing. Diuretics can be ototoxic, but this one is unchanged for 10 years and hearing was adequate on admission.

options.text: No visitors since admission
options.rationale: Lack of visitors affects mood and thinking, not the ability to hear with working aids.

options.text: An aminoglycoside antibiotic started on admission
options.rationale: Aminoglycosides are ototoxic, and this is the one drug that is new since hearing was last adequate.

questions.takeaway: New or sudden changes are not assumed to be age related. Look for what changed: a newly started ototoxic drug such as an aminoglycoside can impair hearing within days.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options are drugs that can harm hearing. Only one of them is new since admission.

steps.detail: Followed conversation on admission, cannot on day 3.
Age and a diuretic taken for 10 years were the same on admission.
No visitors does not change hearing. The aminoglycoside is new and ototoxic.

elimination.verdict: The aminoglycoside antibiotic.

questions.objective: factors that affect sensory function

questions.stem: An 81-year-old who hears poorly even with both hearing aids in is moved to a new room at 2200 and needs call bell teaching now. The client's reading glasses were left at home. Which approach is best?

options.text: Give a printed instruction sheet and point to each step
options.rationale: Written information is a correct strategy for hearing loss, but this client cannot read it without the glasses.

options.text: Wait until family bring the glasses in the morning
options.rationale: Leaves the client overnight without knowing how to call for help.

options.text: Face the client, speak slowly and watch the client use it
options.rationale: Face to face, slow clear speech is the hearing loss strategy this client can use tonight, and watching confirms the client can call.

options.text: Speak loudly near the client's ear and repeat the steps twice
options.rationale: Shouting is to be avoided, and repeating the steps does not confirm understanding.

questions.takeaway: Pick the communication strategy the client can actually use tonight. Written information helps hearing loss only when the client can read it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Written information and face to face speech are both correct for hearing loss. The missing glasses tip it.

steps.detail: The aids are already in. The reading glasses are not here.
Call bell access is a safety measure for tonight.
Louder is not clearer.

elimination.verdict: Face to face, slow speech, and watch the client use the call bell.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with diabetes and worsening vision in both eyes lives alone and draws up her own insulin. Which assessment tells the nurse most about her safety at home?

options.text: Have her read the insulin label and syringe markings
options.rationale: Functional ability: can she safely do the task she does alone every day? Reading labels is the slide's own example.

options.text: Ask how often family or friends come to the house
options.rationale: Social support matters, but it does not show whether each dose is drawn up correctly.

options.text: Ask her to state the date, the place and her address
options.rationale: Mental status is part of the assessment, yet no cue suggests a thinking problem.

options.text: Ask whether she keeps her glasses where she can find them
options.rationale: Device access is worth knowing, but having glasses does not prove she can read the syringe.

questions.takeaway: Assess functional ability by watching the task: can the client read labels, dress and groom safely? Match the assessment to the highest risk task.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four belong in the assessment. Choose the one tied to the task that can hurt her today.

steps.detail: Poor vision plus self drawn insulin.
Watching her read the syringe beats asking about it.
Support, glasses and orientation come after.

elimination.verdict: Have her read the label and syringe.

questions.objective: assessing sensory deficits and safety risks

questions.stem: On a home visit to a 72-year-old with low vision in both eyes who tripped twice this month, the nurse sees fluorescent tube lights, throw rugs in the hall and plain gray stairs. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Tape the throw rugs down firmly and add more fluorescent tubes
options.rationale: Right targets, wrong fixes. Rugs are removed, and warm incandescent light is preferred to fluorescent.

options.text: Remove the throw rugs and paint the stair edges bright yellow
options.rationale: Clear pathways and sharp contrast on stair edges are the slide's adaptations.

options.text: Fit the brightest bulbs available in every room
options.rationale: More light is not the goal. Brightness is adjusted to reduce glare.

options.text: Move the furniture every few weeks to widen the paths
options.rationale: Objects stay in consistent locations so the space is predictable.

questions.takeaway: Home adaptations: warm incandescent light adjusted to reduce glare, no clutter or throw rugs, bright yellow stair edges, objects in consistent places.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option starts from a real hazard and then applies the wrong fix.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluorescent light, rugs, stairs without contrast.
Tape, more fluorescent, maximum brightness and moving furniture all miss.
Remove rugs, mark stair edges.

elimination.verdict: Remove the rugs and paint the stair edges yellow.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with severe vision loss in both eyes and normal hearing is admitted. Assistive personnel say, 'I talk loudly and slowly so she understands.' Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: 'keep the slow pace and add large written labels on her things.'
options.rationale: Slow speech and written information are strategies for hearing loss, which she does not have.

options.text: 'do her grooming and meal setup for her so she is not injured.'
options.rationale: Takes away independence. The goal is safety while she adapts.

options.text: 'speak normally, and put the call bell wherever is handy each time.'
options.rationale: Normal speech is right, but objects must stay in the same place for a client who cannot see.

options.text: 'speak normally, describe where things are in detail, and let her touch them.'
options.rationale: The slide's strategy for vision loss: speak normally, describe objects in detail, allow touch.

questions.takeaway: Vision loss: speak normally, describe objects in detail, allow touch, keep objects in consistent places. Loud, slow speech belongs to hearing loss.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options start with the right tone. Read to the end of each.

steps.detail: Her hearing is normal.
Slow speech and written labels.
Moving the call bell breaks consistency.

elimination.verdict: Speak normally, describe in detail, allow touch.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A nurse taught home safety to the daughter of a 72-year-old with low vision in both eyes. Which statement by the daughter shows the teaching needs follow up?

options.text: 'we took up the rugs in the hall and the bedroom.'
options.rationale: Correct. Throw rugs are removed.

options.text: 'i painted the edge of each step bright yellow.'
options.rationale: Correct. Sharp contrast marks the stair edges.

options.text: 'each visit i put her kitchen things in better spots.'
options.rationale: Moving objects makes the space unpredictable. Objects stay in consistent locations.

options.text: 'we changed the tube lights to warm bulbs with shades.'
options.rationale: Correct. Warm incandescent light, adjusted to reduce glare.

questions.takeaway: For low vision, consistent beats tidy. Remove clutter once, then keep every object in the same place.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. The helpful sounding one hides the error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the statement that is wrong.
Rugs up, yellow edges, warm shaded light.
'Better spots' means changed spots.

elimination.verdict: Rearranging her kitchen each visit.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with diabetes says print has grown harder to read over several years. She adds that since this morning she cannot see clearly with her right eye. Her yearly eye examination is next month. Which action is best?

options.text: Teach her to use a magnifier and large print labels
options.rationale: Helps the gradual loss. It does nothing about a change that began today.

options.text: Arrange a home safety assessment for this week
options.rationale: Useful for long term risk, but it leaves the new change unreported.

options.text: Tell her to mention the right eye at next month's examination
options.rationale: Screening is right for the gradual change. A change since this morning cannot wait a month.

options.text: Report the change in the right eye to the provider today
options.rationale: New or sudden changes are not assumed to be age related or part of the old problem. Detection and referral are the nurse's role.

questions.takeaway: Gradual change over years goes to routine screening. A new or sudden change is never assumed to be age related: report and refer the same day.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two time frames are in the stem. 'Over several years' and 'since this morning' need different answers.

steps.detail: Years of gradual change, plus a change today.
Screening fits the first, same day referral fits the second.
The new change comes first.

elimination.verdict: Report the right eye change today.

questions.objective: assessing sensory deficits and safety risks

questions.stem: A 69-year-old with aphasia after a stroke understands speech but struggles to produce words. He tries to tell the nurse where his pain is, stops, and grows frustrated. Which action is best?

options.text: Finish his sentences for him to ease the frustration
options.rationale: Guessing replaces his message. The strategy is to listen patiently and allow time.

options.text: Face him and repeat the question slowly in a louder voice
options.rationale: A hearing loss strategy. He already understands the question.

options.text: Offer a communication board and yes or no questions
options.rationale: The slide's strategy for aphasia, with time allowed. It gives him a way to answer without producing words.

options.text: Ask a family member where they think the pain is
options.rationale: Family help find what works, but pain location must come from him.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia: listen patiently, use yes or no questions and communication boards, allow time. Do not answer for the client.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The problem is output, not input. Cut anything that changes how the nurse speaks.

steps.detail: He understands. He cannot produce words.
Louder and slower do not help output.
Finishing sentences and asking family replace his answer.

elimination.verdict: A board, yes or no questions, and time.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A 69-year-old with aphasia understands speech but cannot produce words. He pushes the picture board away. His wife says that at home he draws what he wants. Which action is best?

options.text: Give him paper and a pen and ask his wife what else works
options.rationale: Engage the client and family in finding what works best. Drawing already works for him.

options.text: Keep offering the picture board until he gets used to it
options.rationale: A correct tool for aphasia, but he has refused it and a method that works is being ignored.

options.text: Have his wife answer for him while he is in the hospital
options.rationale: Family help find the method. They do not replace his own answers.

options.text: Write the questions down and have him answer them aloud
options.rationale: Written questions help a hearing problem. His barrier is producing words, which this still demands.

questions.takeaway: No single aphasia tool suits every client. Engage the client and family in finding what works best, then use it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The wife's report is the cue. Pick the option that uses the method he already has.

steps.detail: He rejects the board. He draws at home.
Answering aloud needs the words he cannot produce.
His wife answering replaces his message.

elimination.verdict: Paper and pen, and ask his wife what else works.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A 69-year-old with aphasia after a stroke does not answer when asked his name or the date, and assistive personnel report him as confused. He follows a two step command and points correctly on a picture board. Which action is best?

options.text: Reorient him to person, place and date at every visit
options.rationale: Correct for confusion. Following commands and using the board show he understands, so the barrier is speech.

options.text: Chart that he understands but cannot speak, and keep the board
options.rationale: Separates a speech barrier from a mental status change, using the cues the stem gives.

options.text: Repeat the mental status questions and wait longer for spoken answers
options.rationale: Time helps aphasia, but a test that needs spoken answers still cannot measure his thinking.

options.text: Add a bed alarm and move him to a room near the station
options.rationale: Safety measures for a confused client. The cues do not support confusion.

questions.takeaway: Assess how the client communicates before judging mental status. No spoken answer is not the same as confusion when the client follows commands and uses a board correctly.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Reorienting and reframing are both reasonable. The two step command and correct pointing tip it.

steps.detail: No spoken answers, but correct commands and pointing.
Understanding is intact. Speech is the barrier.
Reorientation and a bed alarm treat a problem he does not show.

elimination.verdict: Chart the speech barrier and keep using the board.

questions.objective: assessing sensory deficits and safety risks

questions.stem: At a workplace screening a 45-year-old machinist says he turns the television up more than last year. He works 10 hours daily beside grinding machines, wearing safety glasses but no ear protection. Which action is best?

options.text: Tell him hearing changes start in the 40s and recheck next year
options.rationale: True that changes begin in the 40s, but a change within a year with noise exposure is not assumed to be age related.

options.text: Teach ear protection at work and refer him for a hearing test
options.rationale: Noise exposure is an occupational factor. The nurse's role is education, detection and referral.

options.text: Advise him to add side shields to his safety glasses
options.rationale: Eye protection is right for flying objects, but he already wears it and the cue is hearing.

options.text: Suggest he keep the television volume low to protect his ears
options.rationale: Treats the result. The grinding machines are the exposure.

questions.takeaway: Occupational noise needs hearing protection. The nurse educates, detects and refers. Do not explain a change away by age when a hazard is present.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: One option names a true fact about age. Check whether it answers a 1 year change with an obvious exposure.

steps.detail: Grinding machines, no ear protection.
A true statement that does not answer the question.
Education and referral together.

elimination.verdict: Ear protection and a hearing test.

questions.objective: factors that affect sensory function

questions.stem: A 45-year-old who now spends 6 hours daily at a computer reports tired, burning eyes by afternoon. An eye examination last month was normal. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Every 2 hours, leave the screen and rest the eyes for a 20 minute break
options.rationale: Right idea with the wrong interval. Two hours is too long between breaks.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, close both eyes tightly for 20 seconds
options.rationale: Right interval and length, wrong action. The eyes need a distant target.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: The 20-20-20 rule for digital eyestrain, exactly as the slides state it.

options.text: Book another eye examination for this month
options.rationale: Screening is important, but the examination was normal last month and the pattern fits screen use.

questions.takeaway: Digital eyestrain: the 20-20-20 rule. Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options use the number 20. Check all three parts: how often, how far, how long.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tired eyes by afternoon with 6 hours of screen work.
Interval, distance, duration.
Normal a month ago.

elimination.verdict: Every 20 minutes, 20 feet, 20 seconds.

questions.objective: interventions for safety and communication

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the health history of a 45-year-old machinist. Which items raise his risk of a sensory alteration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Works 10 hours daily beside grinding machines
options.rationale: Noise exposure is an occupational factor.

options.text: Has had type 2 diabetes for 8 years
options.rationale: Diabetes is a health status factor that raises risk.

options.text: Has hypertension
options.rationale: Hypertension is listed with diabetes as raising risk.

options.text: Started an opioid this week for back pain
options.rationale: Opioids can impair perception.

options.text: Keeps family photos at his workstation
options.rationale: Meaningful stimuli protect against deprivation.

options.text: Eats lunch with coworkers every day
options.rationale: Social interaction protects. Its absence is the risk.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors: age, noise and other occupational hazards, diabetes, hypertension, chronic illness, and ototoxic, psychotropic and opioid drugs. Meaningful stimuli and social contact protect.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort each item into raises risk or protects. Two of these are protective factors written to look like history items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Noise at work.
Diabetes, hypertension, an opioid.
Photos and daily social contact.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: factors that affect sensory function

questions.stem: A 45-year-old machinist says that for 2 days he has felt slowed and has misjudged distances at the grinder. He started an opioid for back pain 2 days ago. His eye examination last month was normal. Which action is best?

options.text: Keep him off the grinder and have the prescriber review the drug
options.rationale: Opioids can impair perception and the change began with the drug. Misjudged distance at a grinder is an injury risk now, so the hazard is removed while the drug is reviewed.

options.text: Refer him for a repeat eye examination this week
options.rationale: Defensible for a visual complaint, but the examination was normal last month, and he stays at the grinder meanwhile.

options.text: Have him report the change to the prescriber at the next routine visit
options.rationale: Right person, wrong time. He keeps misjudging distances at a grinder until then.

options.text: Explain that position sense declines with age and teach extra caution
options.rationale: Proprioceptive changes come after 60. He is 45 and the change is 2 days old.

questions.takeaway: When a new drug changes perception, protect the client from the hazard first and get the drug reviewed. A new change is not assumed to be age related.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options send him to the prescriber. The grinder decides which: one removes the hazard today.

steps.detail: Opioid started 2 days ago, slowed for 2 days, eye examination normal.
Misjudged distances at a grinder.
Only one stops the exposure while the drug is reviewed.

elimination.verdict: Off the grinder, and the prescriber reviews the drug.

questions.objective: factors that affect sensory function

questions.stem: A 72-year-old taking a loop diuretic for heart failure has a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L (reference 3.5 to 5.0). Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Hypoactive bowel sounds and no stool for 2 days
options.rationale: Low potassium slows the gut, so this is expected at 2.9 mEq/L. It needs follow-up, but it is not the first threat.

options.text: Leg weakness with decreased deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Expected skeletal muscle weakness and a fall risk. It ranks below a breathing problem.

options.text: Respirations 10 per minute and shallow
options.rationale: Shallow breathing means the low potassium is severe and the respiratory muscles are weakening. Breathing comes first.

options.text: Flat T waves with a U wave on the monitor
options.rationale: The expected ECG pattern of low potassium. It warns of dysrhythmia, but the breathing is already failing.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium weakens every muscle. When the breathing muscles are involved, that outranks the gut, the legs and an expected ECG pattern.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four findings belong to low potassium. Rank them by airway, breathing, circulation instead of asking which one is abnormal.

steps.detail: Slow gut, weak legs, shallow breathing and a U wave all come from a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L.
Respirations of 10 per minute and shallow is a breathing problem happening now.
A U wave is a warning that keeps the monitor on. It is not yet a dysrhythmia.

elimination.verdict: Shallow respirations at 10 per minute. Breathing first.

questions.objective: low potassium: causes, findings, ECG, safety

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L (reference 3.5 to 5.0) has a prescription for IV potassium 20 mEq diluted in 250 mL of IV fluid through a peripheral catheter. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run it on an infusion pump at no more than 10 mEq per hour
options.rationale: IV potassium is diluted, on a pump, and slow: 5 to 10 mEq per hour.

options.text: Check the IV site every hour and ask about burning or pain
options.rationale: Potassium is a severe tissue irritant, so the site is assessed hourly.

options.text: Keep the cardiac monitor and pulse oximeter on during the infusion
options.rationale: Both low potassium and its replacement can disturb the rhythm, and severe low potassium weakens breathing.

options.text: Run it by gravity, counting drops, until a pump is free
options.rationale: Right drug and right dilution, wrong delivery. Without a pump the rate is not controlled.

options.text: Give the first 5 mEq by slow IV push because the level is below 3.0
options.rationale: A low level never justifies a push. IV push potassium can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: If the catheter fails, give the remaining dose subcutaneously
options.rationale: Potassium is never given subcutaneously or intramuscularly. It destroys tissue.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium is high alert: diluted, on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq per hour, site checked hourly, client monitored. Never push, never IM or subcutaneous.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options sound like ways to solve a practical problem (no pump, very low level, lost access). Each one breaks a rule that has no exception.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pump, rate limit, hourly site check, cardiac monitor and oximeter.
Gravity loses rate control. A push and a subcutaneous dose are never allowed.
A level of 2.9 mEq/L does not change the route or the rate.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C.

questions.objective: IV and oral potassium safety rules

questions.stem: A 72-year-old is receiving diluted IV potassium by pump at 10 mEq per hour through a left forearm catheter. At the hourly check the client reports burning at the site. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Pause the infusion and inspect the site
options.rationale: Burning at a potassium site can mean phlebitis or tissue injury. Pausing stops the irritant while the nurse looks.

options.text: Slow the pump to 5 mEq per hour and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: 5 mEq per hour is within the safe range and may be the eventual plan, but it is chosen before anyone has looked at the vein.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and keep the infusion running
options.rationale: A comfort measure that keeps a tissue irritant flowing into a vein that may be damaged.

options.text: Remove the catheter and give the rest of the dose by mouth
options.rationale: Changes the route without an assessment and without a prescription.

questions.takeaway: Burning during IV potassium is a cue, not a side effect to manage. Pause, look at the site, then decide.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a report of burning and no site assessment. That missing piece tells you an assessment option should win.

steps.detail: The stem says burning. It does not say what the site looks like.

steps.action: Cut the options that continue the infusion unassessed
steps.detail: A slower rate and a warm compress both keep potassium running.

steps.action: Cut the jump to a new route
steps.detail: Removing the catheter and switching to oral skips assessment and needs a prescription.

elimination.verdict: Pause and inspect the site.

questions.objective: IV and oral potassium safety rules

questions.stem: A 72-year-old is receiving IV potassium by pump at 10 mEq per hour. Ectopic beats become frequent, and a potassium drawn 20 minutes ago is 2.8 mEq/L (reference 3.5 to 5.0). The provider says to push 10 mEq now. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the push over 10 minutes while watching the monitor
options.rationale: Going slowly with a monitor sounds careful, but potassium is never given IV push. A bolus can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: Stop the infusion because the ectopic beats began while it ran
options.rationale: Tempting, since a new rhythm during an infusion usually means stop. The potassium is still 2.8 mEq/L, so the low level explains the ectopy and stopping removes the treatment.

options.text: Raise the pump to 20 mEq per hour to correct the level sooner
options.rationale: Uses the pump correctly but doubles the upper limit of 5 to 10 mEq per hour.

options.text: Decline the push, keep the pump running, and ask for another plan
options.rationale: The level of 2.8 mEq/L is the likely source of the ectopy, the infusion is at the safe limit, and a push is never acceptable from anyone.

questions.takeaway: Never push IV potassium, whoever asks. A potassium that is still low explains new ectopy better than a correctly running replacement does.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options protect the client from too much potassium too fast. Read the level again: 2.8 mEq/L means the client still needs the infusion.

steps.action: Apply the rule with no exception
steps.detail: IV push potassium is out, even slowly and even on a verbal order.
20 mEq per hour is above 5 to 10 mEq per hour.
The potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and the rate is within limits, so the ectopy fits the deficit, not the infusion.

elimination.verdict: Decline the push, keep the pump at 10 mEq per hour, and ask for another plan.

questions.objective: IV and oral potassium safety rules

questions.stem: A 72-year-old going home on a loop diuretic and oral potassium has a potassium of 3.6 mEq/L. The client says the tablets cause nausea and plans to skip them. Which instruction is best?

options.text: Replace the tablets with bananas and oranges every day
options.rationale: Dietary potassium is encouraged, but it is added to the prescribed dose. It does not replace it while the loop diuretic continues.

options.text: Take each tablet with a meal or right after eating
options.rationale: Oral potassium is given with food to reduce nausea, which solves the reason the client wants to skip it.

options.text: Take the tablet at bedtime on an empty stomach
options.rationale: The right drug at a time that makes the nausea worse, since there is no food with it.

options.text: Skip the diuretic on days when the nausea is bad
options.rationale: The diuretic is not what causes the nausea, and stopping it is not the client's or the nurse's decision.

questions.takeaway: Oral potassium goes with food. Fix the nausea so the client keeps taking the dose that the diuretic makes necessary.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The client's problem is nausea, so pick the option that removes the nausea and keeps the prescription intact.

steps.detail: Nausea from the tablets, with a potassium of 3.6 mEq/L that is barely in range.

steps.action: Cut options that drop a prescribed drug
steps.detail: Replacing tablets with fruit and skipping the diuretic both change the regimen.
With a meal reduces nausea. An empty stomach does not.

elimination.verdict: Take it with a meal.

questions.objective: IV and oral potassium safety rules

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with chronic kidney disease who takes an ACE inhibitor reports new tingling in both hands and frequent watery stools. Heart rate is 52 per minute. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Start cardiac monitoring and request a potassium level
options.rationale: Kidney disease and an ACE inhibitor both raise potassium. Tingling, watery stools and a slow heart rate fit, and the heart is where high potassium kills.

options.text: Check for hand spasm with a blood pressure cuff inflated
options.rationale: Tingling with diarrhea also fits low calcium, so this is the right test for the look-alike. The ACE inhibitor and the heart rate of 52 per minute point to potassium, and the heart is protected first.

options.text: Offer orange juice to replace fluid lost in the stools
options.rationale: Replacing fluid is reasonable, but orange juice adds potassium to a client who may already have too much.

options.text: Collect a stool specimen and start an intake and output record
options.rationale: Treats the diarrhea as the problem when it is one cue in a larger pattern.

questions.takeaway: Impaired excretion plus an ACE inhibitor, early tingling, watery stools and bradycardia: think high potassium and get the heart on a monitor.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Do not chase the symptoms one at a time. Ask what single imbalance the history and all three cues share.

steps.detail: Tingling, watery stools and a heart rate of 52 per minute in a client with two causes of potassium retention.
Low calcium shares tingling and diarrhea. The ACE inhibitor and the slow heart rate fit potassium.

steps.action: Pick the action that protects circulation
steps.detail: A monitor and a level address the lethal risk.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac monitor and a potassium level.

questions.objective: high potassium: causes, findings, ECG, drug roles, monitoring

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with potassium 6.8 mEq/L and a widened QRS has prescriptions for IV calcium, regular insulin with dextrose, and a potassium binder. The nurse gives the calcium first. Which finding shows the calcium worked?

options.text: The repeat potassium is lower than 6.8 mEq/L
options.rationale: Calcium does not lower potassium. A falling level is the work of insulin and the binder.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose stays above 70 mg/dL
options.rationale: That is the dextrose doing its job, which is to prevent hypoglycemia from the insulin.

options.text: The client passes a large loose stool
options.rationale: That is the binder, which removes potassium through the GI tract.

options.text: The QRS on the monitor becomes narrower
options.rationale: IV calcium stabilizes and protects the heart, so its effect is read on the monitor, not on the laboratory report.

questions.takeaway: Each hyperkalemia drug has one job: calcium protects the heart, insulin shifts potassium into cells, dextrose protects the glucose, a binder removes potassium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real sign that one of the prescribed drugs worked. Match each sign to its drug and keep the one that belongs to calcium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A lower level comes from shifting or removing potassium. Calcium does neither.

steps.action: Match the glucose and the stool
steps.detail: Dextrose and the binder.
The widened QRS was the cardiac effect, and calcium acts on the heart.

elimination.verdict: A narrower QRS.

questions.objective: high potassium: causes, findings, ECG, drug roles, monitoring

questions.stem: One hour after regular insulin with dextrose for a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L, a 68-year-old is sweaty, shaky and newly irritable. The cardiac rhythm is unchanged. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Request a repeat serum potassium level
options.rationale: Potassium falling too far is also watched for during treatment, and a repeat level is due. These cues match low glucose, which a bedside test answers at once.

options.text: Give the prescribed potassium binder
options.rationale: A correct part of the plan that does nothing for a new change one hour after insulin.

options.text: Check the capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia is the expected risk after insulin, and sweating, shakiness and irritability are how it shows.

options.text: Prepare another dose of IV calcium
options.rationale: Calcium is for cardiac protection, and the rhythm is unchanged.

questions.takeaway: During hyperkalemia treatment watch for two overshoots: low glucose from the insulin and low potassium from the shift and removal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask which drug was given an hour ago and what its known risk is. The new symptoms should be read through that drug.

steps.action: Tie the timing to the drug
steps.detail: One hour after insulin.
Sweaty, shaky and irritable fit low glucose. The rhythm is unchanged, so calcium is not the need.
A capillary glucose comes before a serum level.

elimination.verdict: Check the capillary blood glucose.

questions.objective: high potassium: causes, findings, ECG, drug roles, monitoring

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with chronic kidney disease was treated for a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L with insulin, dextrose and a binder. The potassium is now 3.3 mEq/L and another binder dose is due. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the binder, since kidney disease will raise the potassium again
options.rationale: Tempting, because the kidneys still cannot excrete potassium. The level is already below 3.5 mEq/L, and the binder would remove more.

options.text: Hold the binder and report the potassium of 3.3 mEq/L
options.rationale: Treatment has overshot into low potassium. Another dose of a potassium remover is unsafe until the plan is revised.

options.text: Give the binder with a glass of orange juice
options.rationale: Gives a potassium remover and a potassium source together, which is not a plan.

options.text: Give the binder and recheck the potassium in 4 hours
options.rationale: Rechecking is right. Giving the dose first removes more potassium from a client who is already low.

questions.takeaway: Treating high potassium can overshoot. Once the level is under 3.5 mEq/L, stop removing potassium and get the plan revised.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The long-term risk (kidney disease) pulls you toward giving the dose. The number on the page, 3.3 mEq/L, is the actual problem right now.

steps.detail: 3.3 mEq/L is below 3.5 mEq/L, so this is now low potassium.

steps.action: Ask what the due drug does
steps.detail: A binder removes potassium.
Low potassium is present now. A rise from kidney disease is possible later.

elimination.verdict: Hold the binder and report 3.3 mEq/L.

questions.objective: high potassium: causes, findings, ECG, drug roles, monitoring

questions.stem: A 45-year-old is 18 hours after thyroid surgery. Assistive personnel reports that the client's lips and fingertips are tingling. Which assessment does the nurse perform next?

options.text: Measure both calves and compare the temperature of the feet
options.rationale: A real electrolyte assessment, but it screens for clots in high calcium.

options.text: Test ankle reflexes, expecting them to be decreased
options.rationale: Low calcium makes nerves and muscles fire too easily, so decreased responses are the wrong thing to expect.

options.text: Reposition the arms and recheck the tingling in 1 hour
options.rationale: Explains the cue away and delays, when tingling of the lips and fingers after thyroid surgery is the early sign of low calcium.

options.text: Inflate a blood pressure cuff on the arm and watch the hand
options.rationale: Trousseau sign. Carpal spasm with the cuff inflated confirms the increased excitability of low calcium.

questions.takeaway: Tingling of the lips and fingers after neck surgery means possible parathyroid injury and low calcium. Test for it with Trousseau or Chvostek.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Thyroid surgery is the risk factor and tingling is the first step toward tetany. Pick the assessment built for that imbalance.

steps.action: Link the surgery to the electrolyte
steps.detail: Thyroid surgery can damage or remove the parathyroid glands, which lowers calcium.
Calf and foot checks belong to clot risk.

steps.action: Cut the wrong direction and the delay
steps.detail: Low calcium increases excitability, and waiting 1 hour lets tingling progress.

elimination.verdict: Cuff on the arm, watch the hand for spasm.

questions.objective: low calcium: findings, Trousseau and Chvostek, QT, treatment, low stimulation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old after thyroid surgery has a calcium of 7.6 mg/dL (reference 9.0 to 10.5), painful spasms of both hands and a prolonged QT interval. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate carrying out first?

options.text: Oral calcium with vitamin D at the next meal
options.rationale: The right replacement for mild or chronic low calcium. Spasms and a QT change make this severe and symptomatic.

options.text: IV calcium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe, symptomatic low calcium is replaced IV, and the QT change means the heart is watched.

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate with frequent reflex checks
options.rationale: Correct pairing of drug and monitoring for low magnesium, the look-alike. The abnormal value here is calcium.

options.text: Calcitonin, followed by a repeat calcium level
options.rationale: Calcitonin lowers calcium. It treats the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: Mild or chronic low calcium gets oral calcium and vitamin D. Spasms, tetany or ECG change means IV calcium on a monitor.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options replace calcium. The spasms and the QT interval decide which route.

steps.detail: Calcitonin moves calcium the wrong way.
Magnesium sulfate treats low magnesium, and the stated value is calcium 7.6 mg/dL.
Painful spasms and a prolonged QT are severe findings, so IV.

elimination.verdict: IV calcium with cardiac monitoring.

questions.objective: low calcium: findings, Trousseau and Chvostek, QT, treatment, low stimulation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with a calcium of 7.5 mg/dL still has muscle twitching while IV calcium infuses. The client is anxious and asks for the lights on and all five relatives to stay. Which plan is best?

options.text: All five relatives stay, since anxiety also raises stimulation
options.rationale: Defensible, because the client asked and anxiety matters. Five visitors and bright light are stimulation for nerves that are still firing too easily.

options.text: Relatives leave, the door is closed, and checks are every 2 hours
options.rationale: Quiet, but it leaves an anxious client who is still twitching alone during an infusion with too little observation.

options.text: One calm relative stays, lights are dimmed, voices are kept low
options.rationale: Keeps stimulation low while the twitching continues and still answers the anxiety with a familiar person.

options.text: Lights stay on and the television plays to distract from twitching
options.rationale: Adds light and noise, the opposite of reducing stimulation.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium calls for a quiet room, limited visitors and a soft voice. Meet the client's need for support inside that limit.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: One option gives the client everything asked for and one gives nothing. The twitching tells you stimulation still matters, so look for the option that honors both.

steps.detail: The muscles are still twitching, so excitability is still high.
Five relatives with lights on, and lights with television.
One leaves the client alone with 2 hour checks. The other keeps one calm person present.

elimination.verdict: One calm relative, dim lights, low voices.

questions.objective: low calcium: findings, Trousseau and Chvostek, QT, treatment, low stimulation

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with cancer on bed rest has a calcium of 12.8 mg/dL (reference 9.0 to 10.5), lethargy and no stool for 4 days. Which scheduled item does the nurse hold and question?

options.text: A daily vitamin D supplement
options.rationale: Vitamin D increases calcium absorption from the GI tract, so calcium and vitamin D supplements are held when calcium is high.

options.text: An IV loop diuretic
options.rationale: A loop diuretic promotes calcium excretion. It is part of the treatment. A thiazide diuretic is the one that is stopped.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV infusion
options.rationale: Normal saline promotes renal calcium excretion. It is part of the treatment.

options.text: A stool softener by mouth
options.rationale: It addresses the slowed gut that high calcium causes and adds no calcium.

questions.takeaway: In high calcium, stop the sources: hold calcium and vitamin D supplements, stop calcium-containing IV fluids and stop thiazide diuretics.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three of these items help a client with a calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. Find the one that feeds the problem.

steps.detail: The question asks which item to hold.
Saline and a loop diuretic remove calcium. A stool softener treats a symptom.
Vitamin D increases calcium absorption from the gut.

elimination.verdict: Hold the vitamin D supplement.

questions.objective: high calcium: causes, findings, clot risk, treatment

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on bed rest has a calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. Assistive personnel reports the left foot is cooler and paler than the right. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Massage the left calf and raise the leg on pillows
options.rationale: Massage is unsafe when a clot is possible, and nothing has been assessed yet.

options.text: Measure both calves and check capillary refill in both feet
options.rationale: High calcium raises clot risk in the legs and pelvis. Calf circumference, foot temperature, color and capillary refill are the assessment.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to recheck the left foot in 1 hour
options.rationale: An assessment, but delayed by an hour, delegated, and limited to one foot when both legs need comparing now.

options.text: Test patellar and ankle reflexes in both legs
options.rationale: High calcium does decrease reflexes, so this is a real assessment for this client. It does not explain one foot that is cooler and paler than the other.

questions.takeaway: High calcium means clot risk. A foot that changes temperature or color gets a full comparison of both legs now.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options assess. Match the assessment to the cue: a one-sided change in temperature and color is a perfusion question, and it cannot wait.

steps.action: Connect the cue to the imbalance
steps.detail: Calcium 12.8 mg/dL plus bed rest equals clot risk.
Massage acts on a leg that may hold a clot before anyone has examined it.
Reflexes answer a different question, and a recheck in 1 hour delays. Comparing both calves and capillary refill fits the cue now.

elimination.verdict: Measure both calves and check capillary refill.

questions.objective: high calcium: causes, findings, clot risk, treatment

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has received IV 0.9% sodium chloride and a loop diuretic for 6 hours for a calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. Which finding needs prompt follow-up?

options.text: Urine output of 250 mL per hour
options.rationale: A large output is the intended effect. Saline and a loop diuretic increase urine output so calcium leaves.

options.text: Calcium of 11.9 mg/dL on the repeat level
options.rationale: Still above 10.5 mg/dL, but it is falling, which is what the treatment is for.

options.text: No bowel movement yet today
options.rationale: The gut slows with high calcium and recovers as the level falls. It is expected at this point.

options.text: Heart rate of 48 per minute, down from 92
options.rationale: Severe or prolonged high calcium slows the heart and causes dysrhythmias. The cardiac effect is the most serious one.

questions.takeaway: In high calcium the heart is the most serious system: fast early, slow when severe. A falling heart rate is unexpected during treatment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as expected or unexpected for a client being treated. Only one is moving the wrong way.

steps.detail: High urine output and a falling calcium.
Constipation lags behind the calcium level.
Heart rate from 92 to 48 per minute is a circulation problem.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate of 48 per minute.

questions.objective: high calcium: causes, findings, clot risk, treatment

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with alcohol use disorder and poor intake has a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L (reference 1.3 to 2.1), hyperactive reflexes and muscle twitching. Which addition to the plan is the priority?

options.text: Seizure precautions with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Low magnesium increases nerve and muscle excitability. Seizures and dysrhythmias are its major complications, and the reflexes and twitching show the excitability is already there.

options.text: Calf measurements every shift for clot detection
options.rationale: A valid electrolyte assessment that belongs to high calcium.

options.text: A magnesium antacid from the client's home supply
options.rationale: The right mineral in the wrong way: an unprescribed product instead of ordered oral or IV replacement.

options.text: A nutrition referral for a balanced meal plan
options.rationale: Addresses the cause and belongs in the plan. It does not protect the client today.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium, like low calcium, makes nerves and muscle overreact. Plan for seizures and dysrhythmias first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask what a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L can do to this client in the next few hours, then choose the option that guards against it.

steps.detail: Low magnesium means increased excitability.
Seizures and dysrhythmias.
A nutrition referral is later, calf checks are for another imbalance, and a home antacid is not prescribed.

elimination.verdict: Seizure precautions and cardiac monitoring.

questions.objective: low magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, monitoring during IV magnesium

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which check best tells the nurse the infusion is delivering too much magnesium?

options.text: Facial twitch when the cheek is tapped
options.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign shows excitability is still high, which means too little magnesium, not too much.

options.text: Length of the QT interval on the monitor
options.rationale: A prolonged QT is a sign of low magnesium. It tracks the deficit, not toxicity.

options.text: Patellar reflexes at each check
options.rationale: Deep tendon reflexes are monitored frequently during IV magnesium. Reflexes that become depressed or absent signal toxicity.

options.text: Burning at the IV site at the hourly check
options.rationale: Site checks matter for any infusion and are the named rule for IV potassium. They do not detect a high magnesium level.

questions.takeaway: During IV magnesium, check deep tendon reflexes often. Hyperactive means still low. Depressed or absent means too much.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options detect too little magnesium. The question asks for too much, so pick the check that changes when magnesium is high.

steps.detail: Too much magnesium.
Chvostek sign and a long QT belong to low magnesium.
Hourly site checks for burning are the potassium rule.

elimination.verdict: Patellar reflexes.

questions.objective: low magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, monitoring during IV magnesium

questions.stem: During IV magnesium sulfate for a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L, a 52-year-old's patellar reflexes go from 4+ to 2+ (normal). Tingling is gone, respirations are 16 per minute, and the client is alert. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the infusion and keep checking reflexes
options.rationale: Reflexes moving from hyperactive to normal, with tingling gone, normal respirations and an alert client, is the intended response.

options.text: Stop the infusion because the reflexes are falling
options.rationale: Tempting, because falling reflexes are the toxicity warning. They have fallen to normal, not below it, and nothing else suggests toxicity.

options.text: Slow the infusion by half until a level returns
options.rationale: Changes a prescribed rate on the nurse's own decision when there is no sign of toxicity.

options.text: Request IV calcium to reverse the magnesium
options.rationale: IV calcium is the antidote for magnesium toxicity. This client is responding, not toxic.

questions.takeaway: Reflexes are read against normal. From 4+ to 2+ is recovery. Below normal or absent, with drowsiness or slow breathing, is toxicity.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A falling number can be good news. Ask where it landed: 2+ is normal, respirations are 16 per minute and the client is alert.

steps.action: Place the reflex on the scale
steps.detail: 4+ is hyperactive. 2+ is normal.
Respirations 16 per minute and alert, with tingling resolved.

steps.action: Reject treatment for a problem that is absent
steps.detail: Stopping, slowing and the antidote all answer toxicity.

elimination.verdict: Continue the infusion and keep checking reflexes.

questions.objective: low magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, monitoring during IV magnesium

questions.stem: During IV magnesium sulfate, a 52-year-old becomes drowsy. Patellar reflexes that were 4+ (hyperactive) are now absent and respirations are 10 per minute. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the infusion by half and recheck reflexes in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Slowing still delivers magnesium to a client whose reflexes are gone and whose breathing is slowing.

options.text: Request a magnesium level and continue until it results
options.rationale: A level will be wanted, but the bedside findings already show toxicity and the infusion is the source.

options.text: Wake the client and coach deep breaths every 5 minutes
options.rationale: Supports breathing for the moment and leaves the cause running.

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion and stay with the client
options.rationale: Absent reflexes, drowsiness and slow respirations are high magnesium. All magnesium sources are stopped first.

questions.takeaway: Absent reflexes, drowsiness and slow breathing during IV magnesium mean toxicity. Stop the magnesium first, then treat.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The assessment is complete: three toxicity cues are stated. This is the point where acting beats assessing again.

steps.detail: Absent reflexes, drowsy and respirations of 10 per minute.
The infusion is delivering the magnesium.

steps.action: Cut options that keep it running
steps.detail: Half rate, waiting for a level and coaching breaths all leave magnesium infusing.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion and stay with the client.

questions.objective: low magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, monitoring during IV magnesium

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with kidney failure has a magnesium of 4.2 mEq/L (reference 1.3 to 2.1), drowsiness and a heart rate of 50 per minute. Which question about home routines is most useful?

options.text: Do you season your food with a salt substitute?
options.rationale: A good question in kidney failure, but salt substitutes are a potassium source.

options.text: Which antacids or laxatives do you take?
options.rationale: High magnesium comes from kidney failure plus magnesium intake, and antacids and laxatives are the usual sources.

options.text: Do you take calcium or vitamin D tablets?
options.rationale: Those raise calcium. The abnormal value here is magnesium.

options.text: How often do you take your water pill?
options.rationale: Loop and thiazide diuretics cause magnesium loss, so they explain a low level, not a high one.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium needs two things: kidneys that cannot clear it and a source. Ask about antacids and laxatives.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each question hunts for the source of a different electrolyte problem. Match the question to the value that is abnormal.

steps.detail: Magnesium 4.2 mEq/L.
Salt substitute is potassium. Calcium and vitamin D tablets are calcium.
Diuretics lower magnesium.

elimination.verdict: Ask about antacids and laxatives.

questions.objective: high magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, antidote

questions.scenario: An 80-year-old with kidney failure takes a magnesium antacid and a magnesium laxative every day. The client is drowsy, with a heart rate of 48 per minute, blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, respirations 10 per minute and shallow, and absent patellar reflexes. Urine output is 5 mL per hour. Magnesium is 4.6 mEq/L (reference 1.3 to 2.1).
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Hold the magnesium antacid and laxative
options.rationale: All magnesium sources are stopped first.

options.text: Give IV calcium as prescribed
options.rationale: IV calcium is the antidote. It counters the cardiac and neuromuscular depression shown by the heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and reflexes.

options.text: Give IV fluids with a loop diuretic as the main treatment
options.rationale: A correct treatment only when kidney function is adequate. With kidney failure and 5 mL of urine per hour it will not clear magnesium.

options.text: Give IV magnesium sulfate as prescribed
options.rationale: This is the treatment for the opposite imbalance.

options.text: Hypermagnesemia
options.rationale: Kidney failure, daily magnesium products, a level of 4.6 mEq/L and depressed heart, breathing and reflexes.

options.text: Hypomagnesemia
options.rationale: Low magnesium gives hyperactive reflexes and twitching. These reflexes are absent.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: Shallow breathing and weak reflexes can fit, but the stated abnormal value and the history are for magnesium.

options.text: Hypocalcemia
options.rationale: Low calcium increases excitability, with spasms and tetany, not absent reflexes.

options.text: Respiratory rate and depth
options.rationale: Severe muscle weakness from high magnesium leads to respiratory failure.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Reflexes return as the magnesium effect is reversed.

options.text: Trousseau sign
options.rationale: A test for the increased excitability of low calcium or low magnesium.

options.text: Calf circumference
options.rationale: The clot assessment for high calcium.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium: stop every source, give IV calcium for severe cardiac and neuromuscular depression, and use fluids with a loop diuretic only when the kidneys work. Watch breathing and reflexes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Fluids with a loop diuretic is a real treatment for this imbalance. The urine output of 5 mL per hour is the detail that removes it here.

steps.action: Name the condition from the value and the reflexes
steps.detail: Magnesium 4.6 mEq/L with absent reflexes.

steps.action: Pick actions that fit these kidneys
steps.detail: Stop the sources and give the antidote. Excretion through the kidneys needs urine output.
Breathing and reflexes.

elimination.verdict: Hypermagnesemia; hold magnesium products and give IV calcium; respirations and deep tendon reflexes.

questions.objective: high magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, antidote

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with kidney failure and a magnesium of 4.6 mEq/L (reference 1.3 to 2.1) has respirations of 8 per minute, oxygen saturation 86% on room air and absent patellar reflexes. Prescribed IV calcium is coming from pharmacy. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Stay at the monitor and give the calcium when it arrives
options.rationale: The calcium is the antidote and must be given the moment it comes. It is not at the bedside, and the client is not oxygenating now.

options.text: Check patellar reflexes again to confirm the change
options.rationale: The reflexes are already known to be absent. Repeating the assessment delays action.

options.text: Support breathing with oxygen and a bag-mask device
options.rationale: Respirations of 8 per minute with a saturation of 86% is respiratory failure from muscle weakness. Breathing is supported while the antidote is on its way.

options.text: Start IV fluids with a loop diuretic
options.rationale: Depends on adequate kidney function, which a client with kidney failure does not have, and it does nothing for breathing.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium kills by respiratory failure and cardiac arrest. Support breathing now and give the IV calcium antidote as soon as it is in hand.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The antidote is the right drug, but look at where it is. Until it arrives, the only thing the nurse can fix is the breathing.

steps.detail: Respirations 8 per minute and saturation 86%.
The calcium is still on its way from pharmacy.

steps.action: Cut the repeat assessment and the kidney route
steps.detail: Reflexes are already documented as absent, and the client has kidney failure.

elimination.verdict: Support breathing with oxygen and a bag-mask device.

questions.objective: high magnesium: causes, findings, treatment, antidote

questions.stem: A 66-year-old who takes a loop diuretic has weakness in both legs. Laboratory results are pending. Which finding points to low potassium rather than high potassium?

options.text: Weakness that began in the feet and is moving upward
options.rationale: Weakness that moves up from the hands and feet is the pattern of high potassium.

options.text: Frequent watery stools with abdominal cramping
options.rationale: High potassium increases gut motility. Low potassium slows it.

options.text: A dysrhythmia on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Both low and high potassium cause dysrhythmias, so this does not separate them.

options.text: Hypoactive bowel sounds with constipation
options.rationale: Low potassium decreases peristalsis, and a loop diuretic is a cause of potassium loss.

questions.takeaway: Both potassium imbalances cause weakness and dysrhythmias. The gut separates them: slow and quiet when low, fast and watery when high.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Weakness and rhythm changes belong to both sides. Look for the body system that behaves in opposite ways.

steps.detail: A dysrhythmia fits either imbalance.
Watery stools against hypoactive bowel sounds.
A loop diuretic loses potassium, which agrees with the slow gut.

elimination.verdict: Hypoactive bowel sounds with constipation.

questions.objective: low potassium: causes, findings, ECG, safety

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with poor intake has a positive Chvostek sign, hyperactive reflexes and a prolonged QT interval. The calcium returns at 9.6 mg/dL (reference 9.0 to 10.5). Which step makes sense next?

options.text: Ask whether a magnesium level was drawn
options.rationale: Low magnesium produces the same picture: positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, hyperreflexia and a long QT. Poor intake is one of its causes.

options.text: Repeat the calcium level in the morning
options.rationale: The right electrolyte family, but the value is in range and the findings need an explanation today.

options.text: Give the as needed oral calcium with vitamin D
options.rationale: Treats a calcium level that is not low.

options.text: Recheck the Chvostek sign each shift and document it
options.rationale: Keeps watching a sign of high excitability without looking for its cause, while the QT interval is prolonged.

questions.takeaway: Chvostek and Trousseau signs are not specific to calcium. When calcium is in range, think magnesium.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The findings say increased excitability. The calcium says it is not calcium. Ask which other electrolyte causes the same signs.

steps.detail: Calcium 9.6 mg/dL is within 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL.

steps.action: Cut the options that stay with calcium
steps.detail: Repeating it and treating it.
Low magnesium shares the signs, and poor intake causes it.

elimination.verdict: Ask about a magnesium level.

questions.objective: telling the paired imbalances apart by cues

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old with poor intake who takes a loop diuretic has a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L (reference 3.5 to 5.0) and a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L (reference 1.3 to 2.1). Calcium is 9.6 mg/dL (reference 9.0 to 10.5). The nurse reviews which low result each possible finding would point to.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it points to the low potassium or to the low magnesium.

rows.text: Patellar reflexes weaker than normal
rows.rationale: Low potassium makes excitable cells less responsive, so reflexes decrease.

rows.text: Hand and fingers spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated
rows.rationale: A positive Trousseau sign shows increased excitability, which low magnesium causes.

rows.text: Flat T wave with a prominent U wave
rows.rationale: The ECG pattern of low potassium.

rows.text: Tingling around the lips and in the fingers
rows.rationale: Tingling is the early sign of nerves firing too easily, the low magnesium picture.

rows.text: Prolonged QT interval
rows.rationale: Low magnesium prolongs the QT interval.

rows.text: Shallow respirations with weak legs
rows.rationale: Weak skeletal and respiratory muscle is the severe picture of low potassium.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium quiets cells: weak muscle, weak reflexes, U wave. Low magnesium, like low calcium, excites them: tingling, spasm, positive Trousseau and Chvostek, long QT.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask one thing for each row: is the tissue doing too little or too much? Too little is potassium. Too much is magnesium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weak reflexes and weak breathing are decreased activity. Tingling and spasm are increased activity.
U wave with a flat T wave is potassium. A long QT is magnesium.
Three rows on each side.

elimination.verdict: Potassium, magnesium, potassium, magnesium, magnesium, potassium.

questions.objective: telling the paired imbalances apart by cues

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has vomited for 2 days. Blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg, heart rate is 118 per minute, and the oral mucosa is dry. Which prescription does the nurse expect to start first?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride through a peripheral IV
options.rationale: Right idea that she needs fluid, wrong tonicity. A hypotonic solution moves water into cells and is contraindicated in hypotension.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride through a peripheral IV
options.rationale: An isotonic solution stays in the vessels and expands volume, which a blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg needs.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride through a peripheral IV
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is for severe hyponatremia or cerebral edema. No cue here points to either, and it risks hypernatremia and overload.

options.text: Isotonic fluid by subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen
options.rationale: Right tonicity, wrong route. Subcutaneous infusion is for mild to moderate dehydration and is avoided in severe dehydration or shock.

questions.takeaway: Low blood pressure means the vessels are empty. Isotonic fluid fills vessels; hypotonic fluid leaves them for the cells and is contraindicated in hypotension.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Read the blood pressure before the fluid names. The question is where the water needs to go: into the vessels.

steps.detail: 86/50 mm Hg with a rate of 118 per minute is low circulating volume.

steps.action: Cut the fluid that leaves the vessels
steps.detail: 0.45% is hypotonic and contraindicated in hypotension.

steps.action: Cut the fluid and route with no matching cue
steps.detail: 3% treats severe hyponatremia. Subcutaneous infusion is too slow for hypotension.

elimination.verdict: 0.9% sodium chloride IV. Isotonic fluid expands volume.

questions.objective: fluid and electrolyte balance in choosing a solution

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with thin, fragile skin and rolling veins needs a peripheral IV for 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL per hour. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: 22-gauge catheter in a dorsal vein of the hand
options.rationale: Right gauge, wrong site. Dorsal hand veins are avoided in older adults when possible because the skin and veins there tear easily.

options.text: 18-gauge catheter in a straight forearm vein
options.rationale: Right site, wrong gauge. An 18 gauge is for blood products and contrast and causes more vein trauma than this infusion needs.

options.text: 24-gauge catheter in the antecubital fossa
options.rationale: A small gauge suits fragile veins, but the antecubital fossa is avoided for short peripheral catheters.

options.text: 22-gauge catheter in a straight forearm vein
options.rationale: Smallest effective gauge for an older adult, placed in the preferred forearm site.

questions.takeaway: For an older adult use the smallest effective gauge (22 to 24) in a forearm vein, and stay off the back of the hand and the antecubital fossa.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option has two parts, a gauge and a site. Only one option gets both right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A maintenance rate of 75 mL per hour does not need an 18 gauge.
Dorsal hand and antecubital fossa are both sites to avoid for this client.

steps.action: Keep the option with no flaw
steps.detail: 22 gauge in the forearm.

elimination.verdict: 22-gauge catheter in a straight forearm vein.

questions.objective: clinical judgment, older adults and delegation

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has received 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour for 4 hours. She now has new confusion, dyspnea and crackles in both lung bases. Which problem do these cues indicate?

options.text: Fluid overload from the infusion rate
options.rationale: Older adults have less renal reserve. Confusion, dyspnea and crackles are the three cues to check for when fluid is outpacing the heart and kidneys.

options.text: Speed shock from fluid entering the vein too fast
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a drug or fluid given too fast and shows flushing, headache and chest tightness. Crackles after 4 hours of fluid do not fit it.

options.text: Air embolism from air entering the line
options.rationale: Dyspnea fits, but air embolism is sudden and comes with chest pain and hypotension. Crackles after 600 mL of fluid point elsewhere.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Confusion can appear with a bloodstream infection, but it comes with fever, chills and hypotension, and none of those is reported.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult on IV fluid, new confusion, dyspnea and crackles mean fluid overload until proven otherwise. Infuse at lower rates and check for these three often.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four options can cause dyspnea or confusion. Sort them by what else comes with it and by how fast it started.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 150 mL per hour for 4 hours is 600 mL in a 78-year-old.
Crackles with dyspnea is fluid in the lungs.
Speed shock flushes, air embolism is sudden with chest pain, infection brings fever and chills.

elimination.verdict: Fluid overload.

questions.objective: clinical judgment, older adults and delegation

questions.stem: A nurse inserts a peripheral IV in a 78-year-old woman on the second attempt. Which note documents the insertion completely?

options.text: 22-gauge in left forearm cephalic vein, 2 attempts, transparent dressing applied, client tolerated without pain, daughter at bedside during insertion.
options.rationale: Close, but it leaves out the vein condition and the reason for the site. Who was at the bedside is not a required element.

options.text: IV started in left arm on second attempt, vein soft and straight, transparent dressing applied, tolerated without pain, arm chosen to spare fragile hand veins.
options.rationale: It gives the reason and the attempts but no gauge, and "left arm" is not a site location.

options.text: 22-gauge in left forearm cephalic vein, 2 attempts, vein soft and straight, transparent dressing, tolerated without pain, forearm chosen to spare fragile hand veins.
options.rationale: Site location, gauge, number of attempts, vein condition, dressing, tolerance and the reason for the site are all present.

options.text: 22-gauge in left forearm cephalic vein, vein soft and straight, transparent dressing, tolerated without pain, 0.9% sodium chloride infusing at 75 mL per hour.
options.rationale: The rate is true and useful, but the note omits the number of attempts and the reason for the site.

questions.takeaway: An insertion note has seven parts: site location, gauge, number of attempts, vein condition, dressing, client tolerance and the reason for the site.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Run the seven-part list against each note. Extra true details do not replace a missing part.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stem says second attempt, so a note without the count is incomplete.

steps.action: Look for gauge and exact site
steps.detail: "Left arm" with no gauge fails.

steps.action: Look for vein condition and reason
steps.detail: Only one note has both.

elimination.verdict: The note with all seven parts.

questions.objective: document infusion care

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL (reference 14 to 18) is prescribed 1 unit of packed red blood cells. Type and crossmatch are complete. No signed consent is in the chart. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Make sure signed consent is on file before sending for the unit
options.rationale: Consent must be documented before the product is retrieved from the blood bank, and once issued the unit has only 4 hours.

options.text: Take baseline vital signs so the unit can start on arrival
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are required, but they come right before the infusion, after consent is on file.

options.text: Send for the unit and have consent signed during the bedside check
options.rationale: Right that consent is needed, wrong time. It must be on file before the unit leaves the blood bank.

options.text: Prime the blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Correct fluid and a real step, but setting up before consent exists puts the steps out of order.

questions.takeaway: No consent on file, no blood out of the blood bank. Consent comes before retrieval, then verification, baseline vital signs and the start.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are real transfusion steps. The question is which one unlocks the others.

steps.detail: Order and crossmatch are done. Consent is not.
It must be on file before the unit is retrieved.
Vital signs and priming happen once the transfusion can legally proceed.

elimination.verdict: Confirm signed consent first.

questions.objective: safety protocols

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is receiving lactated Ringer's through his only peripheral IV. A unit of packed red blood cells has arrived, and two nurses have completed verification. How does the nurse set up the transfusion?

options.text: Piggyback the blood into the lactated Ringer's line above the pump
options.rationale: Blood runs with 0.9% sodium chloride only, so it cannot share a line with lactated Ringer's.

options.text: Pause the lactated Ringer's and run the blood through that same tubing
options.rationale: Pausing is the right idea, but the tubing still holds lactated Ringer's, and blood needs its own tubing primed with saline.

options.text: Stop the lactated Ringer's and use blood tubing primed with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Blood products require dedicated access and 0.9% sodium chloride only.

options.text: Stop the lactated Ringer's and use blood tubing primed with 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Dedicated tubing is right, the priming fluid is wrong. Only 0.9% sodium chloride is used with blood.

questions.takeaway: Blood gets a dedicated line and one companion fluid: 0.9% sodium chloride. Nothing else is primed, piggybacked or flushed with it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options fix the tubing and two do not. Then check the fluid in the tubing.

steps.detail: Any option that leaves lactated Ringer's in the path fails.
They differ only in the priming fluid.
0.9% sodium chloride only.

elimination.verdict: Stop the lactated Ringer's and use tubing primed with 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: IV solution types and blood products

questions.stem: A registered nurse (RN) has started packed red blood cells for a 58-year-old man and has completed the 15-minute check. A licensed practical nurse (LPN) and assistive personnel (AP) are on the team. Which assignments are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The AP takes vital signs every 30 minutes and gives the values to the RN
options.rationale: Taking vital signs is an AP task. The RN still reads the numbers and decides what they mean.

options.text: The AP tells the RN at once if the client reports chills or itching
options.rationale: Reporting what the client says is within the AP role. It passes the cue to the RN without asking the AP to interpret it.

options.text: The AP serves as the second verifier when the next unit arrives
options.rationale: Verification takes two licensed nurses. The AP is not licensed.

options.text: The LPN starts the next unit while the RN is at lunch
options.rationale: The LPN can monitor sites and hang non-high-alert fluids, but initiating a blood product is an RN task.

options.text: The AP decides whether a rise in temperature is a reaction
options.rationale: Measuring the temperature is fine. Interpreting the client's response is the RN's clinical judgment.

questions.takeaway: The AP measures and reports. The RN initiates blood, interprets the response and stays accountable, and verification needs two licensed nurses.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: For each option ask whether the task is collecting data or deciding what it means. Deciding stays with the RN.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vital signs and passing on a client report are AP tasks.

steps.action: Cut anything that needs a license
steps.detail: The second verifier must be a licensed nurse.
Starting blood and judging a reaction belong to the RN.

elimination.verdict: A and B.
