questions.objective: clinical judgment, older adults and delegation

questions.stem: A unit of packed red blood cells was issued from the blood bank at 0900 and started at 0930 for a 58-year-old man. At 1300, 60 mL remain and his vital signs match baseline. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Raise the rate so the last 60 mL finish in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because so little is left, but the 4 hours are already up at 1300 and a fast finish adds risk without fixing that.

options.text: Discontinue the unit now and record the volume infused
options.rationale: The unit must be infused within 4 hours of issue. At 1300 that limit is reached, so the rest is not given.

options.text: Continue the current rate, since 4 hours from the start is 1330
options.rationale: Defensible, because a unit runs over no more than 4 hours. But the unit must also be infused within 4 hours of issue, and it was issued at 0900, so the earlier limit of 1300 governs.

options.text: Return the remaining blood to the blood bank refrigerator for later
options.rationale: Right that it should not keep infusing, but blood that has been out for 4 hours cannot be stored and given later.

questions.takeaway: Two limits apply to packed red blood cells: within 4 hours of issue and over no more than 4 hours. The clock that started first, the issue time, runs out first. When it is reached, stop and document what was given.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two times appear in the stem. Decide which one starts the clock before reading the options.

steps.detail: Issued at 0900, so the limit is 1300.
Continuing relies on the 0930 start time, which is not the reference point.
Hurrying it in or saving it for later both give blood that is past its limit.

elimination.verdict: Discontinue the unit and record the volume infused.

questions.objective: IV solution types and blood products

questions.stem: A 46-year-old left-handed woman had a right mastectomy with lymph node removal. She needs a peripheral IV for 2 days of antibiotics. Which site does the nurse choose?

options.text: Right forearm, because it is her nondominant arm
options.rationale: Sparing the dominant hand is a preference. The arm on the mastectomy side is a site to avoid.

options.text: Left antecubital fossa, where the vein is largest
options.rationale: Correct arm, but the antecubital fossa is avoided for short peripheral catheters.

options.text: Dorsal vein of the left foot, leaving both arms free
options.rationale: Lower extremities are avoided for IV sites in adults.

options.text: Left forearm, in the cephalic vein
options.rationale: The forearm is the preferred site, and the left arm is the one not affected by the mastectomy.

questions.takeaway: A contraindicated limb outranks hand dominance. Avoid the mastectomy side, the antecubital fossa and the legs, and use the forearm of the other arm.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem sets a preference (dominant hand) against a contraindication (mastectomy side). The contraindication wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Right arm is out whatever her handedness.
Antecubital fossa and foot.
Left forearm uses her dominant arm, which is allowed.

elimination.verdict: Left forearm cephalic vein.

questions.objective: vascular access devices

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman will receive a vesicant chemotherapy drug one day every 3 weeks for 6 months. She swims several times a week. Which device does the nurse expect to discuss with her?

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: A central line that can take vesicants, so it is close. Its external catheter and dressing cannot be submerged, and she swims.

options.text: An implanted port under the skin of the chest
options.rationale: Central access for a vesicant, suited to intermittent long-term therapy, with nothing external, so she can swim and bathe.

options.text: A midline catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: A midline ends below the axilla, dwells up to 4 weeks and is for non-vesicant drugs only.

options.text: A nontunneled catheter in the subclavian vein
options.rationale: Central, but meant for short-term acute care and carries the highest infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Intermittent, long-term, vesicant therapy in a client who wants no external catheter points to an implanted port.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three cues choose the device: vesicant, every 3 weeks for 6 months, and swimming. Each cue removes one option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs a central line, so the midline is out.
A nontunneled catheter is short term.
A PICC arm cannot go under water. A port has no external part.

elimination.verdict: Implanted port.

questions.objective: vascular access devices

questions.stem: A nurse watches a colleague give a dose of medication through the needleless connector on a 46-year-old woman's accessed implanted port. Which step by the colleague requires the nurse to step in?

options.text: Performs hand hygiene before touching the connector
options.rationale: Correct practice before any catheter access.

options.text: Confirms that the port is accessed with a noncoring needle
options.rationale: Correct. A port is accessed only with a noncoring needle.

options.text: Wipes the connector for 3 seconds before access
options.rationale: Cleaning the connector is right, the time is not. The hub is scrubbed for at least 15 seconds before access to prevent bloodstream infection.

options.text: Flushes with saline before and after the medication
options.rationale: Correct. The line is flushed before and after use.

questions.takeaway: Scrub the hub for at least 15 seconds before every access. A quick wipe is the same as not cleaning it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong step. Three options are correct practice, and one is correct practice done too briefly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the step to stop.
Hand hygiene, noncoring needle and saline flushes are all right.
3 seconds is far short of 15.

elimination.verdict: The 3-second wipe.

questions.objective: safety protocols

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with an implanted port has a temperature of 38.9 C, shaking chills, blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg and new confusion. No other source is found. Two sets of blood cultures and an IV antibiotic are prescribed. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Draw both sets of blood cultures, then start the antibiotic
options.rationale: These cues with no other source mean a catheter-related bloodstream infection. Cultures drawn before the first dose can still grow the organism, and both steps happen within minutes.

options.text: Start the antibiotic now, then draw the cultures within the hour
options.rationale: Defensible with a pressure of 88/52 mm Hg, but an antibiotic given first can keep the cultures from growing the organism.

options.text: Ask for the port to be removed before other treatment
options.rationale: Removal is considered if needed. It does not come before cultures and antibiotics.

options.text: Swab the skin over the port and send it for culture
options.rationale: A culture is the right idea, but the infection is in the blood, and blood cultures are what is prescribed.

questions.takeaway: Suspected catheter-related bloodstream infection: blood cultures times two, then IV antibiotics, back to back. Catheter removal is decided after.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides.
questions.strategy: Both prescriptions are urgent. One of them ruins the other if it goes first.

steps.detail: Fever, chills, hypotension and confusion with a central device and no other source.
Cultures take minutes and must come before the first antibiotic dose.
A skin swab and port removal do not come first.

elimination.verdict: Blood cultures, then the antibiotic.

questions.objective: recognize complications

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man had a PICC placed at the bedside 20 minutes ago for 6 weeks of IV antibiotics. The first dose is due. Blood return is brisk, and the chest x-ray has not been done. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Start the dose, because brisk blood return shows the tip is in place
options.rationale: Blood return shows the catheter is in a vein. It does not show where the tip ends.

options.text: Hold the dose until the x-ray confirms the tip position
options.rationale: X-ray confirmation of tip placement is required before a PICC is used.

options.text: Start the dose at half the rate and watch the arm closely
options.rationale: Watching closely is good practice, but a slower rate does not make an unconfirmed tip safe to use.

options.text: Start the dose if the external length matches the insertion record
options.rationale: Checking external length is a real check for later movement. It does not replace the first x-ray.

questions.takeaway: A PICC is not used until its tip position is confirmed by x-ray. Blood return and catheter length are not substitutes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options find a way to give the dose on time. Ask what has to be true before this line can be used at all.

steps.detail: The x-ray has not been done.
Blood return and length do not locate the tip.
The dose waits for confirmation.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose until the x-ray confirms tip position.

questions.objective: vascular access devices

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has had a left arm PICC for 10 days. His whole left arm is swollen, painful and warm, and the pump shows a slower flow. Temperature is 36.9 C, and the insertion site is not red. Which complication is most likely?

options.text: Infiltration of fluid into the tissue
options.rationale: Swelling and slow flow fit, but infiltrated tissue is cool and pale, and his arm is warm.

options.text: Phlebitis of the vein at the insertion site
options.rationale: Pain fits, but phlebitis shows redness and a streak or cord along the vein, and the site is not red.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A PICC raises this risk, but it shows fever, chills and hypotension, and his temperature is 36.9 C.

options.text: Thrombosis in the vein around the catheter
options.rationale: A swollen, painful limb with a decreased flow rate is how a clot in or around the catheter presents.

questions.takeaway: Whole limb swollen and painful with slowing flow means thrombosis. Cool and pale means infiltration; red with a streak or cord means phlebitis; fever and chills mean infection.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each complication has one cue the others lack. Check skin temperature, redness and body temperature in turn.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm, so not infiltration.
None at the site, so not phlebitis.
36.9 C, so not a bloodstream infection.

elimination.verdict: Thrombosis.

questions.objective: recognize complications

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man is going home with a left arm PICC. Which statements show that he understands the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will have my blood pressure taken on my right arm."
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuffs or needle sticks on the PICC arm.

options.text: "I will put a waterproof cover over the site when I shower."
options.rationale: Showering is allowed with a waterproof cover so the dressing stays dry.

options.text: "If the flush is hard to push, I will press harder to clear it."
options.rationale: Flushing as instructed is right, but resistance means do not use the PICC. Forcing it is unsafe.

options.text: "I will call right away for a temperature above 38 C or chills."
options.rationale: Fever above 38 C and chills are warning signs that need care immediately.

options.text: "A short swim is fine as long as the dressing is still sealed."
options.rationale: Checking the dressing is right, but the arm is never submerged. No swimming or baths.

questions.takeaway: PICC at home: dressing clean, dry and intact, no cuff or sticks on that arm, never submerge it, never flush against resistance, and report fever above 38 C or chills at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two statements start with a sound habit and end with an unsafe action. Read each statement to its last word.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Other arm for blood pressure, waterproof cover, call for fever or chills.
Resistance means stop, not push.
A sealed dressing does not allow submerging.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D.

questions.objective: safety protocols

questions.stem: A nurse is changing the tubing on a 67-year-old man's PICC when the open hub is left unclamped. He suddenly has dyspnea and chest pain, and his blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and give oxygen by face mask
options.rationale: Oxygen is part of the response and upright is the usual answer for dyspnea, but the hub is still open and this is air in the vein, which calls for left side with head down.

options.text: Call the rapid response team and stay at the bedside
options.rationale: The team is needed. Air keeps entering while the call is made, and closing the catheter takes one second.

options.text: Clamp the catheter and turn him left side, head down
options.rationale: An open central line with sudden dyspnea, chest pain and hypotension is air embolism. Clamping stops the air and left lateral Trendelenburg is the emergency position.

options.text: Connect the new tubing and flush the line with saline
options.rationale: Closing the system is the right idea, but flushing pushes any air in the catheter into him.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: clamp the line, left lateral Trendelenburg, call rapid response, oxygen at 100%. Stop the air first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Dyspnea pulls you toward sitting him up. The open hub in the stem tells you why he is short of breath.

steps.detail: Open central line plus sudden dyspnea, chest pain and low pressure.
Clamp before anything else.
Head down on the left side, the opposite of head up.

elimination.verdict: Clamp and position left side, head down.

questions.objective: recognize complications

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with head trauma is becoming harder to wake over the past hour. Which prescription does the nurse question before carrying it out?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride IV at 100 mL per hour
options.rationale: A hypotonic solution moves water into cells, including brain cells. It is contraindicated in head trauma and increased intracranial pressure.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV at 75 mL per hour
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid causes no net water shift into brain cells, so it is acceptable.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride IV by pump with sodium checks
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells and is used for cerebral edema, with sodium monitoring.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride flush before and after IV drugs
options.rationale: A routine saline flush that keeps the line patent.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid swells cells. In head trauma or rising intracranial pressure that means a swelling brain, so 0.45% sodium chloride is questioned.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask of each fluid which way it moves water across the brain cell wall.

steps.detail: You are looking for the unsafe prescription.
Isotonic: none. Hypertonic: out of cells. Hypotonic: into cells.
Head trauma with a falling level of consciousness cannot take water into brain cells.

elimination.verdict: 0.45% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: IV solution types and blood products

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with head trauma has a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145) and is receiving 3% sodium chloride by pump. Four hours later, which finding shows the infusion is causing harm?

options.text: Serum sodium of 123 mEq/L
options.rationale: Still low, but rising toward the reference range, which is the intended effect.

options.text: He opens his eyes to voice sooner than before
options.rationale: Neurologic status is watched closely on this infusion, and this change is an improvement.

options.text: Urine output of 60 mL per hour
options.rationale: Fluid balance is monitored on this infusion, and this output is adequate.

options.text: New crackles in both lung bases with dyspnea
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water into the vessels. Crackles with dyspnea are circulatory overload, a key risk of the infusion.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic saline draws water into the bloodstream. Monitor sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance, and treat new crackles as overload.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three findings are things you monitor that are moving the right way. One is the known risk showing up.

steps.detail: 123 mEq/L is up from 118.

steps.action: Check the brain and the kidneys
steps.detail: More responsive, and 60 mL per hour.
New crackles with dyspnea is the abnormal finding.

elimination.verdict: New crackles with dyspnea.

questions.objective: fluid and electrolyte balance in choosing a solution

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man's right forearm peripheral IV is removed before transfer. The site bleeds briefly and stops with pressure. Which note documents the removal completely?

options.text: Right forearm IV removed at 1410, pressure held until bleeding stopped, client transferred to the rehabilitation unit by wheelchair with belongings.
options.rationale: It has the time, but no tip check, no site appearance and no client tolerance. The transfer details belong in a different note.

options.text: Right forearm IV removed at 1410, catheter tip intact, site without redness or swelling, bleeding stopped with pressure, client tolerated removal without pain.
options.rationale: Time, tip integrity, site appearance and client tolerance are all recorded.

options.text: Right forearm IV removed, catheter tip intact, site without redness or swelling, gauze dressing applied to site, client tolerated removal without pain.
options.rationale: Nearly complete, but the time of removal is missing.

options.text: Right forearm IV removed at 1410, site without redness or swelling, bleeding stopped with pressure, gauze dressing applied, new IV not needed per provider.
options.rationale: It has time and site appearance but omits the tip check and how the client tolerated it.

questions.takeaway: A removal note records the time, the site appearance, that the catheter tip was intact, and how the client tolerated it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check each note for four things: time, tip, site, tolerance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One note has no time.
Two notes never mention the catheter tip.
Only one note has all four.

elimination.verdict: The note with time, tip, site appearance and tolerance.

questions.objective: document infusion care

questions.stem: An 88-year-old woman in long-term care has mild dehydration and poor oral intake. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Two nurses have each failed twice to place a peripheral IV in her fragile veins. Which route does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia
options.rationale: It delivers any IV fluid, but it is emergency access for arrest or trauma when IV fails. Her blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg.

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter
options.rationale: It would solve the access problem, but a PICC is for long-term therapy, vesicants or parenteral nutrition, not brief hydration.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen
options.rationale: Hypodermoclysis is used for mild to moderate dehydration in older adults, and the abdomen is a common site.

options.text: A peripheral IV in a dorsal vein of the foot
options.rationale: Lower extremities are avoided for IV sites in adults, and this would be a fifth attempt in fragile veins.

questions.takeaway: Mild to moderate dehydration in an older adult with no veins and a normal blood pressure is the case for hypodermoclysis.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match the size of the access to the size of the problem: mild dehydration, not an emergency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mild dehydration, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg.

steps.action: Cut the emergency and long-term devices
steps.detail: Intraosseous and PICC are more than she needs.
No foot veins in adults.

elimination.verdict: Subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen.

questions.objective: define infusion therapy, purposes and routes

questions.stem: An 88-year-old woman is receiving isotonic fluid by subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen. The nurse finds the pump set at 120 mL per hour. The site is soft and not painful. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Lower the rate to 60 mL per hour or less
options.rationale: The maximum for subcutaneous infusion is about 1 mL per minute, which is 60 mL per hour. The pump is running at twice that.

options.text: Keep the rate, because a soft site shows the fluid is absorbing
options.rationale: A soft, painless site is reassuring, but it does not change the maximum rate for this route.

options.text: Keep the rate and move the needle to the forearm
options.rationale: The usual sites are the abdomen, thighs and scapula. Moving the needle does not correct the rate.

options.text: Stop the infusion and ask for intraosseous access
options.rationale: Intraosseous access is for emergencies. The route is appropriate here; only the rate is wrong.

questions.takeaway: Subcutaneous infusion runs at about 1 mL per minute at most. Convert that to 60 mL per hour and compare it with the pump.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Convert the limit into the pump's units before judging the setting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 1 mL per minute is 60 mL per hour.
120 mL per hour is double the maximum.
The route and site are fine. The rate is not.

elimination.verdict: Lower the rate to 60 mL per hour or less.

questions.objective: define infusion therapy, purposes and routes

questions.stem: An 88-year-old woman receiving subcutaneous fluids becomes unresponsive, with blood pressure 72/40 mm Hg and heart rate 132 per minute. Two peripheral IV attempts fail. The rapid response team is at the bedside. Which access does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A faster subcutaneous infusion with a second site added
options.rationale: More fluid is the right goal, but subcutaneous infusion is avoided in shock.

options.text: An ultrasound-guided IV in a deep vein of the upper arm
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the standard for difficult access, so this is defensible. She is unresponsive and in shock, and IV attempts have already failed.

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter placed by the IV team
options.rationale: A PICC needs x-ray confirmation before use. It is not emergency access.

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia
options.rationale: Intraosseous access is rapid emergency access when IV fails, and it delivers all IV fluids, drugs and blood products.

questions.takeaway: When IV access fails in an emergency, go intraosseous. It takes every IV fluid and drug, and it is limited to 24 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ultrasound is the answer for difficult access with time to spare. Look at her blood pressure and responsiveness to see whether there is time.

steps.detail: Unresponsive at 72/40 mm Hg is shock.
Subcutaneous infusion is avoided in shock, and a PICC waits for an x-ray.

steps.action: Choose between the two fast options
steps.detail: IV has already failed twice, which is the trigger for intraosseous access.

elimination.verdict: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia.

questions.objective: define infusion therapy, purposes and routes

questions.stem: A nurse is inserting a peripheral IV near the left wrist of a 52-year-old woman. Blood appears in the flashback chamber, and she reports shooting pain with tingling into her thumb. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Advance the catheter, since the blood return confirms vein entry
options.rationale: The catheter may be in the vein, but shooting pain and tingling signal a nerve, and advancing can worsen the injury.

options.text: Pause for one minute, then secure it if the tingling fades
options.rationale: Pausing leaves the catheter against the nerve. These signs mean stop, not wait.

options.text: Stop, remove the catheter and assess sensation in the hand
options.rationale: Shooting pain and tingling during insertion are nerve injury signs: stop at once, remove the catheter and assess neurologic function.

options.text: Pull the catheter back slightly and redirect it at this site
options.rationale: Pulling back is partly right, but redirecting keeps the needle moving beside the nerve.

questions.takeaway: Shooting pain, burning, numbness or pins and needles during insertion means a nerve. Stop, take the catheter out, check function, then document and report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The blood return is there to make you feel the insertion succeeded. Her symptoms outrank it.

steps.detail: Shooting pain with tingling is a nerve sign.

steps.action: Cut every option that keeps the catheter in
steps.detail: Advance, wait and redirect all do.
Check sensation in the hand.

elimination.verdict: Stop, remove the catheter and assess sensation.

questions.objective: recognize complications

questions.scenario: A 52-year-old woman is receiving an IV antibiotic through a left forearm peripheral catheter. The site is red, warm and painful, with a red streak and a firm cord about 3 cm long along the vein.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.

rows.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
rows.rationale: Redness, warmth, pain, a streak and a cord are phlebitis. The infusion stops and the catheter comes out.

rows.text: Apply a warm moist compress to the site
rows.rationale: A warm moist compress is the comfort measure for phlebitis.

rows.text: Slow the infusion and keep the catheter for the next dose
rows.rationale: Slowing reduces irritation but leaves the catheter in an inflamed vein.

rows.text: Record the phlebitis grade in the chart
rows.rationale: Phlebitis is graded on a scale from 0 to 4 and the grade is documented.

rows.text: Tell the provider about the site findings
rows.rationale: Phlebitis is reported to the provider, and she still needs her antibiotic.

rows.text: Have assistive personnel assign the phlebitis grade
rows.rationale: Assistive personnel report how a site looks. Grading it is interpreting the findings, which stays with the registered nurse.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: stop, remove the catheter, warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade. The nurse, not assistive personnel, assigns the grade.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the complication from the streak and cord first. Then judge each action: does it treat phlebitis, and is the right person doing it?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red, warm, painful with a streak and cord is phlebitis, not infiltration.
Stop and remove, warm moist compress, notify, document the grade.

steps.action: Cut what keeps the catheter or hands off judgment
steps.detail: Keeping the catheter for the next dose, or having assistive personnel grade the site.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: r1, r2, r4, r5. Not indicated: r3, r6.

questions.objective: recognize complications

questions.stem: A 52-year-old right-handed woman had a left forearm IV removed for phlebitis. She needs 3 more days of IV antibiotics. Both arms have soft, visible veins. Which site does the nurse choose?

options.text: Right forearm, in a straight vein
options.rationale: The forearm is the preferred site, and the right arm is clear of the phlebitis. Using the dominant arm is acceptable.

options.text: Dorsal vein of the left hand, nondominant and most distal
options.rationale: Defensible on two rules, nondominant and distal first, but the left hand is distal to the phlebitis, which is a site to avoid.

options.text: Left antecubital fossa, above the old site
options.rationale: It is proximal to the phlebitis, which is the right direction, but the antecubital fossa is avoided for short peripheral catheters.

options.text: Left forearm, 2 cm below the old site
options.rationale: Forearm is the right region, but below the old site is distal to the phlebitis.

questions.takeaway: Never place a catheter distal to a prior phlebitis or infiltration. That rule outranks nondominant arm and most distal site first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options share one flaw: they sit below the inflamed vein. Remove them together.

steps.action: Cut the sites distal to phlebitis
steps.detail: Left hand and left forearm below the old site.
Antecubital fossa.
Right forearm uses her dominant arm, which is a preference only.

elimination.verdict: Right forearm.

questions.objective: vascular access devices

questions.stem: A 72-year-old reports 1 year of painless, slowly worsening blurred vision in both eyes, colors that look faded and trouble driving at night. The client blames the glasses and asks for a stronger pair. Which interpretation best fits these cues?

options.text: The pattern fits open angle glaucoma, so tonometry is the only test needed
options.rationale: Open angle glaucoma is also gradual and painless, but its cues are loss of side vision and halos, not faded colors and overall blur.

options.text: The pattern fits cataracts, so an eye examination is needed before new glasses
options.rationale: Painless, gradual blurring with faded colors and poor night driving is the cataract pattern, and clients often blame their glasses first.

options.text: The pattern fits presbyopia, so a stronger reading prescription should correct it
options.rationale: Presbyopia is an aging change too, but it affects near focus. It does not fade colors or single out night driving.

options.text: The pattern fits retinal detachment, so the client needs emergency surgery today
options.rationale: Retinal detachment is painless as well, but it is sudden, with flashes, floaters and a curtain. One year of slow change does not fit.

questions.takeaway: Painless, gradual blur plus faded colors plus night driving trouble points to cataracts. Glasses are often blamed first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four conditions can be painless. Sort them by speed of onset and by what kind of vision is lost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One year of slow change removes retinal detachment.
Faded colors and night driving point to the lens, not side vision or near focus.

elimination.verdict: Cataracts. Get the eyes examined before changing the glasses.

questions.objective: differentiating eye conditions by client cues

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with cataracts in both eyes can no longer read medication labels or cook safely because of blurred vision. The client asks whether eyedrops could clear the lenses. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Surgery is the only treatment, and it is done once the pupil has turned bluish white"
options.rationale: Right treatment, wrong trigger. A bluish white pupil describes a mature cataract. The timing is set by daily activities.

options.text: "Eyedrops used every day lower the pressure in the eye and slow the clouding of the lens"
options.rationale: Daily pressure lowering drops are glaucoma care. They do nothing for a cloudy lens.

options.text: "Surgery is the only treatment, and it is done once vision reaches 20/200 in the better eye"
options.rationale: 20/200 in the better eye is the line for legal blindness, not the trigger for cataract surgery.

options.text: "Surgery is the only treatment, and it is done once daily activities are affected"
options.rationale: Surgery is the only treatment for cataracts and it is timed by function. Unsafe cooking and unreadable labels meet that point.

questions.takeaway: Cataracts are treated only by surgery, and the timing is set by function: when daily activities are affected.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options name the right treatment. Compare the trigger each one attaches to it.

steps.detail: Pressure lowering drops belong to glaucoma.
Pupil color, an acuity number, or daily function. The stem gives a loss of function.

elimination.verdict: Surgery, timed by daily activities.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 72-year-old is going home 2 hours after phacoemulsification of the right eye with a lens implant. Which statement shows that the discharge teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will not bend over to tie my shoes or carry my 20 lb laundry basket"
options.rationale: Bending, straining and lifting more than 10 lb raise the pressure inside the eye after surgery. This client avoids both.

options.text: "I will put on my dark glasses whenever the right eye starts to hurt in bright light"
options.rationale: Dark glasses are correct, but they are worn after surgery as protection, not only once the eye already hurts.

options.text: "I should have my best vision in the right eye by the end of the first week"
options.rationale: Vision does improve, but the best vision is reached at 4 to 6 weeks. Expecting it in one week sets up a false alarm or false reassurance.

options.text: "If I get sudden pain in the right eye, I will rest and mention it at my next visit"
options.rationale: Sudden pain is on the report list. It is reported when it happens, not held for the next visit.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery: dark glasses, no bending, no straining, no lifting more than 10 lb, report sudden pain or vision loss, best vision at 4 to 6 weeks.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each statement holds a correct topic. Look for the one with nothing off in timing or amount.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glasses only when it hurts, best vision in one week and waiting to report sudden pain each have one wrong detail.
20 lb is more than 10 lb, so leaving the basket to someone else is right.

elimination.verdict: No bending and no heavy lifting.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: Two days after cataract removal from the right eye, a 72-year-old phones the clinic. The right eye felt mildly scratchy yesterday. One hour ago it developed sudden sharp pain, and vision in that eye is now dimmer. Which advice is best?

options.text: Tell the client to rest with dark glasses on and to call again if the pain lasts 24 hours
options.rationale: Rest and dark glasses fit the mild scratchiness of yesterday. The new cues are sudden pain and dimmer vision, which cannot wait a day.

options.text: Tell the client that the best vision is not reached until 4 to 6 weeks after the surgery
options.rationale: True, and it would answer a client whose vision is slowly clearing. It does not explain vision that got worse within an hour.

options.text: Tell the client that sudden pain with vision loss must be examined by the surgeon today
options.rationale: Sudden pain and vision loss are the two findings the client is taught to report after cataract surgery. Both are present, so the eye is examined now.

options.text: Tell the client to stop bending and lifting, then recheck the right eye in the morning
options.rationale: Avoiding bending and lifting is correct aftercare, but it is prevention. It does not deal with a complication that has already started.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, sudden pain or sudden vision loss is reported and examined right away. Slow improvement over 4 to 6 weeks is the expected course.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Yesterday's scratchiness and today's pain are different findings. Answer the newest cue, and note the word sudden.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mild scratchiness was yesterday. Sudden sharp pain and dimmer vision began one hour ago.
Sudden pain and vision loss are both on it.

steps.action: Drop the true but off target option
steps.detail: 4 to 6 weeks explains slow clearing, not sudden dimming.

elimination.verdict: Seen by the surgeon today.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 64-year-old African American client whose father had glaucoma has no eye symptoms at a wellness visit. Tonometry reads 26 mmHg in each eye. Which conclusion should guide the nurse's next step?

options.text: The pressure is high, and having no symptoms does not rule out open angle glaucoma
options.rationale: 26 mmHg is above normal and inside the open angle range of 22 to 32 mmHg. This type often has no symptoms until late, and the client has two risk factors.

options.text: The pressure is high, and the client needs emergency laser treatment within the hour
options.rationale: Emergency laser care belongs to angle closure, which shows sudden pain, redness and pressures of 30 mmHg or more.

options.text: The pressure is acceptable at age 64, so the next screening is due in one year
options.rationale: Yearly screening after 40 is right, but 26 mmHg is not an acceptable reading at any age.

options.text: The pressure is high, and referral can wait until halos or side vision loss appear
options.rationale: The reading is judged correctly, but waiting for symptoms means waiting for nerve damage that cannot be reversed.

questions.takeaway: Open angle glaucoma is often silent. A pressure of 22 to 32 mmHg in a client at risk is acted on without waiting for symptoms.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options call the pressure high. Decide between them on urgency: emergency, referral now, or wait for symptoms.

steps.detail: 26 mmHg is above normal, so the option calling it acceptable goes.
No pain, no redness and under 30 mmHg rule out the emergency.
Symptoms in this type mean damage is already done.

elimination.verdict: High pressure with no symptoms still needs follow up.

questions.objective: eye assessment and health promotion

questions.stem: A 64-year-old reports bumping into door frames on both sides for several months, halos around lights and a mild ache in both eyes. Reading vision straight ahead is unchanged. Which problem should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma, because halos and aching mean the pressure is rising
options.rationale: Pressure is the shared idea, but angle closure is sudden, with severe pain, a red eye and vision loss, not months of mild aching.

options.text: Cataracts, because the change is gradual and affects both of the eyes
options.rationale: Cataracts are gradual and often in both eyes, but they blur the whole image and fade colors. This client's straight ahead vision is unchanged.

options.text: Open angle glaucoma, because side vision is lost first and onset is gradual
options.rationale: Gradual loss of side vision with halos and a mild ache is the open angle pattern. Damage moves from the edge of the visual field toward the center.

options.text: Retinal detachment, because part of the visual field is missing in each eye
options.rationale: A missing part of the field fits, but detachment is sudden, with flashes and floaters, and comes on as a curtain.

questions.takeaway: Gradual loss of side vision, halos and mild aching with central vision kept: think open angle glaucoma.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use two sorters: how fast it came on, and which part of the vision is lost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Several months removes angle closure and retinal detachment.
Side vision gone with central vision kept is not the overall blur of a cataract.

elimination.verdict: Open angle glaucoma.

questions.objective: differentiating eye conditions by client cues

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with open angle glaucoma and a resting heart rate of 58 per minute is starting beta blocker eyedrops. Which instruction best limits the amount of drug that reaches the rest of the body?

options.text: Count the pulse before each dose and leave out the drop when it is below 60
options.rationale: Checking the pulse is reasonable, but skipping doses breaks the strict adherence glaucoma drops need, and it does not reduce absorption.

options.text: Blink quickly several times after each drop to spread the drug across the eye
options.rationale: Blinking does not close the drainage point, so it does nothing to limit absorption into the body.

options.text: Put in half of the prescribed number of drops until the heart rate is above 60
options.rationale: Changing the dose is not the client's or the nurse's decision, and under treating lets the pressure keep damaging the nerve.

options.text: Press a finger on the inner corner of the eye beside the nose after each drop
options.rationale: This is punctal occlusion. It closes the tear drainage point so less drug is absorbed into the body.

questions.takeaway: Punctal occlusion after each eyedrop limits systemic absorption. It lets the client stay on the full prescribed dose.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The question asks how to limit absorption, not how to monitor the heart. Only one option changes where the drug goes.

steps.detail: It asks about drug reaching the rest of the body.

steps.action: Drop the options that cut doses
steps.detail: Skipping and halving both break adherence.
Pressing the inner corner blocks drainage. Blinking does not.

elimination.verdict: Punctal occlusion.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: After 6 months of prostaglandin eyedrops, a 64-year-old with open angle glaucoma has a pressure of 16 mmHg in each eye. The client says, "My side vision has not come back, so the drops failed." Which response is best?

options.text: "The drops did not work for you, so laser trabeculoplasty is the next step to discuss"
options.rationale: Laser trabeculoplasty is the right next step when drops fail. Here the pressure is normal, so they have not failed.

options.text: "The drops are working. They prevent more loss, cannot restore vision, and are lifelong"
options.rationale: The goal of glaucoma treatment is to prevent further damage, not to restore vision, and it is lifelong. A pressure of 16 mmHg shows the drops are doing that.

options.text: "The drops are working. With the pressure normal you can stop them and be checked yearly"
options.rationale: The first half is right. Stopping is wrong, because treatment is lifelong and the pressure rises again without it.

options.text: "The drops are working. A new glasses prescription will bring the side vision back"
options.rationale: Vision lost to open angle glaucoma is not reversible with glasses.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma treatment prevents further damage. It does not restore lost vision, and it is lifelong.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge the drops by the pressure, not by the vision that was already lost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 16 mmHg is normal, so the drops have not failed.

steps.action: Check the second half of each remaining option
steps.detail: Stopping the drops and glasses restoring side vision are both false.

elimination.verdict: Working, not restoring, lifelong.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with open angle glaucoma had pressures of 17 mmHg on prostaglandin eyedrops 6 months ago. Today both eyes read 27 mmHg. Pharmacy records show one bottle refilled in 6 months. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask how the client has been using the drops and what makes daily use difficult
options.rationale: The pressure was controlled on these drops and only one bottle was refilled in 6 months. The likely cause is missed doses, and strict adherence is the point of treatment.

options.text: Prepare the client for teaching about laser trabeculoplasty as the next treatment
options.rationale: Laser treatment follows when drops fail. Drops that have not been used have not failed, and the refill record shows that gap.

options.text: Reteach punctal occlusion so that more of each drop stays in the eye
options.rationale: Good technique teaching, but it limits systemic absorption. It does not fix drops that are not being put in.

options.text: Ask the provider to add a second class of pressure lowering eyedrops
options.rationale: Adding a drug is reasonable when one drug taken as prescribed is not enough. Adding a second bottle to a client who is not using the first solves nothing.

questions.takeaway: When glaucoma pressure rises on a drug that worked before, check adherence before deciding the drug failed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options treat this as drug failure. One stated cue, the refill record, says the drug was not tested.

steps.detail: One bottle in 6 months.
Laser and a second drug both assume the first drug was taken.

steps.action: Pick the option that involves the client
steps.detail: Asking about use finds the real barrier.

elimination.verdict: Explore how the drops are being used.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 68-year-old who does not wear contact lenses and reports no injury has severe left eye pain that began suddenly 1 hour ago, with blurred vision, a red conjunctiva and a hazy cornea. Which interpretation should direct triage?

options.text: Open angle glaucoma is likely, so the client needs a clinic visit this week
options.rationale: Glaucoma is the right family, but the open angle type is gradual and often without symptoms. It does not start with sudden severe pain.

options.text: Retinal detachment is likely, so the client needs an eye patch and bed rest
options.rationale: Detachment is also sudden and an emergency, but it is painless and shows flashes, floaters and a curtain, not a red eye.

options.text: Corneal abrasion is likely, so the client needs fluorescein staining in turn
options.rationale: A painful eye with a hazy cornea can be an abrasion, but this client has no lens wear or injury to cause one, and a red eye with sudden vision loss fits a pressure emergency.

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma is likely, so the client needs emergency eye care now
options.rationale: Sudden pain, vision loss, redness and corneal edema are the angle closure pattern, and angle closure is a medical emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden eye pain with vision loss, a red eye and a hazy cornea is angle closure glaucoma until shown otherwise. It is an emergency.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Pain separates this from retinal detachment. Sudden onset separates it from open angle glaucoma. No injury or lens wear weakens abrasion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Retinal detachment is painless.
One hour, not months.
No contact lenses and no injury.

elimination.verdict: Angle closure glaucoma, treated as an emergency.

questions.objective: differentiating eye conditions by client cues

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has sudden left eye pain, redness and vision loss that began 2 hours ago. Tonometry reads 44 mmHg in the left eye and 15 mmHg in the right eye. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Start daily pressure lowering eyedrops and recheck the left eye in one week
options.rationale: Drops are how raised pressure is usually managed, and that fits the gradual open angle type. A sudden rise to 44 mmHg with pain cannot wait a week.

options.text: Prepare the client for emergency laser peripheral iridotomy on the left eye
options.rationale: A pressure of 30 mmHg or more with sudden pain, redness and vision loss is angle closure. Laser peripheral iridotomy is the first line emergency treatment.

options.text: Schedule laser trabeculoplasty for the left eye once a trial of eyedrops fails
options.rationale: A laser procedure is right, but trabeculoplasty is the step after drops fail in open angle glaucoma.

options.text: Begin fluorescein staining, then antibiotic eyedrops every hour to the left eye
options.rationale: Staining and hourly antibiotics are the corneal infection plan. They do not open blocked drainage or lower the pressure.

questions.takeaway: Pressure of 30 mmHg or more with sudden pain is angle closure. First line emergency treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options are real glaucoma treatments. The speed of onset and the size of the number decide which type this is.

steps.action: Read the number with the onset
steps.detail: 44 mmHg and 2 hours, not the 20s over months.
Iridotomy is the emergency one. Trabeculoplasty follows failed drops.
It treats infection.

elimination.verdict: Emergency laser peripheral iridotomy.

questions.objective: eye function and intraocular pressure

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with sudden left eye pain, a red left eye and a left eye pressure of 44 mmHg asks to go home and return tomorrow when her daughter can drive. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Glaucoma takes vision slowly over years, so one night is safe if you return in the morning"
options.rationale: Slow loss over years is true of open angle glaucoma. This sudden, painful rise is the other type.

options.text: "You may go home if the pain medicine works, and come back sooner if the pain returns"
options.rationale: Treating pain is kind, but it hides the cue while the pressure keeps damaging the nerve.

options.text: "Pressure this high starves the nerve of blood and the damage is permanent, so we treat now"
options.rationale: Raised pressure compresses the retinal vessels and nerve fibers, which causes ischemia and permanent nerve damage. Angle closure is an emergency.

options.text: "You may go home if you wear dark glasses and avoid bending or lifting until tomorrow"
options.rationale: Those are aftercare measures for eye surgery. They do not lower a pressure of 44 mmHg.

questions.takeaway: High pressure in the eye starves the nerve of blood, and the loss is permanent. Angle closure is treated now, not tomorrow.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options allow her to leave. Ask what the pressure is doing to the eye while she waits.

steps.detail: Only one option keeps her for treatment.
Slow loss belongs to the other type, and pain relief or dark glasses do not lower pressure.

elimination.verdict: Treat now, because the damage is permanent.

questions.objective: eye function and intraocular pressure

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with extreme nearsightedness reports that 2 hours ago he suddenly saw flashes of light and new floaters in the right eye, then a dark curtain across part of his vision. He has no pain. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: Retinal detachment is likely, and it is an emergency even though he has no pain
options.rationale: Sudden flashes, floaters and a curtain with no pain are the classic cues, and extreme myopia is a risk factor. Retinal detachment is an emergency.

options.text: Retinal detachment is possible, but with no pain a routine visit this week is enough
options.rationale: The condition is named correctly. The error is using pain to set urgency, because detachment is painless.

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma is likely, and he needs his eye pressure lowered at once
options.rationale: Angle closure is also a sudden emergency, but it brings severe pain and a red eye.

options.text: A cataract is likely, since painless vision change is expected at his age
options.rationale: Cataracts are painless too, but they develop gradually with blur and faded colors, not in 2 hours with a curtain.

questions.takeaway: Sudden, painless flashes, floaters and a curtain mean retinal detachment. Painless does not mean it can wait.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Do not let the absence of pain lower the urgency. Use sudden plus curtain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 hours removes cataract.
No pain removes angle closure.
Detachment is an emergency without pain.

elimination.verdict: Retinal detachment, emergency.

questions.objective: differentiating eye conditions by client cues

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man waiting for scleral buckling surgery for a right retinal detachment wants to walk the hall and read on his phone to pass the time. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Let him read in bed, since close work is restricted only in the week after surgery
options.rationale: Close work is restricted after surgery, but reading moves the eyes, and reducing eye movement is the goal before surgery as well.

options.text: Let him walk the hall wearing dark glasses, with a staff member beside him
options.rationale: Dark glasses and an escort address light and falls. Walking still breaks the activity and head movement restriction.

options.text: Keep him resting with head movement limited and apply the prescribed eye patch
options.rationale: Before surgery, activity and head movement are restricted and the eye is patched to reduce eye movement. Walking and reading both work against that.

options.text: Keep him in bed and begin the position he will need after the gas bubble is placed
options.rationale: Positioning is set by the surgeon after the procedure. The care before surgery is restricted movement and a patch.

questions.takeaway: Before retinal detachment surgery: restrict activity and head movement, and patch the eye to reduce eye movement.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: He asks for two things. Both move the head or the eyes, so look for the option that limits both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Less head movement and less eye movement.
Walking moves the head. Reading moves the eyes.
Positioning comes from the surgeon after the procedure.

elimination.verdict: Rest, limited head movement, eye patch.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.scenario: A 61-year-old man is going home after scleral buckling surgery with a gas bubble in the right eye. The nurse evaluates his statements about care at home.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or a need for more teaching.

rows.text: "I will not read or do other close work for the first week."
rows.rationale: Reading and close work are avoided for the first week after surgery.

rows.text: "If I get eye pain with nausea, I will take something for the nausea and wait for my appointment."
rows.rationale: Pain with nausea is reported immediately. Treating the nausea hides a warning sign.

rows.text: "I will have someone else carry the groceries, and I will not bend over."
rows.rationale: Lifting and bending raise the pressure inside the eye, and those activities are avoided after surgery.

rows.text: "A sudden change in my vision is part of healing, so I do not need to call about it."
rows.rationale: Sudden vision changes are reported immediately.

rows.text: "I will keep my head in the position my surgeon showed me."
rows.rationale: Positioning after this surgery follows the surgeon's instructions.

rows.text: "Sudden pain in the eye is expected, so I will mention it at my next visit."
rows.rationale: Sudden pain is reported immediately, not at the next visit.

questions.takeaway: After retinal detachment repair: keep the surgeon's position, avoid bending, lifting and close work for the first week, and report sudden pain, pain with nausea or sudden vision change at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sort the statements into restrictions he keeps and warning signs he reports. Any plan to wait on a sudden symptom needs more teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position, no close work, no lifting or bending are all correct.
Sudden pain, pain with nausea and sudden vision change are each reported immediately.

elimination.verdict: Understands: r1, r3, r5. Needs teaching: r2, r4, r6.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: Eight weeks after scleral buckling repair of a right retinal detachment, a 61-year-old man with extreme nearsightedness is cleared by his surgeon to play racquetball again. He asks how to lower his chance of another detachment. Which teaching fits best?

options.text: Wear sunglasses outdoors, because ultraviolet light is what detaches the retina
options.rationale: Sunglasses are real eye protection, but ultraviolet light is tied to cataracts and ocular melanoma. It does not address the trauma risk of a ball sport.

options.text: Wear protective eyewear for every game, because eye trauma is a risk factor
options.rationale: Eye trauma is a risk factor for retinal detachment, and eye protection is taught for sports. A fast ball near the face is the hazard he can control.

options.text: Keep limiting head movement and close work, as in the first week after surgery
options.rationale: Those limits are correct around the surgery itself. At eight weeks, cleared for sport, they no longer apply and they do not protect the eye from a ball.

options.text: Have a yearly eye examination, because screening keeps the retina attached
options.rationale: Yearly screening after 40 is right and finds problems early. It detects damage. It does not prevent an injury on the court.

questions.takeaway: Eye trauma is a risk factor for retinal detachment. Protective eyewear for sports and work hazards is the prevention the client controls.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are real eye health teaching. Match the teaching to the hazard in the stem, a ball sport.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Racquetball means a risk of a blow to the eye, and trauma is a detachment risk factor.
Ultraviolet light is a cataract risk. Screening detects and does not prevent. First week limits have ended.

elimination.verdict: Protective eyewear every game.

questions.objective: eye assessment and health promotion

questions.stem: A 24-year-old who sleeps in contact lenses has right eye pain, tearing and a cloudy right cornea. Fluorescein shows a green stained area. The client asks to come back next week after exams. What is the nurse's best judgment?

options.text: Treatment can wait a week, as long as the client leaves the contact lenses out
options.rationale: Leaving the lenses out is correct and is part of care. It does not treat an injury that is already at risk of infection.

options.text: Treatment waits until tonometry rules out angle closure glaucoma as the cause of the pain
options.rationale: Angle closure also gives a painful eye with a hazy cornea. Here the staining and the lens wear already explain the pain.

options.text: Treatment is saline irrigation today, and the client then returns after exams
options.rationale: Irrigation is how a loose foreign body is handled. A stained, cloudy cornea needs antibiotics.

options.text: Treatment starts today, because the cornea has no blood supply of its own
options.rationale: A cloudy cornea with green staining after contact lens wear is a corneal abrasion or ulcer. With no separate blood supply, the risk of infection makes this an emergency.

questions.takeaway: A cloudy cornea that stains green is a corneal injury. The cornea has no separate blood supply, so infection risk makes it an emergency.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The staining result is already in the stem, so the cause is known. The question is how soon to treat.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Green staining plus lens wear explains the pain.
No blood supply means infection is an emergency, so a week is out.
Irrigation alone is for a loose foreign body.

elimination.verdict: Treat today.

questions.objective: differentiating eye conditions by client cues

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with a right corneal ulcer is prescribed broad spectrum antibiotic eyedrops every hour for the first 24 hours. The client plans to sleep through the night and catch up in the morning. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Set an alarm and give every hourly dose overnight for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: The drops are ordered hourly for the first 24 hours because the infection is an emergency. That schedule includes the night.

options.text: Use the drops every hour while awake, then put in several drops on waking
options.rationale: Hourly use is right, but only for part of the day. Extra drops later do not replace the missed hours.

options.text: Use the drops every hour until the pain eases, then switch to morning and night
options.rationale: Hourly dosing is right, but the end point is wrong. The schedule is set by the order, and the full course is completed.

options.text: Sleep tonight to help healing, and wear the contact lens only during the day
options.rationale: Rest is reasonable, but it gives up the hourly dosing, and contact lenses stay out until the cornea is fully healed.

questions.takeaway: For corneal infection, antibiotic drops are often ordered hourly for the first 24 hours. Hourly means day and night.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options keep some hourly dosing. Find the one that keeps all 24 hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every hour for the first 24 hours.
While awake only, until the pain eases, and sleeping all shorten it.

elimination.verdict: Every hour, including overnight.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 24-year-old being treated with antibiotic eyedrops for corneal infection in both eyes reports on day 4 that the pain is gone. Which statements show that the client understood the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I use one bottle for the right eye and a different bottle for the left eye."
options.rationale: When both eyes are infected, each eye has its own bottle.

options.text: "Now that the pain is gone, I wear my contact lenses for a few hours each day."
options.rationale: No pain is not the same as healed. Contact lenses stay out until the cornea is fully healed.

options.text: "I will finish all of the antibiotic even though my eyes feel normal."
options.rationale: The full antibiotic course is completed.

options.text: "I will keep the leftover drops in case this happens again."
options.rationale: There should be no leftover drops, because the full course is completed.

options.text: "My contact lenses stay out until I am told the cornea has fully healed."
options.rationale: No contact lenses until the cornea is fully healed.

options.text: "I use the same bottle for both eyes but wipe the tip between them."
options.rationale: Wiping the tip shows concern for spread, but the teaching is a separate bottle for each eye.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infection teaching: a separate bottle for each eye, finish the full antibiotic course, no contact lenses until fully healed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Pain relief is the trap. Judge each statement against the three teaching points, not against how the eyes feel.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Separate for each eye. Wiping a shared tip is not the same.
Finished, so nothing is left over.
Out until fully healed, not until the pain stops.

elimination.verdict: A, C and E.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 35-year-old machinist felt grit blow into the right eye 20 minutes ago. The eye is tearing, irritated and sensitive to light. A loose speck lies on the surface of the eye, and nothing protrudes from it. Which plan fits?

options.text: Leave the speck untouched until the eye care provider arrives to remove it
options.rationale: That is the rule for a protruding object in a penetrating injury. This speck is loose on the surface and nothing protrudes.

options.text: Send the client for a CT scan of the orbit before the right eye is touched
options.rationale: CT is used when a fragment may be inside the eye. A loose speck on the surface does not call for imaging first.

options.text: Assist with a fluorescein examination and saline irrigation of the right eye
options.rationale: Irritation, tearing and photophobia with a loose surface speck are the cues of a foreign body, which is treated with a fluorescein exam and saline irrigation.

options.text: Start antibiotic eyedrops every hour and have the client return in 24 hours
options.rationale: Hourly antibiotics treat a corneal infection. They leave the foreign body in the eye.

questions.takeaway: A loose foreign body on the eye surface gets a fluorescein exam and saline irrigation. The hands off rule is for an object that protrudes or penetrates.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two safety rules compete: irrigate a foreign body, never remove a protruding object. The stem says which kind this is.

steps.detail: Loose on the surface, nothing protruding.
Surface foreign body means stain and irrigate.

steps.action: Drop the plans for other problems
steps.detail: CT is for a fragment inside the eye. Hourly antibiotics are for infection.

elimination.verdict: Fluorescein exam and saline irrigation.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 35-year-old machinist arrives after a nail gun accident with a metal fragment protruding from the left eye. He asks the nurse to pull it out because it hurts. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the left eye with saline to wash away loose metal around the fragment
options.rationale: Saline irrigation is right for a surface foreign body. This object has penetrated the eye.

options.text: Leave the fragment as it is for the eye care provider to assess and remove
options.rationale: A protruding object is never removed by the nurse. Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.

options.text: Ease the fragment out gently, then cover the left eye until the provider arrives
options.rationale: Covering the eye sounds protective, but removing the object is the one thing the nurse must not do.

options.text: Stain the left eye with fluorescein to see how much of the cornea is damaged
options.rationale: Fluorescein is used for abrasions and surface foreign bodies. Assessment of a penetrating injury belongs to the eye care provider.

questions.takeaway: Never remove a protruding object from the eye. Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The word protruding changes every rule. Actions that are right for a surface speck become wrong here.

steps.detail: Protruding means penetrating.
Irrigation and fluorescein belong to a foreign body on the surface.
Never by the nurse.

elimination.verdict: Leave it in place for the eye care provider.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: A 35-year-old machinist may have a metal fragment inside the left eye after a nail gun accident. Orders before surgery are: MRI of the orbits, CT of the orbits, IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster. Which order should the nurse question?

options.text: The CT of the orbits
options.rationale: CT or X-ray is the preferred imaging when metal may be in the eye.

options.text: The IV antibiotics
options.rationale: IV antibiotics are given before surgery for a penetrating eye injury.

options.text: The tetanus booster
options.rationale: A tetanus booster is given before surgery for a penetrating eye injury.

options.text: The MRI of the orbits
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected, because the magnet can move the metal and cause further injury.

questions.takeaway: Suspected metal in the eye: no MRI. Use X-ray or CT, and give IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster before surgery.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the one unsafe order. The word metal should stop you at the magnet.

steps.detail: Three orders are correct and one is not.
CT is preferred. MRI is contraindicated with metal.

elimination.verdict: Question the MRI.

questions.objective: priority care, treatment, teaching and prevention

questions.stem: An alert 78-year-old admitted after 2 days of vomiting has dry looking eyes and yellowish sclerae. Assistive personnel say she looks dehydrated and jaundiced. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Recheck her sclerae and tear film in brighter light to confirm both findings
options.rationale: Rechecking is assessment, but it repeats the same unreliable cue. In an older adult the eyes are not used to judge hydration or jaundice, however good the light.

options.text: Record both findings as normal aging and continue routine care for the shift
options.rationale: The eye findings may be aging, but 2 days of vomiting is a real risk for fluid loss that still has to be assessed.

options.text: Assess her hydration and skin color using findings other than the eyes
options.rationale: In older adults the eyes are not used to judge hydration or jaundice, because aging reduces tear production and changes eye appearance. Two days of vomiting still call for an assessment.

options.text: Begin hourly oral fluids now, because dry eyes confirm that she is dehydrated
options.rationale: Fluids may be needed, but dry eyes confirm nothing in an older adult, and she has been vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Do not use the appearance of the sclera or eyes to judge hydration or jaundice in an older adult. Assess another way.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options rely on the eyes and one dismisses the client. Find the option that neither trusts the eyes nor ignores the vomiting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eye appearance is unreliable at 78.
2 days of vomiting still needs a hydration assessment.
Use findings other than the eyes. Looking at the sclerae again only repeats the unreliable cue.

elimination.verdict: Assess hydration and color another way.

questions.objective: age related vision changes

questions.stem: A 78-year-old who is alert and oriented has knocked over her water glass twice in her dim room at night. She also cannot tell her blue pill box from her green one. Which change to the plan best fits these cues?

options.text: Add more light to the room and mark the pill boxes in contrasting colors
options.rationale: The aging pupil dilates less, so she adapts poorly to the dark and needs more light. Aging also reduces the ability to tell blues, greens and violets apart.

options.text: Keep the room dim to spare her eyes and relabel the pill boxes in violet
options.rationale: Reducing glare is a real goal, but she needs more light, not less, and violet is one of the colors she tells apart poorly.

options.text: Ask for an evaluation of new confusion, since she is mixing up her pill boxes
options.rationale: Mixing up pills can signal confusion, but she is alert and oriented and both cues are explained by aging eyes.

options.text: Add more light to the room and have staff give all of her pills from now on
options.rationale: The lighting is right. Taking over her pills removes independence when a contrast label solves the problem.

questions.takeaway: Aging eyes need more light and lose blue, green and violet discrimination. Fix the environment before blaming the mind or taking over.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Both cues are about seeing, not thinking. Look for the option that fixes light and color and takes nothing away from her.

steps.detail: Poor dark adaptation and poor blue and green discrimination.
Both make the problem worse.
Contrast labels keep her managing her own pills.

elimination.verdict: More light and contrasting colors.

questions.objective: age related vision changes

questions.stem: A 78-year-old wearing her glasses reads 20/200 with the right eye and 20/40 with the left eye on the Snellen chart. Her daughter asks whether she now counts as legally blind. Which response is accurate?

options.text: "Yes. A reading of 20/200 with glasses on in either eye meets the definition"
options.rationale: 20/200 with correction is the right number, and that is why this is tempting. The definition uses the best eye, not either eye.

options.text: "No. It is judged by the better eye with glasses on, and that eye reads 20/40"
options.rationale: Legal blindness is 20/200 or worse in the best eye with correction. Her better eye reads 20/40, so she does not meet it.

options.text: "No. Legal blindness is judged without glasses, so she needs to be tested again"
options.rationale: The measurement is taken with correction, which is how she was tested.

options.text: "Yes. Her right eye qualifies, and her left eye is also below the normal 20/20"
options.rationale: Neither fact meets the definition. One eye at 20/200 is not enough, and 20/40 is far from 20/200.

questions.takeaway: Legally blind means 20/200 or worse in the best eye with correction. One poor eye does not meet it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The number 20/200 is in the stem to pull you to yes. Check which eye the definition uses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 20/200 or worse, best eye, corrected.
She was tested with glasses. Her best eye is the left at 20/40.

elimination.verdict: No, because her better eye reads 20/40.

questions.objective: eye assessment and health promotion

questions.stem: A 78-year-old admitted for pneumonia heard the television at a usual volume last week. For 2 days the client has not heard speech from the left side. The daughter says it is just old age. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Record the loss as an expected aging change and continue routine care
options.rationale: Aging changes come on gradually. A drop over 2 days in one ear is new, and a new change is not assumed to be age related.

options.text: Check the left ear canal for patency and ask how the loss began
options.rationale: A new, one sided change needs an individual assessment. Canal patency and onset are the first data, and dry cerumen impacts easily in older adults.

options.text: Ask the provider for a hearing aid referral before discharge
options.rationale: A hearing aid may help some losses, but the cause of this 2 day change has not been looked for yet.

options.text: Speak into the right ear for the remainder of the hospital stay
options.rationale: Moving to the better ear is a sound way to communicate. It works around the new loss without finding its cause.

questions.takeaway: A new or sudden hearing change is not assumed to be aging. Assess each older adult individually, starting with onset and the canal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The daughter's explanation is the trap. Two days and one ear do not match a slow aging change.

steps.detail: Last week normal, 2 days of loss on the left.

steps.action: Cut the option that accepts the label
steps.detail: Documenting it as aging ends the assessment.
Referral and using the right ear both skip the cause.

elimination.verdict: Check the left canal and ask about onset.

questions.objective: age related ear changes

questions.stem: A 78-year-old has impacted cerumen in the left ear. A ceruminolytic was given and irrigation is ordered. Which finding in the left ear leads the nurse to hold the irrigation?

options.text: A feeling of fullness that began 2 days ago
options.rationale: Fullness is a sign of the impaction itself. It is the reason for the irrigation.

options.text: Itching deep inside the canal since yesterday
options.rationale: Itching is a listed sign of cerumen impaction and does not make irrigation unsafe.

options.text: Mild dizziness when the client stands up
options.rationale: Dizziness can come with impaction. It calls for help with standing, and it does not by itself forbid irrigation.

options.text: Ear pain with a temperature of 38.4 C
options.rationale: Pain with fever suggests otitis media. Irrigation is never done when otitis media or a perforated eardrum is suspected, because it spreads infection.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate an ear when otitis media or eardrum perforation is suspected. Fullness, itching, hearing loss and dizziness are the expected signs of impaction.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three of the findings are the impaction itself. Find the one that points to infection behind the eardrum.

steps.detail: Fullness, itching and dizziness are on the impaction list.
Pain plus 38.4 C is not explained by wax.
Suspected otitis media means no irrigation.

elimination.verdict: Ear pain with fever of 38.4 C.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 78-year-old had impacted cerumen removed from the left ear. The canal is now clear. With that ear the client hears a man's low voice but still misses a granddaughter's high voice. What does the nurse plan next?

options.text: Ask about a referral to an audiologist for audiometry
options.rationale: High pitched sounds are lost first with aging. The canal is clear, so the remaining loss needs audiometry, the most reliable hearing measurement.

options.text: Request a second irrigation of the left ear canal
options.rationale: Irrigation treats a blocked canal. The stem says the canal is clear, so more irrigation cannot help.

options.text: Tell the family that hearing is restored now that the canal is clear
options.rationale: The low voice is heard, but the high voice is still missed. The outcome is only partly met.

options.text: Start a ceruminolytic twice a day to keep the canal clear
options.rationale: A ceruminolytic softens wax before removal. No wax remains to explain a loss of high pitches.

questions.takeaway: In aging, high frequency sounds are lost first. When a clear canal does not restore them, refer for audiometry.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The pattern of what is heard and missed tells you this is not a wax problem any more.
