steps.detail: Canal clear, low voice heard, high voice missed.
Irrigation and a ceruminolytic both treat wax that is gone.
Hearing is not restored, so it needs measurement.

elimination.verdict: Ask about audiometry with an audiologist.

questions.objective: age related ear changes

questions.stem: An audiologist reports that a 78-year-old has a 30 dB hearing loss in both ears. The nurse must give discharge teaching on a busy unit. Which plan fits this result?

options.text: Stand right next to the client's ear for every sentence
options.rationale: Being right next to the speaker is needed at a 71 to 90 dB loss. This client's loss is 30 dB.

options.text: Give all of the teaching in writing and skip the spoken review
options.rationale: Written material supports teaching. A 30 dB loss does not stop the client from hearing speech in a quiet place.

options.text: Teach face to face in a quiet room with the door closed
options.rationale: A 20 to 40 dB loss causes mild difficulty in noise. Removing the noise and facing the client is the matching plan.

options.text: Raise the voice to a shout so it carries over the unit noise
options.rationale: Shouting is avoided with hearing loss. The problem at 30 dB is background noise, which a quiet room removes.

questions.takeaway: A 20 to 40 dB loss means mild difficulty in noise, so control the noise. A 71 to 90 dB loss means the listener must be right next to the speaker.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Match the plan to the number. One option is the right plan for a much larger loss.

steps.detail: It falls in the 20 to 40 dB range.

steps.action: Name the problem at that level
steps.detail: Mild difficulty in noise.

steps.action: Cut the plans for worse loss
steps.detail: Standing at the ear and writing everything fit a severe loss.

elimination.verdict: Teach face to face in a quiet room.

questions.objective: hearing assessment

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on day 2 of an IV aminoglycoside antibiotic reports muffled hearing only in the right ear, with fullness and itching in that ear. The left ear is unchanged and there is no ringing. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the next antibiotic dose until audiometry is completed
options.rationale: Holding the drug is right when the cues point to ototoxicity. Fullness and itching in one ear point to the canal, and that has not been checked.

options.text: Instil a ceruminolytic into the right ear canal
options.rationale: A ceruminolytic is the treatment if wax is found. Giving it before looking at the canal treats a guess.

options.text: Move to the client's left side when giving instructions
options.rationale: Using the better ear helps communication. It does not find out why the right ear changed.

options.text: Inspect the right ear canal for patency
options.rationale: One ear, fullness and itching are the signs of cerumen impaction, a conductive and often correctable cause. Canal patency is the missing piece before the drug is blamed.

questions.takeaway: Fullness, itching and hearing loss in one ear suggest cerumen impaction. Check canal patency before deciding a hearing change is drug damage.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Holding the drug and checking the canal are both defensible. Fullness and itching on one side tip it to the canal.

steps.detail: One ear, fullness, itching, no ringing.
Drug damage has no fullness or itching. Wax has both.
Nobody has looked in the canal.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the right canal first.

questions.objective: types of hearing loss, risk factors and ototoxic drugs

questions.stem: A 66-year-old retired office clerk is on day 4 of an IV aminoglycoside antibiotic and a daily diuretic. The client reports new ringing in both ears, with no ear pain or fever. Which explanation does the nurse consider first?

options.text: Inner ear effects of the two prescribed drugs
options.rationale: Aminoglycosides and diuretics are both ototoxic, and ototoxic drugs contribute to tinnitus. The ringing is new, in both ears, and began after 4 days of both drugs.

options.text: Dry cerumen that has become impacted with increasing age
options.rationale: Impaction is common in older adults. It gives fullness, itching and muffled hearing, usually without new ringing in both ears at once.

options.text: Acute infection of the middle ear
options.rationale: Otitis media can cause tinnitus, but it comes with ear pain and fever. The stem says there is neither.

options.text: Damage from years of loud noise at work
options.rationale: Noise is a major cause of tinnitus. An office clerk has no stated noise exposure, and the ringing is 4 days new.

questions.takeaway: New ringing in a client taking an aminoglycoside, a diuretic, an NSAID, a quinine based drug or chemotherapy is a drug cue until shown otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real cause of ringing. Use the timing and the missing findings to rule three out.

steps.detail: Ringing began on day 4 of two ototoxic drug classes.
No pain and no fever argue against otitis media.
Office work gives no noise exposure.

elimination.verdict: The two ototoxic drugs.

questions.objective: types of hearing loss, risk factors and ototoxic drugs

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on day 4 of an IV aminoglycoside antibiotic reported new ringing in both ears 20 minutes ago. Both ear canals are clear. The next dose is due now. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose on time and recheck the ringing in 1 hour
options.rationale: Rechecking is good practice, but giving another dose of the suspected drug first adds to the possible injury.

options.text: Offer a sound machine to mask the ringing, then give the dose
options.rationale: Masking is a real treatment for tinnitus. It covers a warning sign here and does nothing about the cause.

options.text: Hold the dose and report the new ringing to the prescriber
options.rationale: The assessment is done: new ringing, clear canals, an ototoxic drug. Inner ear damage is often permanent, so the dose waits for the prescriber's decision.

options.text: Hold the dose and restart it once the ringing has eased
options.rationale: Holding is right. Restarting on the nurse's own judgment leaves the prescriber unaware, and ringing that eases does not show the inner ear is safe.

questions.takeaway: When a client on an ototoxic drug reports new ringing or hearing change, hold the next dose and report it. Sensorineural damage is often permanent.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the dose. Ask who decides what happens to the drug after that.

steps.action: Check that the data are complete
steps.detail: New ringing, clear canals, ototoxic drug, dose due.

steps.action: Cut the options that give the dose
steps.detail: Two options give the suspected drug first.
One reports the ringing. The other restarts the drug without the prescriber.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report the ringing.

questions.objective: types of hearing loss, risk factors and ototoxic drugs

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has ringing and reduced hearing in both ears after an IV aminoglycoside antibiotic. The client now says the floor seems to tilt when walking to the bathroom. What does the nurse add to the plan of care?

options.text: A quiet room with the lights dimmed to reduce stimulation
options.rationale: Lowering stimulation helps sensory overload. It does not protect a client who is unsteady on the way to the bathroom.

options.text: Fall precautions with help for every trip out of bed
options.rationale: The inner ear holds the cochlea for hearing and the semicircular canals for balance. Injury there can affect both, so the unsteadiness is a fall risk to act on.

options.text: A written communication board kept at the bedside
options.rationale: A board helps communication with reduced hearing. It does not address the new report about walking.

options.text: Bed rest with a bedpan until the antibiotic course is finished
options.rationale: This removes the fall risk but is more restrictive than needed. Assisted walking is tried before bed rest.

questions.takeaway: The inner ear serves hearing and balance. When an inner ear problem shows hearing cues, look for balance cues and protect against falls.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The new cue is about walking, not hearing. Choose the option that answers it with the least restriction.

steps.detail: The floor seems to tilt when walking.
Cochlea and balance organs share the inner ear.

steps.action: Choose the least restrictive safe plan
steps.detail: Assisted walking, not bed rest.

elimination.verdict: Fall precautions with assistance.

questions.objective: ear structure and the sound pathway

questions.stem: A 66-year-old who developed ringing in both ears while on an IV aminoglycoside antibiotic is going home. Which facts from the home history does the nurse address as added risks to this client's hearing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Takes an over the counter NSAID every day for knee pain
options.rationale: NSAIDs are on the ototoxic drug list.

options.text: Uses a chain saw and leaf blower weekly without ear protection
options.rationale: Prolonged loud noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss.

options.text: Takes a quinine based drug at night for leg cramps
options.rationale: Quinine based drugs are ototoxic.

options.text: Has a flashing light alert connected to the doorbell
options.rationale: This is an assistive device for hearing loss. It does not harm hearing.

options.text: Listens to the radio at the volume of normal conversation
options.rationale: Normal conversation is about 60 dB, which is not prolonged loud noise.

options.text: Wears reading glasses for small print on drug labels
options.rationale: This is a vision aid. It helps the client read labels and has no effect on hearing.

questions.takeaway: Ototoxic drug classes: NSAIDs, aminoglycoside antibiotics, diuretics, quinine based drugs and chemotherapy. Loud noise without protection is the major preventable cause.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each fact alone: does it add drug or noise injury to the inner ear, or is it a neutral or helpful habit?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NSAID and quinine based drug are both on the list.
Power tools with no protection.

steps.action: Leave the aids and normal sound
steps.detail: Alert light, glasses and 60 dB radio are not risks.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: types of hearing loss, risk factors and ototoxic drugs

questions.stem: During a preoperative interview a 52-year-old with otosclerosis leans forward, tilts her head, and answers "Tuesday" when asked about allergies. Assistive personnel tell the nurse she seems confused. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Face her in good light and ask the question again slowly
options.rationale: Leaning forward, tilting the head and a mismatched answer are behavior cues of hearing loss. Repeating the question so she can hear it tests that before any other label is used.

options.text: Complete a mental status screening before continuing the interview
options.rationale: Mental status belongs in a sensory assessment. Her cues match hearing loss, and a screening she cannot hear would give a false result.

options.text: Ask a family member to answer the remaining history questions
options.rationale: Family can add information. Replacing her as the source skips the fix that would let her answer.

options.text: Document new confusion and place her on fall precautions
options.rationale: A mismatched answer alone is not confusion. Charting it as such mislabels a hearing cue.

questions.takeaway: Tilting the head, leaning forward, saying "What?" often and mismatched answers are hearing cues. Rule out not hearing before calling it confusion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the answer as a thinking problem. Her body language says she is working to hear.

steps.detail: Leaning in and tilting the head.
"Tuesday" is a mismatched response, a listed hearing cue.
Face her, good light, slow speech.

elimination.verdict: Face her and ask again.

questions.objective: hearing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse is giving preoperative instructions to a 52-year-old woman who has otosclerosis. She hears better with her right ear. Which actions does the nurse use? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sit on her right side, facing her
options.rationale: Moving to the better hearing ear and facing the client are both taught strategies.

options.text: Stand with the bright window behind the nurse
options.rationale: Good lighting is right, but light behind the speaker puts the face in shadow. Avoid standing in front of windows.

options.text: Speak slowly and clearly in a lower pitch
options.rationale: Slow, clear speech in a lower pitch is easier to hear.

options.text: Raise the voice to a shout for key points
options.rationale: Emphasis on key points is reasonable. Shouting is avoided.

options.text: Give the instructions in writing as well
options.rationale: Written communication supports the spoken teaching.

options.text: Arrange interpreter services if she uses sign language
options.rationale: Interpreter services are used as needed, and effective communication is a legal and ethical duty.

questions.takeaway: Face the client in good light, away from windows, on the better ear side. Speak slowly and clearly in a lower pitch, never shouting, and add written information.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options start with a good idea and then go wrong. Read each one to the end.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Better ear, face to face, slow and low.
A window behind the nurse hides the face.
Shouting is never the method.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: communicating with and managing hearing loss

questions.stem: Two hours after a left stapedectomy, a 52-year-old woman says she feels steady and wants to walk 3 meters to the bathroom by herself. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Let her walk alone with the call light within reach
options.rationale: A call light does not prevent a fall that happens on the way. Vertigo risk is high after this surgery even when she feels steady.

options.text: Walk beside her and assist her to the bathroom
options.rationale: Assisted ambulation is the action alert after stapedectomy because vertigo risk is high. It keeps her safe and is the least restrictive choice.

options.text: Keep her in bed and offer a bedpan until the morning
options.rationale: This prevents a fall but restricts her more than needed. She may walk with assistance.

options.text: Ask her to sit at the bedside for 10 minutes, then walk alone
options.rationale: Sitting first is a good step for any first walk. She still ends up walking alone with a high vertigo risk.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, assist every ambulation. Vertigo risk is high regardless of how steady the client feels.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Her report of feeling steady is the bait. The surgery sets the risk, and the answer is the least restrictive safe option.

steps.detail: High vertigo risk after stapedectomy.

steps.action: Cut the options that leave her alone
steps.detail: Call light and sitting first both end with her walking alone.
A bedpan is more than she needs.

elimination.verdict: Walk with her.

questions.objective: communicating with and managing hearing loss

questions.stem: One day after a left stapedectomy, a 52-year-old reports dizziness when she turns her head. Assistive personnel add that the left corner of her mouth did not lift when she smiled. Which action is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Remind her to call for help before getting out of bed
options.rationale: Dizziness after stapedectomy is expected and assistance is the right precaution. It does not address the new finding on her face.

options.text: Teach her to avoid straining, nose blowing and air travel
options.rationale: These are the correct discharge precautions. Teaching can wait until the unexpected finding is dealt with.

options.text: Assess movement on both sides of her face, then report it
options.rationale: The facial nerve runs close to the surgical site, and weakness on the operative side is the complication to watch for. It is unexpected, so the nurse confirms it and reports it.

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic and recheck her in 30 minutes
options.rationale: An antiemetic suits vertigo with nausea. The stem reports no nausea, and it delays the facial finding.

questions.takeaway: After ear surgery, dizziness is expected and managed with assistance. Facial weakness on the operative side is unexpected and suggests facial nerve damage.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two findings compete. One is expected after this surgery and already has a plan. The other is new and on the operative side.

steps.detail: Dizziness is expected. A mouth that does not lift is not.
Left surgery, left facial change.
Assess both sides of the face first.

elimination.verdict: Assess facial movement and report it.

questions.objective: communicating with and managing hearing loss

questions.stem: Three days after a left stapedectomy, a 52-year-old phones the clinic. Hearing in the left ear is no better than before surgery. She has no pain, fever, dizziness or drainage. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Come in today so the prosthesis can be checked for failure."
options.rationale: Unchanged hearing at 3 days is not a sign of failure. She has no pain, fever, dizziness or drainage that would need a same day visit.

options.text: "A hearing aid can be fitted to that ear this week."
options.rationale: Hearing aids do help conductive loss. Fitting one at 3 days treats a result that is not final yet.

options.text: "Blow your nose gently to open the ear and test it."
options.rationale: Nose blowing is avoided after this surgery, so this advice risks harm.

options.text: "Hearing usually improves about 4 to 6 weeks after this surgery."
options.rationale: This is the expected course. With no other symptoms, day 3 without improvement is on schedule.

questions.takeaway: Hearing improves about 4 to 6 weeks after stapedectomy. Until then the client avoids straining, nose blowing and air travel.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Decide whether day 3 with no change is expected or unexpected before choosing an action.

steps.detail: Improvement comes at about 4 to 6 weeks.
No pain, fever, dizziness or drainage.
Nose blowing is a postoperative restriction.

elimination.verdict: Hearing improves at about 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.objective: communicating with and managing hearing loss

questions.stem: A 34-year-old has had three episodes of spinning with nausea this month. Each came with ringing and reduced hearing in the right ear. There is no ear pain or fever. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: An oral antibiotic to be taken for the full course
options.rationale: This fits otitis media, which can cause dizziness and tinnitus. Otitis media brings ear pain and fever, and the stem has neither.

options.text: A ceruminolytic followed by irrigation of the right ear
options.rationale: This fits cerumen impaction, which gives fullness and hearing loss. Impaction does not cause repeated spinning episodes with nausea.

options.text: A low sodium diet with a diuretic
options.rationale: Episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss are the triad of Meniere disease. A low sodium diet and a diuretic reduce endolymph volume.

options.text: Topical antibiotic and steroid ear drops
options.rationale: These treat external otitis, which causes pain when the pinna is moved. This client has no pain.

questions.takeaway: Episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss together mean Meniere disease: low sodium diet, diuretic, antiemetic, fall precautions.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each option treats a different ear condition. Match the triad and use the missing pain and fever to drop the infections.

steps.detail: Episodes of spinning, ringing, hearing loss.
No pain or fever rules out both infections.
Sodium restriction and a diuretic lower endolymph.

elimination.verdict: Low sodium diet with a diuretic.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a 34-year-old with Meniere disease who takes a diuretic and follows a low sodium diet. Which statement shows that the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will drink extra coffee so fatigue does not set off an attack."
options.rationale: Fatigue is a trigger, so the goal is right. Caffeine is also a trigger, so the method is wrong.

options.text: "I will add salt back because the water pill removes sodium."
options.rationale: The diuretic and the low sodium diet work together to lower endolymph volume. Adding salt undoes both.

options.text: "I can stop the diet after a month without any spinning."
options.rationale: A month without attacks is a good result. The condition is progressive, so the lifestyle changes continue.

options.text: "If spinning starts, I will not drive or climb a ladder."
options.rationale: Avoiding driving and ladders during attacks is the taught safety measure.

questions.takeaway: Meniere teaching: low sodium diet, avoid caffeine, stress and fatigue, fall precautions, no ladders or driving during attacks.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three statements start from something true and then draw the wrong conclusion. Check the second half of each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fatigue and caffeine are both triggers.
Sodium stays low, and it stays low long term.
No driving or ladders in an attack.

elimination.verdict: No driving or ladders during an attack.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 34-year-old roofer with Meniere disease says that twice this week he dropped to the ground with no dizziness beforehand and did not lose consciousness. Which teaching point is the priority?

options.text: Lie down as soon as the first sign of dizziness begins
options.rationale: This is good advice for an ordinary attack. These falls came with no dizziness beforehand, so there is no first sign to act on.

options.text: Stay off roofs and ladders while these episodes are occurring
options.rationale: Sudden drop attacks give no warning and carry a significant fall risk. Working at height is the danger that can be removed today.

options.text: Use background sound at night to cover the ringing
options.rationale: Masking helps tinnitus. Ringing is not what put him on the ground.

options.text: Begin balance exercises with vestibular rehabilitation therapy
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation improves balance over time. It cannot stop a fall that comes without warning this week.

questions.takeaway: A drop attack (Tumarkin crisis) comes with no warning. Safety teaching removes the hazard, because the client cannot react in time.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: One option depends on a warning sign. The stem says there was none.

steps.detail: No dizziness beforehand.

steps.action: Cut the option that needs a warning
steps.detail: Lying down at the first sign cannot work.
Height plus sudden falls is the immediate danger.

elimination.verdict: Stay off roofs and ladders.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 34-year-old in an acute Meniere attack has severe spinning and vomiting. Blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg and pulse is 108 per minute. An antiemetic is prescribed as needed. The client is trying to get out of bed. What is the priority?

options.text: Recheck the blood pressure in both arms to confirm the reading
options.rationale: Rechecking an abnormal reading is sound practice. Blood pressure and pulse can rise during an acute attack, and the recheck leaves the client on the way to a fall.

options.text: Request an antihypertensive for the blood pressure of 158/94 mm Hg
options.rationale: A raised pressure deserves attention in other settings. Here it is a possible effect of the attack, and it is not the immediate danger.

options.text: Start balance exercises to help the client adapt to the spinning
options.rationale: Vestibular exercises are part of long term management. An acute attack with vomiting is the wrong time.

options.text: Keep the client in bed, offer a bedpan, and give the antiemetic
options.rationale: A spinning client who stands will fall. Safety comes first, then the antiemetic for the vomiting. The vital signs are expected to change during an attack.

questions.takeaway: In an acute Meniere attack, blood pressure, pulse and respirations may rise. The priority is preventing a fall and controlling nausea.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The vital signs pull attention. Ask which problem can injure the client in the next minute.

steps.detail: A rise is possible during an attack.
Spinning and trying to stand.

steps.action: Act, since the data are complete
steps.detail: Keep in bed and treat the vomiting.

elimination.verdict: Keep in bed and give the antiemetic.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 34-year-old roofer with Meniere disease is scheduled for a right labyrinthectomy. He says, "The spinning will stop and I will finally hear my crew on that side again." What does the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that hearing in the right ear will be lost, and pause consent
options.rationale: Labyrinthectomy stops vertigo but causes total hearing loss on the operative side. His statement shows he does not understand the result, so consent cannot go forward yet.

options.text: Agree that the spinning should stop after the operation
options.rationale: This half of his statement is true. Confirming only that half leaves his false belief about hearing in place.

options.text: Tell him that hearing improves about 4 to 6 weeks after surgery
options.rationale: That timeline belongs to stapedectomy. After labyrinthectomy the hearing on that side does not return.

options.text: Review the fall precautions he will need after the operation
options.rationale: Fall precautions matter after ear surgery. They are not the priority while he misunderstands what the surgery does.

questions.takeaway: Labyrinthectomy is a last resort: it stops vertigo and ends hearing on the operative side. A client who expects hearing to return has not given informed consent.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: His sentence has a true half and a false half. Agreeing and correcting are both tempting, and the false half is the one consent depends on.

steps.detail: Spinning stops: true. Hearing returns: false.
4 to 6 weeks is stapedectomy.
Correct the belief before the surgery proceeds.

elimination.verdict: Explain the hearing loss and pause consent.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 41-year-old with acute otitis media has muffled hearing in the left ear and fears the nerve is damaged for good. The eardrum is bulging and intact. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The hearing nerve is inflamed, and it recovers slowly over months."
options.rationale: The infection is in the middle ear. The nerve lies beyond the cochlea and is not where this problem is.

options.text: "Hearing lost during an ear infection does not come back."
options.rationale: Loss can become permanent if the infection is left untreated and damages the eardrum or ossicles. A treated infection usually does not.

options.text: "Fluid is blocking sound in the middle ear. It often clears."
options.rationale: Sound must pass the eardrum and ossicles to reach the cochlea and nerve. Fluid blocks that step, which is a conductive loss and is often correctable.

options.text: "A cochlear implant can restore the hearing if it does not return."
options.rationale: A cochlear implant is for sensorineural loss. It bypasses a damaged cochlea, which is not this client's problem.

questions.takeaway: Sound travels eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, nerve. A block before the cochlea is conductive and often correctable. Damage at the cochlea or nerve is sensorineural and often permanent.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Locate the problem on the sound pathway first. The stem puts it behind an intact, bulging eardrum.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Middle ear, behind the eardrum.
Blocked transmission is conductive.

steps.action: Cut the nerve and cochlea answers
steps.detail: Nothing in the stem involves the inner ear.

elimination.verdict: Fluid is blocking sound, and it often clears.

questions.objective: ear structure and the sound pathway

questions.stem: A 41-year-old with acute otitis media of the left ear rated ear pain 8 of 10 an hour ago. The pain is now 2 of 10, with no analgesic given, and there is fresh drainage on the pillow. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Record the lower pain score as a sign the infection is resolving
options.rationale: A drop in pain looks like improvement. Sudden relief with new drainage and no analgesic fits a perforated eardrum.

options.text: Suspect a perforated eardrum and assess the drainage
options.rationale: Otitis media progresses to bulging and then perforation, and the pain is relieved when the eardrum perforates. The drainage is the supporting cue to assess and report.

options.text: Irrigate the left ear canal to clear the drainage
options.rationale: Irrigation is never done when perforation or otitis media is suspected, because it spreads infection.

options.text: Give the scheduled analgesic to keep the pain controlled
options.rationale: Staying ahead of pain is good practice. Pain at 2 of 10 is not the problem now, and the drainage is unexplained.

questions.takeaway: In otitis media, sudden pain relief with drainage means the eardrum has perforated. It is not a sign of recovery.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The pain score fell without any treatment for pain. Ask what else changed in the same hour.

steps.detail: Pain down from 8 to 2, new drainage.
An infection does not resolve in an hour.
No irrigation.

elimination.verdict: Suspect perforation and assess the drainage.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 41-year-old is on day 4 of a 10 day oral antibiotic for acute otitis media. Pain is 0 of 10 and temperature is 36.9 C. The client plans to stop the antibiotic. Which response is best?

options.text: "Take every dose. Untreated infection can cause permanent hearing loss."
options.rationale: Antibiotics for otitis media are taken for the full course. Incompletely treated infection can lead to perforation, ossicle damage and permanent conductive hearing loss.

options.text: "Stop now and save the remaining doses in case the pain returns."
options.rationale: Watching for returning pain is sensible. Stopping at day 4 and keeping doses for later leaves the infection partly treated.

options.text: "Stop the antibiotic and use mild heat until the ear feels normal."
options.rationale: Mild heat is a real comfort measure. It does not replace the remaining 6 days of antibiotic.

options.text: "Take it until day 7, when acute infections have resolved."
options.rationale: Acute otitis media resolves within about 3 weeks, not by a set day 7. The prescribed course is 10 days.

questions.takeaway: Feeling better is not the end point for an antibiotic. The full course is completed to prevent perforation and permanent conductive hearing loss.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The good outcome data are real. The question is whether symptoms or the prescribed course decide when to stop.

steps.detail: No pain, no fever on day 4 of 10.
Three options stop before day 10.
Permanent conductive hearing loss.

elimination.verdict: Take every dose.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 23-year-old competitive swimmer has right ear pain that sharply worsens when the nurse moves the pinna. The canal is swollen. Temperature is 36.8 C. Which instruction belongs in this client's teaching?

options.text: Dry the canal with a cotton swab after each shower
options.rationale: Keeping the ear dry is the right goal. Cotton swabs injure the canal skin and are a cause of this condition.

options.text: Avoid air travel and nose blowing until the ear heals
options.rationale: These are precautions after middle ear surgery. This client's problem is the skin of the outer canal.

options.text: Flush the canal with warm water each evening to clean it
options.rationale: Cleaning is done by the provider. Adding water to a canal inflamed by water works against healing.

options.text: Keep water and earbuds out of the ear for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: Pain with pinna movement and a swollen canal are the signs of external otitis. Treatment includes avoiding water and earbuds for 7 to 10 days.

questions.takeaway: Pain when the pinna or tragus is moved means external otitis. Use the prescribed drops, heat for comfort, and no water or earbuds for 7 to 10 days.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options sound like ear hygiene. Check whether each one puts something into the canal.

steps.detail: Pain with pinna movement, swollen canal, a swimmer.
Swabs and flushing both do.
Air travel and nose blowing belong to middle ear surgery.

elimination.verdict: No water or earbuds for 7 to 10 days.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 23-year-old has used topical antibiotic and steroid drops for external otitis of the right ear for 3 days. Pain with pinna movement fell from 7 to 3 of 10. Right ear hearing is still muffled. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: Expected progress; hearing loss with this condition is temporary
options.rationale: Pain is falling on treatment, and external otitis causes a plugged sensation with temporary hearing loss from canal swelling. Treatment continues.

options.text: Treatment failure; the drops should be changed to an oral antibiotic
options.rationale: Failure would show as pain that is unchanged or rising. Pain has fallen from 7 to 3 of 10 in 3 days.

options.text: Possible nerve damage; audiometry is needed this week
options.rationale: Audiometry measures hearing reliably. Muffled hearing with a swollen canal is a blocked canal, not a nerve problem.

options.text: Resolved infection; swimming can resume now
options.rationale: Pain of 3 of 10 and muffled hearing show the canal is not healed. Water is avoided for 7 to 10 days, and this is day 3.

questions.takeaway: External otitis causes a plugged feeling and temporary hearing loss. Falling pain on drops is expected progress, and water stays out for the full 7 to 10 days.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two outcome measures are given. One is improving and the other is expected to lag behind.

steps.detail: 7 down to 3 of 10.
Swelling still narrows the canal.
Day 3 of a 7 to 10 day restriction.

elimination.verdict: Expected progress with temporary hearing loss.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 23-year-old with type 1 diabetes phones the clinic on day 5 of drops for external otitis of the right ear. Ear pain was 3 of 10 two days ago and is now 9 of 10. Temperature is 38.9 C. What does the nurse advise?

options.text: Continue the drops, since treatment takes 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: The 7 to 10 day figure is real, and day 5 is inside it. Pain should be falling by now, and here it has tripled with fever.

options.text: Apply heat to the ear and call back in 48 hours
options.rationale: Heat is a correct comfort measure for external otitis. Waiting 48 hours is unsafe with rising pain, fever and diabetes.

options.text: Come in to be examined today
options.rationale: Clients with diabetes are at risk for necrotizing external otitis, which can be fatal. Worsening pain with fever on treatment needs examination now.

options.text: Rinse the ear with warm water to clear the canal before the next drops
options.rationale: Clearing debris helps drops reach the skin, but cleaning is done by the provider and water is kept out of this ear.

questions.takeaway: External otitis that worsens on treatment in a client with diabetes or weak immunity may be necrotizing otitis, a rare complication that can be fatal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Staying the course is defensible at day 5 for most clients. The diagnosis in the first line and the direction of the pain change the answer.

steps.detail: Pain 3 to 9 of 10, new fever of 38.9 C.
Diabetes raises the risk of the dangerous form.

steps.action: Choose the option that gets an examination
steps.detail: The other three keep the client at home.

elimination.verdict: Come in today.

questions.objective: ear conditions: cues, priority care, safety and teaching

questions.stem: A 78-year-old walks more slowly, has slightly less shoulder movement in both arms and has thinner calf muscles on both legs than five years ago. Strength is equal on both sides. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Expected changes of aging to record as the baseline
options.rationale: Slower movement, less range of motion and muscle atrophy are the aging changes. They are gradual and the same on both sides.

options.text: Red flag findings to report before continuing the assessment
options.rationale: Red flags are sudden or one sided: lost movement, new numbness, a new deformity. These changes took five years and match on both sides.

options.text: Signs of joint injury that call for an x-ray of both shoulders
options.rationale: An x-ray looks for fracture, dislocation or alignment problems after a new complaint. A slow, equal loss of movement in both shoulders is not an injury pattern.

options.text: Signs of muscle disease that call for a creatine kinase level
options.rationale: Muscle wasting is worth inspecting, but equal strength and a five year course fit atrophy of aging, not muscle damage.

questions.takeaway: Gradual, symmetric slowing, stiffness and muscle thinning are aging. Record them so a later change can be seen against them.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look at the two words that describe every finding: gradual and both sides.

steps.detail: Five years, not hours or days.
Both arms and both legs match.
Movement slows, range of motion decreases, muscle atrophies.

elimination.verdict: Expected aging changes. Baseline, not alarm.

questions.objective: aging changes versus new findings

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with osteopenia is assessed after a fall this morning. Which finding does the nurse treat as new, and not as an expected change of aging?

options.text: Walking more slowly than at a visit one year ago
options.rationale: Movement slows with age. A change over a year is the expected pace.

options.text: Both knees bending less far than they once did
options.rationale: Range of motion decreases with age, and it is the same on both sides.

options.text: Thigh muscles on both legs smaller than they were in past years
options.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with age. Both legs match, so this is the baseline.

options.text: Right wrist swollen and misshapen; left wrist is not
options.rationale: A new deformity with swelling on one side after a fall is a red flag, and bone that has lost density breaks easily.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are slow and symmetric. Swelling or deformity on one side after an injury is new.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options describe both sides or a slow change. One describes one side, today.

steps.detail: Three findings are bilateral or general.
Only the wrist changed this morning.
Osteopenia plus a fall makes a fracture likely.

elimination.verdict: The swollen, misshapen right wrist.

questions.objective: aging changes versus new findings

questions.stem: A 78-year-old says walking is no problem. The nurse needs data on posture and gait before planning care. Which approach gives the most useful information?

options.text: Ask the client to rate difficulty with walking from 0 to 10
options.rationale: A self rating is worth having, but the client already says there is no problem. It cannot show alignment or an uneven step.

options.text: Watch the client walk, noting alignment and symmetry
options.rationale: Gait and posture are assessed by observing movement. Alignment and symmetry can only be seen while the client stands and walks.

options.text: Palpate both hips and knees while the client lies in bed
options.rationale: Palpation finds tenderness and swelling. It shows nothing about posture or how the client walks.

options.text: Test strength in both legs against resistance in bed
options.rationale: Strength is part of the assessment, but strong legs in bed do not show balance, alignment or gait.

questions.takeaway: Posture and gait are inspected. Watch the client stand and move, and look for alignment and symmetry.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem asks about posture and gait. Pick the option where the client is upright and moving.

steps.detail: Posture and gait.
Palpation and strength testing in bed show neither.
A rating repeats what the client already said.

elimination.verdict: Observe the client walking.

questions.objective: focused assessment

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with osteoporosis has had a rounded upper back for years. Today the client reports mid back pain of 8 of 10 that began an hour ago while lifting a bag. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Chart the curved spine as an aging change and recheck pain in one hour
options.rationale: The long standing curve is an aging change and should be charted. The pain is the new part: sudden, severe and one hour old, so waiting is the error.

options.text: Teach weight-bearing exercise to slow further bone loss
options.rationale: Correct teaching for osteoporosis at the wrong time. A client with sudden pain of 8 of 10 needs the cause found first.

options.text: Report the sudden severe back pain as a new finding
options.rationale: Severe pain that starts suddenly is a red flag. With osteoporosis, a lift can be enough to break a vertebra.

options.text: Arrange the bone density scan that measures bone loss
options.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone density, which is already known to be low. It does not explain pain that began an hour ago.

questions.takeaway: An old finding stays baseline. Sudden severe pain in a client with fragile bone is new and is reported.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two things are in the stem: a curve that is years old and a pain that is one hour old. Answer the new one.

steps.detail: Curve for years; pain for one hour.

steps.action: Check the pain against the red flags
steps.detail: Severe pain is on the list.

steps.action: Hold the right ideas for later
steps.detail: Exercise teaching and bone density testing do not address today's pain.

elimination.verdict: Report the sudden severe pain.

questions.objective: aging changes versus new findings

questions.stem: A 52-year-old arrives with a swollen left forearm after a fall. The right arm is uninjured. Which approach does the nurse use for the neurovascular assessment?

options.text: Assess the left hand only, since the right arm is uninjured
options.rationale: The uninjured side is the comparison. Without it a slightly cool or pale left hand cannot be judged.

options.text: Check the left radial pulse and add sensation once swelling settles
options.rationale: A pulse alone is not the full check. Sensation and movement are assessed now, because swelling is what threatens them.

options.text: Check left hand movement by testing grip against firm resistance
options.rationale: Movement is part of the check, but it means asking the client to move the fingers. Forceful resistance on a swollen forearm adds pain and tells no more.

options.text: Assess both hands and compare the left with the right
options.rationale: Comparing sides shows what is normal for this client, so a cooler, paler or weaker left hand stands out.

questions.takeaway: A neurovascular check covers color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement and pain, always compared with the other side.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The uninjured arm is not a reason to skip it. It is the measuring stick.

steps.detail: Both hands, compared.
Pulse only and left hand only leave gaps.
Movement is checked gently.

elimination.verdict: Assess both hands and compare.

questions.objective: neurovascular assessment and red flags

questions.nursesNote: 1400: 52-year-old with a splinted left forearm after a fall this morning. Left hand pale and cool to touch; right hand pink and warm. Left radial pulse weaker than the right radial pulse. Reports tingling in the left fingers that was not present at 1200. Wiggles all left fingers when asked. Pain in the left forearm 3 of 10, the same as at 1200. Bruise on the left elbow, unchanged in size since 1200.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the nurse reports as red flags.

segments.text: Left hand pale and cool to touch; right hand pink and warm
segments.rationale: A cool, pale extremity that differs from the other side points to reduced blood flow.

segments.text: Left radial pulse weaker than the right radial pulse
segments.rationale: A diminished pulse on the injured side is a red flag.

segments.text: Reports tingling in the left fingers that was not present at 1200
segments.rationale: New tingling means sensation has changed since the last check.

segments.text: Wiggles all left fingers when asked
segments.rationale: Movement is intact. Record it and keep checking.

segments.text: Pain in the left forearm 3 of 10, the same as at 1200
segments.rationale: Pain is mild and unchanged. Severe pain would be the red flag.

segments.text: Bruise on the left elbow, unchanged in size since 1200
segments.rationale: An unchanged bruise is expected after a fall. Rapid swelling would be the concern.

questions.takeaway: Cool or pale skin, a weaker pulse and new tingling are reported. Compare with the other side and with the last check.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: For each line ask two things: is it different from the right hand, and is it different from 1200?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Color, temperature and pulse differ from the right hand.
Tingling is new since 1200.

steps.action: Leave what is unchanged or intact
steps.detail: Movement, mild pain and the bruise.

elimination.verdict: Pale cool hand, weaker pulse, new tingling.

questions.objective: neurovascular assessment and red flags

questions.stem: A 52-year-old has a splinted, swollen left forearm. The nurse cannot feel the left radial pulse. The left hand is pink and warm, and the right radial pulse is strong. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Chart the left radial pulse as absent and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: An absent pulse is a red flag, so an hour is too long, and the pink warm hand suggests flow that fingers cannot feel through swelling.

options.text: Use a Doppler to check for blood flow at the left wrist
options.rationale: A Doppler uses sound waves to detect blood flow. Swelling can hide a pulse from the fingers, so flow is confirmed before deciding the pulse is gone.

options.text: Raise the left arm on pillows and feel for the pulse again
options.rationale: Elevation helps swelling over time. It does not answer whether blood is reaching the hand now.

options.text: Ask for an x-ray to see whether the bone has shifted
options.rationale: An x-ray shows bone alignment. It does not measure blood flow.

questions.takeaway: When a pulse cannot be felt, check blood flow with a Doppler before calling it absent.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The hand is pink and warm but the pulse cannot be felt. The data conflict, so get better data.

steps.detail: No palpable pulse, yet good color and warmth.

steps.action: Pick the tool that measures flow
steps.detail: Doppler.
Waiting an hour or repositioning leaves the question open.

elimination.verdict: Doppler at the left wrist.

questions.objective: neurovascular assessment and red flags

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with a splinted left forearm rated pain 4 of 10 one hour ago. Now pain is 9 of 10, the forearm has swollen quickly and the fingers tingle. An analgesic is due. What is the priority?

options.text: Give the analgesic that is due and reassess pain in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Treating pain is right and the dose is due. Given alone, it quiets the warning sign while swelling and tingling go unreported for another 30 minutes.

options.text: Raise the arm, apply ice and recheck the swelling in one hour
options.rationale: Comfort measures for an injured limb, but an hour of waiting is unsafe when swelling is rapid and sensation is changing.

options.text: Report the severe pain, rapid swelling and new tingling now
options.rationale: Three red flags have appeared together within an hour. The limb is at risk, and the assessment is already complete enough to act on.

options.text: Request a Doppler, since swelling makes pulses hard to feel
options.rationale: A Doppler is for a pulse that cannot be felt. The stem gives no pulse problem, and it gives three findings that already need reporting.

questions.takeaway: Severe pain, rapid swelling and new tingling are red flags. Report them first; pain relief does not replace the report.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The analgesic is tempting because it is due. Ask what changed in the last hour and whether pain medicine fixes that.

steps.detail: Pain 4 to 9 of 10, quick swelling, tingling.

steps.action: Check each against the red flags
steps.detail: All three are on the list.
The analgesic treats one sign and reports none.

elimination.verdict: Report the three red flags now.

questions.objective: neurovascular assessment and red flags

questions.stem: A 34-year-old twisted the right knee during a soccer game. An x-ray shows no fracture, but the knee gives way and a torn ligament is suspected. Which test does the nurse expect next?

options.text: A CT scan of the right knee
options.rationale: CT gives more detailed images of bone and suits complex fractures. The x-ray found no fracture, and the question is a ligament.

options.text: An MRI of the right knee
options.rationale: MRI is the best test for soft tissue such as ligaments, tendons and cartilage.

options.text: A bone scan of both legs
options.rationale: A bone scan looks for hidden fractures, infection or tumors in bone. It does not show a ligament.

options.text: A DEXA scan of the right hip
options.rationale: DEXA measures bone mineral density for osteoporosis. It has no role in a knee ligament injury.

questions.takeaway: Bone question: x-ray, then CT for detail. Soft tissue question such as a ligament: MRI.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the tissue in question first. A ligament is soft tissue.

steps.detail: Ligament.
CT, bone scan and DEXA all look at bone.
MRI.

elimination.verdict: MRI.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with a twisted right knee bends it partway, then stops and says it hurts. The left knee bends fully without pain. What does the nurse record?

options.text: Right knee movement limited by pain and less than the left
options.rationale: Joint movement is compared side to side, and pain, limitation and asymmetry are what the nurse notes.

options.text: Right knee movement decreased, as expected with aging
options.rationale: Range of motion does decrease with age, but in both knees and slowly. This client is 34 and only the injured knee is limited.

options.text: Right leg muscle strength 3 of 5, with 5 as full strength
options.rationale: Strength is a separate test using gravity and resistance. Stopping because of pain says nothing about the grade.

options.text: Right knee movement normal, since the client moved it unaided
options.rationale: Moving it without help makes it active movement. It was still incomplete and painful.

questions.takeaway: When checking joint movement, compare both sides and record pain, limitation and asymmetry.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Record what was seen: how far, what stopped it, and how the other side compares.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Partial bend on the right, stopped by pain.
Left bends fully.
No resistance test was done.

elimination.verdict: Limited by pain, less than the left.

questions.objective: focused assessment

questions.stem: A 34-year-old returned from arthroscopy of the right knee one hour ago. Which assessment of the right leg does the nurse perform first?

options.text: How far the right knee bends and straightens without pain
options.rationale: Joint movement matters later. Exercises may not be allowed straight after the procedure, and circulation and nerve function come first.

options.text: Right leg strength when pushing against the nurse's resistance
options.rationale: Resistance testing strains a joint that was entered an hour ago and does not show whether blood and nerve supply are intact.

options.text: Gait and balance while the client walks to the bathroom
options.rationale: Gait is a useful observation once the limb is known to be safe. It is not the first check after a joint procedure.

options.text: Pulses, color, sensation and movement of the right foot
options.rationale: After arthroscopy the priority is the neurovascular status of the limb below the joint, compared with the left foot.

questions.takeaway: After arthroscopy, check the neurovascular status of the affected limb first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Circulation comes before function. One option checks blood and nerve supply to the foot.

steps.detail: Three test function; one tests circulation and nerves.
A foot without blood flow cannot wait.
Movement, strength and gait follow.

elimination.verdict: Neurovascular check of the right foot.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 34-year-old is two days past arthroscopy of the right knee. Which report from the client shows that recovery is not going as expected?

options.text: An ache of 2 of 10 when bending the right knee
options.rationale: Mild discomfort is expected after arthroscopy.

options.text: Right knee swelling unchanged since yesterday, pain 3 of 10
options.rationale: Swelling is worth watching, but it is not growing and the pain is mild. The red flag is swelling that is rapid or pain that is severe.

options.text: Swelling that doubled overnight, with pain now 8 of 10
options.rationale: Rapid swelling with severe pain is a red flag after a joint procedure and needs to be reported.

options.text: A small dry scab over each right knee incision
options.rationale: Dry scabs show the small incisions are closing.

questions.takeaway: Mild ache and stiffness are expected after arthroscopy. Rapid swelling or severe pain is not.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options mention swelling or pain. Look for the one with speed and severity in it.

steps.detail: You are looking for the bad sign.
2 of 10, unchanged swelling with 3 of 10, dry scabs.
Rapid swelling and severe pain.

elimination.verdict: Swelling that doubled with pain 8 of 10.

questions.objective: neurovascular assessment and red flags

questions.stem: A 66-year-old lifts the right arm off the bed and holds it up, but it drops when the nurse presses down lightly. On the scale where 0 is no contraction and 5 is full strength, what grade applies?

options.text: Grade 2 of 5
options.rationale: Grade 2 is movement without gravity. This arm lifts off the bed against gravity.

options.text: Grade 3 of 5
options.rationale: Grade 3 is movement against gravity. The arm lifts and holds, and it cannot take any added resistance.

options.text: Grade 4 of 5
options.rationale: Grade 4 is movement against some resistance. This arm drops with light pressure.

options.text: Grade 5 of 5
options.rationale: Grade 5 is full strength. This arm drops with light pressure.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the gravity line: the limb lifts against gravity but takes no resistance. Grade 4 takes some resistance; grade 2 needs gravity removed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions in order: does it beat gravity, and does it beat any resistance?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yes, the arm lifts and holds.
No, it drops with light pressure.
Against gravity only is grade 3.

elimination.verdict: Grade 3.

questions.objective: muscle strength grading

questions.stem: A 66-year-old had right leg strength of 4 of 5 at 0800, with 5 as full strength. At 1200 the client slides the right leg across the mattress but cannot lift it. What does this show?

options.text: No real change; grade 4 with tiredness late in the morning
options.rationale: Grade 4 means lifting against some resistance. A leg that cannot leave the mattress is not grade 4, whatever the cause.

options.text: A drop to grade 3, since the leg still moves on its own
options.rationale: Moving on its own is not the test. Grade 3 requires lifting against gravity, and this leg cannot.

options.text: A drop to grade 1, since only a trace contraction is left
options.rationale: Grade 1 is a flicker of contraction with no movement. This leg still moves across the bed.

options.text: A drop to grade 2, which is a new loss of movement
options.rationale: Sliding with the bed taking the weight is movement without gravity, grade 2. Falling two grades in four hours is a sudden loss of movement.

questions.takeaway: Grade 2 is movement with gravity removed. A fall of two grades within hours is a sudden loss of movement, a red flag.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Lifting off the bed is the gravity test. Sliding along it is not.

steps.detail: Slides, cannot lift: grade 2.
Grade 4 to grade 2.
Four hours is sudden.

elimination.verdict: Grade 2, a new loss of movement.

questions.objective: muscle strength grading

questions.stem: A 66-year-old's left arm strength was charted 5 of 5 yesterday, with 5 as full strength. Today the arm holds against light resistance but gives way to firm resistance. The client says it is tired from therapy. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Record grade 4 as a decline, then check the right arm and sensation
options.rationale: The finding is a measured drop from 5 to 4. It is charted as found, and comparing sides and checking sensation shows whether this is fatigue or a new deficit.

options.text: Let the arm rest for an hour, then retest before recording a grade
options.rationale: Fatigue is a fair explanation and a retest is reasonable later. Waiting to record or assess means a new deficit could go unnoticed for an hour.

options.text: Record grade 5, since the arm resists and fatigue explains the rest
options.rationale: Grade 5 is full strength. An arm that gives way to firm resistance is not at full strength, and charting yesterday's grade hides a real change.

options.text: Record grade 3, since the arm cannot hold against firm resistance
options.rationale: Grade 3 is movement against gravity with no resistance. This arm still takes some resistance, which is grade 4.

questions.takeaway: A change from the charted grade is recorded as measured and assessed further now. The client's explanation does not replace the comparison.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The client offers a reason. The nurse still has a number that changed, and more data to collect.

steps.detail: Takes some resistance, not full: grade 4.
Down from grade 5.
Compare sides and check sensation.

elimination.verdict: Record grade 4 and assess further now.

questions.objective: muscle strength grading

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has weak, tender muscles in both thighs after lying on the floor for many hours following a fall. Which laboratory result would support skeletal muscle damage?

options.text: Elevated alkaline phosphatase
options.rationale: Alkaline phosphatase rises with bone or liver problems. It is a bone test, not a muscle enzyme.

options.text: Low serum calcium with low phosphorus
options.rationale: Calcium and phosphorus reflect bone and parathyroid problems. They do not show muscle injury.

options.text: Elevated creatine kinase (CK-MM)
options.rationale: Damaged skeletal muscle releases its enzymes into the blood, and CK-MM is the muscle form of creatine kinase.

options.text: Elevated serum phosphorus alone
options.rationale: Phosphorus is followed with calcium for bone disorders. It is not a marker of muscle damage.

questions.takeaway: Muscle damage raises the muscle enzymes: creatine kinase (CK-MM), lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase and aldolase.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the labs into bone tests and muscle enzymes. The client's problem is muscle.

steps.detail: Tender, weak thigh muscle.
Three are bone related; one is a muscle enzyme.
Injured muscle leaks enzyme, so the level rises.

elimination.verdict: Elevated CK-MM.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 45-year-old fell from a ladder and holds the left ankle still. What does the nurse do first to assess the ankle?

options.text: Move the left ankle gently through its full range of motion
options.rationale: Joint movement is part of the assessment, but moving an ankle that may be broken through its full range before looking at it risks further injury.

options.text: Test left ankle strength against resistance
options.rationale: Strength testing loads the injured area. It waits until inspection shows it is safe.

options.text: Ask the client to walk so that gait can be observed
options.rationale: Gait is a standard observation. Bearing weight on a newly injured ankle before inspecting it is unsafe.

options.text: Inspect both ankles for swelling, redness and deformity
options.rationale: Inspection comes first and costs the client nothing. Looking at both ankles shows what is different about the left.

questions.takeaway: Start with inspection and compare sides. Movement, strength and gait come after you know what you are dealing with.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options put load or motion on an ankle no one has looked at yet.

steps.detail: Inspection.
Each moves or loads the ankle.
Both ankles, side by side.

elimination.verdict: Inspect both ankles first.

questions.objective: focused assessment

questions.stem: A 45-year-old's left ankle is swollen and visibly out of line after a fall from a ladder. Which imaging test does the nurse expect to be ordered first?

options.text: An x-ray of the left ankle
options.rationale: X-ray shows fractures, dislocations and alignment, which is the question a deformed ankle raises.

options.text: An MRI of the left ankle
options.rationale: MRI is best for soft tissue such as ligaments. With a visible deformity, the first question is bone and alignment.

options.text: A bone scan of both legs
options.rationale: A bone scan is for hidden fractures, infection or tumors when simpler imaging has not explained the problem.

options.text: An ultrasound of the left ankle
options.rationale: Ultrasound looks at tendons, muscle and fluid collections. It is not the first test for a suspected fracture.

questions.takeaway: A new deformity after trauma is a bone and alignment question. X-ray comes first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The deformity tells you the question is bone alignment. Start with the simplest test that answers it.

steps.detail: Fracture or dislocation.
X-ray shows both, plus alignment.
MRI and ultrasound are soft tissue tests; a bone scan is for what x-ray misses.

elimination.verdict: X-ray.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 45-year-old's left ankle x-ray shows a fracture in several pieces. The surgeon wants more detail of the bone before repair. The client asks why the next test is not an MRI. Which reply is accurate?

options.text: "An MRI comes next, since it is the best test for an injured joint."
options.rationale: MRI is the best test for soft tissue such as ligaments and cartilage, so it sounds right for an ankle. The stated need is bone detail, which is CT.

options.text: "A CT scan shows bone in more detail, which a complex fracture needs."
options.rationale: CT provides more detailed images of bone and is the test for complex fractures. The surgeon's question is about bone.

options.text: "A bone scan is next, since it finds fractures an x-ray misses."
options.rationale: A bone scan does find hidden fractures. This fracture is already seen; what is missing is detail.

options.text: "Another x-ray from a new angle gives the same detail as a CT."
options.rationale: More x-ray views help with alignment. They do not give the detail of bone that a CT does.

questions.takeaway: Choose the test by the question. Bone detail for a complex fracture is CT; soft tissue is MRI.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: CT and MRI both sound reasonable for an ankle. The stem says what the surgeon wants: detail of bone.

steps.detail: More detail of the bone.
CT for bone and complex fractures.
MRI answers a soft tissue question nobody asked.

elimination.verdict: CT for bone detail.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has low bone density on a DEXA scan. She smokes and asks how to protect her bones and muscles. Which teaching points does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walk briskly on most days of the week
options.rationale: Walking is weight-bearing exercise, which slows bone loss and keeps muscle.

options.text: Choose foods that supply calcium and vitamin D
options.rationale: Bone needs both, and adequate nutrition is part of bone health.

options.text: Limit activity so that a fall is less likely
options.rationale: Fall safety matters, but inactivity speeds the loss of bone and muscle.

options.text: Work on stopping tobacco use
options.rationale: Tobacco harms bone. Avoiding it is part of the plan.

options.text: Keep alcohol intake low
options.rationale: Excessive alcohol works against bone and muscle health.

options.text: Rely on a calcium supplement in place of exercise
options.rationale: Calcium supports bone, but it does not replace the loading that weight-bearing exercise gives.

questions.takeaway: Bone and muscle health: regular activity with weight-bearing exercise, adequate nutrition with calcium and vitamin D, no tobacco, limited alcohol.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options sound protective but take something away: activity. Bone needs loading.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Activity, nutrition, no tobacco, low alcohol.
Limiting activity weakens bone and muscle.
A supplement does not replace exercise.

elimination.verdict: Walk, calcium and vitamin D, stop tobacco, limit alcohol.

questions.objective: promoting bone and muscle health

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with low bone density was taught how to protect her bones. At a follow-up visit, which statement shows the plan needs more work?

options.text: "I walk for 30 minutes with a neighbor five days a week."
options.rationale: Regular weight-bearing exercise, as taught.

options.text: "I eat yogurt daily and take the vitamin D my provider approved."
options.rationale: Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, as taught.

options.text: "I quit cigarettes and now have four glasses of wine most nights."
options.rationale: Stopping tobacco is a gain. Four glasses most nights is excessive alcohol, which the plan asks her to limit.

options.text: "I do light strengthening exercises twice a week."
options.rationale: Regular physical activity that keeps muscle and function, as taught.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate teaching against every part of the plan. One good change does not cancel a harmful one.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read each statement to the end. One starts well and finishes badly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the statement that is off.
Walking, nutrition and strengthening all fit.
Four glasses of wine most nights is not limiting alcohol.

elimination.verdict: The wine statement.

questions.objective: promoting bone and muscle health

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with low bone density stopped her daily walks because she fears a fall will break a bone. She now does seated arm exercises only. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Explain that walking loads the bones, and plan a safe way to restart
options.rationale: Weight-bearing exercise is what protects bone. Her fear is real, so the plan keeps the walking and makes it safer.

options.text: Praise the seated exercises and add calcium to make up for the walking
options.rationale: Staying active deserves praise and calcium helps. Neither replaces weight-bearing, so bone loss continues.

options.text: Agree that avoiding walks is safest until her next bone density scan
options.rationale: It respects her fear, but time without weight-bearing lowers bone density and leg strength, which raises fracture risk.

options.text: Advise resting on alternate days so her muscles can recover
options.rationale: Rest days suit hard training. Her problem is too little loading, not too much.

questions.takeaway: Fear of falling is answered with safer weight-bearing activity, not with less of it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options protect her from falls today. Ask which one also protects her bones over the next year.

steps.detail: Weight-bearing exercise.
Seated arm work, which does not load the legs or spine.

steps.action: Pick the option that restores it
steps.detail: Restart walking with a safety plan.

elimination.verdict: Restart walking safely.

questions.objective: promoting bone and muscle health

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has had deep right thigh pain for four weeks. An x-ray of the right femur shows nothing abnormal, and the provider suspects a bone problem the x-ray missed. Which test does the nurse prepare the client for?

options.text: A DEXA scan
options.rationale: DEXA measures bone mineral density. It shows thinning, not a hidden fracture, infection or tumor.

options.text: An ultrasound of the right thigh
options.rationale: Ultrasound looks at tendons, muscle and fluid collections. The suspected problem is inside the bone.

options.text: An arthroscopy of the right hip
options.rationale: Arthroscopy looks inside a joint. The pain is in the thigh and the question is about the bone.

options.text: A bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan can detect hidden fractures, infection, tumors and areas of increased bone activity that an x-ray does not show.

questions.takeaway: When an x-ray is clear and a bone problem is still suspected, a bone scan looks for hidden fracture, infection, tumor or increased bone activity.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem says the problem is in bone and the x-ray missed it. Which test finds what x-ray cannot?

steps.detail: A hidden problem in bone.
DEXA measures how dense, not what is wrong.

steps.action: Cut soft tissue and joint tests
steps.detail: Ultrasound and arthroscopy.

elimination.verdict: Bone scan.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with right thigh pain is scheduled for a bone scan tomorrow and asks what will happen. Which explanation does the nurse give?

options.text: "Remove all metal, since the scanner uses a strong magnet."
options.rationale: This describes an MRI, the soft tissue test.

options.text: "A tracer is injected hours before the pictures are taken."
options.rationale: A bone scan uses an injected radioactive tracer that bone takes up slowly, so scanning follows hours later.

options.text: "A table scanner measures bone density at your hip and spine."
options.rationale: This describes a DEXA scan, which measures bone mineral density.

options.text: "Gel goes on your thigh and a probe is moved over the skin."
options.rationale: This describes an ultrasound, which uses sound waves.

questions.takeaway: Bone scan: tracer injection, a wait of several hours, then lying still for the pictures. Extra fluids afterward help clear the tracer.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option describes a real test. Match the description to the test that was ordered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Magnet is MRI, density is DEXA, gel and probe is ultrasound.
Injected tracer and a wait.
Bone takes the tracer up slowly, so the pictures come hours later.

elimination.verdict: Tracer injection, then delayed pictures.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old had a needle bone biopsy of the right femur two hours ago, after a bone scan showed an area of increased activity.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected after the biopsy or needs to be reported.

rows.text: Tenderness at the biopsy site rated 2 of 10
rows.rationale: Mild soreness after a needle biopsy is expected.

rows.text: Bright red blood spreading across the dressing
rows.rationale: Bleeding from the puncture site is the main thing to watch for after a bone biopsy.

rows.text: Biopsy site red and warm to touch
rows.rationale: Redness and warmth point to infection.

rows.text: Right foot pink and warm, with pulses equal to the left foot
rows.rationale: Circulation matches the other side.

rows.text: New numbness in the right foot
rows.rationale: New numbness is a red flag in any limb.

rows.text: Small dressing, dry and intact
rows.rationale: A dry, intact dressing shows no bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After a bone biopsy watch the site for bleeding and for redness or warmth, and check the limb beyond it. Mild tenderness is expected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort by three questions: is it bleeding, is it infected, is the limb beyond it changing?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A spreading stain is reported; a dry dressing is not.
Red and warm is reported; mild tenderness is not.
New numbness is reported; a pink warm foot with equal pulses is not.

elimination.verdict: Expected, report, report, expected, report, expected.

questions.objective: diagnostic tests

questions.stem: A 79-year-old admitted with pneumonia was alert and oriented at 0800. At 1000 assistive personnel report that she does not know where she is and is pulling at her oxygen tubing. Which assessment does the nurse perform first?

options.text: Tympanic temperature, to look for a new fever
options.rationale: Infection is one of the causes to consider in a sudden mental status change. It comes after oxygenation, which can harm the brain within minutes.

options.text: Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry
options.rationale: Oxygenation is the first cause to check in a sudden change. It is fast, it is a breathing problem, and she has pneumonia and is pulling at her oxygen.

options.text: A review of the medications given since 0800
options.rationale: Medications are a real cause of new confusion. The review takes longer and does not come before a breathing check.

options.text: Her most recent serum electrolyte results
options.rationale: Electrolytes belong on the list of causes. A lab review comes after the bedside check of oxygenation.

questions.takeaway: A sudden change in mental status is a new cue that needs assessment now. Check oxygenation first, then glucose, infection, medications and electrolytes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are causes the slides tell you to consider. The question is the order, and breathing comes first.

steps.detail: Oriented at 0800, disoriented at 1000. That is a sudden change from baseline.
Low oxygen injures the brain fastest and takes seconds to measure.
Temperature, medications and electrolytes follow.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen saturation first.

questions.objective: Neurologic changes requiring intervention

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with pneumonia and diabetes became confused within 2 hours. Oxygen saturation is 95% on 2 L per minute by nasal cannula, unchanged from 0800. She ate none of her breakfast after her morning insulin dose. Which action is next?

options.text: Reorient her each hour and recheck orientation at noon
options.rationale: Reorienting is good care for a confused client. Waiting until noon leaves the cause of a sudden change unfound.

options.text: Raise the oxygen flow to 4 L per minute
options.rationale: Right idea for low oxygen. Her saturation is 95% and unchanged, so oxygenation has already been checked and is not the cause.

options.text: Request a sedative to settle her until the confusion passes
options.rationale: A sedative hides the mental status the nurse is trying to assess, and medications are themselves a cause of confusion.

options.text: Check a capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Oxygenation is ruled out, and insulin without food points straight at blood glucose, the next cause on the list.

questions.takeaway: When oxygenation is not the cause of sudden confusion, move to the next cause the client's own facts point to. Insulin without food means check the glucose.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem has already answered the oxygen question. Use the missed breakfast after insulin to pick the next cause.

steps.detail: Saturation 95% and unchanged. Oxygen is not the cause.
Insulin given, no food eaten.
Hourly reorientation waits, and a sedative covers the change.

elimination.verdict: Capillary blood glucose.
