questions.objective: Neurologic changes requiring intervention

questions.stem: A 79-year-old became confused with a capillary blood glucose of 52 mg/dL and was treated. Her baseline is oriented to person, place, time and situation. Which finding 30 minutes later shows that she has returned to baseline?

options.text: She states her name, the hospital, the date and why she was admitted
options.rationale: This is orientation to person, place, time and situation, which is exactly the baseline the stem gives.

options.text: She opens her eyes and looks at the nurse each time her name is spoken
options.rationale: This shows alertness, which is level of consciousness. A client can be awake and still disoriented.

options.text: She squeezes the nurse's hand and lets go when asked to
options.rationale: Command following is one part of level of consciousness. It does not show that she knows place, time or situation.

options.text: Her repeat capillary blood glucose is 104 mg/dL
options.rationale: The cause is corrected, which is needed. The number does not show how her brain is working; only the client can show that.

questions.takeaway: Level of consciousness is how awake the client is. Orientation is whether the client understands person, place, time and situation. Evaluate against the client's own baseline.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options are true signs of recovery. Only one matches the baseline named in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oriented to person, place, time and situation.
Eye opening and hand squeeze are level of consciousness. Glucose is a lab.
Only the four answers about herself show orientation.

elimination.verdict: Stating name, place, date and reason for admission.

questions.objective: Level of consciousness, language, speech, movement and sensation

questions.stem: A 66-year-old was alert and oriented 30 minutes ago. The nurse now notices new confusion, slurred speech and right-sided weakness. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Compare the findings with the baseline from 30 minutes ago
options.rationale: Second. The comparison shows what changed and how much.

options.text: Assess airway, breathing, circulation and vital signs
options.rationale: Third in the sequence taught for this scenario, done within the same bedside visit.

options.text: Assess the client immediately at the bedside
options.rationale: First. A change from baseline has been recognized, so the nurse assesses without delay.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the appropriate response
options.rationale: Last. The nurse reports with the findings, the baseline comparison and the vital signs in hand.

questions.takeaway: A new neurologic change means act now: assess at once, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, then notify the provider or activate the response.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Start at the bedside. The call is last because the nurse needs findings to report, and it still happens within minutes.

steps.detail: The nurse goes to the client and assesses immediately.
Findings mean something only against what the client was 30 minutes ago.
ABCs and vital signs, then the provider or the response team.

elimination.verdict: Assess immediately, compare with baseline, ABCs and vital signs, notify or activate.

questions.objective: Neurologic changes requiring intervention

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has new slurred, garbled words. He points to the correct object when asked, follows a two-step command and writes his daughter's name correctly. Which approach to communication fits these findings?

options.text: Use a picture board because he cannot understand spoken words
options.rationale: A picture board suits a language problem. He understands and uses words correctly, so language is intact.

options.text: Speak louder and repeat each instruction twice
options.rationale: He follows a two-step command the first time, so hearing and understanding are not the problem.

options.text: Give him extra time to speak and a pad to write on
options.rationale: His language works and the physical production of words does not. Time and writing let him use the language he still has.

options.text: Ask only questions he can answer by nodding yes or no
options.rationale: This suits a client who cannot produce language at all. He can write, so it limits him more than his findings require.

questions.takeaway: Language is understanding and using words, a cognitive function. Speech is the physical production of words, a motor function. Test both, then match the help to the one that is impaired.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Slurred words with correct pointing, command following and writing means the motor side is impaired and the cognitive side is not.

steps.detail: Slurred and garbled is speech. Pointing, following and writing are language.
Speech is impaired. Language is intact.
Time and a writing pad use his intact language.

elimination.verdict: Extra time and a writing pad.

questions.objective: Level of consciousness, language, speech, movement and sensation

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a new right-sided facial droop is NPO by order. Assistive personnel ask to give him small sips of water to see whether he coughs. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Give the sips with him sitting upright at 90 degrees."
options.rationale: Upright positioning is correct for a client who is cleared to swallow. He is NPO, so nothing is given.

options.text: "Give nothing. Swallowing is not tested while he is NPO."
options.rationale: Swallowing is observed only when clinically appropriate and is never tested on a client who is NPO. A new facial droop adds aspiration risk.

options.text: "Start with a thickened liquid, which is easier to control."
options.rationale: Thickened liquid is a real measure for swallowing difficulty. It is still something by mouth for a client who is NPO.

options.text: "Give ice chips only, and tell me if he coughs."
options.rationale: Watching for coughing is the right concern. Ice chips melt into thin liquid, and he is NPO.

questions.takeaway: Do not test swallowing if the client is NPO. With new facial weakness, note aspiration risk and keep everything out of the mouth.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three options change how the fluid is given. The order says no fluid is given.

steps.detail: He is NPO.
Sips, thickened liquid and ice chips all put something in his mouth.
A new facial droop raises aspiration risk.

elimination.verdict: Nothing by mouth; swallowing is not tested.

questions.objective: Cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with a head injury opens his eyes only to his name, says single words that do not answer the question, and pulls his hand away from nail bed pressure. Which Glasgow Coma Scale total (range 3 to 15) does the nurse record?

options.rationale: This scores eye opening as to pain (2) and the motor response as flexion (3). His eyes open to voice and he withdraws.
Eye opening and verbal are right, and the motor response is scored as flexion (3). Pulling away from the stimulus is withdrawal (4).
Eyes to voice is 3, words is 3 and withdraws is 4, for a total of 10.
This scores the verbal response as confused (4). Single words that do not answer the question score as words (3).

questions.takeaway: Score each part on what the client does: eyes to voice 3, words 3, withdraws 4. Record the total so the next score can be compared with it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Score the three parts separately, then add. The near misses come from mixing up words with confused, and withdraws with flexion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Opens to his name: to voice, 3.
Single words, not confused sentences: 3.
Pulls away from pressure: withdraws, 4.

questions.objective: Purpose of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with a head injury had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 at 1400 and 14 at 1500. At 1600 his score is 12 (range 3 to 15, lower is worse). His next check is due at 1700. Which action is correct?

options.text: Do a focused neurologic assessment now and report the decline
options.rationale: A falling score signals deterioration and needs immediate action. A focused assessment is done when a change from baseline is noted.

options.text: Recheck the score at 1700 as scheduled, then compare the trend
options.rationale: Tracking the trend is right. Waiting an hour after a 2 point drop is the wrong time.

options.text: Record 12 as a mild change because it is nearer 15 than 3
options.rationale: This reads a single score by itself. The meaning is in the drop from 14.

options.text: Let him rest now and rescore him after he has slept
options.rationale: Rest does not explain a 2 point drop, and a declining score needs action now. Waiting delays the assessment.

questions.takeaway: The trend in the Glasgow Coma Scale matters more than any one score. A declining score needs immediate action.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options track the trend. Only one of them acts at 1600.

steps.detail: A decline, which is deterioration.
Now, with a focused assessment and a report.

elimination.verdict: Focused assessment now and report the decline.

questions.objective: Purpose of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with a head injury had pupils that were 3 mm, equal and brisk at 1400. At 1600 his right pupil is 3 mm and brisk and his left pupil is 5 mm and sluggish. How does the nurse act on this finding?

options.text: Document both pupils as normal, since each is within 2 to 6 mm
options.rationale: The range is correct. Pupils should also be equal and briskly reactive, and his are now neither.

options.text: Recheck both pupils at the next hourly check in a darker room
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable for a doubtful reading. An unequal, sluggish pupil that was normal 2 hours ago does not wait an hour.

options.text: Record the sizes in millimeters and continue the hourly schedule
options.rationale: Recording in millimeters is correct. Continuing the routine misses that the finding is new.

options.text: Treat it as a change from baseline and assess him fully now
options.rationale: The left pupil is larger and slower than it was at 1400. A change from the client's baseline is the most significant pupil finding.

questions.takeaway: Ask whether the pupils are equal and reactive, and compare with baseline. A new unequal or sluggish pupil is a change that needs assessment now.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A pupil inside the normal range can still be abnormal for this client. Compare left with right and now with 1400.

steps.detail: Right 3 mm, left 5 mm: not equal.
Both were 3 mm and brisk at 1400.
New inequality and sluggish reaction mean assess now.

elimination.verdict: Change from baseline; assess fully now.

questions.objective: Cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has scored 9 on the Glasgow Coma Scale at every check for 8 hours. A 24-year-old man with a head injury scored 15 one hour ago and now scores 13 (range 3 to 15, lower is worse). Whom does the nurse assess first?

options.text: The 70-year-old, because 9 is the lower of the two scores
options.rationale: Tempting, since a lower score is worse. A score of 9 that has not moved for 8 hours is that client's known state.

options.text: The 70-year-old, because a score of 9 means deep coma
options.rationale: Deep coma is a score of 3. A score of 9 is serious and unchanged.

options.text: The 24-year-old, after the 70-year-old's scheduled check is done
options.rationale: Right client, wrong time. A falling score needs immediate action.

options.text: The 24-year-old, because his score is falling
options.rationale: A drop from 15 to 13 in one hour is a declining trend, which signals deterioration.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize the client whose score is changing. A declining Glasgow Coma Scale trend outranks a lower score that is unchanged.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Both clients have an abnormal score. The cue that tips it is which score moved.

steps.detail: 9 for 8 hours against 15 to 13 in one hour.
The falling score is the new cue.
First means now, not after another task.

elimination.verdict: The 24-year-old with the falling score.

questions.objective: Purpose of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a brain hemorrhage flexed his arms inward toward his chest with painful stimulation at 0600. At 0800 the same stimulation makes both arms extend and rotate outward and his feet point down. How does the nurse interpret this change?

options.text: Improvement, because his arms now move away from the stimulus
options.rationale: Extension is posturing. It is a lower motor response than flexion.

options.text: No real change, because both responses are abnormal posturing
options.rationale: Both are abnormal, which is true. Extension is the more severe of the two, so this is a change for the worse.

options.text: Worsening with brainstem involvement, needing immediate action
options.rationale: Flexion points to damage above the brainstem. Extension with feet pointing down indicates brainstem involvement and is more severe.

options.text: An expected reflex, to be compared at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: Neither posture is expected, and both need immediate assessment and intervention.

questions.takeaway: Decorticate is flexion toward the core, with damage above the brainstem. Decerebrate is extension away from the body, with brainstem involvement, and is more severe. A move from flexion to extension is deterioration.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Picture the arms: toward the core at 0600, away from the body at 0800. Away is worse.

steps.detail: Arms flex inward: decorticate.
Arms extend and rotate, feet point down: decerebrate.
Decerebrate is more severe.

elimination.verdict: Worsening, brainstem involvement, act immediately.

questions.objective: Abnormal motor responses

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a brain hemorrhage does not open his eyes or speak. With painful stimulation his arms flex inward toward his core and his wrists and fingers curl inward. Which actions or conclusions by the nurse are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Describe the response as flexion (decorticate) posturing
options.rationale: Arms flexing toward the core with wrists and fingers curled inward is decorticate posturing.

options.text: Score the motor response as 3 on the Glasgow Coma Scale
options.rationale: Flexion scores 3 on the motor part, which runs from 1 (none) to 6 (obeys).

options.text: Recognize that this points to damage above the brainstem
options.rationale: Decorticate posturing indicates damage above the brainstem.

options.text: Record it as withdrawal, a motor score of 4
options.rationale: Withdrawal is pulling away from the stimulus. A fixed inward flexion posture scores 3.

options.text: Assess him immediately, since any posturing is abnormal
options.rationale: Both kinds of posturing are abnormal signs that need immediate assessment and intervention.

options.text: Wait to report until extension appears, since flexion is milder
options.rationale: Flexion is less severe than extension, which is true. Waiting for the worse sign delays care.

questions.takeaway: Flexion posturing scores 3 on the motor part of the Glasgow Coma Scale and indicates damage above the brainstem. Any posturing needs immediate assessment and intervention.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement by itself. Flexion is less severe than extension, and it is still not a reason to wait.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Arms inward toward the core with curled wrists and fingers is flexion.
Flexion is 3. Withdrawal is 4 and is a different response.
Both postures need immediate assessment.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and E.

questions.objective: Abnormal motor responses

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a brain hemorrhage has flexion posturing, a Glasgow Coma Scale motor score of 3 (range 1 to 6, lower is worse). Assistive personnel report that he now straightens both arms away from his body and call this improvement. Which action is correct?

options.text: Go to the bedside now and assess his motor response
options.rationale: The description fits extension, which would be a decline. The report comes from assistive personnel, so the nurse confirms it at the bedside at once.

options.text: Call the provider now to report extension posturing
options.rationale: Defensible, since extension needs immediate action. The nurse has not seen the response, and a report rests on the nurse's own assessment.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to apply painful stimulation and report back
options.rationale: Applying a stimulus and judging the response is assessment, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Document the arm movement as an improved motor response
options.rationale: Arms extending away from the body is extension, motor score 2, which is lower than flexion.

questions.takeaway: Arms extending away from the body is decerebrate posturing, a decline from flexion. When the cue comes secondhand, the nurse assesses the client immediately and then acts on the findings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options take the report seriously. The cue is who saw it: assistive personnel, not the nurse.

steps.detail: Arms straight and away from the body is extension, motor score 2.
Assistive personnel observed it. The nurse has not assessed it.
Assess now, then report with findings.

elimination.verdict: Assess the motor response at the bedside now.

questions.objective: Abnormal motor responses

questions.scenario: An 84-year-old is admitted with a urinary tract infection. The nurse compares today's findings with her record from a visit 6 months ago.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with aging or a new change that the nurse assesses now.

rows.text: She walks slowly with short steps, as recorded 6 months ago
rows.rationale: Slower movement and gait changes are expected, and this is unchanged.

rows.text: Both pupils are 3 mm and react slowly to light
rows.rationale: Pupils react more slowly with age. They are equal and the finding is in both eyes.

rows.text: Deep tendon reflexes are diminished in both legs
rows.rationale: Diminished deep tendon reflexes are expected with aging, and the finding is on both sides.

rows.text: Her right hand grip is weaker than her left; grips were equal 6 months ago
rows.rationale: Weakness on one side that was not there before is a new motor change.

rows.text: She wakes several times each night and is oriented each time
rows.rationale: More nighttime wakefulness is expected. Her orientation is intact.

rows.text: Since this morning she cannot say where she is; she was oriented yesterday
rows.rationale: A sudden change in mental status is never put down to age. It needs immediate assessment.

questions.takeaway: Slower movement, slower pupil reaction, diminished reflexes and nighttime waking are expected with aging. A finding that is new or one-sided is not explained by age and needs assessment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: For each row ask two things: is it the same on both sides, and is it the same as before?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark the unchanged and two-sided findings
steps.detail: Gait, pupils, reflexes and sleep match expected aging.
The right grip was equal 6 months ago. Orientation was intact yesterday.
New changes need assessment now.

elimination.verdict: Expected, expected, expected, new, expected, new.

questions.objective: Applying neurologic findings to clinical situations

questions.stem: An 84-year-old says light touch feels duller on her left forearm than on her right. Six months ago sensation was recorded as equal on both sides. Her daughter says numbness comes with age. Which action is correct?

options.text: Agree, and teach her to protect the skin of the left arm
options.rationale: Skin protection suits decreased sensation. Accepting age as the cause skips a new one-sided change.

options.text: Compare sensation on both sides and report the new difference
options.rationale: Sensation is always compared right with left, and a new sensory change is documented and reported.

options.text: Retest the left forearm alone, pressing more firmly this time
options.rationale: Testing one side gives nothing to compare with, and firmer pressure tests a different sensation.

options.text: Record decreased sensation in the left arm as an age related change
options.rationale: Aging does lower sensitivity to touch. It does not explain a difference between sides that was absent 6 months ago.

questions.takeaway: Sensory assessment compares right with left. Asymmetry that is new gets documented and reported, whatever the client's age.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Aging explains dull sensation in general. The cue here is one side, and new since the last record.

steps.detail: Left duller than right; equal 6 months ago.
Do not assume a new change is aging.
Compare both sides, then report.

elimination.verdict: Compare both sides and report the new difference.

questions.objective: Level of consciousness, language, speech, movement and sensation

questions.stem: An 84-year-old has pupils that are 3 mm, equal and slow to react to light in both eyes, recorded the same way at admission 2 days ago. She is alert and oriented. A new nurse wants to call a rapid response. Which guidance is best?

options.text: Call the rapid response, since a sluggish pupil reaction needs immediate action
options.rationale: Defensible for a new sluggish pupil. These are equal, in both eyes and the same as her admission baseline.

options.text: Continue scheduled checks, since this matches her baseline and expected aging
options.rationale: Pupils react more slowly with age. Nothing has changed from baseline, and change is what makes a pupil finding significant.

options.text: Stop the pupil checks, since slow reaction is normal at her age
options.rationale: The finding is expected, and the checks are how the nurse would catch a change from it.

options.text: Darken the room and recheck until both pupils react briskly
options.rationale: A brisk reaction is not her baseline, so the nurse would be chasing a finding she does not have.

questions.takeaway: Changes from the client's baseline are the most significant pupil findings. Slow reaction in both eyes that is unchanged in an older adult is expected, and the nurse keeps monitoring.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Sluggish pupils can mean an emergency or nothing new. Equal, both eyes and same as admission tip it.

steps.detail: Same as admission 2 days ago.
Equal size and equal reaction.
No emergency call, and no stopping the checks.

elimination.verdict: Continue scheduled checks.

questions.objective: Cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: A 47-year-old is admitted to the unit for the first time with a newly found cerebellar tumor. No neurologic findings have been recorded for him on this unit. Which assessment does the nurse perform?

options.text: A comprehensive head to toe neurologic exam to set his baseline
options.rationale: A comprehensive exam is used for new admissions and neurologic concerns. Without a baseline, later changes cannot be detected.

options.text: A focused exam of gait and balance, the functions his tumor affects
options.rationale: A focused exam monitors a known problem after a baseline exists. He has no recorded baseline yet.

options.text: A Glasgow Coma Scale score, repeated at each scheduled check
options.rationale: The score measures level of consciousness only and leaves out pupils, movement and sensation.

options.text: A pupil check and orientation questions, since he is awake
options.rationale: These are parts of the exam. A baseline also needs speech, movement and sensation.

questions.takeaway: A new admission or a new neurologic concern gets a comprehensive assessment to establish the baseline. Focused assessments then monitor for change from it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The focused exam looks efficient. With nothing recorded, there is nothing to compare a focused finding with.

steps.detail: New admission, no baseline on this unit.
Comprehensive sets the baseline.
Focused exam, coma score and pupil check are all parts of it.

elimination.verdict: Comprehensive exam to set the baseline.

questions.objective: Focused neurologic assessment

questions.stem: A 47-year-old with a cerebellar tumor is alert, oriented and follows commands. His grip is strong and equal in both hands. He asks to walk to the bathroom alone. Which plan fits the part of the brain involved?

options.text: Let him walk alone, since his strength and orientation are intact
options.rationale: Strength and orientation are not what the cerebellum controls, so intact findings there do not make walking safe.

options.text: Keep him in bed with a urinal and all four side rails raised
options.rationale: Fall prevention is the right goal. This restricts a client who can walk with help more than his findings require.

options.text: Walk with him, since his balance and coordination are at risk
options.rationale: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, so gait is the function to protect.

options.text: Give him a picture board in case he cannot find his words
options.rationale: Word finding is a language function of the cerebrum. His tumor is in the cerebellum.

questions.takeaway: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination. A client with a cerebellar problem can be strong and oriented and still fall.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The normal findings in the stem are true and belong to other parts of the brain.

steps.detail: Cerebellum: balance and coordination.
Grip and orientation do not test balance.
Walk with him; do not confine him.

elimination.verdict: Walk with him.

questions.objective: Nervous system organization and function

questions.stem: A 47-year-old with a cerebellar tumor has new swelling that presses on the brainstem, according to today's CT report. He is drowsy. Which assessment is the priority, given what the brainstem controls?

options.text: Balance and steadiness when he stands at the bedside
options.rationale: This assesses the cerebellum. It also asks a drowsy client to stand.

options.text: Memory of events from earlier today
options.rationale: Memory is a cognitive function of the cerebrum.

options.text: Light touch compared on both arms and both legs
options.rationale: Part of a full exam. It does not measure a vital function.

options.text: Respiratory rate and pattern with heart rate
options.rationale: The brainstem controls vital functions, so breathing and heart rate show first whether it is being affected.

questions.takeaway: The brainstem controls vital functions. When it is threatened, breathing and heart rate are the priority assessments.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Each option tests a real part of the nervous system. Match the test to the structure named in the stem.

steps.detail: Brainstem: vital functions.
Breathing and circulation come before balance, memory and touch.
A drowsy client is not stood up for a balance test.

elimination.verdict: Respirations and heart rate.

questions.objective: Nervous system organization and function

questions.stem: A 38-year-old with a frontal lobe injury asks the nurse several times why he is in the hospital. The nurse wants to check his memory of recent events. Which request does this best?

options.text: "Count backward from 100 by 7s."
options.rationale: This checks attention and calculation. It needs no recall of events.

options.text: "Tell me what 'a stitch in time saves nine' means."
options.rationale: This checks abstract thinking, the ability to explain a saying.

options.text: "Tell me how you came to the hospital."
options.rationale: He has to recall a recent event from his own life, and the nurse can check the answer against the record.

options.text: "Copy this word onto the paper for me."
options.rationale: This checks whether he can see and reproduce a word. Nothing has to be remembered.

questions.takeaway: Test memory by asking for a recent event the nurse can verify. Counting, explaining a saying and copying test other parts of cognition.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: All four are real mental status tasks. Ask which one cannot be done without remembering something.

steps.detail: Memory of recent events.
Counting is attention, a saying is abstraction, copying is reproduction.
Only the trip to the hospital must be remembered.

elimination.verdict: "Tell me how you came to the hospital."

questions.objective: Focused neurologic assessment

questions.stem: A 38-year-old, 3 weeks after a frontal lobe injury, says he has stopped answering his friends' calls and sees no point in going to therapy. His motor and pupil findings are unchanged from yesterday. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell him that most people his age recover well with therapy
options.rationale: Reassurance closes the conversation and passes over what he just said about himself.

options.text: Screen him for depression and ask about coping and supports
options.rationale: A complete neurologic assessment includes emotional response, coping, support systems and depression screening, and his words point there.

options.text: Repeat the full motor and pupil assessment now
options.rationale: Those findings are unchanged. The new cue is emotional, not physical.

options.text: Ask therapy to shorten his sessions until he feels ready
options.rationale: This changes the plan before anyone has assessed why he has withdrawn.

questions.takeaway: Neurologic assessment covers the whole client. Withdrawal and hopelessness after a neurologic injury call for depression screening and a look at coping and supports.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The physical findings are settled in the stem. Follow the cue that is new.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Avoiding friends and seeing no point.
Screening comes before shortening therapy.
It denies what he feels.

elimination.verdict: Depression screening, coping and supports.

questions.objective: Applying neurologic findings to clinical situations

questions.stem: A 38-year-old with a frontal lobe injury is impulsive and has poor judgment. He repeated call light teaching correctly an hour ago, then was found standing unsteadily at the bedside without having called. Which intervention is most appropriate now?

options.text: Reteach the call light and have him demonstrate it once more
options.rationale: Defensible, and teaching is the least restrictive measure. He already demonstrated it and did not use it, because using it depends on the judgment he has lost.

options.text: Enable the bed alarm
options.rationale: The alarm alerts staff without relying on his judgment, and it does not restrain him.

options.text: Apply a vest restraint while he is in bed
options.rationale: A restraint is not the least restrictive measure, and an alarm has not yet been tried.

options.text: Raise all four side rails so that he stays in bed
options.rationale: Four raised rails act as a restraint and add a fall from a greater height if he climbs over them.

questions.takeaway: With frontal lobe injury, judgment and impulse control are impaired, so safety cannot rest on the client choosing to call. Use the least restrictive measure that works without his judgment.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is not on the slides, and the Reading was not available to check.
questions.strategy: Teaching and the alarm are both least restrictive. The cue is that correct teach-back did not change what he did.

steps.detail: He knew the teaching and still got up.

steps.action: Find what does not depend on him
steps.detail: An alarm brings staff to him.
Restraint and four rails go too far.

elimination.verdict: Enable the bed alarm.

questions.objective: Nervous system organization and function

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with a compressed spinal nerve in his lower back cannot feel light touch or pain on the top of his right foot. He moves the right foot and ankle with full strength. Which plan fits these findings?

options.text: Inspect the right foot daily and wear shoes when walking
options.rationale: Signals from the foot toward the central nervous system are blocked, so an injury there will not be felt and has to be seen.

options.text: Perform passive range of motion on the right ankle each shift
options.rationale: Passive movement is for a limb the client cannot move. His signals to the muscles work and strength is full.

options.text: Check his level of consciousness and orientation every hour
options.rationale: Those assess the brain. A spinal nerve is part of the peripheral nervous system.

options.text: Keep the right leg elevated and avoid bearing weight on it
options.rationale: Strength is full, so there is no motor reason to stop him walking.

questions.takeaway: Spinal nerves connect the cord to the body. When signals toward the central nervous system are lost and signals to the muscles remain, the client can move but cannot feel, so protect the numb area.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Separate what goes in from what goes out. Sensation is lost and movement is kept.

steps.detail: No touch or pain: incoming signals lost. Full strength: outgoing signals intact.
A spinal nerve, not the brain.
Protect and inspect what he cannot feel.

elimination.verdict: Daily inspection and shoes.

questions.objective: CNS, PNS and autonomic nervous system

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with numbness on the top of his right foot from a compressed spinal nerve is scheduled for electromyography (EMG). Which statement shows that he understood the nurse's teaching about what the test looks at?

options.text: "It records the electrical activity of my brain."
options.rationale: That describes an EEG. The names are close and the target is different.

options.text: "It takes detailed pictures of my soft tissues."
options.rationale: That describes MRI, which images structure.

options.text: "It samples the fluid around my spinal cord."
options.rationale: That describes a lumbar puncture, which assesses cerebrospinal fluid.

options.text: "It checks for disorders of my nerves and muscles."
options.rationale: EMG looks at nerve and muscle disorders, which fits numbness from a compressed spinal nerve.

questions.takeaway: Know what each test looks at: EEG brain electrical activity, EMG nerve and muscle disorders, MRI soft tissue detail, CT structure, lumbar puncture cerebrospinal fluid, transcranial Doppler cerebral blood flow.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: EEG and EMG differ by one letter. E for encephalon, the brain; M for muscle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match the test to the problem
steps.detail: His problem is a compressed spinal nerve, a nerve problem outside the brain.
EEG is the brain.
MRI and lumbar puncture look at other things.

elimination.verdict: Nerves and muscles.

questions.objective: Applying neurologic findings to clinical situations

questions.stem: A 52-year-old rates back pain 9 of 10 and fears his procedure. Heart rate is 116 per minute, up from 78 an hour ago. Pupils are 5 mm, equal and brisk, up from 3 mm. He is alert and oriented. Which action is correct?

options.text: Report the larger pupils as a new neurologic change needing urgent imaging
options.rationale: Defensible, since pupil size changed from baseline. Both are equal, brisk and within 2 to 6 mm, he is alert and oriented, and pain and fear explain it.

options.text: Record the findings as normal and continue preparing him for the procedure
options.rationale: The pupils are within range. Pain of 9 of 10 and fear are left untreated.

options.text: Treat his pain and fear, then recheck his heart rate and pupils
options.rationale: Fight or flight raises heart rate and dilates pupils. Treating the trigger and rechecking confirms the cause.

options.text: Hold the procedure and begin hourly Glasgow Coma Scale scoring
options.rationale: His level of consciousness is intact, so this monitors a problem the findings do not show.

questions.takeaway: The sympathetic nervous system raises heart rate and dilates the pupils. Equal, brisk pupils in an alert client in pain and fear point to fight or flight, so treat the trigger and reassess.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: A pupil change can be the brain or the autonomic system. Equal, brisk, alert and a clear trigger tip it.

steps.detail: Fast heart rate and larger pupils rose together with pain and fear.
Pupils equal and brisk, client alert and oriented.
Relieve pain and fear, then recheck.

elimination.verdict: Treat pain and fear, then recheck.

questions.objective: CNS, PNS and autonomic nervous system

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man arrives at the emergency department at 1430 with left facial droop. A coworker saw him speaking normally at 1310 and found him slumped at 1400. Which time does the nurse report as last known well?

options.text: 1400, when the coworker found him with symptoms
options.rationale: This is when the symptoms were discovered. The stroke could have started any time after 1310, so the clock cannot start here.

options.text: 1310, when he was last seen speaking normally
options.rationale: Last known well is the last moment he was known to be normal. It starts the treatment clock.

options.text: 1430, when he arrived and was first assessed
options.rationale: Arrival time matters for how fast the team works. It says nothing about when the brain lost blood flow.

options.text: Unknown, because no one witnessed the onset
options.rationale: Tempting because the onset was unwitnessed. A last normal time of 1310 is known, and calling it unknown could wrongly limit his treatment.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last time the client was seen normal, not when symptoms were found. It decides whether time sensitive treatment is possible.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three times are in the stem. Ask which one is the last moment someone saw him without symptoms.

steps.detail: Last known well means last seen normal.
1400 and 1430 both come after symptoms were already present.
A witnessed normal time of 1310 exists, even though the onset itself was not seen.

elimination.verdict: 1310. The clock starts at the last normal moment.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who takes insulin has slurred speech, confusion and left arm weakness that began 80 minutes ago. He is breathing easily. Which assessment does the nurse complete before transport to CT?

options.text: Swallow screen with sips of water
options.rationale: Required before anything goes in his mouth. It does not explain his symptoms or change the decision to image.

options.text: Full medication reconciliation with his pharmacy
options.rationale: Current medications matter, and the key ones can be asked in seconds. A full reconciliation delays imaging, and history must not delay care.

options.text: 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: A reasonable search for a clot source. It does not explain his symptoms or change what happens in the next few minutes.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Low blood glucose causes slurred speech, confusion and weakness that look exactly like a stroke, and he takes insulin. It is fast and its result can change the whole plan.

questions.takeaway: Check blood glucose promptly in every suspected stroke. Hypoglycemia looks like a stroke and is fixed in minutes.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: All four are real stroke assessments. Pick the fast one whose result could explain every symptom in the stem.

steps.detail: Insulin plus confusion, slurred speech and weakness fits low glucose as well as stroke.
Full reconciliation and an ECG take time and do not change the next step.

steps.action: Cut what is not needed yet
steps.detail: A swallow screen comes before oral intake. It does not explain his symptoms.

elimination.verdict: Capillary blood glucose. Rule out the mimic before assuming stroke.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with slurred speech and left arm weakness had a blood glucose of 52 mg/dL. After treatment it is 104 mg/dL, and both deficits are unchanged. Last known well was 95 minutes ago. Which action is next?

options.text: Keep the stroke alert active and take him to noncontrast CT
options.rationale: The glucose is corrected and the deficits remain, so low glucose did not explain them. He is still a possible stroke inside the treatment window, and imaging comes next.

options.text: Cancel the stroke alert because the low glucose explained his symptoms
options.rationale: That would be right if the deficits had cleared when the glucose rose. They did not.

options.text: Recheck the glucose every 15 minutes for an hour before any imaging
options.rationale: Rechecking glucose is good care. Making imaging wait an hour for it uses up treatment time.

options.text: Ask for the fibrinolytic to be started while the time window is open
options.rationale: The time is right and the order of steps is wrong. Imaging must exclude bleeding before a clot dissolving drug.

questions.takeaway: Treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess. If the deficits persist once glucose is normal, the stroke pathway continues without delay.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: This is an evaluate question. The treatment worked on the number and not on the deficits, so ask what that tells you.

steps.detail: Glucose 104 mg/dL with unchanged deficits means the mimic is ruled out.
Canceling the alert and an hour of rechecks both lose time.

steps.action: Cut the step out of order
steps.detail: A fibrinolytic never comes before imaging.

elimination.verdict: Keep the alert active and go to CT.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man's noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage 110 minutes after last known well, and a fibrinolytic is being considered. His daughter now says he takes a blood thinner for atrial fibrillation. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Start a second IV line for the infusion
options.rationale: IV access is part of the nurse's role and would be next if the drug were going ahead. The new history may change that decision, so it comes first.

options.text: Begin frequent neurologic and blood pressure checks for bleeding
options.rationale: This is the plan after a fibrinolytic is given. No drug has been given yet.

options.text: Tell the stroke team about the anticoagulant now
options.rationale: Contraindications are one of the candidate questions, and an anticoagulant raises bleeding risk. The team is deciding now and does not have this fact.

options.text: Reassure the daughter that the clear CT makes the drug safe
options.rationale: The CT shows he is not bleeding now. It does not answer whether he has a contraindication to the drug.

questions.takeaway: A clear CT answers one candidate question. Medication history, especially anticoagulants, answers another, and the nurse's job is to get it to the team before the decision.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options prepare for the drug. One piece of new information could change whether the drug is given at all, and that goes first.

steps.detail: The blood thinner is information the team does not have.
A second IV line only helps if the drug is given. The history decides whether it is.

steps.action: Cut the after drug plan and the false reassurance
steps.detail: Bleeding checks come later, and a clear CT is not the same as no contraindications.

elimination.verdict: Tell the stroke team about the anticoagulant first.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man had 20 minutes of right hand numbness and trouble finding words this morning. Both resolved fully and his neurologic examination is now normal. He asks to go home. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "This was a small stroke, and the damage it left is permanent."
options.rationale: A stroke leaves persistent deficits. His cleared completely, which fits a transient ischemic attack with no permanent damage.

options.text: "There is no lasting damage, so a clinic visit next week is enough."
options.rationale: The first half is true. The conclusion is not, because the episode warns that a stroke may follow.

options.text: "This warns of a stroke to come. You need evaluation today."
options.rationale: Symptoms that came on and then resolved fit a transient ischemic attack. It is an emergency warning, not a false alarm.

options.text: "Learn the BE FAST signs, then call us if they ever come back."
options.rationale: Good teaching for him, and it is not enough alone. Sending him home skips the evaluation that the warning calls for.

questions.takeaway: A transient ischemic attack causes no permanent damage and is still an emergency warning of a coming stroke. Resolved symptoms do not mean the client can leave.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options contain something true. Check whether the true part actually leads to the conclusion attached to it.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Symptoms that resolve fully with a normal examination fit a transient ischemic attack.
Persistent deficits define a stroke. He has none.

steps.action: Cut the two that send him home
steps.detail: Routine follow up and teaching alone both treat a warning as a false alarm.

elimination.verdict: It is a warning, and he needs evaluation today.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man being evaluated after a transient ischemic attack suddenly cannot see objects on his right side and staggers when he stands. His face is symmetric, arm strength is equal and speech is clear. Which action is correct?

options.text: Activate the stroke response and record the time the symptoms began
options.rationale: Sudden vision loss and sudden loss of balance are stroke signs, the B and E of BE FAST. The T means noting the time.

options.text: Measure lying and standing blood pressure to explain the unsteadiness
options.rationale: A fair thought for unsteadiness on standing. It does not explain sudden vision loss, and it delays the stroke response.

options.text: Continue observation because face, arm and speech checks are negative
options.rationale: Face, arm and speech are only three of the signs. Balance and eyes can be the only signs of a stroke.

options.text: Have him rest in bed and recheck in 30 minutes to see if it clears
options.rationale: Waiting to see whether it resolves like the earlier episode spends treatment time on a possible stroke.

questions.takeaway: Sudden vision change or loss of balance is a stroke sign even when face, arms and speech are normal. Act and note the time.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem lists three normal findings to pull you toward watching. Look at what is new and sudden instead.

steps.detail: Vision loss on the right and staggering.
Balance and eyes are stroke signs.
Orthostatic pressures, observation and bed rest all delay the response.

elimination.verdict: Activate the stroke response and record the time.

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has sudden right sided weakness, last known well 60 minutes ago. The CT scanner is occupied, the fibrinolytic has arrived from pharmacy, and his wife says, "time is brain, please start it." Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the bolus now and send him to CT during the infusion
options.rationale: Fast, and unsafe. If the weakness comes from a bleeding vessel, the drug makes the bleeding worse.

options.text: Hold the drug until CT excludes bleeding
options.rationale: Symptoms cannot tell a blocked vessel from a ruptured one. Imaging has to exclude hemorrhage before any clot dissolving drug.

options.text: Draw clotting studies and start the drug once they are sent
options.rationale: Clotting studies are part of the workup. They do not show whether he is bleeding into his brain.

options.text: Repeat the NIHSS and start the drug if the score has risen
options.rationale: A rising score shows he is getting worse. It does not show whether the cause is a clot or a bleed.

questions.takeaway: Ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes can look the same at the bedside. A fibrinolytic is never given until imaging excludes hemorrhage.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Speed matters, and so does the order of steps. Three options start the drug before the one test that makes it safe.

steps.detail: Whether the vessel is blocked or bleeding.

steps.action: Find the test that answers it
steps.detail: Noncontrast CT detects hemorrhage.

steps.action: Cut every option that starts the drug first
steps.detail: Three options give it before bleeding is excluded.

elimination.verdict: Hold the drug and get the CT now.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with an ischemic stroke has a CT showing no hemorrhage, last known well 100 minutes ago. Blood pressure is 204/116 mm Hg. A fibrinolytic and an IV antihypertensive are both prescribed. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Start the fibrinolytic now, then give the antihypertensive during the infusion
options.rationale: Defensible because time is brain. At 204/116 mm Hg the drug carries a high risk of bleeding into the brain, so pressure is treated first.

options.text: Hold both drugs, because high pressure after an ischemic stroke perfuses the brain
options.rationale: True for a client who is not getting a fibrinolytic. This client is, so the pressure must come down first.

options.text: Give the antihypertensive quickly until systolic pressure is under 120 mm Hg
options.rationale: Right drug, wrong target. A sudden drop that low cuts perfusion to brain tissue that is already short of blood.

options.text: Antihypertensive first, then the fibrinolytic once pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg
options.rationale: Pressure must be below 185/110 mm Hg before a fibrinolytic. The antihypertensive goes first, and the fibrinolytic follows as soon as the pressure allows.

questions.takeaway: Before a fibrinolytic, blood pressure must be below 185/110 mm Hg. Lower it first, and lower it only as far as needed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two rules pull against each other here: move fast, and do not give a clot dissolving drug at a very high pressure. The stated pressure decides which one leads.

steps.detail: 204/116 mm Hg is above the limit for a fibrinolytic.
Starting the drug first saves minutes and risks bleeding. Lowering pressure first makes the drug safe.
Leaving pressure alone fits a client with no fibrinolytic, and under 120 systolic is too low too fast.

elimination.verdict: Antihypertensive, confirm below 185/110 mm Hg, then the fibrinolytic.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with right arm weakness from an ischemic stroke is 20 minutes into an alteplase infusion. Which new findings does the nurse treat as possible bleeding that needs immediate attention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sudden severe headache
options.rationale: A severe headache during a fibrinolytic can mean bleeding inside the skull.

options.text: Nausea with vomiting
options.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are on the list of bleeding signs after a fibrinolytic.

options.text: Blood pressure up from 158/88 to 206/112 mm Hg
options.rationale: A sharp rise in pressure is a warning sign of bleeding and also raises the risk of it.

options.text: Blood oozing around the IV puncture site in her left forearm
options.rationale: Bleeding at puncture sites shows the drug's effect on clotting and is reported.

options.text: Right hand grip stronger than before the infusion
options.rationale: Her weakness is on the right, so a stronger grip is improvement. That is the purpose of the drug.

options.text: Asks for water because her mouth is dry
options.rationale: Thirst is not a sign of bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After a fibrinolytic the major concern is bleeding: new or worse deficits, severe headache, acute hypertension, nausea and vomiting, and blood at puncture sites or in urine or stool.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each finding alone. Ask whether it could come from bleeding or whether it is the improvement the drug is meant to produce.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Headache, vomiting, a sharp pressure rise and oozing at the site.
Her weak side is the right, so a stronger right grip is good news.
A dry mouth is not a sign of bleeding.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is 30 minutes into a fibrinolytic infusion for an ischemic stroke. She reports a sudden severe headache, and her speech, which had cleared, is garbled again. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the infusion and call the provider
options.rationale: Severe headache with neurologic worsening during a fibrinolytic suggests bleeding in the brain. The drug stops first, and a head CT is expected.

options.text: Give an analgesic for the headache and reassess pain in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Treating the pain treats the symptom and leaves the drug running while she may be bleeding.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and recheck her in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The right instinct, carried only halfway. A slower rate still delivers the drug that may be causing a bleed.

options.text: Complete a full NIHSS before changing anything
options.rationale: Assessment usually comes first. Here the two cues that trigger action are already in hand, and a full score costs minutes.

questions.takeaway: Severe headache plus neurologic worsening during a fibrinolytic means stop the infusion, call, and expect a head CT.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check whether the stem already gives the assessment. A new headache and returned speech deficit are enough to act on.

steps.detail: New severe headache and a deficit that has returned.
Bleeding in the brain from the drug that is still infusing.

steps.action: Cut what leaves the drug running
steps.detail: Analgesia, a slower rate and a full score all keep it going.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion and call the provider.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman finished a fibrinolytic infusion 2 hours ago. Her right hand grip was weak before treatment, and blood glucose was 108 mg/dL ten minutes ago. Which reported finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Blood oozing at the left forearm IV site, first seen this hour
options.rationale: Real bleeding that needs pressure and reporting. It is visible and controllable, so it ranks below a possible bleed inside the skull.

options.text: Opens her eyes only after three calls; was awake an hour ago
options.rationale: A falling level of consciousness is neurologic worsening and may mean bleeding in the brain. The normal glucose rules out the quick mimic.

options.text: Pink tinged urine in the bedpan, first seen this hour
options.rationale: Blood in the urine is a bleeding sign and is reported. It does not threaten her brain in the next minutes.

options.text: Right hand grip weaker than the left, as it was before treatment
options.rationale: Unchanged from before treatment, so it is not new and not worsening.

questions.takeaway: After a fibrinolytic, every bleeding sign is reported, and a new drop in level of consciousness comes first because the bleed it points to is in the brain.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three of the four are true bleeding or stroke findings. Rank them by which one is new and inside the skull.

steps.detail: The weak right grip was there before treatment.
Oozing at a site and pink urine are outside the skull and can be seen and managed.
108 mg/dL means low glucose does not explain the new drowsiness.

elimination.verdict: The new drowsiness. Possible bleeding in the brain outranks visible bleeding elsewhere.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman received a fibrinolytic for an ischemic stroke 6 hours ago and has passed a swallow screen. Her daily antiplatelet tablet is due now. No follow up CT has been done. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give it, because antiplatelets are started within 24 to 48 hours of a stroke
options.rationale: True for a client who did not receive a fibrinolytic. After one, the antiplatelet waits.

options.text: Give it, because the passed swallow screen makes oral drugs safe
options.rationale: The screen settles whether she can swallow the tablet. It does not settle the bleeding risk.

options.text: Give half the dose now and the rest after the follow up CT
options.rationale: A partial dose still affects clotting during the period of highest bleeding risk.

options.text: Hold it until 24 hours have passed and a follow up CT shows no bleeding
options.rationale: Antiplatelets and anticoagulants are held for 24 hours after a fibrinolytic and until a follow up CT is clear.

questions.takeaway: No antiplatelet or anticoagulant for 24 hours after a fibrinolytic, and not until a follow up CT shows no bleeding.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two facts in the stem matter: 6 hours since the drug, and no follow up CT. The passed swallow screen answers a different question.

steps.detail: After a fibrinolytic, drugs that affect clotting wait 24 hours and a clear CT.
Only 6 hours have passed and no CT has been done.

steps.action: Cut all three that give it
steps.detail: Each one adds bleeding risk now, whatever the reason offered.

elimination.verdict: Hold the antiplatelet.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is 18 hours past a large ischemic stroke. While he dozes, oxygen saturation falls from 96% to 89% on room air; breath sounds are clear. Oxygen is prescribed as needed. Which action protects his brain?

options.text: Recheck the saturation at the next scheduled vital signs
options.rationale: Leaves him at 89% in the meantime. Injured brain tissue does not tolerate low oxygen.

options.text: Suction his airway to clear secretions
options.rationale: Right for a blocked airway. His breath sounds are clear, so there is nothing to remove.

options.text: Apply the prescribed oxygen now and recheck
options.rationale: Low oxygen adds a second injury to brain tissue that is already short of blood flow. The order is in place, so the nurse acts.

options.text: Lay the bed flat to bring more blood to his head
options.rationale: The goal of better perfusion is right. Position does not correct low oxygen, which is the problem in front of the nurse.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke the goal is to protect perfusion and prevent secondary injury. Hypoxia and hypotension are corrected at once.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The data are complete: a clear airway, a low saturation and an oxygen order. This is a time to act, not to recheck later.

steps.detail: Saturation of 89% in a brain that is already injured.

steps.action: Match the fix to the cause
steps.detail: Clear breath sounds mean suction has no target.

steps.action: Cut the delay and the wrong tool
steps.detail: Waiting and repositioning do not raise his oxygen.

elimination.verdict: Apply oxygen now and recheck.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.nursesNote: 1400: 61-year-old man, day 2 after a large left hemisphere ischemic stroke. Right arm weakness, unchanged from admission. Halting speech, unchanged from admission. Restless and pulling at the bed linen since 1300; calm at 1200. Reports a new headache, 6 of 10 where 10 is worst. Vomited twice in the past hour. Both pupils equal but slower to constrict than at 1200. Blood pressure 146/84 mm Hg, the same as at 1200. Oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that suggest rising intracranial pressure and need to be reported now.

segments.text: Right arm weakness, unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: His known deficit from the stroke. It has not changed.

segments.text: Halting speech, unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: A new speech change would count. This one is his baseline.

segments.text: Restless and pulling at the bed linen since 1300; calm at 1200
segments.rationale: Restlessness is a change in level of consciousness, the earliest sign of rising pressure.

segments.text: Reports a new headache, 6 of 10 where 10 is worst
segments.rationale: A new headache is an early sign.

segments.text: Vomited twice in the past hour
segments.rationale: Vomiting is an early sign of rising pressure.

segments.text: Both pupils equal but slower to constrict than at 1200
segments.rationale: Sluggish pupils are an early sign. Fixed pupils come late.

segments.text: Blood pressure 146/84 mm Hg, the same as at 1200
segments.rationale: Unchanged. Blood pressure changes come late, so a steady pressure does not rule out rising pressure in the skull.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 97% on room air
segments.rationale: Normal. Nothing to report.

questions.takeaway: Early signs of increased ICP are a change in level of consciousness (restlessness, irritability, confusion), headache, vomiting, new speech change and sluggish pupils. Vital sign changes come late.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort every line into new or unchanged. On day 2 after a large stroke the risk is at its highest, so new findings count even while the vital signs hold steady.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Arm weakness and halting speech are unchanged from admission.
Blood pressure is unchanged and saturation is 97%.
Restlessness, headache, vomiting and slower pupils all began today.

elimination.verdict: Restlessness, new headache, vomiting and sluggish pupils.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is 2 days past a large ischemic stroke. Blood pressure has gone from 150/84 to 192/70 mm Hg and pulse from 78 to 48 per minute. Breathing is irregular and the left pupil is fixed. How does the nurse interpret this pattern?

options.text: A late sign that pressure is compressing the brainstem
options.rationale: Rising pressure with a wider pulse pressure, a slow pulse and irregular breathing is the Cushing triad, and a fixed pupil is also late. This needs the rapid response team now.

options.text: An early sign that pressure in the skull is starting to rise
options.rationale: The condition is right and the stage is wrong. Early signs are restlessness, headache and vomiting, and these are late ones.

options.text: A hypertensive response to pain that calls for an analgesic
options.rationale: Pain raises both pressure and pulse. His pulse has dropped to 48 per minute.

options.text: A slow pulse from deep sleep with a normal swing in pressure
options.rationale: Sleep can slow the pulse. It does not fix a pupil or make breathing irregular.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension with a widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing is the Cushing triad. With fixed pupils it is a late sign that needs immediate help.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look at the direction of each change together: pressure up, pulse down, breathing irregular. Then ask whether that set is early or late.

steps.detail: Pressure up with the pulse pressure widened from 66 to 122 mm Hg, pulse down, breathing irregular, one pupil fixed.
Pain speeds the pulse and sleep does not fix a pupil.
Vital sign changes and fixed pupils are late.

elimination.verdict: A late sign of brainstem pressure.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man on day 2 after a large stroke has a new headache and restlessness, and increased intracranial pressure is suspected. Assistive personnel plan his bath, linen change and turning. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Do all three back to back so that he gets one long rest afterward
options.rationale: Clustering care is the usual rule for rest. With high pressure in the skull, activities done back to back raise it sharply.

options.text: Space them apart, with his head midline and the head of the bed raised
options.rationale: Spacing care limits pressure spikes. A midline head and a raised bed let venous blood drain from the skull.

options.text: Lay the bed flat for the linen change, then raise it when finished
options.rationale: Convenient for the linen change. Lying flat slows venous drainage from the head while pressure is already high.

options.text: Turn his head fully to one side during care to guard against aspiration
options.rationale: A reasonable thought for airway protection. Turning the neck narrows the veins that drain the skull.

questions.takeaway: With increased ICP, space out care instead of clustering it, keep the head midline and the head of the bed raised per protocol, and avoid sharp neck or hip flexion.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The usual rule is to cluster care. Ask whether the stem gives a reason that rule reverses for this client.

steps.action: Find the reason the rule changes
steps.detail: Suspected high pressure in the skull.
Back to back care spikes the pressure.
Flat and head turned both slow venous drainage.

elimination.verdict: Space the care and keep his head midline with the bed raised.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has left leg weakness after a right hemisphere stroke. Alert and oriented, he says, "my leg is fine," and has twice tried to stand alone despite call light teaching. Which plan fits this client?

options.text: Repeat the call light teaching and have him say it back
options.rationale: Teach back is good practice. He does not believe the leg is weak, so repeating a rule he sees no need for has already failed twice.

options.text: Apply a vest restraint whenever staff are out of the room
options.rationale: It would stop him standing, and it is not the least restrictive choice while supervision has not been tried.

options.text: Ask his family to convince him that the leg is weak
options.rationale: Family support helps. Being unaware of a deficit comes from the brain injury and does not yield to persuasion.

options.text: Supervise him closely at every transfer
options.rationale: Right hemisphere damage brings impulsivity, poor judgment and unawareness of deficits. Safety has to come from the staff, not from his own judgment.

questions.takeaway: A right hemisphere stroke makes a client impulsive and unaware of deficits. Being oriented does not make him safe, so supervision replaces reliance on teaching.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Alert and oriented is the lure. Ask which side of the brain was injured and what that does to judgment.

steps.detail: Right hemisphere: impulsive, poor judgment, unaware of deficits.

steps.action: Cut what depends on his insight
steps.detail: Teaching and persuasion both need him to accept the weakness.
A restraint comes after less restrictive measures.

elimination.verdict: Close supervision at every transfer.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a right hemisphere stroke eats only the food on the right half of his plate and does not notice his left arm hanging off the chair. Which action addresses this finding?

options.text: Offer smaller meals, because his appetite is poor
options.rationale: He leaves food on one side only, which points to attention and not appetite.

options.text: Place all items on his right so that he does not need to look left
options.rationale: This is the fix for a visual field cut. For neglect it lets the ignored side stay ignored, including the arm.

options.text: Cue him to scan left and to touch and use his left arm
options.rationale: Ignoring the left side of the plate and the left arm is left sided neglect. Scanning and using both sides brings that side back into awareness.

options.text: Patch one eye and switch the patch every few hours
options.rationale: Patching treats double vision. Nothing in the stem suggests he sees double.

questions.takeaway: Left sided neglect follows right hemisphere damage. Teach scanning toward the neglected side and touching and using both sides.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The arm is the tipping cue. A visual field cut explains the plate, and only neglect explains ignoring his own arm.

steps.detail: He ignores both the left of the plate and his left arm, which is neglect.

steps.action: Separate it from a field cut
steps.detail: Moving items to the right suits a visual field loss.
Small meals treat appetite and a patch treats double vision.

elimination.verdict: Cue him to scan left and to use his left arm.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man admitted 3 hours ago with a stroke says he is hungry. No swallow screen is documented. Assistive personnel offer to feed him breakfast slowly with the head of the bed raised. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Keep him NPO until the nurse completes a swallow screen
options.rationale: Any stroke can impair swallowing. Nothing goes in by mouth until the nurse has screened him.

options.text: Feed him small bites and stop if he starts to cough
options.rationale: Good feeding technique at the wrong time. It tests his swallow with food, and aspiration can happen without a cough.

options.text: Test his swallow yourself with a few sips of water first
options.rationale: Screening comes first, and it is the nurse's assessment. It cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

options.text: Hold the food and give his oral tablets with a sip of water
options.rationale: NPO before the screen covers food, fluids and medications.

questions.takeaway: NPO until the swallow screen: no food, fluids or medications. The nurse screens, and assistive personnel may feed only after the screen is passed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Hunger is the emotional pull. Check what has not been done yet and who is allowed to do it.

steps.detail: No swallow screen is documented.
Bites, sips and tablets all go in before the screen.
The screen is the nurse's assessment.

elimination.verdict: Keep him NPO until the nurse screens his swallow.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a left hemisphere stroke says, "I want... the... thing... drink," and cries. She raises her left hand when asked. This pattern is unchanged since admission. Her son says she is confused. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: "Her speech muscles are weak, so her words come out slurred."
options.rationale: That describes dysarthria, where the right words come out slurred. She is searching for words, not slurring them.

options.text: "She cannot understand what is said, so explaining will not help."
options.rationale: She raised her left hand when asked, so she understands spoken words.

options.text: "This is new confusion that suggests pressure rising in her skull."
options.rationale: A new language change would be a warning. Hers is unchanged since admission.

options.text: "She understands you. Her brain cannot find the words, and she knows it."
options.rationale: Aphasia is a language problem from left hemisphere damage. She follows a command, and her crying shows she is aware of the gap.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia is a language problem in the brain; dysarthria is a speech muscle problem with the right words slurred. A client who follows commands and struggles for words understands.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Use the two cues the son missed: she follows a command, and she is upset by her own speech.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: She raises her left hand when asked.
Missing words, not slurred words.
Unchanged since admission, so it is not a new decline.

elimination.verdict: She understands, and the words will not come.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman on day 3 after a left hemisphere stroke has had right arm weakness since admission. At 1000 she has a new right facial droop and cannot lift her right leg, which she lifted at 0800. Which action is correct?

options.text: Document the change and watch whether it clears within the hour
options.rationale: Waiting to see whether it resolves treats a possible new stroke like a transient event and spends treatment time.

options.text: Compare her NIHSS score at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: The right tool at the wrong time. A new deficit is scored and acted on when it is found.

options.text: Report the new deficits now, noting baseline at 0800
options.rationale: New facial droop and new weakness in a client already being watched are changes that matter. The 0800 time gives the team a last known well.

options.text: Position the right leg in alignment and request a therapy referral
options.rationale: Good care for a settled deficit. This one appeared in the last 2 hours.

questions.takeaway: In a client already being watched, new weakness, new facial droop, new aphasia or a falling level of consciousness is reported at once, with the time the client was last at baseline.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Separate old from new. The arm is her baseline, and the face and leg changed between 0800 and 1000.

steps.detail: Arm weakness is old. Facial droop and leg weakness are new.
Watching for an hour and the next scheduled check both delay.
Positioning and therapy suit a deficit that is no longer changing.

elimination.verdict: Report the new deficits now, with 0800 as the last time at baseline.

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a stroke passed a swallow screen yesterday. Her NIHSS score is 4 at 0800 and 4 at 1200 (0 is normal; higher is worse). At lunch she coughs with each sip and her voice sounds wet. Which action is correct?

options.text: Continue the meal upright with smaller sips, since the score is unchanged
options.rationale: Defensible because she passed a screen and the score is steady. The score does not measure swallowing, and a wet voice means fluid is reaching her airway.

options.text: Stop the meal, keep her NPO and reassess her swallowing
options.rationale: Coughing with each sip and a wet voice are signs of aspiration. The airway comes before the meal and before any score.

options.text: Repeat the NIHSS now and continue lunch if it is still 4
options.rationale: The score standardizes the neurologic assessment. It does not capture everything, and swallowing is one of the gaps.

options.text: Have assistive personnel finish feeding her at a slower pace
options.rationale: Feeding can be delegated only while her swallow is known to be safe. That is now in doubt.

questions.takeaway: The NIHSS standardizes the neurologic assessment and does not replace it. An unchanged score never outweighs a bedside sign of aspiration.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two reassuring facts sit in the stem: a passed screen and a steady score. One bedside cue overrides both.

steps.detail: A cough with each sip and a wet voice.
It does not measure swallowing, so a steady 4 says nothing about this.
Stop oral intake and reassess before anyone feeds her again.

elimination.verdict: Stop the meal, keep her NPO and reassess.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman reports the worst headache of her life, which began suddenly 40 minutes ago, with vomiting, a stiff neck and light sensitivity. Temperature is 36.9 C; face, arm strength and speech are normal. Which action is correct?

options.text: Treat it as a migraine with a dark, quiet room and an analgesic request
options.rationale: Migraine also brings vomiting and light sensitivity. A sudden worst headache of her life with a stiff neck points to bleeding first.

options.text: Start droplet precautions and prepare her for a lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Stiff neck and light sensitivity fit meningitis too. The sudden onset and normal temperature point away from infection, and imaging comes first.

options.text: Send her to the waiting area, because the stroke screen is negative
options.rationale: Face, arm and speech checks can be normal when the bleeding is around the brain and not within it.

options.text: Treat this as a possible brain bleed and get emergency imaging
options.rationale: Sudden worst headache of her life with vomiting, stiff neck and light sensitivity is the picture of a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

questions.takeaway: A sudden worst headache of the client's life with vomiting, stiff neck and light sensitivity is a subarachnoid hemorrhage until imaging says otherwise, even with normal face, arms and speech.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Three conditions share parts of this picture. The word sudden and the normal temperature separate them.
