steps.detail: Sudden and the worst of her life.
36.9 C makes infection less likely.

steps.action: Do not lean on the normal findings
steps.detail: Normal face, arms and speech do not rule out bleeding around the brain.

elimination.verdict: Possible brain bleed. Emergency imaging.

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman's CT shows a subarachnoid hemorrhage 50 minutes after her headache began. A student nurse asks whether to prepare a fibrinolytic because she is inside the time window. Which reply is correct?

options.text: "Yes, treatment within 4.5 hours of last known well qualifies her."
options.rationale: The time window is right and applies only to an ischemic stroke. Hers is a bleed.

options.text: "Yes, once her blood pressure has been brought down."
options.rationale: Blood pressure limits apply before a fibrinolytic for an ischemic stroke. No pressure makes the drug safe in a bleed.

options.text: "No, a vessel is bleeding, and the drug would make it worse."
options.rationale: A hemorrhagic stroke is a ruptured vessel. A fibrinolytic is never given, because it would add to the bleeding.

options.text: "No, the drug waits until a second scan shows where the clot is."
options.rationale: The answer is right and the reason is wrong. There is no clot to find; the problem is a ruptured vessel.

questions.takeaway: A fibrinolytic is for ischemic stroke only. Hemorrhagic stroke is a ruptured vessel, so the drug is never given, and both types can raise ICP.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Time is one candidate question and it is not the first. Ask what the CT showed.

steps.detail: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, which is a bleeding vessel.
Neither the time window nor a lower pressure makes the drug safe in a bleed.

steps.action: Check the reason in each no
steps.detail: Only one gives the true reason.

elimination.verdict: No. She is bleeding, and the drug would add to it.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a subarachnoid hemorrhage was oriented at 0000. At 0200 she is restless and does not know where she is. Headache is 8 of 10 (10 is worst), unchanged; blood pressure and pulse are unchanged. What does this change mean?

options.text: Pain and lost sleep explain it; treat the pain first, then recheck her orientation
options.rationale: Defensible because pain and agitation do raise pressure in the skull. Her pain is unchanged while her orientation is new, so pain does not explain it.

options.text: It is the earliest sign of rising pressure in the skull
options.rationale: A decline in level of consciousness, including restlessness and confusion, comes first. It is reported immediately.

options.text: It is not a concern until her pulse slows and her blood pressure climbs
options.rationale: Those are late signs. Waiting for them means waiting for brainstem pressure.

options.text: Night time disorientation is expected in hospital; reorient her and dim the lights
options.rationale: Reorienting and a dim room are sound comfort measures. They do not explain a new change two hours after she was oriented.

questions.takeaway: The earliest sign of increased ICP is a decline in level of consciousness: restlessness, irritability, confusion. Vital signs change late, so steady numbers do not reassure.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two findings are unchanged and one is new. Build the answer on the new one.

steps.detail: Orientation and restlessness, between 0000 and 0200.
The headache is the same 8 of 10 as before, so it does not account for a new change.
Pulse and pressure change late.

elimination.verdict: The earliest sign of rising pressure. Report it now.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP

questions.stem: A 58-year-old reports a cough for 3 months. The nurse has recorded a 45 pack-year smoking history, allergies and current medications. Which question should the nurse ask next to complete the focused respiratory history?

options.text: "How many packs do you smoke on a typical day?"
options.rationale: Needed for pack-years, and the 45 pack-year figure shows it has already been obtained.

options.text: "Are you willing to set a quit date some time in the next month?"
options.rationale: A real step in cessation counseling that belongs after the history is complete and after advising the client to quit.

options.text: "What exposures at work or home, and any infections or travel?"
options.rationale: Exposures, infections and travel are the parts of the focused history that are still missing.

options.text: "Which nicotine replacement products have you tried before?"
options.rationale: Useful when assisting a quit attempt later. It does not fill a gap in the respiratory history.

questions.takeaway: A focused respiratory history covers symptom pattern, smoking and vaping, exposures, infections and travel, allergies, medications, family history, and the effect on sleep and daily activities.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: List what the stem says is already recorded, then look for the option that adds a new category of data.

steps.detail: Smoking amount, allergies and medications are recorded.
Three options return to smoking. One opens exposures, infections and travel.
Quit dates and nicotine products are counseling steps, not history.

elimination.verdict: Ask about exposures, infections and travel.

questions.objective: focused history and physical assessment

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a 45 pack-year history has just told the nurse about smoking 1.5 packs per day. The client says, "Nobody ever said my cough was from cigarettes." Using the 5 As, what does the nurse do next?

options.text: Advise the client clearly and personally to quit
options.rationale: Ask is complete. Advise is the next step, and the client's remark shows no one has done it.

options.text: Assess whether the client is willing to try to quit now
options.rationale: The correct step one place too early. Willingness is assessed after the client has been advised.

options.text: Assist by offering nicotine replacement and counseling
options.rationale: The right treatment, offered before the client has been advised or has said anything about readiness.

options.text: Arrange a follow up visit in 1 week to review smoking progress
options.rationale: The last of the 5 As. There is no plan yet to follow up on.

questions.takeaway: The 5 As run in order: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange. Find the last step completed and take the next one.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every option is one of the 5 As, so the question is only about sequence. Identify which step the stem has already finished.

steps.action: Locate the client in the sequence
steps.detail: Tobacco use has been asked about and answered.
Advise follows Ask.
Assess, Assist and Arrange each depend on the step before.

elimination.verdict: Advise the client to quit.

questions.objective: health promotion and smoking cessation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old who smokes 1.5 packs per day is ready to quit and says, "Just give me the patch. I do not need to talk to anybody." Which plan should the nurse propose?

options.text: Nicotine replacement alone, because the plan must follow the client's stated preference
options.rationale: Respects the preference and leaves out half of the recommended strategy without the client hearing why.

options.text: A plan built around the client's routine that pairs nicotine replacement with counseling
options.rationale: Individualized and combines counseling with medication, which is the recommended strategy.

options.text: Counseling first, with medication added later if the first attempt fails
options.rationale: Uses both treatments in sequence. The recommendation is to combine them, and the client is ready now.

options.text: Nicotine replacement plus bupropion and varenicline started together for the strongest effect
options.rationale: All three are real treatments. Stacking them is not individualizing, and it still omits counseling.

questions.takeaway: Smoking cessation works best when the plan is individualized and combines counseling with medication.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options each keep one half of the strategy. Look for the option that keeps both halves and still fits this client.

steps.detail: Counseling and medication.
Patch only and counseling first each drop one.
Three drugs at once is more medication, not a tailored plan.

elimination.verdict: Individualized plan with nicotine replacement and counseling together.

questions.objective: health promotion and smoking cessation

questions.stem: An 82-year-old says the cough has felt weaker for years and stairs have become tiring over the past 5 years. Since yesterday the client is short of breath while sitting. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: All three reports fit respiratory aging, so the nurse reassures the client and documents them
options.rationale: The weaker cough and lower endurance fit aging. New shortness of breath at rest does not.

options.text: The shortness of breath at rest is new and needs focused assessment now
options.rationale: New or severe shortness of breath is not normal aging, so it is assessed as a problem.

options.text: The weaker cough is the main concern, so the nurse begins teaching coughing exercises
options.rationale: A less effective cough is an expected change and worth teaching about, but it is years old and not the acute finding.

options.text: The lower endurance on stairs is the main concern, so activity should be limited
options.rationale: A slow change over 5 years fits reduced muscle strength with aging, and limiting activity does not address the new symptom.

questions.takeaway: Aging weakens the cough and lowers endurance slowly. New or severe shortness of breath is never explained by age.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the three reports by how long each has been present. The one measured in hours is the one to act on.

steps.detail: Years, 5 years, since yesterday.
Weaker cough and less endurance are expected changes.
Dyspnea at rest since yesterday needs assessment.

elimination.verdict: New dyspnea at rest needs a focused assessment now.

questions.objective: gas exchange and aging changes

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is dizzy and exhausted after walking 5 meters. Lungs are clear, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL (expected 12 to 18 g/dL). How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Ventilation is impaired, so the client needs coaching in slow deep breathing before walking again
options.rationale: Clear lungs and a saturation of 97% show air is moving. Breathing coaching would not change oxygen delivery.

options.text: Diffusion is impaired, so the client needs a higher oxygen concentration
options.rationale: A saturation of 97% on room air shows oxygen is crossing into the blood.

options.text: The saturation of 97% shows the tissues are receiving enough oxygen
options.rationale: The saturation reports how full the hemoglobin is. With hemoglobin at 7.2 g/dL there is too little to carry enough.

options.text: Oxygen carrying capacity is low, so tissues can lack oxygen despite the saturation
options.rationale: Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen carrying capacity, and the dizziness and exhaustion show the tissues are affected.

questions.takeaway: Open airways and a normal saturation do not guarantee oxygenation. Decreased oxygen carrying capacity limits delivery even when the lungs work.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check each step of gas exchange against the data. The lungs and the saturation look normal, so the problem lies in what carries the oxygen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear breath sounds and 97% rule out ventilation and diffusion.
Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL is well below the expected range.
Dizziness and exhaustion with activity fit low delivery.

elimination.verdict: Low carrying capacity with tissue oxygen shortage despite 97%.

questions.objective: gas exchange and aging changes

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with hemoglobin of 7.2 g/dL (expected 12 to 18 g/dL) is dizzy when standing. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air and respiratory rate is 20 per minute. Which action addresses the client's problem?

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula per protocol and recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because the tissues are short of oxygen. Oxygen therapy treats hypoxemia, and a saturation of 97% shows there is none to treat.

options.text: Coach pursed lip breathing and reassess the dizziness after 10 minutes
options.rationale: A real breathing technique for airflow problems. The rate of 20 per minute and saturation of 97% show breathing is not the cause.

options.text: Report the hemoglobin with the dizziness so the cause can be treated
options.rationale: The cause is low carrying capacity. Addressing the cause is an oxygen therapy principle, and oxygen cannot replace hemoglobin.

options.text: Continue routine monitoring because the saturation and respiratory rate are within expected ranges
options.rationale: Both values are expected, yet the dizziness shows the tissues are not getting enough oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen therapy treats hypoxemia, not hypoxia. When the saturation is normal and the tissues are still short of oxygen, treat the cause.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Oxygen and reporting the hemoglobin both sound right. The saturation of 97% is the cue: there is no hypoxemia for oxygen to correct.

steps.detail: Tissue hypoxia from low hemoglobin, with normal saturation.
Hemoglobin that is present is already 97% full.
The hemoglobin has to be treated.

elimination.verdict: Report the hemoglobin and symptoms so the cause is treated.

questions.objective: gas exchange and aging changes

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with dyspnea is wearing a sweatshirt. The nurse listened through it to the left posterior chest from apex to base and heard faint sounds. Which change gives reliable findings?

options.text: Listen on bare skin, comparing each left site with the matching right site
options.rationale: Corrects both errors: listening through clothing and not comparing symmetric areas.

options.text: Press the stethoscope firmly through the sweatshirt and listen to the right side from apex to base
options.rationale: Adds the right side but still listens through clothing, which muffles and distorts sounds.

options.text: Listen on bare skin to the whole left side first and then the whole right side
options.rationale: Fixes the clothing problem. Finishing one side before the other loses the side to side comparison.

options.text: Listen on bare skin at matching sites on both sides during inspiration only
options.rationale: Bare skin and symmetry are right. Each site needs the full respiratory cycle, and wheezes are often expiratory.

questions.takeaway: Auscultate on bare skin, compare symmetric areas from apex to base, and listen through a full breath at each site.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options each repair one part of the technique and leave another broken. Find the one with nothing left to fix.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Through clothing, one side only.

steps.action: Check each option against the rules
steps.detail: Bare skin, symmetric comparison, full cycle.
Only one option meets every rule it mentions.

elimination.verdict: Bare skin, side to side comparison, apex to base.

questions.objective: focused history and physical assessment

questions.stem: A 29-year-old had loud wheezes in both lungs 20 minutes ago. Now the nurse hears almost no breath sounds on either side, and the client is drowsy and cannot finish a word. How should the nurse evaluate this change?

options.text: The airways have opened, so the nurse documents the response and rechecks in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Fewer wheezes can mean improvement only when the client looks better. Drowsiness and being unable to speak show the opposite.

options.text: The stethoscope placement is the likely problem, so the nurse listens again at the bases
options.rationale: Rechecking technique is reasonable when the client looks well. This client's speech and alertness have worsened with the sounds.

options.text: The client is tiring, so the nurse dims the lights and allows uninterrupted rest
options.rationale: Fatigue is real here, and it signals failing breathing effort, not a need for sleep.

options.text: Air movement is failing, so the nurse stays and calls for emergency help
options.rationale: Silent breath sounds with a change in mental status and speech are concerning findings that need immediate intervention.

questions.takeaway: A chest that goes quiet while the client gets worse is not improvement. Silent breath sounds and confusion or drowsiness need immediate intervention.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Do not judge the breath sounds alone. Pair them with speech and mental status, which the stem says have worsened.

steps.detail: Quiet chest, drowsy, cannot finish a word.
Improvement would bring easier speech and alertness.
Stay and get help for breathing.

elimination.verdict: Failing air movement. Stay and call for emergency help.

questions.objective: findings requiring immediate intervention

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with wheezes in both lungs has an inhaled bronchodilator due now. The nurse hears a new harsh, high pitched sound over the neck on inspiration and sees retractions. Oxygen saturation is 95%. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the bronchodilator now, then reassess breath sounds in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Defensible for wheezes, which come from narrowed lower airways. The new sound over the neck is stridor, an upper airway problem the inhaler does not address.

options.text: Stay with the client, keep the client upright and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Stridor with retractions means upper airway obstruction and needs immediate intervention.

options.text: Apply the pulse oximeter to another finger to confirm the reading of 95%
options.rationale: The reading is not in doubt. Saturation can stay near normal while the airway closes.

options.text: Auscultate all lung fields from apex to base to compare with the earlier assessment
options.rationale: A complete assessment is good practice, but the cues already identify an airway emergency.

questions.takeaway: Wheezes point to narrowed lower airways. Stridor points to upper airway obstruction and is an emergency whatever the saturation reads.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The due medication and the emergency call both sound correct. The location and timing of the new sound decide it: over the neck, on inspiration, with retractions.

steps.detail: Wheezes were already present. The neck sound is new.
Harsh and high pitched on inspiration over the neck is stridor.
An obstructing upper airway outranks a scheduled inhaler and a saturation of 95%.

elimination.verdict: Stay, keep upright and call rapid response.

questions.objective: findings requiring immediate intervention

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on the first day after surgery is talking in full sentences with pink lips and 16 breaths per minute. The oximeter on a cold finger with dark nail polish reads 84%. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather mask and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: The right response to true severe hypoxemia. The client's speech, color and rate do not match a reading of 84%.

options.text: Record 84% and recheck with the next scheduled vital signs
options.rationale: A reading this low cannot be left unexplained until the next round.

options.text: Move the sensor to a warm site without polish and recheck against the client
options.rationale: Cold extremities and nail polish make readings inaccurate, and the reading is correlated with the client.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and coach deep breathing until the reading is above 90%
options.rationale: Helpful for a client who is short of breath. This client's assessment is normal, so the sensor is the thing to correct.

questions.takeaway: A pulse oximetry reading is correlated with the client. Poor circulation, cold extremities, movement, nail polish and poor placement all make it inaccurate.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The assessment is already in the stem and it is normal. When the number and the client disagree, look for the listed causes of a false reading.

steps.detail: 84% against full sentences, pink lips and a rate of 16.
Cold finger and dark polish.
Warm site, no polish, then compare again.

elimination.verdict: Move the sensor to a warm, polish free site and correlate.

questions.objective: pulse oximetry and diagnostic procedures

questions.stem: A 66-year-old received an opioid 40 minutes ago. Oxygen saturation is 98% on a nasal cannula. The client is hard to wake and is breathing 8 times per minute with shallow breaths. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Stay, wake the client and call for help, because ventilation is failing
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry measures saturation, not ventilation or carbon dioxide. The rate, depth and arousal show the real problem.

options.text: Let the client sleep, because a saturation of 98% shows breathing is adequate
options.rationale: The saturation is supported by the oxygen and says nothing about carbon dioxide.

options.text: Increase the oxygen and recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Oxygen raises saturation. It does not make the client breathe more often or more deeply.

options.text: Start capnography and review the readings at the next hourly check
options.rationale: The right monitor for ventilation, at the wrong pace. A rate of 8 per minute with poor arousal needs action now.

questions.takeaway: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, not ventilation or carbon dioxide. A reassuring number never overrides a slow rate and a client who is hard to wake.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ignore the 98% for a moment and read the rest of the stem. Rate, depth and arousal are the ventilation data.

steps.detail: 8 per minute, shallow, hard to wake.
It cannot show carbon dioxide.

steps.action: Check timing in the monitor option
steps.detail: Capnography is right, hourly review is not.

elimination.verdict: Stay, wake the client and get help.

questions.objective: pulse oximetry and diagnostic procedures

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that a 66-year-old postoperative client's oxygen saturation is 89% and that the client keeps pulling at the sensor and "is not making sense." The client was oriented 2 hours ago. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to tape the sensor to a still finger and repeat the reading
options.rationale: Defensible, because movement makes readings inaccurate. The new confusion is a concerning finding of its own and cannot wait for a repeat number.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to apply oxygen and report the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Oxygen may be needed, but the nurse has not assessed the client and assessment cannot be delegated.

options.text: Review the record for medications that could explain the confusion
options.rationale: A useful step after the client's airway and breathing have been checked.

options.text: Go to the client and assess breathing rate, effort, color and mental status
options.rationale: New confusion with a low reading needs the nurse's immediate assessment, whatever the sensor is doing.

questions.takeaway: Movement can spoil a reading, but new confusion is a concerning respiratory finding in itself. Assess the client before the equipment.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A false reading from movement is a fair thought. The cue that tips it is the change in mental status since 2 hours ago, which the sensor cannot fake.

steps.detail: 89% might be artifact. Not making sense is not artifact.
Assessment belongs to the nurse.
Rate, effort, color and mental status come first.

elimination.verdict: Go and assess the client now.

questions.objective: findings requiring immediate intervention

questions.stem: A 61-year-old is about to have a right thoracentesis. Consent is signed, and allergies and bleeding risk are reviewed. Breath sounds were last documented on admission 2 days ago. What should the nurse do before the procedure starts?

options.text: Plan to compare breath sounds afterward with the admission assessment
options.rationale: Comparison is the right idea. A baseline from 2 days ago does not show the client's condition going into the procedure.

options.text: Assess respiratory rate and breath sounds now as the baseline
options.rationale: Baseline respiratory findings are part of preparation, so later changes can be recognized.

options.text: Ask the client to sign the consent form again with the nurse as witness
options.rationale: Consent is verified, not repeated. The stem says it is signed.

options.text: Review allergies a second time with the client's family
options.rationale: Allergies are already reviewed. This repeats a finished step and leaves the missing one undone.

questions.takeaway: Before thoracentesis: verify preparation and consent, review allergies and bleeding risk, and obtain baseline respiratory findings.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check the preparation list against the stem. Three items are finished, and the fourth is 2 days old.

steps.detail: Consent, allergies, bleeding risk.
No current respiratory baseline.
Admission findings are 2 days old.

elimination.verdict: Obtain baseline respiratory findings now.

questions.objective: pulse oximetry and diagnostic procedures

questions.stem: A 61-year-old returned 30 minutes ago from a bronchoscopy with lung biopsy under sedation. The client is awake, asks for water and does not gag when the nurse checks the reflex. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give small sips of water with the head of the bed raised
options.rationale: Upright positioning lowers aspiration risk in general, but without a gag reflex the airway is unprotected.

options.text: Offer ice chips, because they melt slowly and are safer than water
options.rationale: Ice chips become liquid in the mouth and carry the same risk.

options.text: Give thickened liquid, because it is easier to control than water
options.rationale: Thickened liquid is a real aspiration strategy for swallowing problems. It is still intake by mouth with no gag reflex.

options.text: Hold all oral intake and recheck the gag reflex later
options.rationale: Nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns protects the airway.

questions.takeaway: After bronchoscopy, nothing goes by mouth until the gag reflex returns. Being awake is not the same as having a protected airway.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options change the form of the fluid. Only one responds to the finding in the stem, the absent gag reflex.

steps.detail: No gag reflex.
Sips, ice and thickened liquid are all oral intake.
Hold intake and recheck the reflex.

elimination.verdict: Nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns.

questions.objective: pulse oximetry and diagnostic procedures

questions.stem: Two hours after a right lung biopsy, a 61-year-old who is awake has sudden dyspnea and 30 breaths per minute. Breath sounds heard on the right before the procedure are now absent there. The dressing is dry. Which complication is most likely?

options.text: Pneumothorax, because breath sounds are newly absent on the right
options.rationale: Air in the pleural space after biopsy collapses the lung, which gives sudden dyspnea and absent sounds on that side.

options.text: Bleeding at the site, because the respiratory rate has risen
options.rationale: Bleeding is watched for after biopsy. The dry dressing and one sided loss of breath sounds point elsewhere.

options.text: Oversedation, because sedation is commonly used for this procedure
options.rationale: Sedation is monitored after biopsy. An awake client breathing 30 times per minute is not oversedated.

options.text: Anxiety, because the onset was sudden and the client is awake
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the rate. It does not remove breath sounds from one lung.

questions.takeaway: After lung biopsy, watch for bleeding, pneumothorax and worsening distress. Sudden dyspnea with breath sounds newly absent on the procedure side means pneumothorax.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option is a real concern after biopsy. Match each to the one finding only one of them can produce, the loss of breath sounds on the right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sounds were present on the right before.
Dry dressing, awake, one sided change.
Only air in the pleural space fits all cues.

elimination.verdict: Pneumothorax.

questions.objective: pulse oximetry and diagnostic procedures

questions.stem: A 70-year-old is receiving oxygen by simple face mask. Assistive personnel turned the flow below the prescribed minimum because the client said it felt too strong. Oxygen saturation is 95%. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave the lower flow in place, because the saturation is 95%
options.rationale: The saturation does not show carbon dioxide, which is rebreathed from a simple mask when flow is too low.

options.text: Change to a nasal cannula so the client feels less air on the face
options.rationale: A cannula may be more tolerable, but the nurse uses the ordered device unless the prescription changes.

options.text: Return the flow to the prescribed minimum and explain why
options.rationale: A simple mask needs at least the minimum prescribed flow to reduce carbon dioxide rebreathing.

options.text: Remove the mask for 10 minutes each hour to give the client a rest from the flow
options.rationale: Breaks interrupt prescribed oxygen and do not correct the low flow while the mask is on.

questions.takeaway: A simple face mask needs at least the minimum prescribed flow, because lower flow lets exhaled carbon dioxide collect in the mask.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The saturation is a distraction. Ask what a simple mask does when flow is too low.

steps.detail: Carbon dioxide rebreathing at low flow.
Ordered device, prescribed flow.
Explain the reason so the flow is not turned down again.

elimination.verdict: Restore the prescribed minimum flow and teach why.

questions.objective: oxygen therapy and safety

questions.stem: A 70-year-old was placed on a nonrebreather mask for urgent hypoxemia. Oxygen saturation has fallen from 94% to 88% in 10 minutes, and the reservoir bag is flat. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Loosen the mask straps so some room air can enter around the edges and ease breathing
options.rationale: Dilutes the oxygen and lowers the concentration further.

options.text: Restore the oxygen supply so the reservoir stays inflated and check the valves
options.rationale: The device delivers a high concentration only with an inflated reservoir and working valves.

options.text: Change to a Venturi mask so the concentration is controlled
options.rationale: A Venturi mask gives a controlled concentration, which is a different purpose and not the ordered device.

options.text: Keep the mask as it is and repeat the saturation in 10 minutes
options.rationale: The saturation is already falling and the flat bag shows why.

questions.takeaway: With a nonrebreather mask, check reservoir inflation and the one way valves. A flat bag means the client is not getting the intended oxygen.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The outcome has worsened and the stem hands you an equipment finding. Fix the device before changing devices.

steps.detail: 94% to 88% is a failing response.
The reservoir is flat.
Inflated reservoir, working valves, then reassess.

elimination.verdict: Restore reservoir inflation and check the valves.

questions.objective: oxygen therapy and safety

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on a nasal cannula fed by a portable oxygen cylinder has dry, cracked lips and reddened skin above both ears. A relative has brought petroleum jelly for the lips. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offer a water based lip and nasal moisturizer in place of the petroleum jelly
options.rationale: Petroleum based products are avoided around oxygen. A water based product treats the dryness safely.

options.text: Inspect and pad the skin under the tubing above both ears
options.rationale: Tubing causes pressure injury, and the redness shows it has started.

options.text: Provide oral and nasal care on a regular schedule
options.rationale: Oxygen dries mucous membranes, so oral and nasal care is part of oxygen safety.

options.text: Remove the cannula for 1 hour each shift to rest the skin
options.rationale: Relieving pressure is the right goal. Stopping prescribed oxygen is the wrong way to reach it.

options.text: Check that the portable oxygen cylinder is secured in its holder
options.rationale: Cylinders are secured so they cannot fall.

options.text: Allow the relative to apply the petroleum jelly to the lips only, away from the nares
options.rationale: The lips sit directly in the oxygen flow from the cannula, so the product is still not used.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen safety: no petroleum products, secure cylinders, inspect skin under tubing, and give oral and nasal care for dryness.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each option alone. Two wrong options aim at a real problem, dryness or pressure, and solve it in an unsafe way.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry lips, red skin above the ears.
Petroleum products and removing oxygen are unsafe fixes.
A secured cylinder applies to every client on oxygen.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and E.

questions.objective: oxygen therapy and safety

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has been on a Venturi mask for 6 hours. The prescription allows the nurse to adjust the concentration to keep oxygen saturation at 92% to 96%. The saturation has read 99% for 1 hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Lower the concentration as prescribed and reassess the saturation
options.rationale: The goal is the lowest effective concentration. A reading above the prescribed range means the client is getting more than needed.

options.text: Keep the current setting, because the client is responding well, and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Defensible, since the client is oxygenating. The reading sits above the prescribed range, and extra oxygen adds risk of toxicity and absorption atelectasis.

options.text: Remove the mask and monitor the saturation on room air
options.rationale: Goes past the prescription. The order is to adjust the concentration to a range, not to stop oxygen.

options.text: Change to a nasal cannula, because the client no longer needs a mask
options.rationale: A step down may come later, but the nurse uses the ordered device and the order here is to adjust the Venturi concentration.

questions.takeaway: Use the lowest effective oxygen concentration that meets the prescribed goal. A saturation above the target range is a reason to reduce, not to leave alone.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Leaving a client who looks good untouched feels safe. The stated range of 92% to 96% tips it: 99% is outside the goal.

steps.detail: 99% against 92% to 96%.
Toxicity and absorption atelectasis come with excess oxygen.
Adjust the concentration on the ordered device and reassess.

elimination.verdict: Lower the concentration as prescribed and reassess.

questions.objective: oxygen therapy and safety

questions.stem: A 79-year-old in assisted living developed fever, chills, a severe headache and muscle aches suddenly 10 hours ago. Two other residents have influenza. Which action by the nurse best serves this client?

options.text: Encourage rest and fluids and reassess in 3 days for antiviral treatment
options.rationale: Rest and fluids help, but waiting 3 days passes the period when antiviral medication is useful.

options.text: Arrange an influenza vaccination today to shorten the illness
options.rationale: Vaccination prevents influenza or reduces its severity before infection. It does not treat an illness that has started.

options.text: Wash hands carefully and keep the client in the shared dining room for meals
options.rationale: Handwashing is critical. Keeping a contagious client among other residents spreads a highly contagious infection.

options.text: Arrange evaluation today so antiviral medication can be started early
options.rationale: Rapid onset with these symptoms fits influenza, and antivirals may help when started within 24 to 48 hours.

questions.takeaway: Influenza starts suddenly with severe headache, muscle aches, fever and chills. Antiviral medication may help only when started within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a time, 10 hours. Ask which option depends on acting inside a time window.

steps.detail: Sudden onset, headache, aches, fever, exposure.
10 hours is inside the antiviral window.

steps.action: Cut the right tool at the wrong time
steps.detail: Vaccine is prevention. A 3 day wait is too late.

elimination.verdict: Arrange evaluation today for early antiviral treatment.

questions.objective: influenza, pneumonia and COVID-19

questions.stem: A 79-year-old has had a fever for 4 days. A nursing student reports loud, high pitched breath sounds over the trachea and crackles at the right lung base. How should the nurse use this report?

options.text: Treat the tracheal sounds as the abnormal finding and reassess the upper airway
options.rationale: Loud, high pitched sounds over the trachea are bronchial sounds in their expected place.

options.text: Treat both findings as expected in an older adult and document them
options.rationale: The tracheal sounds are expected. Crackles are adventitious at any age.

options.text: Treat the crackles as the abnormal finding and assess further
options.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the lung, which with 4 days of fever needs follow up for pneumonia.

options.text: Treat both findings as abnormal and ask the client to cough to clear them
options.rationale: Coughing may clear rhonchi from secretions. It does not make the tracheal sounds abnormal or clear fluid crackles.

questions.takeaway: Bronchial sounds are loud and high pitched over the trachea, where they belong. Crackles mean fluid and are never an expected finding.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each sound by where it was heard. One is in its normal location and one is not normal anywhere.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loud and high pitched over the trachea is expected there.
Crackles at the base mean fluid.
Fever for 4 days makes the crackles matter.

elimination.verdict: The crackles are abnormal and need further assessment.

questions.objective: focused history and physical assessment

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with pneumonia has crackles at the right base, 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air, and is lying flat. Oxygen is prescribed. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply the prescribed oxygen
options.rationale: Improving gas exchange comes first in the pneumonia plan, and the cues show hypoxemia that should be treated promptly.

options.text: Collect a sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture
options.rationale: Part of the pneumonia workup. It identifies the organism and does not correct a saturation of 88%.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids toward 3 liters for the day
options.rationale: Fluids help thin secretions when not restricted. They work over hours, not minutes.

options.text: Teach coughing, deep breathing and the value of immunization
options.rationale: Correct health promotion for pneumonia, delivered when the client is breathing 28 times per minute and cannot use it.

questions.takeaway: The pneumonia plan is to improve gas exchange, prevent airflow obstruction and prevent sepsis. With hypoxemia present, positioning and prescribed oxygen come first.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Every option belongs in pneumonia care. The assessment is complete, so pick the action that changes oxygenation within minutes.

steps.detail: 88% on room air, rate of 28, lying flat.
Breathing first.
Specimen, fluids and teaching follow.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed and apply the prescribed oxygen.

questions.objective: influenza, pneumonia and COVID-19

questions.stem: A 52-year-old has had nausea and diarrhea for 2 days and today has a cough and fatigue. Taste and smell are unchanged. A coworker tested positive for COVID-19 last week. How should the nurse proceed at triage?

options.text: Use contact precautions for gastroenteritis, because the illness began with gastrointestinal symptoms
options.rationale: Gastrointestinal symptoms can come before respiratory symptoms in COVID-19, so their order does not rule it out.

options.text: Place the client in facility precautions for possible COVID-19 and arrange testing
options.rationale: Exposure, gastrointestinal symptoms followed by cough and fatigue fit COVID-19, and limiting transmission is a priority.

options.text: Seat the client in the waiting room, because unchanged taste and smell make COVID-19 unlikely
options.rationale: Taste and smell changes are less common now, so their absence is not reassuring.

options.text: Collect a full respiratory history first, then decide about precautions
options.rationale: The history is needed. Precautions come first so others are not exposed while it is taken.

questions.takeaway: COVID-19 can begin with gastrointestinal symptoms, and loss of taste or smell is less common. Exposure plus compatible symptoms means precautions and testing.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Two options use a single symptom to rule COVID-19 out. Check whether either symptom can carry that weight.

steps.detail: Exposure, gastrointestinal symptoms, then cough and fatigue.
Symptom order and normal taste do not exclude it.
Precautions before the long history.

elimination.verdict: Facility precautions for possible COVID-19 and testing.

questions.objective: influenza, pneumonia and COVID-19

questions.scenario: A 52-year-old is admitted with COVID-19. Temperature is 38.4 C, respiratory rate is 22 per minute and oxygen saturation is 94% on a nasal cannula, falling to 91% after walking 3 meters. Mucous membranes are dry. No fluid restriction is prescribed.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.

rows.text: Group vital signs, medications and hygiene into one visit, then leave the client to rest
rows.rationale: Clustering care reduces oxygen demand, which matters when walking 3 meters lowers the saturation.

rows.text: Limit oral fluids to keep the lungs dry
rows.rationale: Fever and dry mucous membranes show fluid loss. Hydration is part of the plan and no restriction is prescribed.

rows.text: Keep the client positioned upright or in another position that supports ventilation
rows.rationale: Positioning supports ventilation and gas exchange.

rows.text: Keep the client on strict bed rest until the fever is gone
rows.rationale: Rest is balanced with mobility. Strict bed rest drops the mobility half of the plan.

rows.text: Record the oxygen saturation trend and respiratory effort at each visit
rows.rationale: The trend in saturation and effort is how deterioration is caught.

rows.text: Wait for the next scheduled provider round to report a rising respiratory rate
rows.rationale: Worsening findings are escalated promptly, not held for a routine round.

questions.takeaway: COVID-19 care: precautions, position for ventilation, monitor oxygenation and effort, hydrate, balance rest with mobility, cluster care and escalate worsening promptly.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Several wrong rows take a correct idea one step too far: rest becomes strict bed rest, monitoring becomes waiting. Read each row for the part that is off.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation falls with activity, membranes are dry, no restriction.

steps.action: Keep actions that lower demand or support breathing
steps.detail: Cluster care, positioning, trend monitoring.
Fluid limits, strict bed rest, delayed reporting.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: r1, r3, r5. Not indicated: r2, r4, r6.

questions.objective: influenza, pneumonia and COVID-19

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with COVID-19 is sitting upright on the prescribed nasal cannula. Over 2 hours, oxygen saturation went from 94% to 91% and respiratory rate from 22 to 28 per minute. The client answers questions appropriately. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue hourly monitoring, because the saturation is above 90% and the client is alert
options.rationale: Defensible if the values were steady. Two measures worsening together over 2 hours is a trend toward deterioration.

options.text: Help the client walk in the room to mobilize secretions and improve lung expansion
options.rationale: Mobility is part of the plan, but activity raises oxygen demand in a client whose saturation is falling.

options.text: Report the 2 hour trend to the provider now and stay to monitor breathing effort
options.rationale: Worsening findings are escalated promptly. The trend, not a single number, is the cue.

options.text: Increase the cannula flow above the prescribed setting and recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: More oxygen may be needed, but it comes through a changed prescription, and it would mask the worsening without reporting it.

questions.takeaway: In COVID-19, follow the trend in saturation and breathing effort. A falling saturation with a rising rate is escalated promptly, even when each value alone looks acceptable.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT.
questions.strategy: Watching and reporting are both reasonable for a single reading of 91%. The stem gives two readings 2 hours apart, and both moved the wrong way.

steps.detail: 94% to 91% and 22 to 28 per minute.
The client is upright on the prescribed oxygen.
Positioning and ordered oxygen have not held the trend.

elimination.verdict: Report the trend now and stay with the client.

questions.objective: influenza, pneumonia and COVID-19

chapters.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with dark brown skin is admitted with pneumonia. Assistive personnel report the skin color looks unchanged, so the client is not cyanotic. Respirations are 26 per minute. Where does the nurse look next?

options.text: The skin of the cheeks, forehead and both forearms for an overall blue tinge to the skin
options.rationale: Right concern, wrong site. A blue tinge is hard to detect in darkly pigmented facial skin, so a normal look there rules nothing out.

options.text: The lips and tongue for gray or white, and the nail beds for a bluish tinge
options.rationale: In dark skin tone, cyanosis shows as gray or white lips and tongue and a bluish tinge in the nail beds, palms, soles and conjunctiva.

options.text: The hard palate and the sclera near the cornea for yellowing
options.rationale: A correct technique for jaundice. It does not answer a question about oxygenation.

options.text: Both forearms for an area darker than the surrounding skin
options.rationale: Darker patches point to inflammation or irritation, not to cyanosis.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin tone, look for cyanosis as gray or white lips and tongue and a bluish tinge in the nail beds, palms, soles and conjunctiva. Unchanged skin color does not rule it out.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option is a real dark skin technique. Match the technique to the problem the stem raises: fast breathing with pneumonia means cyanosis.

steps.detail: Pneumonia with respirations of 26 per minute raises a question of cyanosis.

steps.action: Drop the techniques for other problems
steps.detail: Hard palate and sclera are for jaundice; darker patches are for inflammation.
Facial skin hides blue. Lips, tongue and nail beds show it.

elimination.verdict: Lips and tongue for gray or white, nail beds for a bluish tinge.

questions.objective: Health equity factors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with dark brown skin and pneumonia has gray lips and tongue, bluish nail beds, respirations of 30 per minute and oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. Oxygen is ordered to keep saturation at 92% or higher. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Recheck the lips and nail beds under a halogen light
options.rationale: The color findings already match cyanosis and the saturation agrees. More inspection delays treatment.

options.text: Inspect the conjunctiva and palms to confirm the bluish tinge
options.rationale: These are correct sites for cyanosis, and they add nothing to a picture that is already complete.

options.text: Coach slow deep breaths and recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Deep breathing helps a client with pneumonia, but at 86% with oxygen already ordered it delays the treatment that closes the gap.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply the prescribed oxygen
options.rationale: Gray lips and tongue with bluish nail beds mean cyanosis, the saturation is below the prescribed goal, and the order is in place. Breathing comes first.

questions.takeaway: When gray lips and tongue and bluish nail beds line up with a low oxygen saturation, the assessment is done. Treat the breathing problem.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options ask for more looking. The stem already gives color findings, a respiratory rate and a saturation, so assessment is complete.

steps.detail: Gray lips and tongue, bluish nail beds, 30 per minute, 86%.

steps.action: Cut the extra assessments and the half measure
steps.detail: More sites and better light do not change the plan, and coaching breaths alone leaves 86% untreated.
The oxygen order and its 92% goal are stated.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed and apply the prescribed oxygen.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with dark brown skin has a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL, below the laboratory's reference range. The nurse wants to check for pallor. Which assessment gives the most reliable information?

options.text: Inspect the mucous membranes for an ash-gray tone under ambient or halogen light
options.rationale: Pallor in dark skin tone is read from the mucous membranes, which look gray or ash gray, using ambient or halogen light.

options.text: Press firmly on the skin of the forearm and watch for blanching and return of color
options.rationale: Pressing checks blood flow in one spot. Pigment hides the color change, and it does not show pallor from low hemoglobin.

options.text: Inspect the palms and soles for a yellow tone under ambient light
options.rationale: Yellow palms and soles raise a jaundice question, and calluses can look yellow with no jaundice at all.

options.text: Compare the color of the face with the color of the upper chest
options.rationale: Pigmented skin masks pallor. Brown skin may only look yellow-brown, which is easy to miss.

questions.takeaway: For pallor in dark skin tone, inspect the mucous membranes for a gray or ash-gray tone, using ambient or halogen light.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option is a real way to look at color. Only one looks for the right color change on a surface that pigment does not hide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low hemoglobin means a pallor check.
Forearm and face carry pigment that hides pallor; yellow on palms and soles is a jaundice question.
They show an ash-gray tone in good light.

elimination.verdict: Mucous membranes for an ash-gray tone under ambient or halogen light.

questions.objective: Health equity factors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with dark brown skin works outdoors, and the face and forearms are darker than the trunk. The nurse wants a baseline skin tone to compare with later color changes. Which area does the nurse inspect?

options.text: The face, using a halogen light to see the color well
options.rationale: Good light helps, but the face carries pigment added by sun exposure, so it is not the baseline.

options.text: The backs of both hands, compared side to side
options.rationale: Comparing sides is sound technique, but the backs of the hands are among the most sun exposed areas.

options.text: The inner upper arm, which gets little sun exposure
options.rationale: Genetically determined pigmentation is seen most accurately where ultraviolet exposure is least.

options.text: The forearms, where the skin is easiest to expose
options.rationale: The stem says the forearms are darker from outdoor work. That is pigment added by the sun.

questions.takeaway: Baseline skin tone is the genetically determined pigmentation. Assess it in an area with little ultraviolet exposure, because sun adds pigment on top of it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem tells you which areas the sun has darkened. Remove every option that sits in the sun.

steps.action: Separate the two kinds of pigment
steps.detail: One is inherited, one is added by ultraviolet exposure.
Face, backs of hands and forearms.
The inner upper arm.

elimination.verdict: The inner upper arm.

questions.objective: Genetic implications and physiologic aging

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with dark brown skin has worn a snug identification band on the left wrist for 3 days. Assistive personnel report no redness under it. The nurse sees skin darker than the surrounding skin there. What is the best action?

options.text: Treat the darker skin as possible irritation; palpate it and compare it with the right wrist
options.rationale: In dark skin tone, irritation and erythema may show as an area darker than the surrounding skin instead of redness. The darker patch under a snug band is the cue to assess further.

options.text: Document that no erythema is present and recheck the wrist at the next routine skin check
options.rationale: Tempting, because no redness is a true observation. In dark skin tone, redness may never appear, and the darker patch is the sign that takes its place.

options.text: Inspect the oral mucosa and conjunctiva for small dark spots
options.rationale: That is where to look for petechiae. The cue here is a local change under a band, not bleeding.

options.text: Record the darker skin as baseline pigmentation from sun exposure
options.rationale: Sun adds pigment to exposed areas. A patch limited to the skin under a band does not fit that pattern.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin tone, irritation may appear as skin darker than the area around it. No redness does not mean no irritation.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options accept the report of no redness. The stem adds one cue the report left out: the skin under the band is darker than the skin around it.

steps.detail: Darker than the surrounding skin, only under a snug band.
No redness is true, but redness is not the sign to wait for in dark skin tone.

steps.action: Choose the option that follows the cue
steps.detail: Assess the patch and compare it with the other wrist.

elimination.verdict: Treat the darker skin as possible irritation and assess it.

questions.objective: Health equity factors

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with dark brown skin and liver disease has thick calluses on both palms and both soles. Assistive personnel report that the palms and soles look yellow. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Report new jaundice to the provider and request a bilirubin level
options.rationale: Too early. Callused palms and soles can look yellow with no jaundice, so the finding has not been confirmed.

options.text: Inspect the nail beds and conjunctiva for a bluish tinge
options.rationale: Those sites and that color belong to a cyanosis check, which the stem does not raise.

options.text: Inspect the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea
options.rationale: These are the reliable sites for jaundice in dark skin tone. Yellow calluses alone do not establish it.

options.text: Compare the yellow of the right palm with the yellow of the left palm
options.rationale: Both palms are callused, so both can look yellow. Comparing them cannot separate callus from jaundice.

questions.takeaway: Callused palms and soles may look yellow without jaundice. Confirm at the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Liver disease makes the report believable. The calluses are the cue that the report needs checking before it is passed on.

steps.detail: Thick calluses on the very sites that look yellow.
A finding that may be callus is not yet jaundice.
Hard palate and sclera closest to the cornea.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with dark brown skin has a platelet count of 18,000 per mm3, far below the reference range. The right hip has an area darker than the surrounding skin that is tender and raised to the touch. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: As darkening from skin irritation at the right hip
options.rationale: Irritation can also look darker than the surrounding skin. A tender, raised area in a client with very low platelets points to blood in the tissue.

options.text: As an ecchymosis with a hematoma beneath it
options.rationale: In dark skin tone an ecchymosis appears darker than normal skin tone and may be tender or palpable when a hematoma is present. The low platelet count fits bleeding.

options.text: As petechiae, the expected sign of a low platelet count
options.rationale: Petechiae are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin and are looked for in the oral mucosa or conjunctiva, not felt as a raised area.

options.text: As cyanosis from reduced blood flow to the right hip
options.rationale: Cyanosis is assessed at the lips, tongue, palms, soles, conjunctiva and nail beds, and it is not tender or raised.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin tone, an ecchymosis is darker than the surrounding skin and may be tender or palpable if a hematoma has formed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Darker skin fits more than one condition. The tie breakers are the two findings from palpation and the platelet count.

steps.detail: Darker, tender, raised, platelets 18,000 per mm3.
Petechiae and cyanosis are not raised areas.
Tender and palpable with low platelets means bleeding.

elimination.verdict: An ecchymosis with a hematoma.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with dark brown skin has lengthwise brown bands on several fingernails. The client says the bands have looked the same for many years. Assistive personnel ask whether this is bleeding. How does the nurse interpret the bands?

options.text: As bleeding under the nail plates that calls for a platelet count
options.rationale: Bleeding under a nail would be new. Bands unchanged for many years on several nails do not fit.

options.text: As cyanosis of the nail beds that calls for an oxygen saturation check
options.rationale: Cyanosis gives a bluish tinge across the nail bed, not brown lengthwise bands.

options.text: As an aging change, like the lengthwise ridges of older nails
options.rationale: Right that the bands are harmless, wrong reason. Aging brings ridges, not brown bands, and the client is 44.

options.text: As pigmented nail bands, common in people with dark skin tone
options.rationale: Hyperpigmented nail bands are common, seen in about 75% of people with dark skin. Unchanged for years on several nails fits this.

questions.takeaway: Brown lengthwise nail bands are a common finding in people with dark skin tone, present in about 75%.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options call the bands harmless for different reasons. The skin tone in the stem, not the age, supplies the reason.

steps.detail: Unchanged for many years on several nails rules out bleeding and cyanosis.
Aging gives ridges and the client is 44; dark skin tone gives pigmented bands.

steps.action: Keep the reading that fits the cue
steps.detail: Dark brown skin, brown lengthwise bands.

elimination.verdict: Pigmented nail bands, a common finding in dark skin tone.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with dark brown skin and liver disease has a yellow tint at the outer edges of both sclerae. The sclera next to each cornea is white, and the hard palate is pink. Assistive personnel report jaundice. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: Jaundice is present; report it now because the client has liver disease
options.rationale: Tempting, because liver disease makes jaundice likely and yellow sclera is the classic sign. The most accurate part of the sclera, next to the cornea, is white.

options.text: These findings do not show jaundice; record them and keep checking the same sites
options.rationale: The sclera closest to the cornea and the hard palate are the accurate sites, and both are free of yellow. The yellow at the outer edges alone does not establish jaundice.

options.text: The answer is unknown until the palms and soles are checked for yellow
options.rationale: Palms and soles are less reliable than the sites already checked, since calluses can look yellow without jaundice.

options.text: Jaundice is starting at the outer edges; recheck the sclerae in 1 hour
options.rationale: This treats the least accurate part of the sclera as the early sign. The accurate sites are the ones to trust.

questions.takeaway: Judge jaundice in dark skin tone at the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea. Yellow only at the outer edge of the sclera is not enough.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem gives three sites. Two are the accurate ones and both are normal; one is the less accurate one and it is yellow.

steps.detail: Sclera next to the cornea and hard palate are the accurate ones.
White and pink, no yellow.
Liver disease raises suspicion but does not replace the findings.

elimination.verdict: The findings do not show jaundice; record and keep checking.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with dark brown skin has a platelet count of 18,000 per mm3, far below the reference range. Assistive personnel inspected the arms, legs and trunk in bright light and report no petechiae. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Document that no petechiae are present and repeat the skin inspection each shift
options.rationale: Tempting, because the skin was inspected carefully in good light. Petechiae are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin, so the check is not finished.

options.text: Palpate the arms and legs for tender, raised areas
options.rationale: This finds an ecchymosis with a hematoma. Petechiae cannot be felt.

options.text: Inspect the oral mucosa and conjunctiva before documenting
options.rationale: Petechiae are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin. The oral mucosa and conjunctiva are where they can be seen.

options.text: Repeat the inspection of the arms and legs under a halogen light
options.rationale: Better light does not solve the problem. Pigment hides petechiae on the skin whatever the light.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin tone, look for petechiae in the oral mucosa and the conjunctiva. A clear skin inspection does not rule them out.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The inspection was done well, which makes documenting it defensible. The cue is where it was done: skin only.

steps.detail: Arms, legs and trunk. No mucosa, no conjunctiva.
A negative skin inspection is incomplete in dark skin tone.
Oral mucosa and conjunctiva, then document.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the oral mucosa and conjunctiva before documenting.

questions.objective: Health equity factors

questions.stem: A 52-year-old landscaper with fair skin uses a tanning bed every spring to get a base tan, saying it protects the skin all summer. The client wears no sunscreen at work. Which teaching does the nurse give?

options.text: A tanning bed is ultraviolet exposure to stop; use sunscreen and limit sun at work
options.rationale: The teaching is to use sunscreen and reduce exposure to sun and ultraviolet light. A tanning bed adds ultraviolet exposure.

options.text: Keep the base tan and add sunscreen at work on the days when the sun is at its strongest
options.rationale: Sunscreen is right, but this keeps the tanning bed and leaves most work days unprotected.

options.text: Shorten the tanning bed sessions and check all skin every month
options.rationale: Monthly checks are right, but shorter sessions are still ultraviolet exposure the client chose to add.

options.text: The base tan is reasonable; what matters most is a monthly check of all skin
options.rationale: Monthly checks find changes. They do not prevent the damage that ultraviolet exposure causes.

questions.takeaway: Teach adults to use sunscreen and reduce exposure to sun and ultraviolet light. A tanning bed is ultraviolet exposure, not protection.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options keep the tanning bed in some form. Only one removes it.

steps.detail: A base tan is seen as protection.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the tanning bed
steps.detail: Three of them do.

steps.action: Keep both halves of the teaching
steps.detail: Sunscreen and less ultraviolet exposure.

elimination.verdict: Stop the tanning bed, use sunscreen, limit sun at work.

questions.objective: Health promotion teaching

questions.stem: A 52-year-old landscaper with fair skin shows a mole on the left shoulder. It is 4 mm across, symmetric, one even brown, with a smooth border. The client says it became raised and itchy over the past 2 months. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the client, because the mole is under 6 mm with a smooth border and one color
options.rationale: Four of the five ABCDE features are reassuring, which is why this is tempting. The fifth, evolving, is present.

options.text: Teach monthly skin checks and measure the mole again at the next yearly visit
options.rationale: Monthly checks are correct teaching, but waiting a year ignores a change that has already happened.

options.text: Palpate the mole to confirm its size and whether it is raised
options.rationale: Palpation confirms size and elevation, and the stem already gives both. It delays the next step.

options.text: Arrange an evaluation of the mole now, because it is changing
options.rationale: Becoming raised and itchy over 2 months is an evolving lesion, the E in ABCDE. That one feature is enough to act on.

questions.takeaway: A lesion that is evolving needs evaluation even when its shape, border, color and diameter are all reassuring.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A, B, C and D are all normal in this mole. Read to the end of the stem for E.

steps.detail: Symmetric, smooth border, one color, 4 mm: four reassuring features.
Raised and itchy over 2 months is evolving.

steps.action: Check whether more assessment is needed
steps.detail: Size and elevation are already known.

elimination.verdict: Arrange an evaluation now.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: After teaching skin self-examination, the nurse asks a 52-year-old landscaper with fair skin to describe the plan. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "Every month I will check my face, neck and arms, since those get the sun."
options.rationale: Right schedule, incomplete area. The teaching is to examine all skin.

options.text: "Every month I will check all of my skin, front and back, for new or changing spots."
options.rationale: All skin, every month, looking for new lesions and changes to existing ones.

options.text: "Every year on my birthday I will check all of my skin for new or changing spots."
options.rationale: Right area and right target, wrong interval. The check is monthly.

options.text: "Every month I will check all of my skin, and spots under 6 mm need no attention."
options.rationale: Right schedule and area, but diameter is only one of five features. A small lesion that changes still counts.

questions.takeaway: Teach adults to examine all skin every month for new lesions and for changes to existing lesions, using ABCDE.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement gets two parts right and one wrong. Check area, interval and what to look for, one at a time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All skin, not only sun exposed skin.
Monthly, not yearly.
New or changing lesions of any size.

elimination.verdict: All skin, every month, new or changing spots.

questions.objective: Health promotion teaching

questions.stem: A 52-year-old landscaper with fair skin has a pigmented lesion on the right calf. Which findings does the nurse flag for evaluation using the ABCDE method? Select all that apply.

options.text: One half of the lesion does not match the other half
options.rationale: Asymmetry of shape.

options.text: The lesion measures 8 mm across
options.rationale: Diameter greater than 6 mm.

options.text: The edge of the lesion is notched and blurred
options.rationale: Border irregularity.

options.text: The lesion is flat and cannot be felt
options.rationale: Flat describes a macular lesion. Elevation is not one of the ABCDE features unless it is a change.

options.text: The lesion is one even tan color throughout
options.rationale: The warning sign is color variation within one lesion. One even color is reassuring.

options.text: The client reports the lesion has looked the same for 10 years
options.rationale: The warning sign is evolving or changing features. No change is reassuring.

questions.takeaway: ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation within one lesion, diameter greater than 6 mm, evolving.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options are the reassuring version of a warning sign. Ask of each option whether it states the warning or its opposite.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each option to a letter
steps.detail: Asymmetry, diameter and border are stated as warnings.
One color and no change are the opposite of C and E.
Flat is not an ABCDE feature.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman reports coarse dark hair growing on her chin and chest over 4 months and asks which hair removal method is safest. Which information does the nurse obtain first?

options.text: Which hair removal products she has tried and any skin reaction to them
options.rationale: Useful allergen history, and it answers her question, but it skips why the hair appeared.

options.text: How often she shampoos and which hair care products she uses
options.rationale: Hair hygiene is part of the hair assessment. It does not explain new coarse body hair.

options.text: Which drugs she started in recent months and any signs of hormonal change
options.rationale: Excessive body hair growth comes from hormonal imbalance or is a side effect of drug therapy, so these are the two leads to follow.

options.text: Whether relatives have had thinning hair or early hair loss
options.rationale: Family history matters for hair loss. Her problem is excess growth.

questions.takeaway: New excessive body hair points to a hormonal imbalance or a drug side effect. Ask about both before discussing removal.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: She asks about removal. The nurse's first question is about the cause.

steps.detail: Excessive growth of body hair.
Hormonal imbalance or drug therapy.

steps.action: Pick the history that tests them
steps.detail: Drugs started and hormonal changes.

elimination.verdict: Drugs started in recent months and signs of hormonal change.

questions.objective: Focused assessment using anatomy and physiology

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with new coarse hair on her chin says, "I keep a scarf over my face and I have stopped going out with friends." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "This change is affecting how you see yourself. Tell me more about that."
options.rationale: Skin and hair changes can affect body image. This names what she said and invites her to go on.

options.text: "Many women have this, and it is usually very manageable."
options.rationale: Meant kindly, but it brushes past the distress she just described.

options.text: "Let's find the cause first; once we treat it, the hair should bother you less."
options.rationale: Finding the cause matters, but this postpones her feelings and promises a result.

options.text: "Hair removal works well, so you can go out again soon."
options.rationale: Offers a fix and a promise instead of hearing what the change means to her.

questions.takeaway: Skin and hair conditions can affect body image. Respond to the feeling first, then move to cause and options.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three replies move straight to reassurance or solutions. One stays with what she said.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Covering her face and withdrawing from friends.
They close the conversation.

steps.action: Keep the reply that invites more
steps.detail: It reflects the body image concern.

elimination.verdict: Reflect the effect on how she sees herself and ask her to say more.

questions.objective: Focused assessment using anatomy and physiology

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had an itchy rash on her trunk for 2 days. Her history shows the four facts below. Which fact does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: Her mother has psoriasis
options.rationale: Family history belongs in a skin history, but it does not account for a rash that began 2 days ago.

options.text: She has used the same laundry detergent for 2 years
options.rationale: Allergens belong in the history, but a product unchanged for 2 years is not a new exposure.

options.text: She gardened without gloves 1 month ago
options.rationale: An exposure worth noting, but a month separates it from the rash.

options.text: She started a new prescribed drug 4 days ago
options.rationale: Assess whether skin changes have occurred since a client started a new drug. The rash began 2 days after this one.

questions.takeaway: When a skin change appears, check whether it began after a new drug was started.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four are real parts of a skin history. Line each one up against the date the rash started.

steps.detail: Rash for 2 days.
2 years, 1 month and lifelong do not match.
A new drug 4 days ago.

elimination.verdict: The new prescribed drug started 4 days ago.

questions.objective: Focused assessment using anatomy and physiology

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has pink spots on her trunk 4 days after starting a new drug. By inspection alone the nurse cannot tell whether the spots are flat or raised. Which technique settles it?

options.text: Press a clear glass slide firmly over the spots
options.rationale: That is diascopy, which shows whether color blanches under pressure. It does not show elevation.

options.text: Palpate the spots with gloved fingertips
options.rationale: Palpation confirms the size and consistency of lesions and separates a flat, macular rash from a raised, papular one.

options.text: Shine a Wood lamp on the spots in a darkened room
options.rationale: A Wood lamp shows fluorescence and pigment differences, not whether a spot is raised.

options.text: Measure several of the spots with a ruler
options.rationale: Measuring gives size. It does not show whether the spots are flat or raised.

questions.takeaway: Palpation confirms what inspection suggests: a macular rash is flat and a papular rash is raised.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option is a real skin assessment tool. Ask what each one measures, then match it to the question in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flat or raised.
Slide shows blanching, lamp shows fluorescence, ruler shows size.

steps.action: Keep the one that feels elevation
steps.detail: Fingertips.

elimination.verdict: Palpate with gloved fingertips.

questions.objective: Focused assessment using anatomy and physiology

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on bed rest has skin that stays tented after assistive personnel pinch it. Assistive personnel report that the client is dehydrated. How does the nurse respond?

options.text: Tenting can come from aging skin; check the oral mucosa and fluid intake before deciding
options.rationale: Turgor is skin elasticity, and elasticity falls with normal aging. Tenting alone cannot separate aging from fluid loss, so more data are needed.

options.text: Tenting confirms dehydration; offer oral fluids every hour and record intake and output closely
options.rationale: The right plan once dehydration is established. Tenting in an 84-year-old does not establish it.

options.text: Tenting is expected at this age, so no further fluid assessment is needed
options.rationale: Aging does reduce turgor, but dismissing the finding could miss a real fluid deficit.
