options.text: Tenting points to edema; press over both ankles to check for pitting
options.rationale: Edema stretches the skin. Tenting is the opposite finding.

questions.takeaway: Turgor is skin elasticity, and aging lowers it. In an older adult, tenting alone does not prove dehydration; add other fluid data.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options treat tenting as proof, one for dehydration and one for normal aging. The age in the stem means it could be either.

steps.detail: 84 years: elasticity is already reduced.
Neither confirmed dehydration nor nothing to assess.
Oral mucosa and fluid intake.

elimination.verdict: Tenting may be aging; check the oral mucosa and intake first.

questions.objective: Genetic implications and physiologic aging

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with thin, fragile skin has slid down in bed. Assistive personnel prepare to pull the client up by grasping under both arms. What does the nurse direct instead?

options.text: Turn the client to the left side first, then pull the client up under the arms
options.rationale: Turning changes position but the pull under the arms still drags skin across the sheet.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed first so the pull under the arms is shorter
options.rationale: A shorter drag is still a drag, and it still shears fragile skin.

options.text: Use a lift sheet with a second staff member to move the client up
options.rationale: Lift sheets are used when moving clients to avoid shearing.

options.text: Leave the client as positioned until the next 2-hour position change
options.rationale: The 2-hour schedule is correct, but it does not fix how the client will be moved.

questions.takeaway: Use lift sheets when moving a client so the skin is lifted, not dragged. Dragging causes shear.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the pull under the arms and only change what comes before it.

steps.detail: Pulling drags thin skin across the sheet.

steps.action: Cut both options that still pull
steps.detail: Turning first or raising the bed first.

steps.action: Pick the option that changes the method
steps.detail: A lift sheet.

elimination.verdict: Use a lift sheet with a second staff member.

questions.objective: Health promotion teaching

questions.scenario: An 84-year-old on bed rest has thin skin, a small open area on the right forearm and moist skin under both breasts. The nurse observes assistive personnel giving care.
questions.stem: For each action by assistive personnel, indicate whether it is appropriate or needs correction.

rows.text: Changes the client's position every 4 hours overnight so the client can sleep
rows.rationale: Position changes are at least every 2 hours, overnight included.

rows.text: Positions the client so air reaches the skin under both breasts
rows.rationale: Positioning should promote air circulation to skinfolds.

rows.text: Skips the shampoo and leaves long, soiled fingernails untrimmed because the client is on bed rest
rows.rationale: Hygiene still applies on bed rest: bathing, shampooing the hair and keeping fingernails clean and trimmed.

rows.text: Places pillows to keep pressure off the heels and sacrum
rows.rationale: Positioning should minimize pressure over bony prominences.

rows.text: Tells the nurse at each position change which skin areas look different from before
rows.rationale: Position changes are the time to note areas of compromised tissue integrity, and the nurse then assesses them.

questions.takeaway: Reposition at least every 2 hours and note changed skin areas each time, let air reach skinfolds, keep pressure off bony prominences, and keep up bathing, shampooing and nail care.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both wrong actions come with a kind sounding reason. Judge the action, not the reason given for it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every 4 hours is longer than every 2 hours.
Bed rest is not a reason to drop shampooing and nail care.
Air to skinfolds, pressure relief and reporting changed skin areas are all taught actions.

elimination.verdict: Needs correction: r1 and r3. Appropriate: r2, r4, r5.

questions.objective: Health promotion teaching

questions.stem: An 84-year-old has a 2-day-old skin tear on the left shin with slight redness and swelling. Since this morning, pain at the site rose from 2 of 10 to 6 of 10 and temperature from 36.8 C to 37.9 C. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Continue routine checks, because slight redness and swelling show little inflammation
options.rationale: Tempting, because in a younger adult mild redness and swelling would mean a mild problem. Aging blunts the inflammatory response, so these signs under-report severity.

options.text: Mark the edge of the redness and compare its size on the next shift
options.rationale: A sound way to follow spread, but it postpones acting on rising pain and a raised temperature.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess the pain in 1 hour
options.rationale: Treats the pain and leaves its cause unexplored.

options.text: Report possible infection now; aging skin shows less redness and swelling
options.rationale: With fewer immune cells in aging skin, the degree of redness and swelling cannot be used to judge severity. Rising pain and temperature carry the message.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, do not judge the severity of an injury or infection by how red or swollen it looks. Aging blunts the inflammatory response.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The wound looks mild and the other data are getting worse. The age tells you which of those to believe.

steps.detail: Appearance: slight. Trend: pain 2 to 6 of 10, temperature 36.8 C to 37.9 C.
At 84, redness and swelling under-report.
Routine checks, marking and analgesia all delay.

elimination.verdict: Report possible infection now.

questions.objective: Genetic implications and physiologic aging

questions.stem: A 63-year-old has a signed consent for a punch biopsy of a lesion on the left forearm. As the nurse sets up, the client says, "They are only going to shine a light on it, right?" What does the nurse do?

options.text: Explain how a punch biopsy is done, then continue setting up the sterile field
options.rationale: The nurse can reinforce teaching, but a client who does not know skin will be removed has not given informed consent, and that explanation belongs to the provider.

options.text: Pause the setup and have the provider explain the procedure to the client again
options.rationale: Informed consent must be in place before a biopsy. The client's question shows the procedure is not understood, whatever the form says.

options.text: Tell the client a light examination is painless, then continue the setup
options.rationale: Answers the question the client asked while leaving the misunderstanding in place.

options.text: Point out the signed consent form and reassure the client the procedure is minor
options.rationale: A signature does not make consent informed when the client describes a different procedure.

questions.takeaway: Before a skin biopsy, make sure consent is informed. If the client's words show a misunderstanding, stop and bring the provider back.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The form is signed, which makes continuing look safe. The client's own words are the cue that outweighs the form.

steps.detail: The client expects a light, the plan is removal of skin.
Explaining the procedure for consent is the provider's part.
Nothing proceeds until the client understands.

elimination.verdict: Pause and have the provider explain again.

questions.objective: Care for diagnostic testing

questions.stem: A 63-year-old is scheduled for a Wood lamp examination of a pale patch on the left forearm and asks whether it will hurt and how it is done. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It is a painless light examination done in a darkened room. Nothing is cut."
options.rationale: A Wood lamp is a handheld ultraviolet light used in a darkened room. It is noninvasive and painless.

options.text: "A numbing injection stings briefly, then a small round plug of skin is taken."
options.rationale: That describes a punch biopsy, a different test on the same list.

options.text: "A glass slide is pressed firmly on the patch to see whether the color fades."
options.rationale: That describes diascopy. It is also painless, but it is not the test scheduled.

options.text: "Scales are scraped from the patch and sent to the laboratory for culture."
options.rationale: That describes collecting a specimen for a fungal culture, not a light examination.

questions.takeaway: A Wood lamp examination is a painless ultraviolet light examination done in a darkened room. Nothing is removed from the skin.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each reply correctly describes a real skin test. Only one describes the test this client is having.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wood lamp.
Punch biopsy, diascopy, culture.
Light, darkened room, painless.

elimination.verdict: A painless light examination in a darkened room.

questions.objective: Care for diagnostic testing

questions.stem: A 63-year-old has a draining lesion on the left forearm, and a culture is ordered. Assistive personnel offer to steady the arm with bare hands, saying they will touch only intact skin. What does the nurse direct?

options.text: Steady the arm with bare hands, then wash hands once the culture is done
options.rationale: Handwashing afterward is right, but it does not replace gloves near a draining lesion.

options.text: Stand back so that only the nurse touches the client during the culture
options.rationale: Avoids the exposure, but the arm still needs steadying and gloves solve the problem.

options.text: Wash hands and put on gloves before touching the client's arm
options.rationale: Wash hands and use standard precautions when caring for a client with impaired tissue integrity. Drainage does not stay on the lesion.

options.text: Cover the lesion with a dry dressing, then steady the arm with bare hands
options.rationale: Covering the lesion blocks the culture, and bare hands are still near drainage.

questions.takeaway: Wash hands and use standard precautions whenever a client has impaired tissue integrity, including while a culture is collected.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options either keep bare hands or remove the helper. One keeps the helper and adds protection.

steps.detail: A draining lesion is impaired tissue integrity.
Two of them.

steps.action: Keep the help and add protection
steps.detail: Hand hygiene and gloves.

elimination.verdict: Wash hands and put on gloves first.

questions.objective: Care for diagnostic testing

chapters.title: Care of Clients with Conditions of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on bed rest after hip repair has intact skin and a Braden score of 13. Lower scores mean higher risk, and this unit flags 18 or less. What does the nurse do with this result?

options.text: Start turning every 2 hours, floating the heels and moisture care now
options.rationale: A score of 13 is below the unit's cutoff of 18, so the client is at increased risk. Prevention starts while the skin is still intact.

options.text: Repeat the Braden score daily and start prevention measures if redness appears
options.rationale: Daily assessment is right. Waiting for redness is the part that is off, because redness means damage has already begun.

options.text: Ask the wound care nurse to stage the skin over the sacrum and heels
options.rationale: Staging is for an existing injury. This skin is intact, so there is nothing to stage.

options.text: Record the score as low risk and continue daily skin inspection
options.rationale: Reads the scale backward. On the Braden scale a lower score means higher risk.

questions.takeaway: A Braden score at or below the facility cutoff means act now. The score triggers prevention; redness is not the trigger.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read the direction of the scale first. Then ask whether the plan waits for damage or prevents it.

steps.detail: 13 is under the cutoff of 18, and lower is worse.
Low risk does not fit a score of 13.

steps.action: Compare the two plans that use the score
steps.detail: One waits for redness. One prevents it.

elimination.verdict: Start turning, heel floating and moisture care now.

questions.objective: Preventing pressure injuries

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on bed rest is lying directly on the right hip at a 90 degree side lying angle. The head of the bed is at 30 degrees. Which correction does the nurse make?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed until it is completely flat
options.rationale: The head of the bed is already at 30 degrees, which meets the limit. Lowering it leaves the weight on the right hip.

options.text: Keep the position and shorten the turning interval to every hour
options.rationale: More frequent turning is a sound idea. The angle is what is off, because 90 degrees puts the body weight straight onto the hip bone.

options.text: Tilt the client back to a 30 degree side lying angle with a wedge
options.rationale: A 30 degree tilt moves weight off the hip bone. Side lying is done at 30 degrees, not 90.

options.text: Place a donut cushion under the right hip to relieve the pressure
options.rationale: Donut cushions damage capillaries around the area and are never used.

questions.takeaway: Side lying means a 30 degree tilt, not 90. The head of the bed stays at or below 30 degrees.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two numbers are in the stem. One is already correct. Fix the one that is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Head of bed 30 degrees is fine. A 90 degree side lying angle is not.
Donut cushions are never used.
Turning more often on a bad angle still loads the hip.

elimination.verdict: Tilt back to 30 degrees with a wedge.

questions.objective: Preventing pressure injuries

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on bed rest is kept at a 60 degree head of bed between meals to watch television and slides down while the sacral skin stays against the sheet. Which action targets this mechanism of injury?

options.text: Have two staff use a lift sheet when moving the client up in bed
options.rationale: Right action for friction, which comes from dragging skin across linen. Here the skin stays still while deeper tissue slides.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to 30 degrees or less between meals
options.rationale: Skin that stays put while the body slides is shear, which kinks vessels. Keeping the head of the bed at or below 30 degrees prevents it.

options.text: Apply a moisturizer to the sacral skin twice a day
options.rationale: Protects the skin surface. It does nothing about deeper tissue sliding under the skin.

options.text: Turn the client every hour in place of every 2 hours
options.rationale: Shortens time on one spot, but the sliding at 60 degrees still happens between meals.

questions.takeaway: Skin that stays still while deeper tissue slides is shear. Prevent it by keeping the head of the bed at 30 degrees or less.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide whether the stem describes rubbing or sliding under fixed skin. Then pick the action for that one.

steps.detail: Skin fixed, body sliding: shear.
A lift sheet prevents dragging, which is a different mechanism.
The 60 degree angle is what makes the client slide.

elimination.verdict: Lower the head of the bed to 30 degrees or less between meals.

questions.objective: Factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report a red area on the left heel of an 84-year-old on bed rest and offer to rub it with lotion. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to rub lotion around the red area, not on it
options.rationale: Reddened areas are never massaged. Rubbing near the area still damages fragile capillaries.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to press on the area and report whether it blanches
options.rationale: A blanch check is the right assessment. The person doing it is what is off, because assessment stays with the nurse.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel place a donut cushion under the left heel
options.rationale: Donut cushions damage capillaries and are never used.

options.text: Go check the heel for blanching, and have both heels floated off the bed
options.rationale: The nurse assesses the new finding, and floating the heels removes the pressure. No massage.

questions.takeaway: A new red area gets a nurse's blanch check and pressure relief. Never massage it and never use a donut cushion.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options hand something to assistive personnel. Ask which of those tasks is theirs to do.

steps.detail: Massage and donut cushions damage capillaries.
Pressing for blanching is assessment, which the nurse does.
Floating the heels takes the weight off.

elimination.verdict: The nurse checks the heel and the heels are floated.

questions.objective: Acting on wound and skin assessment findings

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with dark brown skin is immobile after a stroke. On admission the sacral skin is intact and the nurse sees no redness. Which assessment best detects early pressure damage in this client?

options.text: Press and release the sacral skin, and record it as intact if no redness shows
options.rationale: Press and release is a real technique. Relying on redness is what is off, because redness is less visible in darker skin.

options.text: Compare the sacrum with nearby skin for warmth, swelling, firmness and pain
options.rationale: In darker skin, temperature, edema, induration and pain show early damage when color does not.

options.text: Photograph the sacrum now and look for redness on tomorrow's photograph
options.rationale: Serial photographs help track a wound. This still depends on redness and delays the assessment by a day.

options.text: Measure the sacral area with a cotton tipped applicator marked at skin level
options.rationale: That measures the depth of an open wound. This skin has no opening to measure.

questions.takeaway: In darker skin tones, do not wait for redness. Feel for temperature, swelling, firmness and tenderness compared with the surrounding skin.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem says no redness is seen in dark brown skin. Reject any option that still depends on seeing redness.

steps.detail: Two options depend on seeing redness.
An applicator measures an open wound.

steps.action: Keep the option that uses touch
steps.detail: Warmth, swelling, firmness and pain do not depend on color.

elimination.verdict: Compare the sacrum with nearby skin by touch.

questions.objective: Acting on wound and skin assessment findings

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with dark brown skin, immobile after a stroke, has intact sacral skin that is darker than the surrounding skin, warmer and firmer. No purple or maroon color is present. What does the nurse conclude and do?

options.text: Normal pigment variation; continue the current plan and recheck the sacrum tomorrow
options.rationale: A color difference alone could be pigment. Warmth and firmness over a bony area in an immobile client point to tissue damage.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury; expect full thickness loss and request a surgical consult
options.rationale: Deep tissue injury shows persistent deep red, maroon or purple color. The stem says that color is absent.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury; offload the sacrum and keep turning every 2 hours
options.rationale: Intact skin whose color differs from the surrounding skin, with temperature and firmness changes and no purple or maroon, is stage 1.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury; cover the exposed dermis with a moist dressing
options.rationale: Stage 2 needs partial thickness loss with exposed dermis. This skin is intact.

questions.takeaway: Stage 1 in darker skin: intact skin that differs in color from the skin around it, often with temperature or firmness changes, and not purple or maroon.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two cues sort this: the skin is intact, and the color is not purple or maroon.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That removes stage 2.
No purple or maroon removes deep tissue injury.
Those are damage cues, so this is not normal pigment.

elimination.verdict: Stage 1. Offload and keep turning.

questions.objective: Wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with dark brown skin, immobile after a stroke, develops a 3 cm sacral blister filled with dark blood. The intact skin around the blister is persistently maroon. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury, because a blister means partial thickness loss
options.rationale: Tempting, because stage 2 can look like a blister. A stage 2 blister is filled with serum, and this one holds blood over maroon skin.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury, because the skin around the blister is still intact
options.rationale: Stage 1 color is not purple or maroon, and stage 1 has no blister.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury, because the blister hides the wound bed
options.rationale: Unstageable means slough or eschar covers a full thickness wound. Neither is described.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury, because the damage is rising from deeper tissue
options.rationale: A blood filled blister with persistent maroon color is deep tissue injury. It starts at the muscle and bone interface and can progress to full thickness loss.

questions.takeaway: Serum filled blister: stage 2. Blood filled blister or persistent maroon or purple skin: deep tissue pressure injury.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both blister answers are defensible until you read what fills the blister and what color surrounds it.

steps.detail: Dark blood, not serum.
Persistent maroon rules out stage 1.
None, so not unstageable.

elimination.verdict: Deep tissue pressure injury.

questions.objective: Wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A 67-year-old, immobile after a stroke, has a sacral pressure injury that has opened. Tan slough and black eschar cover the whole wound bed. A student plans to chart stage 3. Which guidance does the nurse give?

options.text: Chart it as unstageable, because slough and eschar hide the wound base
options.rationale: When slough or eschar obscures the base, the extent of full thickness loss cannot be confirmed, so no number is given.

options.text: Chart stage 3, because slough and eschar can be present in a stage 3 wound
options.rationale: A true statement about stage 3. It does not answer the problem, because the base that would show the depth cannot be seen.

options.text: Chart stage 4, because black eschar means muscle or bone is involved
options.rationale: Eschar is dead tissue of any depth. No muscle or bone is seen or felt.

options.text: Chart a deep tissue pressure injury, because the wound bed is dark
options.rationale: Dark eschar is necrotic tissue covering the wound. That is different from a maroon or purple area of deep damage.

questions.takeaway: If slough or eschar covers the wound bed, the injury is unstageable. You cannot assign a number to a base you cannot see.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what the nurse can actually see at the base of this wound. The answer is nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Completely covered by slough and eschar.
Stage 3 and stage 4 both need a visible or palpable base.

steps.action: Separate eschar from deep tissue injury
steps.detail: Eschar covers a wound. It is not a color change in tissue.

elimination.verdict: Unstageable.

questions.objective: Wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has a full thickness sacral pressure injury with visible fat, rolled edges and tunneling. No bone is visible, but the nurse's applicator touches hard bone at the wound base. Which stage does the nurse record?

options.text: Stage 3, because fat is visible and no bone can be seen in the wound
options.rationale: Tempting, since visible fat and rolled edges fit stage 3. Stage 3 requires that bone is not exposed, and here bone can be felt.

options.text: Unstageable, because the tunneling keeps the full depth from being confirmed
options.rationale: Unstageable applies when slough or eschar hides the base. Tunneling can be probed, and no slough or eschar is described.

options.text: Stage 4, because bone that can be felt counts the same as bone that is seen
options.rationale: Stage 4 is full thickness loss with exposed or palpable bone, muscle, tendon or similar structures.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury, because the damage reaches the bone
options.rationale: Deep tissue injury is a maroon or purple area or blood filled blister. This is an open full thickness wound.

questions.takeaway: Stage 4 means bone, muscle or tendon is exposed or can be felt. Seeing it is not required.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Fat, rolled edges and tunneling appear in both stage 3 and stage 4. Only one cue in the stem separates them.

steps.detail: Fat, rolled edges and tunneling.
The applicator touches bone.
Palpable bone is stage 4.

elimination.verdict: Stage 4.

questions.objective: Wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A 72-year-old's sacral pressure injury measured 5 x 4 x 1.5 cm three weeks ago and measures 4 x 3 x 1 cm today. The wound bed is beefy red, moist and slightly spongy. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: Infection is developing; the beefy red color should be reported today
options.rationale: Beefy red is the color of healthy granulation. The stem gives no spreading redness, drainage change or growth in size.

options.text: The wound is healing; continue the current plan and keep measuring
options.rationale: Healthy granulation is beefy red, moist and slightly spongy, and all three measurements are smaller.

options.text: The spongy tissue is necrotic; ask about debridement before the next dressing
options.rationale: Necrotic tissue is eschar: black, brown or gray. Slightly spongy red tissue is healthy granulation.

options.text: The wound is too wet; change to a dressing that dries the wound bed
options.rationale: Moist is the normal state of healthy granulation, so drying it would work against healing.

questions.takeaway: Beefy red, moist, slightly spongy tissue plus shrinking measurements means healing. Keep doing what is working.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option takes one normal word in the stem and treats it as a problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Length, width and depth are all smaller.
Beefy red, moist and spongy is healthy granulation.
Red is not infection, spongy is not necrosis, moist is not too wet.

elimination.verdict: Healing. Continue the plan.

questions.objective: Monitoring healing or deterioration

questions.stem: A 72-year-old's sacral pressure injury still measures 4 x 3 x 1 cm with red granulation tissue. Today redness and warmth extend 3 cm onto the surrounding skin, and pain has risen from 3 to 6 of 10. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Report the spreading redness, warmth and increased pain to the provider today
options.rationale: Inflammation spreading beyond the wound is cellulitis. Signs of infection are reported, even when the wound bed looks healthy.

options.text: Offer pain relief before the dressing change and continue the current plan
options.rationale: Tempting, because the pain needs care and the wound bed looks healthy. Continuing the plan treats the new pain as routine when it arrived with spreading redness.

options.text: Remeasure the wound in one week, because the size has not changed
options.rationale: Regular measurement is right. Waiting a week is off, because the new finding is in the surrounding skin, not the size.

options.text: Turn the client every hour to take more pressure off the sacrum
options.rationale: Offloading helps a pressure injury heal. It does not address redness and warmth spreading into the skin around it.

questions.takeaway: Redness and warmth spreading beyond the wound edge is cellulitis. A healthy looking wound bed does not cancel it; report it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The wound bed and the size say healing. The surrounding skin says something new. Ask which finding changed today.

steps.detail: Size and granulation are unchanged. Spreading redness, warmth and pain are new.
Inflammation beyond the wound is cellulitis.

steps.action: Choose the response to infection signs
steps.detail: Report them. Comfort care alone treats one symptom.

elimination.verdict: Report the spreading redness, warmth and pain today.

questions.objective: Monitoring healing or deterioration

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with a full thickness sacral pressure injury has had negative pressure wound therapy for one week. Which finding tells the nurse the therapy is doing what it is meant to do?

options.text: The wound bed is dry and the canister has stayed empty for 2 days
options.rationale: Less drainage sounds like progress. A dry bed is what is off, because healthy granulation is moist.

options.text: The wound edges have separated further from the tissue underneath
options.rationale: Skin separating from tissue at the edges is undermining, which is the wound getting worse.

options.text: The skin around the wound is firmer and more swollen than last week
options.rationale: The therapy is meant to minimize edema. More swelling is the opposite result.

options.text: The wound bed has more granulation and less swelling
options.rationale: Negative pressure wound therapy increases blood flow, minimizes edema and enhances granulation.

questions.takeaway: Negative pressure wound therapy is working when you see more granulation and less edema.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Recall what the therapy is for, then match the findings to those goals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More blood flow, less edema, more granulation.
More swelling and more undermining are worsening.
Healthy granulation is moist, so dry is not the goal.

elimination.verdict: More granulation tissue and less swelling.

questions.objective: Care for impaired skin integrity

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes who takes a high dose corticosteroid is 2 days past abdominal surgery. The stapled incision is slightly red and warm, and the client eats about 30% of each meal. Which factors does the nurse expect to slow healing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Diabetes causes poor circulation, which slows healing.

options.text: The high dose corticosteroid
options.rationale: High dose steroids slow healing.

options.text: Eating about 30% of each meal
options.rationale: Poor nutrition slows healing, and healing needs protein and calories.

options.text: Staples holding the wound edges together
options.rationale: Edges brought together heal by first intention, the fastest pattern with a thin scar.

options.text: Slight redness and warmth at the incision on day 2
options.rationale: Redness and warmth are expected in the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 5.

questions.takeaway: Poor circulation from diabetes, high dose steroids and poor nutrition slow healing. Closed edges and early redness are normal healing, not barriers.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each option into a barrier or a normal part of healing. Redness on day 2 is the inflammatory phase.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark the disease and the drug
steps.detail: Diabetes and high dose steroids both slow healing.
Eating 30% of meals is poor nutrition.
Staples and day 2 redness are expected.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with diabetes is 3 days past abdominal surgery. The stapled incision edges are together, red, warm, slightly swollen and tender, with no drainage. Temperature is 37.2 C. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Expected inflammatory phase; keep assessing the incision as scheduled
options.rationale: Redness, warmth, edema and pain are the normal findings of the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 5.

options.text: Early wound infection; report the redness and warmth to the provider now
options.rationale: Infection is the right worry in a client with diabetes. The timing is off, because these findings on day 3 with no drainage are normal inflammation.

options.text: Delayed healing from diabetes; the incision should be pale and flat by day 3
options.rationale: A pale, flat, thin scar belongs to maturation, which starts around 3 weeks.

options.text: Proliferative phase; the swelling is new granulation tissue filling the wound
options.rationale: Granulation fills an open wound. These edges are closed, and day 3 is still the inflammatory phase.

questions.takeaway: Redness, warmth, swelling and pain at an incision during days 1 to 5 are the inflammatory phase. Watch it; do not treat it as infection.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Put the day number against the healing phases before you judge the redness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inside the inflammatory phase of days 1 to 5.
Redness, warmth, swelling and pain are that phase.
No drainage, and the edges are together.

elimination.verdict: Expected inflammatory phase. Keep assessing.

questions.objective: Wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A 58-year-old's infected abdominal incision was opened and drained. The surgeon is leaving it open and plans to suture it closed in several days. The family asks why it was not stitched today. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: It will fill in from the bottom with new tissue and close without stitches
options.rationale: That is second intention. It is the similar pattern, but the surgeon plans to suture this wound closed.

options.text: The edges are already together, so it will heal quickly with a thin scar
options.rationale: That is first intention. This wound is open.

options.text: It stays open until the infection risk clears, and then it is closed
options.rationale: Third intention, or delayed primary closure: the wound is left open until the infection risk clears, then closed.

options.text: It is in the final healing phase, when the scar remodels for up to a year
options.rationale: That describes maturation, a phase of healing. It does not explain why the wound is open.

questions.takeaway: Third intention: leave the wound open until the infection risk clears, then close it. Second intention is never closed.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: An open wound could be second or third intention. The surgeon's plan to suture it later decides which.

steps.detail: That removes first intention.
Sutures in several days.
Open now and closed later is third intention.

elimination.verdict: Open until the infection risk clears, then closed.

questions.objective: Wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with diabetes has an abdominal wound, left open after an infection, that has not changed in 3 weeks. The client eats about 30% of meals and has lost 6% of usual body weight. Which referral does the nurse request first?

options.text: Wound care nurse, to choose a different dressing for the wound
options.rationale: A reasonable consult for a wound that is not progressing. The cues in this stem are about intake and weight, which a dressing cannot fix.

options.text: Registered dietitian nutritionist, to plan protein and calories
options.rationale: Weight loss over 5% and poor intake are nutrition cues, and severe protein deficiency stops healing.

options.text: Physical therapist, to increase activity and help offload pressure
options.rationale: Physical therapy offloads pressure and builds function. No pressure or mobility problem is given.

options.text: Surgeon, to evaluate the wound for a graft or a flap
options.rationale: Surgery is an option for wounds that do not heal. Correcting nutrition comes first, since healing of any repair depends on it.

questions.takeaway: When a wound stalls and the client has lost more than 5% of body weight, fix nutrition first. Without protein, nothing else heals it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every team member listed helps wounds heal. Match the referral to the cues the stem actually gives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 30% of meals eaten and 6% weight loss.
Undernutrition.
The dietitian plans protein and calories.

elimination.verdict: Registered dietitian nutritionist.

questions.objective: Care for impaired skin integrity

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with diabetes has dry, itchy skin and scratch marks on both shins. The fingernails and toenails are long. Assistive personnel offer to cut all of the nails. What does the nurse arrange?

options.text: Assistive personnel cut the fingernails and the toenails straight across today
options.rationale: Short nails are right for the fingers. Toenails are the part that is off, because a client with diabetes is referred to podiatry for them.

options.text: The nails are left as they are, and mittens are put on both hands at night
options.rationale: Mittens limit scratching at night only, and long nails keep breaking the skin during the day.

options.text: The nurse cuts the toenails, and assistive personnel file the fingernails
options.rationale: The toenails of a client with diabetes go to a podiatrist, not to the nurse.

options.text: Fingernails are trimmed short and filed, and a podiatrist cares for the toenails
options.rationale: Short, filed fingernails limit skin damage from scratching. Toenails in diabetes are referred to podiatry.

questions.takeaway: For itching, keep fingernails short and filed. In a client with diabetes, toenails belong to the podiatrist.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem has two kinds of nails and one diagnosis that changes the rule for one of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Short and filed reduces scratch damage.
Diabetes means a podiatry referral.

steps.action: Cut the options that have staff cut toenails
steps.detail: Two options do that.

elimination.verdict: Fingernails trimmed and filed; podiatry for toenails.

questions.objective: Differentiating common skin disorders

questions.stem: A 76-year-old develops raised, red, swollen plaques on the trunk an hour after eating a new food. Breathing is unlabored, and the lips and tongue are not swollen. An antihistamine is ordered as needed. Besides removing the trigger, which plan fits?

options.text: Give the antihistamine and keep the room cool
options.rationale: Hives are treated by removing the trigger and giving antihistamines, and heat is avoided because it dilates vessels.

options.text: Offer a warm bath to relax the skin and ease the itching
options.rationale: A bath is a comfort measure. Warm is what is off, because heat dilates vessels and worsens hives.

options.text: Apply a moisturizer to the plaques to treat dry skin
options.rationale: Right for itching caused by dry skin. These swollen plaques are an allergic reaction to a food.

options.text: Encourage a brisk hallway walk to distract from the itching
options.rationale: Overexertion dilates vessels and makes hives worse.

questions.takeaway: Hives: remove the trigger, give antihistamines, and avoid heat, alcohol and overexertion, which dilate vessels.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options warm the client up or treat a different itch. Hives get worse with anything that dilates vessels.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Swollen plaques after a new food are hives.
A warm bath and brisk exercise.
Moisturizer treats a different cause of itching.

elimination.verdict: Antihistamine and a cool room.

questions.objective: Differentiating common skin disorders

questions.stem: A 76-year-old in long-term care has itching that is now much worse at night. The nurse sees thin curved ridges between the fingers and on the inner wrists. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Add a second daily moisturizer application and reassess in the morning
options.rationale: Right for itching from dry skin. Ridges between the fingers are burrows, which dry skin does not cause.

options.text: Request an antihistamine for bedtime and recheck the itching tomorrow
options.rationale: Eases the itch for one night and leaves a contagious infestation free to spread to other residents.

options.text: Begin contact precautions now and request a skin scraping to confirm
options.rationale: Night itching with burrow ridges in the finger webs and inner wrists suggests scabies, which is contagious. Precautions start on suspicion, and a scraping confirms it.

options.text: Request a skin scraping and begin contact precautions if it is positive
options.rationale: A scraping is the right test. The timing of the precautions is off, because other residents are exposed while the result is pending.

questions.takeaway: Itching that is worse at night with burrow ridges in the finger webs and wrists points to scabies. Start contact precautions on suspicion; do not wait for the scraping.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The ridges change this from a comfort problem to a contagious one. Two options test for it. Choose the one that protects the other residents now.

steps.detail: Curved ridges between the fingers are burrows.
Moisturizer and an antihistamine do not stop spread.
One starts precautions now. One waits for the result.

elimination.verdict: Contact precautions now, with a skin scraping to confirm.

questions.objective: Differentiating common skin disorders

questions.stem: A 54-year-old landscaper whose father had melanoma works outdoors from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. and asks how to lower the risk of skin cancer. Which plan does the nurse recommend?

options.text: Apply sunscreen every morning and keep the schedule, since sunscreen replaces shade
options.rationale: Sunscreen is part of the plan. Treating it as a replacement for avoiding midday sun is what is off.

options.text: Shift outdoor tasks away from midday, and wear a hat, sleeves and sunscreen
options.rationale: Prevention is avoiding midday sun plus sunscreen and protective clothing that covers the skin.

options.text: Build a gradual tan in a tanning bed before summer so the skin does not burn
options.rationale: Tanning beds are a source of ultraviolet exposure and are avoided.

options.text: Wear sunglasses and a cap, and leave the arms uncovered to stay cool
options.rationale: Sunglasses and a cap are right. Uncovered arms through an 8 hour outdoor shift leave skin exposed.

questions.takeaway: Prevention has three parts that work together: avoid midday sun and tanning beds, use sunscreen, and cover the skin.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one good habit and drops another. Pick the plan that drops nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It adds ultraviolet exposure.

steps.action: Find what each remaining option leaves out
steps.detail: One keeps midday sun. One leaves the arms bare.
Timing, clothing and sunscreen together.

elimination.verdict: Shift tasks away from midday, with hat, sleeves and sunscreen.

questions.objective: Skin cancer prevention and early detection

questions.stem: A 54-year-old landscaper whose father had melanoma has many moles on the back and arms. The client asks how to catch a problem early. Which plan does the nurse teach?

options.text: Have a provider check the skin every year, and skip self checks in between
options.rationale: A provider's skin check is useful. Skipping self checks is off, because a mole can change in the months between visits.

options.text: Check the face, neck and arms every month, since those get the most sun
options.rationale: Monthly is right. The area is off, because this client's moles are also on the back.

options.text: Watch the moles and report any that become painful or start to bleed
options.rationale: Bleeding is reportable, but waiting for it misses earlier changes in color, size and shape.

options.text: Check all of the skin every month, and photograph the moles to compare
options.rationale: A monthly skin self exam with photographs or a body map shows new or changing lesions.

questions.takeaway: Teach a monthly self exam of all the skin, with photographs or a body map so a change can be seen.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the option that covers the whole skin, on a schedule, with a way to compare over time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Monthly, not yearly.
All of the skin, including the back.
Any change, not only pain or bleeding.

elimination.verdict: Monthly whole skin check with photographs.

questions.objective: Skin cancer prevention and early detection

questions.stem: A 54-year-old landscaper tracks a mole on the left shoulder with monthly photographs. The size, shape and color match last month's photograph, but the mole is newly itchy and tender. What does the nurse advise?

options.text: Have the mole evaluated now, because new itching or tenderness is a change to report
options.rationale: Reportable changes include new itching or tenderness, not only changes in color, size or shape.

options.text: Keep taking monthly photographs, and report the mole if its size, shape or color changes
options.rationale: Tempting, because the photographs match and those three changes are reportable. New itching and tenderness are on the same list and are already present.

options.text: Apply a moisturizer and sunscreen to the shoulder, and recheck the mole in one month
options.rationale: Treats the itch as dry skin and delays evaluation of a changing mole by a month.

options.text: Take an antihistamine for the itching, and keep the shoulder covered while at work
options.rationale: Covering the skin is good prevention. Quieting the itch hides the symptom that needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: A mole that starts to itch or feel tender has changed, even if it looks the same in the photograph. Report it.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The photographs say no change. The client's symptoms say change. Decide which one the reporting list counts.

steps.detail: Appearance is the same. Itching and tenderness are new.
New itching or tenderness is on it.
Moisturizer or an antihistamine only covers the cue.

elimination.verdict: Have the mole evaluated now.

questions.objective: Skin cancer prevention and early detection

questions.stem: A 34-year-old who started an anticonvulsant 2 weeks ago is admitted with painful red skin, blisters on the chest and mouth sores. The next anticonvulsant dose is due now. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the dose to prevent a seizure, and report the rash on rounds
options.rationale: Tempting, because missing an anticonvulsant has a real risk. Blistering skin with mouth sores after a new high risk drug is a life threatening reaction, and the first step is stopping the drug.

options.text: Give the dose, and watch the rash for an hour for further spread
options.rationale: Observation is reasonable for a mild rash. Each further dose of the trigger feeds a blistering reaction.

options.text: Hold the dose, and tell the provider the drug may be the trigger
options.rationale: The first step in a suspected severe skin reaction to a drug is to stop the drug. Anticonvulsants are a high risk group.

options.text: Estimate the percentage of body surface involved before deciding on the dose
options.rationale: The percentage classifies the reaction. It does not change the first step, and the data to act are already present.

questions.takeaway: Blisters and mouth sores after a new high risk drug: stop the drug first. Classifying the reaction comes after.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Weigh the two risks. One is possible. One is already happening and gets worse with every dose.

steps.detail: A new anticonvulsant 2 weeks ago, then blistering and mouth sores.
The skin reaction is actual. A seizure is potential.

steps.action: Check whether more data are needed
steps.detail: No. The cues are enough to hold the dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and tell the provider.

questions.objective: Differentiating common skin disorders

questions.scenario: A 34-year-old has toxic epidermal necrolysis covering 35% of the body surface after starting an anticonvulsant 2 weeks ago. The client is transferred to the burn unit.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.

rows.text: Monitor the airway and breathing closely
rows.rationale: Airway is the first item of supportive care.

rows.text: Track intake, output and electrolyte results
rows.rationale: Skin loss over 35% of the body means fluid and electrolyte loss.

rows.text: Restart the anticonvulsant at a lower dose
rows.rationale: The drug is the trigger. The first step is stopping it, and a lower dose is still the trigger.

rows.text: Monitor body temperature
rows.rationale: Temperature control is part of supportive care when this much skin is lost.

rows.text: Provide eye care
rows.rationale: Eye care is part of supportive care.

rows.text: Hold pain medication so the skin can be assessed accurately
rows.rationale: Pain management is part of supportive care. Skin is assessed by looking, not by the client's pain.

rows.text: Use strict hand hygiene with all skin care
rows.rationale: The skin barrier is gone, so infection prevention is essential.

questions.takeaway: Care for toxic epidermal necrolysis is supportive: airway, fluids and electrolytes, temperature, pain, eye care and infection prevention. The trigger drug is never restarted.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Most rows are the supportive care list. Find the two rows that undo it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Airway, fluids, temperature, eyes and infection prevention.
Any dose of the trigger is wrong.
Pain is treated, not withheld.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: r1, r2, r4, r5, r7. Not indicated: r3, r6.

questions.objective: Care for impaired skin integrity

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with toxic epidermal necrolysis over 35% of the body surface has mouth sores. Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Pain rated 7 of 10 during linen changes
options.rationale: Pain needs treatment and is part of supportive care. It does not threaten life the way an airway change does.

options.text: New hoarseness with trouble swallowing saliva
options.rationale: With mouth sores, new hoarseness and trouble swallowing mean the airway is becoming involved. Airway comes first.

options.text: A temperature of 37.9 C
options.rationale: Temperature is monitored when skin is lost, and this value comes after an airway change.

options.text: Urine output of 35 mL per hour over the last 2 hours
options.rationale: Fluid balance matters with this much skin loss. This output is adequate, and airway outranks it.

questions.takeaway: In toxic epidermal necrolysis the supportive care list starts with airway. A voice or swallowing change outranks pain, temperature and fluids.
questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four belong to the supportive care list. Rank them with airway, breathing, circulation.

steps.detail: Hoarseness and trouble swallowing saliva.
35 mL per hour is adequate.
Both matter and both wait.

elimination.verdict: The hoarse voice with trouble swallowing.

questions.objective: Differentiating common skin disorders

skills.title: FSBS/Insulin Administration Check-Off
skills.subtitle: Interpreting the value, recognizing hypoglycemia, insulin types and timing, and injection technique

questions.stem: A 67-year-old on sliding scale NovoLog has a prelunch fingerstick of 92 mg/dL after readings of 210 and 198 mg/dL this morning. The assistive personnel says the finger was still wet and was squeezed hard. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Chart 92 mg/dL and give the meal insulin with no correction dose
options.rationale: Correct handling of a trusted 92 mg/dL. This value came from a wet, squeezed finger, so it cannot be trusted yet.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on a dry finger without squeezing
options.rationale: Water and squeezing both dilute the sample and can give a false low. A clean, dry finger gives a value the dose can rest on.

options.text: Give a snack now, since the glucose fell more than 100 mg/dL
options.rationale: Food for a falling glucose is reasonable when the fall is real. Here the fall may be a diluted sample.

options.text: Report the drop from 198 mg/dL to 92 mg/dL to the provider
options.rationale: Reporting a sudden change is sound once the value is confirmed. The nurse confirms it first.

questions.takeaway: A reading that does not fit the trend and came from a wet or squeezed finger is repeated before any dose is based on it.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a number and two reasons to doubt it. Settle the doubt before charting, feeding or calling.

steps.action: Compare the value with the morning
steps.detail: 92 mg/dL after 210 and 198 mg/dL does not fit.
A wet finger and hard squeezing dilute the drop.

steps.action: Cut the options that trust the number
steps.detail: Charting, feeding and reporting all act on 92 mg/dL.

elimination.verdict: Repeat the fingerstick on a dry finger without squeezing.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 1130 a 67-year-old has a fingerstick of 224 mg/dL. NovoLog 5 units and a NovoLog correction scale are both ordered with meals. The kitchen says the lunch tray will arrive at 1300. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give both doses now so they are working when the tray comes
options.rationale: Giving ahead of the meal fits regular insulin. Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes, long before a 1300 tray.

options.text: Give the correction dose now and the meal dose at 1300
options.rationale: Treating the high sounds prompt. The correction is ordered with meals, and rapid-acting insulin with no food for 90 minutes sets up a low.

options.text: Wait for the tray, then repeat the fingerstick and dose from it
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin follows the food, and a value 90 minutes old no longer describes the client. A fresh fingerstick at 1300 sets the dose.

options.text: Wait for the tray, then give the doses the scale lists for 224 mg/dL
options.rationale: Right time, wrong number. By 1300 the 1130 value is 90 minutes old.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting insulin is given when the food is present, and a sliding scale dose is based on the glucose at the time it is given.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two questions decide it: when is the food here, and how old will the number be by then.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes. The tray is 90 minutes away.

steps.action: Cut the options that give insulin now
steps.detail: Both put rapid-acting insulin in with no food.
One doses from a current value, one from a 90 minute old value.

elimination.verdict: Wait for the tray, repeat the fingerstick and dose from the new value.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A 67-year-old received NovoLog with lunch at 1300 for a glucose of 224 mg/dL and ate the whole meal. At 1500 the fingerstick is 171 mg/dL with no symptoms. The correction scale starts at 151 mg/dL, with meals only. Which conclusion does the nurse reach?

options.text: The value is in the 70 to 180 mg/dL target, so the dose worked
options.rationale: 171 mg/dL sits inside the inpatient target and the client has no symptoms. That is the expected response.

options.text: The value is on the correction scale, so another dose is due now
options.rationale: 171 mg/dL is above 151 mg/dL, but the scale is ordered with meals only. No meal is present at 1500.

options.text: The value is hyperglycemia and is reported to the provider now
options.rationale: Reporting fits a value above 180 mg/dL. This one is below that line.

options.text: The value fell quickly, so fast-acting carbohydrate is given now
options.rationale: Carbohydrate treats a value under 70 mg/dL. A fall from 224 to 171 mg/dL is the insulin doing its job.

questions.takeaway: Effective glucose treatment lands between 70 and 180 mg/dL. A correction scale ordered with meals is not used between meals.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Check the number against the target range first, then read exactly when the scale applies.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 171 mg/dL is between 70 and 180 mg/dL.
The scale applies only with meals.

steps.action: Cut the options built on a wrong line
steps.detail: 180 mg/dL for a high and 70 mg/dL for a low are not crossed.

elimination.verdict: The value is in the target range, so the dose worked.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 0730 a 67-year-old with NovoLog 5 units ordered with meals has a fingerstick of 68 mg/dL. The client is alert, swallows safely and reports no symptoms. The breakfast tray has arrived. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the NovoLog now, since the tray is here and the client will eat
options.rationale: Food present is the usual signal for rapid-acting insulin. Insulin is never given while the glucose is under 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Let the client eat breakfast, hold the NovoLog and recheck before lunch
options.rationale: Holding the insulin is right and food will help. A meal with fat and protein raises glucose slowly, and a low is rechecked in 15 minutes, not hours later.

options.text: Let the client eat half the tray, then give the NovoLog as ordered
options.rationale: Waiting for intake is sound for a normal value. This still puts insulin into a client whose glucose has not been shown to be over 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Give fast-acting carbohydrate, hold the NovoLog, recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Under 70 mg/dL is treated with or without symptoms. 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and a 15 minute recheck come first, and insulin waits.

questions.takeaway: A value under 70 mg/dL is a low even with no symptoms. Treat it, recheck in 15 minutes and do not give insulin to a client who is low.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the insulin. The one stated cue is 68 mg/dL, which is under 70 mg/dL, so the low itself needs treatment and a timed recheck.

steps.detail: 68 mg/dL is under 70 mg/dL.

steps.action: Cut the options that give NovoLog
steps.detail: Now or after half the tray, it is insulin during a low.

steps.action: Compare the two that hold it
steps.detail: Breakfast alone is slow and has no 15 minute recheck.

elimination.verdict: Give fast-acting carbohydrate, hold the NovoLog and recheck in 15 minutes.

questions.objective: hold, question or report

questions.stem: A 71-year-old is ordered Novolin R 6 units and Novolin N 14 units in one syringe before breakfast. The nurse rolls the Novolin N vial, then sees that the unrolled Novolin R vial also looks cloudy. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Discard the cloudy Novolin R vial and obtain a clear one
options.rationale: Regular insulin is a clear solution. A cloudy vial of it is not used, and the dose still has to be prepared.

options.text: Roll the Novolin R vial gently until the cloudiness is even
options.rationale: Rolling is correct for NPH, a suspension. Regular insulin should never look cloudy, so rolling fixes nothing.

options.text: Draw the Novolin N first so the cloudy R vial matters less
options.rationale: The order of drawing is clear before cloudy. Reversing it does not make a spoiled vial usable.

options.text: Mix the dose as planned, since the final syringe looks cloudy
options.rationale: The mixed syringe does look cloudy because of the NPH. That does not excuse a regular vial that has changed.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin is clear and NPH is cloudy. A cloudy vial of regular insulin is discarded and replaced before mixing.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask which vial is supposed to be cloudy. Only one of the two is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Novolin R is clear. Novolin N is cloudy.
Rolling belongs to the suspension.

steps.action: Cut the options that use the vial
steps.detail: Drawing order and the look of the final mix do not make it safe.

elimination.verdict: Discard the cloudy Novolin R vial and get a clear one.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A nurse prepares regular insulin 6 units and NPH insulin 14 units in one syringe for a 71-year-old before breakfast. Place the steps in order.

options.text: Roll the NPH vial gently between the palms
options.rationale: The cloudy suspension is mixed first so the NPH dose is even.

options.text: Inject air into the NPH vial
options.rationale: Air goes into the cloudy vial first, with nothing drawn out yet.

options.text: Inject air into the regular insulin vial
options.rationale: Air goes into the clear vial second, and the needle stays in for the draw.

options.text: Withdraw regular insulin to the 6 unit mark
options.rationale: Clear is drawn first so the regular vial is never contaminated with suspension.

options.text: Withdraw NPH insulin until the plunger is at the 20 unit mark
options.rationale: The syringe already holds 6 units, so 14 units of NPH brings the total to 20.

questions.takeaway: Roll the NPH, air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, then draw cloudy to the total of both doses.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Fix two anchors: the clear insulin is drawn before the cloudy, and the last mark is the sum.

steps.detail: NPH is rolled so the dose is even.
Air goes into the NPH vial first, then the regular vial.
Regular to 6 units, then NPH to 6 plus 14, the 20 unit mark.

elimination.verdict: Roll NPH, air into NPH, air into regular, draw regular to 6, draw NPH to 20.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 71-year-old received regular and NPH insulin in one syringe at 0730 and ate a quarter of the breakfast tray at 0800. The client is alert with no symptoms. Which plan addresses the earliest risk?

options.text: Check the glucose at 0745, since regular insulin starts in 10 minutes
options.rationale: A 15 minute interval belongs to the recheck after treating a low. Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Check the glucose at 1530, when the NPH is working hardest
options.rationale: The NPH peak, 1130 to 1930, is a real risk for this client. It is the later risk, not the earliest.

options.text: Check the glucose between 0930 and 1130 and offer carbohydrate
options.rationale: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose. With a quarter of breakfast eaten, that window is the first setup for a low.

options.text: Check the glucose before lunch as scheduled and chart the intake
options.rationale: Charting intake is needed. A routine prelunch check may come after the regular insulin peak has already caused a low.

questions.takeaway: Reduced intake at an insulin's peak is the setup for a low. Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, NPH at 4 to 12 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Count the hours from 0730 for each insulin and pick the window that opens first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular peaks 0930 to 1130. NPH peaks 1130 to 1930.
Earliest means the regular insulin window.
Regular insulin does not start in 10 minutes.

elimination.verdict: Check between 0930 and 1130 and offer carbohydrate.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: At 1545 an assistive personnel reports that a 71-year-old who received NPH insulin before breakfast at 0730 slept through the 1500 snack, has damp skin and is hard to wake. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have the assistive personnel wake the client and give 4 ounces of juice
options.rationale: A low is likely, and juice treats one. Oral treatment is for a client who is alert and can swallow, and this client is hard to wake.

options.text: Go to the client, check responsiveness and get a fingerstick
options.rationale: A missed snack, damp skin and poor arousal at the NPH peak point to a low. The nurse assesses a changed client in person, and the value and swallowing ability decide the route of treatment.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel obtain a fingerstick and report the value
options.rationale: An assistive personnel can obtain a routine fingerstick. A client whose condition has changed is assessed by the nurse, and this adds a delay.

options.text: Let the client sleep and check the glucose before the dinner tray
options.rationale: Sleep is a reasonable guess for a tired client. Damp skin and a missed snack 8 hours after NPH make a low more likely than sleep.

questions.takeaway: New drowsiness and sweating in a client on insulin is a low until a fingerstick says otherwise. The nurse assesses the unstable client, and the mouth is used only if the client is alert and can swallow.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Juice and a delegated fingerstick are both defensible. The cue that tips it is hard to wake: that rules out the mouth and makes this the nurse's assessment.

steps.detail: 0730 to 1545 is just over 8 hours, inside the NPH peak.
Waiting for dinner ignores the cues.
Hard to wake means swallowing is not safe to assume.
Routine checks are delegated. A changed client is not.

elimination.verdict: Go to the client, check responsiveness and obtain a fingerstick now.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: At 1045 a 76-year-old who received regular insulin before breakfast at 0700 and ate half of breakfast is being helped with a bath. Which findings point to a low blood glucose? Select all that apply.

options.text: Snaps at the nurse, which is new behavior
options.rationale: A behavior change in a client on insulin is a warning sign of a low.

options.text: Reports strong thirst
options.rationale: Thirst goes with a high glucose, not a low one.

options.text: Says twice that the hunger is hard to ignore
options.rationale: Hunger is a warning sign of a low, so the glucose is checked before it is treated as a food request.

options.text: Is sweating while sitting still
options.rationale: Sweating without exertion is a sign of a low.

options.text: Has deep, rapid breathing with abdominal pain
options.rationale: That pattern goes with a very high glucose and ketoacidosis.

questions.takeaway: Irritability, hunger and sweating in a client on insulin are warning signs of a low, most of all at the insulin's peak with reduced intake.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as a sign of too little glucose or too much. Thirst and deep rapid breathing belong to a high.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 1045 is inside the 2 to 4 hour peak of regular insulin given at 0700.

steps.action: Keep the signs of a low
steps.detail: New irritability, hunger and sweating.

steps.action: Cut the signs of a high
steps.detail: Thirst, and deep rapid breathing with abdominal pain.

elimination.verdict: A, C and D.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: At 1050 a 76-year-old who received regular insulin before breakfast at 0700 has a fingerstick glucose of 58 mg/dL. The client is alert, shaky and able to swallow. The lunch tray is due at 1200. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Send for an early lunch tray and use the meal as the treatment
options.rationale: Food is the right idea. A meal with fat and protein raises the glucose slowly, and the tray is not at the bedside.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand before treating
options.rationale: Confirming a doubtful value is sound. Nothing in the stem makes this value doubtful, and the symptoms match it.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck when shakiness eases
options.rationale: Right treatment, wrong endpoint. Symptoms easing does not show the glucose is back over 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The client is alert and can swallow, so the low is treated by mouth with simple sugar and rechecked on the clock.

questions.takeaway: Alert and able to swallow with a glucose under 70 mg/dL: 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, then a fingerstick recheck in 15 minutes.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The assessment is complete in the stem, so act. Then check each option for the amount, the type of food and the recheck time.

steps.detail: 58 mg/dL, alert, able to swallow.
The value fits the symptoms.
A meal is not fast-acting.
One rechecks by the clock, one by symptoms.

elimination.verdict: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: At 1050 a 76-year-old on insulin with a fingerstick glucose of 58 mg/dL was given 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. Lunch is due at 1200. Which finding shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: Fingerstick glucose of 76 mg/dL at 1105
options.rationale: The 15 minute recheck is at least 70 mg/dL. The number is what shows the low has resolved.

options.text: Client says the shakiness is gone at 1055
options.rationale: Feeling better is encouraging. Symptoms can ease while the glucose is still under 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Fingerstick glucose of 67 mg/dL at 1105 with no symptoms
options.rationale: The recheck was done on time, but 67 mg/dL is still a low and the treatment is repeated.

options.text: Client eats the whole lunch tray at 1200
options.rationale: Good intake helps later. It does not show what the glucose was 15 minutes after treatment.

questions.takeaway: A treated low has resolved when the 15 minute recheck is 70 mg/dL or higher. Symptoms do not decide it.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Evaluate with the measure the treatment was aimed at: a number, at 15 minutes, at or above 70 mg/dL.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fingerstick at 15 minutes.

steps.action: Cut the options with no number
steps.detail: A symptom report and a meal.
67 mg/dL is under 70 mg/dL. 76 mg/dL is not.

elimination.verdict: Fingerstick glucose of 76 mg/dL at 1105.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 76-year-old on insulin with a fingerstick glucose of 55 mg/dL was alert 10 minutes ago and was given juice. The client now slurs words and coughs with each sip. There is no IV access. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and continue the juice in small sips
options.rationale: Juice was right while the client swallowed safely. Coughing with each sip means oral treatment now risks aspiration.

options.text: Stop the juice and start an IV line so dextrose can be given
options.rationale: IV dextrose is the route when access is already in place. With no access, starting a line delays treatment of a worsening low.

options.text: Stop the juice, give glucagon by injection, turn client to the side
options.rationale: The client can no longer swallow safely and has no IV access. Glucagon by injection treats the low without the mouth, and side positioning protects the airway.

options.text: Stop the juice, keep the head raised and repeat the fingerstick in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Stopping the juice is right. Waiting 15 minutes leaves a low untreated while the client is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: When a client with a low can no longer swallow safely, stop oral treatment. IV access present means IV dextrose. No IV access means glucagon by injection and side positioning.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Three options stop the juice. The stated cue, no IV access, picks the route that works right now.

steps.detail: Slurred words and coughing with sips mean the mouth is no longer safe.
More juice risks the airway.
The low is still untreated.
Dextrose needs a line that is not there.

elimination.verdict: Stop the juice, give glucagon by injection and turn the client to the side.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has Humalog 6 units ordered with meals. At 0750 the fingerstick is 162 mg/dL, and the kitchen says the breakfast tray will come at 0820. When does the nurse give the Humalog?

options.text: At 0750, so the insulin is working when the tray arrives
options.rationale: Thirty minutes ahead is the timing for regular insulin. Humalog starts in 10 to 30 minutes and could act before any food is present.

options.text: At 0820, when the tray is in front of the client
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is given with the food. The glucose is above 70 mg/dL, so the dose is safe once the meal is present.

options.text: At 0920, one hour after the client begins eating
options.rationale: Waiting for intake sounds careful. An hour later the meal has already raised the glucose with no insulin to cover it.

options.text: Not at breakfast, because the tray is running late
options.rationale: A late tray moves the dose. It does not cancel it, since the client will still eat.

questions.takeaway: Insulin timing follows the food: rapid-acting as the tray arrives, regular about 30 minutes before, basal on the clock.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Name the insulin type before you look at the clock. One option is the correct timing for a different insulin.

steps.detail: Humalog is rapid-acting, onset 10 to 30 minutes.
30 minutes ahead leaves it acting before the tray.

steps.action: Cut the late and the omitted dose
steps.detail: Both leave the meal uncovered.

elimination.verdict: At 0820, when the tray is in front of the client.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A 62-year-old takes Lantus 22 units at 2100 and Humalog with meals. The client vomited and ate no dinner, so the Humalog was held. At 2100 the fingerstick is 148 mg/dL and the client asks to skip the Lantus. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the Lantus tonight, because the client ate no dinner at all
options.rationale: That reasoning is correct for mealtime Humalog. Lantus is basal insulin with no pronounced peak and is not timed to food.

options.text: Give half of the Lantus dose to match the missed meal
options.rationale: Lantus is not matched to meals, and a changed dose needs an order.

options.text: Hold the Lantus and recheck the fingerstick at 0200
options.rationale: Checking overnight is cautious. Without basal insulin the glucose climbs, and illness raises it further.

options.text: Give the Lantus as ordered and explain it is not tied to meals
options.rationale: Basal insulin continues through a missed meal and through illness. At 148 mg/dL there is no low to stop it.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin follows the meal the client actually eats. Basal insulin is given on the clock and continues through illness.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The same missed meal has opposite effects on the two insulins. Decide which kind Lantus is.

steps.detail: Humalog is mealtime. Lantus is basal.
Three options tie the Lantus to the missed dinner.
148 mg/dL is above 70 mg/dL.

elimination.verdict: Give the Lantus as ordered and explain why.

questions.objective: hold, question or report

questions.stem: At 2100 a nurse preparing Lantus 22 units for a 62-year-old takes a vial from the client's bin. The solution is clear, and the label reads Humalog. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Return it and obtain the vial labeled Lantus
options.rationale: Both insulins are clear, so only the label separates them. The nurse gives the insulin that was ordered.

options.text: Draw up 22 units, because a clear solution matches Lantus
options.rationale: Checking appearance is a real step. It cannot tell two clear insulins apart.

options.text: Give the Humalog 22 units with a bedtime snack to cover it
options.rationale: Food does make rapid-acting insulin safer. It does not turn the wrong insulin into the ordered one.

options.text: Ask the provider to change the bedtime order to Humalog
options.rationale: Calling the provider fits a questionable order. The order is correct here. The vial is wrong.
