questions.takeaway: Read the label against the order every time. Appearance separates clear from cloudy insulin, not one clear insulin from another.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask what is actually wrong: the order, or the vial in the hand.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Order says Lantus. Label says Humalog.

steps.action: Cut the options that give Humalog
steps.detail: With or without a snack it is the wrong insulin.
The order needs no change.

elimination.verdict: Return it, obtain the Lantus vial and read its label against the order.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 62-year-old takes Lantus at 2100 and Humalog with meals. Over 4 days the fasting readings were 104 to 126 mg/dL with no overnight lows, and readings after meals were 232 to 258 mg/dL. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The Lantus is not holding the glucose through the night
options.rationale: That would show as high fasting readings. The fasting values are in range.

options.text: An overnight low is rebounding into high readings
options.rationale: A rebound follows an overnight low and shows in the morning. No overnight lows were found.

options.text: The mealtime Humalog is not covering the meals
options.rationale: Glucose after meals reflects the rapid-acting insulin. Those are the only readings above range.

options.text: The Lantus should be moved from bedtime to mealtimes
options.rationale: Long-acting insulin is given on the clock, not with meals. The fasting readings show it is working.

questions.takeaway: Fasting glucose reflects the long-acting insulin. Glucose after meals reflects the rapid-acting insulin.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Match each set of readings to the insulin that is responsible for it, then see which set is out of range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fasting goes with Lantus. After meals goes with Humalog.

steps.action: Find the set out of range
steps.detail: 232 to 258 mg/dL after meals.

steps.action: Cut the options that blame Lantus
steps.detail: Fasting values of 104 to 126 mg/dL are in range.

elimination.verdict: The mealtime Humalog is not covering the meals.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: For each action by the student, indicate whether it is correct technique or needs correction.
questions.scenario: A student gives a 62-year-old Humalog 6 units at 1700 as the dinner tray arrives while the nurse observes. The client's injections are given in the abdomen. Lantus is due at 2100.

rows.text: Draws the dose in an insulin syringe marked in units
rows.rationale: Insulin is drawn up only in an insulin syringe marked in units.

rows.text: Chooses a spot on the abdomen away from the lunch injection
rows.rationale: One region is kept and the spot within it changes each time.

rows.text: Pinches up the skin and inserts the needle at 90 degrees
rows.rationale: This keeps the dose in the subcutaneous tissue.

rows.text: Pulls back on the plunger to look for blood
rows.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

rows.text: Rubs the site firmly after withdrawing the needle
rows.rationale: Massage speeds absorption and makes the dose act unpredictably.

rows.text: Offers to add the 2100 Lantus to this syringe to save an injection
rows.rationale: Long-acting insulin is never mixed with another insulin, and it is given on its own schedule.

questions.takeaway: Insulin syringe in units, one region with a new spot, pinch and 90 degrees. No aspiration, no rubbing, and long-acting insulin is never mixed.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Judge each action alone. Three of them are habits that sound careful or kind and are still wrong for subcutaneous insulin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check the equipment and the spot
steps.detail: Unit syringe, same region, new spot.
Pinch and 90 degrees, no aspiration, no rubbing.
Lantus goes in its own syringe.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2 and 3 are correct technique. Rows 4, 5 and 6 need correction.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects NPH insulin before breakfast each day into the same firm, raised area on the left abdomen because it does not hurt there. Readings before lunch are near 240 mg/dL. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Keep using that spot and massage it after each injection
options.rationale: Massage does speed absorption. It is not a taught fix, and the thickened tissue stays in use.

options.text: Use the thigh on one day and the upper arm on the next
options.rationale: Leaving the damaged area is right. Moving between regions changes absorption from dose to dose.

options.text: Keep using that spot until the provider raises the NPH dose
options.rationale: A higher dose answers the high readings. The cause is poor absorption, and a larger dose becomes dangerous once healthy tissue is used.

options.text: Use intact abdominal spots and check the glucose more often
options.rationale: Thickened tissue absorbs insulin poorly. In healthy tissue the same dose works harder, so the client rotates within the region and watches for lows.

questions.takeaway: Avoid damaged or thickened areas and rotate within one region. When a client moves to healthy tissue the same dose absorbs better, so watch for lows.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The high readings have a cause in the stem. Fix the site, keep the region and plan for what better absorption does.

steps.detail: A firm, raised area absorbs poorly.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the spot
steps.detail: Two of them stay in damaged tissue.
Thigh and arm absorb at different rates.

elimination.verdict: Use intact abdominal spots and check the glucose more often.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects regular insulin into the abdomen before breakfast and asks to move that dose to the buttock because it would hurt less there. Which response does the nurse give?

options.text: "The buttock absorbs fastest, so you would need to eat much sooner."
options.rationale: This reverses the order. The abdomen is fastest and the buttock is slowest.

options.text: "The buttock absorbs slowest, so the dose may lag behind the meal."
options.rationale: Absorption runs abdomen, upper arm, thigh, then buttock. A slower site can leave a mealtime dose acting after the food.

options.text: "All sites absorb alike, so choose whichever one hurts the least."
options.rationale: Comfort matters to the client. Sites do not absorb alike, so the choice changes how the dose acts.

options.text: "Alternate the abdomen and the buttock so each area can rest."
options.rationale: Resting tissue is a kind thought. Switching regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate.

questions.takeaway: Absorption is fastest from the abdomen, then the upper arm, then the thigh, then the buttock. Changing the region changes when the dose acts.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two responses state an absorption speed for the buttock and they are opposites. Settle that pair first.

steps.detail: Abdomen, upper arm, thigh, buttock.
Slowest is true of the buttock.
Alternating regions varies absorption.

elimination.verdict: The buttock absorbs slowest, so the dose may lag behind the meal.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects regular insulin at 0700, drives 50 minutes to work and eats breakfast there at 0815. The client reports feeling shaky during the drive on most days. Which change does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Inject at home and eat about 30 minutes later, before driving
options.rationale: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes. Eating about 30 minutes after the dose puts food in before the insulin acts on the road.

options.text: Keep the routine, since regular insulin takes 2 hours to start working
options.rationale: Two hours is where the peak begins. The onset is 30 to 60 minutes, which matches the shakiness on the drive.

options.text: Eat breakfast at work first, then inject once the meal is finished
options.rationale: Tying insulin to food is right. Regular insulin given after a meal acts too late to cover it.

options.text: Leave out the morning dose on the days the client drives to work
options.rationale: This stops the shakiness by removing a prescribed dose, which is not the nurse's or the client's decision.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before the meal because its onset is 30 to 60 minutes. Food that comes later than that leaves the insulin working alone.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Line up the injection, the onset and the meal on the clock. The gap between them is the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Onset 0730 to 0800. Breakfast at 0815.
Regular insulin does not wait 2 hours.
Skipping or moving the dose after the meal is not the fix.

elimination.verdict: Inject at home and eat breakfast about 30 minutes later, before driving.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects regular and NPH insulin into the abdomen before breakfast at 0700. The client began a 40 minute walk at 1430 this week, with fingersticks of 58 and 62 mg/dL at 1500 twice. Meals are unchanged. Which plan does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Stop the afternoon walks for now and restart once the lows have ended
options.rationale: This would stop the lows. It gives up the client's exercise when the timing, not the walking, is the problem.

options.text: Move the morning injection to the thigh for slower absorption
options.rationale: The thigh is slower than the abdomen at rest. It is the working limb on a walk, and exercise speeds absorption from it.

options.text: Check the glucose before each walk and eat a carbohydrate snack first
options.rationale: The walk lands in the NPH peak, 1100 to 1900, and meals have not changed. A check and a snack before activity cover the peak and keep the client walking.

options.text: Take 2 units less NPH on the days a walk is planned
options.rationale: Too much insulin for the activity is one cause of a low. A dose change is the provider's decision, not the client's or the nurse's.

questions.takeaway: Exercise lowers glucose most when it lands on an insulin's peak. Check before activity and put food ahead of it. Do not inject a limb that is about to work.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Stopping the walk and covering the walk both end the lows. The stated cue is the time: 1430 sits inside the NPH peak, so cover that window and keep the activity.

steps.detail: NPH at 0700 peaks 1100 to 1900. The walk is at 1430.
That needs an order.
A working limb absorbs faster.
Covering keeps the client active and safe.

elimination.verdict: Check the glucose before each walk and eat a carbohydrate snack first.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A nurse watches an assistive personnel check an 80-year-old's fingerstick with a shared meter: two identifiers, clean dry hands, new lancet, side of the fingertip. The assistive personnel then carries the meter toward the next room. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Let the morning checks continue, since each step was correct
options.rationale: Every step at this bedside was correct. The problem is the one that comes next.

options.text: Remind the assistive personnel to use the center of the finger pad
options.rationale: The side of the fingertip is the taught site. The center pad hurts more.

options.text: Take over the remaining fingersticks for the rest of the shift
options.rationale: Stepping in is right. A routine fingerstick stays a task the assistive personnel can do once the error is corrected.

options.text: Stop the assistive personnel and have the meter disinfected first
options.rationale: A meter used on more than one client is cleaned and disinfected between clients. This is the step about to be missed.

questions.takeaway: A glucose meter used on more than one client is cleaned and disinfected between clients. Lancets are single use.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Check off what the stem says was done. The answer is the step that is missing, not a step that was done well.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identifiers, clean dry hands, new lancet, side of the fingertip.
Nothing was done to the shared meter.
Correct the step. Do not remove the task.

elimination.verdict: Stop the assistive personnel and have the meter disinfected first.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 0730 an 80-year-old has regular insulin 10 units ordered before breakfast, and the tray comes at 0800. The fingerstick is 112 mg/dL. The client has been nauseated since 0500 and says no breakfast will be eaten. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose now, because 30 minutes before the tray is correct
options.rationale: The timing is correct for regular insulin. The client has said no food will follow it.

options.text: Hold the dose and report the nausea and lack of intake
options.rationale: Insulin is held and clarified when the client will not be eating. Reduced intake is a key cause of inpatient lows.

options.text: Give 5 units now and 5 more if the client eats
options.rationale: Matching insulin to intake is the right instinct. A split dose is a dose nobody ordered.

options.text: Give the dose now and add juice to the breakfast tray
options.rationale: Carbohydrate behind the insulin is sensible. A nauseated client who refuses breakfast may not take the juice.

questions.takeaway: Hold mealtime insulin and clarify it when the glucose is under 70 mg/dL or the client will not be eating.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The number is fine and the timing is fine. The cue that decides it is what the client says about eating.

steps.detail: 112 mg/dL is not the problem.
Nausea and no plan to eat.

steps.action: Cut the options that give insulin
steps.detail: Full dose, half dose or dose with juice all go in without a meal.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report the nausea and lack of intake.

questions.objective: hold, question or report

questions.stem: An 80-year-old on scheduled insulin with meals and no correction scale has prelunch fingersticks of 176, 184 and 192 mg/dL on three days. The client is alert with no symptoms. Each value was charted without action. Which action does the nurse take today?

options.text: Chart today's value, because the client has no symptoms
options.rationale: Charting is required. A value above 180 mg/dL that keeps rising is not left at charting.

options.text: Give 2 extra units of the scheduled insulin with lunch
options.rationale: More insulin may be what is needed. Units added without an order are outside the nurse's scope.

options.text: Assess the client and review the orders against the trend
options.rationale: Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia that calls for assessment and a review of orders. The three day climb makes it worth acting on.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand to confirm the value
options.rationale: A repeat is for a reading that does not fit the trend or came from poor technique. Three days of rising values fit each other, so this adds a puncture and no answer.

questions.takeaway: Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia. Read the trend, assess the client and review the orders. Do not ignore it, recheck it away or treat it without an order.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Know the top of the range and read the three values as a line. Two options assess: one gathers what the provider needs, one only repeats a number that already fits.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 184 and 192 mg/dL are above 180 mg/dL.
Each day is higher than the last.

steps.action: Cut the unordered fix and the repeat
steps.detail: Extra units need an order. A repeat fingerstick only confirms a value that fits the trend.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client and review the orders against the rising trend.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 2100 an 80-year-old has NPH insulin 12 units ordered at bedtime. The fingerstick is 72 mg/dL, down from 140 mg/dL before dinner at 1700, and the client ate half of dinner. The client has no symptoms. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Call the provider with the value and intake before giving it
options.rationale: The value is barely above 70 mg/dL and falling after a half eaten dinner, and NPH would peak from 0100 to 0900 while the client sleeps. The dose is questioned before it is given.

options.text: Give the NPH as ordered, since 72 mg/dL is inside the target range
options.rationale: 72 mg/dL is inside 70 to 180 mg/dL, and that is why this is tempting. The falling trend and reduced intake point to a low once the NPH peaks.

options.text: Give fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, then give the NPH
options.rationale: This is the treatment for a value under 70 mg/dL, and 72 mg/dL is not under it. It also gives the full 12 units without anyone weighing the fall and the half eaten dinner.

options.text: Hold the NPH tonight and recheck the fingerstick at 0700
options.rationale: Caution is right. Leaving out a dose without telling the provider is not the nurse's decision.

questions.takeaway: Read the trend, not only the number. A glucose falling toward 70 mg/dL with reduced intake, ahead of an insulin's peak, is a reason to question the dose before giving it.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Giving it and questioning it are both defensible at 72 mg/dL. The cues that tip it are the fall from 140 mg/dL and the half eaten dinner.

steps.detail: 72 mg/dL is in range by 2 points.
Down 68 mg/dL in 4 hours, half of dinner eaten.
NPH at 2100 peaks 0100 to 0900.
Holding without reporting is not within scope.

elimination.verdict: Call the provider with the value, intake and trend before giving it.
